title: Campaigns
content: Campaigns A campaign brings together a specific actor and the instruments and techniques they used against a specific indigenous people in a specific historical period. They are listed below and can be filtered by the peoples affected by Russian aggression. Filter by peoples: Sort by date: Campaigns: 178 September 1941 – August 1942 C1190 "Bombs Rained Down on the Auls": Repression and Air Strikes on Mountain Chechnya on the Eve of the Deportation (1941-1942) In the autumn of 1941 the Second World War was underway: Germany was advancing on the USSR, and the front was moving toward the Caucasus. The USSR was taking Chechens to its war: during the first mass mobilization, from 29 August to 2 September 1941, the military commissariats took almost 8 thousand men - 269 managed to evade, and another 450 fled on the way to the dispatch point[1]. In October they took another 4.4 thousand - 362 did not report to the recruitment stations[1]. The commissariats sent up to 13 thousand more men, unfit for combat service, to the "labor army" - construction battalions[2]. Already in September 1941 the labor-army trains found themselves in the frontline zone, where more than 10 thousand of these men died[2]. The colonizer recorded as "deserters" those who fled death in the "labor army", those who evaded mobilization into it, and even those who failed to appear at a recruitment station because of disability or their own death; the Chechen historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "The unfortunate citizens were forced either to hide from arrest or to pay bribes to the officials of the military commissariats and the NKVD" - and add: "Mass bribes taken from the highlanders became the everyday practice of the military commissariats"[2]. In early October 1941 the mountain villages of Chechnya rose against the collective farms and the mobilization - according to the report of the commander of the 141st Regiment of the NKVD Internal Troops (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia), Lieutenant Colonel Khalukhaev, dated 26 June 1943, the protest covered the Shatoy (Shatoevsky), Itum-Kale, Galanchozh, Cheberloy and Sharoy districts[1]. Even by the data of the secret services this was an economic protest: the population of the mountain villages "proceeded to a spontaneous division of collective-farm property" - property the colonizer had merged into collective farms during collectivization (campaign C1178); the same records charged the people with mass non-payment of taxes and evasion of mobilization; Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov likewise see "features of social protest" in the events[2]. The USSR's response was a military operation across the mountain districts, the declaration of this protest a "kulak-bandit uprising", and operational groups and NKVD troops left behind in the mountains. The historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that, "besides the operational groups and internal troops, three flights of combat aircraft were brought in" for the suppression, and "Bombs rained down on auls whose population did not even suspect any 'uprising'"[2]. "In the period from 30 October to 15 November 1941 the 141st rifle regiment, together with other units, crushed the c[ounter]-r[evolutionary] uprising in heavy multi-day fighting," Khalukhaev reported to Sheredega, head of the NKVD Internal Troops of the USSR[1]. June 1840 – December 1846 C1165 "Constriction of Chechnya from all sides": blockade, secret war, punitive expeditions and the Sunzha Line (1840-1846) In 1840-1846 the empire constricted Chechnya from all sides at once: by trade blockade and hostage-taking, by secret war - contract killings, agents and bribery, - by punitive expeditions and by building the Sunzha Line of fortresses with the eviction of the inhabitants. The programme was named by general Golovin, commander of the Separate Caucasus Corps (head of the empire's troops and administration in the Caucasus), in a report to Minister of War Chernyshev of 24 February 1841: ""the constriction of Chechnya in this way from all sides will place the chiefs of this populous tribe in the most disadvantageous position for them... It is quite probable that the Chechens, having remained inactive for a long time, will become tamer""[3]. Historian N. I. Pokrovsky formulates the policy's calculation from the documents: ""Starving Chechnya, by tsarism's reckoning, was to surrender in order to restore trade relations and obtain grain""[4]. The empire supplemented armed force with secrecy: in a secret letter to Golovin of 19 July 1842 Chernyshev named the model - ""The English knew how to establish their dominion in India by political means. By this path they spared their troops and gained time in the subjugation of the country. Should not we too try this system?""[3]. The result of the six years was summed up by the imperial officer Poltoratsky, a participant in the December 1846 expedition: ""the plain of Lesser Chechnya in the triangle between the fortresses of Groznaya, Vozdvizhenskaya and Zakan-Yurt has been cleared completely of dwellings and forests""[5]. January 1847 – November 1851 C1166 "Death sentence" for Lesser Chechnya: the massacre of Duba's hamlet, forest clearings, fortresses, annihilation of the population and stanitsas on the sites of burned auls (1847-1851) In 1847-1851 the empire destroyed the auls of Lesser Chechnya (the lowland-piedmont western part of Chechnya) and forced out its population: it cut forest clearings (prosekas) through the woods, built fortresses, struck the auls with short blows annihilating their inhabitants. The policy was named by its participant, imperial officer Poltoratsky, who wrote of the winter expedition of 1847-1848: by the building of the Sunzha Line "we greatly constricted Lesser Chechnya," and by the construction of fortresses "we were finally carrying out her death sentence" - the sentence on Lesser Chechnya[5]. On 6 March 1847 an imperial detachment slaughtered the hamlet of naib Duba (a deputy of Imam Shamil, leader of the highlanders' resistance to the Russian conquest) - Poltoratsky wrote: "old and young, women, children and nursing infants, drowned in their own blood from the sharply honed bayonets that pardoned no one, spared no one"[5]; historian N. I. Pokrovsky gives the frame: "the Russian command did not renounce separate short strikes aimed at terrifying the Chechens... What took place was an outright massacre"[4]. General Sleptsov summed up the result in a report of 4 October 1850: "the rich lands between the Sunzha and the Russian road have passed into the unaccountable possession of the government, so that the entire plain of Lesser Chechnya is now completely cleared of the hostile population"[6]. Imperial historian Volkonsky wrote of Sleptsov in retrospect: he "annihilated the entire enemy population nesting in the gorges from Bumut... to Roshnya"[7]. On the sites of the burned auls the empire planted Cossack stanitsas - seven stanitsas in 1847 and 1851[2]. January 1686 – May 1686 C0009 "Eternal Peace" with Poland (1686) The legal legitimation of the partition of territories between the Tsardom of Muscovy and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth behind the Hetmanate's back, definitively turning Ukraine into a rightless object of bargaining. The deal was sealed financially – under the text of the 1686 treaty Moscow undertook "for eternal peace to count out a genuine sum of money, that is, one hundred forty-six thousand Muscovite rubles, and hand it over to the Commonwealth"[8]. "Russian historians usually assess the Eternal Peace as Golitsyn's great diplomatic success, Polish ones – as their major defeat, and contemporary Ukrainian ones – as a national tragedy of Ukraine"[9]. March 1949 – December 1965 C1181 "Exiled Forever": Life in Special Settlement and Return to an Occupied Homeland (1949-1965) After the deportation of the Chechens in 1944 (campaign C1180) the occupiers took over their homes, auls and fields. By 1952 there were more than a million of them on the lands of the deported peoples of the North Caucasus[10]. By its decree of 26 November 1948 the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR had already declared the exile eternal: the Chechens and Ingush were "exiled forever," with up to 20 years of hard labor for escape[2]. The exile itself was built as a prison without walls. The secret police admitted: "In 1949 a series of measures was carried out to track down and detain fugitives, as well as to establish a strict regime in the places of settlement"[1]. Under the resolution of the government of the USSR of 8 January 1945, "any unauthorized absence of a deportee beyond the bounds of the resettlement district served by the special commandant's office shall be regarded as escape and shall entail criminal liability," and that district was at times limited to a few streets in a town or a single village soviet[1]. Those whom the agency listed among the "malicious evaders of work on the collective farms" faced 8 years of imprisonment[1], and in July 1952 the occupiers' court sent ten religious mentors and their followers to the camps for terms of up to 25 years with confiscation of property[1]. The "eternal" term of exile rested on Stalin's decrees. The tightening of 1948-1949 followed his late-1940s course of crushing any self-reliance, and to the secret police, which demanded that fugitives be jailed indiscriminately, he handed as a reward both the supervision of the special settlers and the disposal of their labor[1]. After his death the term of the Chechens' exile became a matter of bargaining between agencies: in the summer of 1953 a department of the Central Committee of the Bolshevik party proposed removing 560,710 people from the special-settlement rolls, Chechens and Ingush among them, while the police ministry demanded that "the said categories of persons temporarily remain in special settlement"[1]; in September Kruglov, Minister of Internal Affairs of the USSR, asked Malenkov, chairman of the Council of Ministers of the USSR, to keep the Chechens and Ingush in settlement for another five years, deeming their release from surveillance premature. No decision on his memorandum was ever taken[1]. The empire did not return the seized lands even when it let the people out of exile: by its decree of 16 July 1956 the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR lifted the special-settlement regime from the Chechen people (forced residence in Kazakhstan and Kirghizia under the surveillance of commandants' offices) - and in the same article laid down that the lifting of restrictions "does not entail the return to them of property confiscated at deportation, and that they do not have the right to return to the places from which they were deported"[11]. The ministries explained the ban by saying the land had already been handed out. Barsukov, head of the occupier's police, reported on 26 June 1956 that housing the Chechens and Ingush in their districts "is not possible," because "these districts are settled by migrants from the central oblasts of the RSFSR"[1], while Dudorov, Minister of Internal Affairs of the USSR, reported to the leadership of the Bolshevik party (the "TsK KPSS"): "the possibility of restoring autonomy for the Chechens and Ingush within their former territory is a difficult matter and hardly feasible... the return of the Chechens and Ingush to their former places of residence will inevitably provoke a whole range of undesirable consequences"[1]. The people returned on their own, without waiting for permissions: already on 15 June 1957 the bureau of the regional committee of the Bolshevik party (the "Checheno-Ingush obkom of the KPSS") admitted that "more than 122 thousand Chechens and Ingush have already arrived in the republic instead of the 70 thousand provided for by the plan for 1957"[1], and the resettlement department of the colonial administration (the "Orgkomitet for the ChIASSR") counted in a report of 20 January 1958: under the plan 23,503 families were to resettle - 52,037 families, 201,746 people, had arrived[12]. "Almost a third of the adult Chechens, Ingush and Karachais (up to 80 thousand people) refused to give" the pledge renouncing their property, write historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov, "and returned home regardless of the bans"[2]. People arrived to a homeland occupied by settlers and cut down by a redrawing of borders: they had to buy their own houses back from the new owners[2], the mountain auls remained closed, and the Ingush lands of the Tarskaya valley, where the Ingush people had taken shape, the empire did not return to the Chechens and Ingush: in 1944 it gave them to North Ossetia and, restoring the republic in 1957, left 1,600 square kilometers of black earth with Ossetia, adding to the republic in exchange 5,000 square kilometers of the sands of the Burun steppe beyond the Terek; the protests of the Chechen-Ingush delegation were rejected by the leadership of the Bolshevik party[2]. Historians reckon the outcome in shares: "by 1961 the Chechens and Ingush made up 41% of the republic's population, whereas in 1939 their share had reached 58.4%"[2]. April 1858 – March 1917 C1170 "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) In 1858-1917 conquered Chechnya lived under a regime the empire itself named "military-popular administration": administrative power over the people lay in the hands of officers of the active army. The system was named by Baryatinsky, viceroy in the Caucasus - historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "A. I. Baryatinsky called the system of governing the highlanders that he was creating 'military-popular' and considered it temporary", and add what the name contained: "Contemporaries, without embarrassment, called this system of administration 'military'"[2]. The system was defined by a later viceroy, Vorontsov-Dashkov: it was "based on the concentration of administrative power in the hands of individual officers, under the supreme direction of the commander-in-chief of the Caucasus Army, and on allowing the population to manage its internal affairs according to its own adats" (adats - the customary law of the highlanders)[13]. The imperial general Chernyavsky explained why the regime was needed: "for these savage peoples such privileges are still premature... What is needed here is a power that commands, bridles and governs"[13]. Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes of the order thus imposed: "In the restless Terek oblast a 'military-popular' regime was established, which was in essence a state-of-emergency regime"; the outcome of the war he states separately: "A colonial 'military-popular' regime was established in the land"[14]. April 1877 – May 1878 C1172 "Mow Down Everything, Beat and Hang Without Mercy": Suppression of the 1877 Uprising and the Executions in Grozny (1877-1878) The uprising of 1877 - historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov call it a peasant war - was suppressed by the empire through the annihilation of everything that could sustain the insurgents. The methods were summed up by historian A. I. Ismailova: "The burning of auls, the deportation of the population, the destruction of crops - these are the main methods of struggle that the tsarist command applies with merciless consistency"[15]. The tone of the orders was set by Svistunov, head of the Terek oblast - in his instructions to General Smekalov, according to historian A. I. Ismailova, one demand was invariably repeated: "For God's sake, just do not fall back, but advance at least little by little, mercilessly destroying everything and everyone before you... Our forces will keep arriving; just mow down everything without pity, beat and hang without mercy"[15]. The principle of punishment was formulated by the viceroy in a memorandum: "so that punishment falls not only upon the fanatics seeking the feat of self-sacrifice, but also upon the guilty milieu surrounding them, so that by the fear of inevitable collective punishment... the mass is induced to counteract them"[16]. The people's answer was recorded by the same imperial side - the inhabitants of Mekhkety refused the head of the Terek oblast, who threatened to deport the aul, the surrender of Uma Duev, leader of the uprising in mountain Chechnya: "...only the possible should be demanded of a people. You know how hard it is for us to part with the graves of our fathers and with our homeland, yet we submit without protest. But we cannot hand over Uma. He was our guest"[2]. January 1852 – December 1857 C1167 "Neither plow nor sow": the pogrom of Chechnya, organized famine, the buying-up of elites and the institutions of subjugation (1852-1857) In 1852-1857 the empire used famine to force Greater Chechnya (the lowland eastern part of Chechnya) into submission or off its land. The period was opened by the winter expedition of Baryatinsky, who commanded the left flank of the Caucasus Line (the chain of imperial fortifications on the land of the Nokhchi) - imperial historian Volkonsky, its participant, published his account under the title "The Pogrom of Chechnya"; the task of the detachment of more than ten thousand bayonets he recorded thus: "to smash the enemy hordes, destroy all means of subsistence of the inhabitants and the enemy, and then act according to circumstances"[7]. The destruction of food became doctrine: Vorontsov, viceroy and commander-in-chief in the Caucasus, in an official letter (otnosheniye) to Minister of War Chernyshev of 28 August 1852, reported that the Chechens, deprived of crops and hay, "must - either resettle into our bounds, or go into the very depth of the mountains"[6]. Back in March Vorontsov wrote to Baryatinsky: "we will not allow them to sow or to mow, unless they declare submission" - the letter of 21 March 1852 is cited by historian N. I. Pokrovsky[4]; historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov convey the same policy in the formula of the proclamations - the command warned the Chechens that it would let them "neither plow nor sow," and conclude: "This promise was kept in the literal sense, and in 1856-1857 a famine set in in Chechnya such as the Chechens had almost never known"[2]. In the same period the empire was buying up the leadership of the resistance - Bata Shamurzayev, a naib of Shamil (deputy of the Imam, leader of the highlanders' resistance of Dagestan and Chechnya to the Russian conquest), who went over to the empire in the autumn of 1851, received a rank, a pension and land "as an example for other potential defectors"[2] - and was building institutions of subordination: in 1852 in the Groznaya fortress the "Chechen People's Court" was instituted, which worked out the "Rules for the Governance of Submissive Chechens"[2]. January 1965 – July 1989 C1182 "Only Pardoned": Alien Rule and the Suppression of Chechen and Ingush National Life (1965-1989) In 1965-1989 the Chechens and the Ingush, whom the coloniser had merged into a single region (the Chechen-Ingush ASSR), were ruled by Russian officials sent from Moscow. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "in the early 1970s, of the 60 ministries and agencies of the Council of Ministers of the ChIASSR only 17 were headed by Chechens or Ingush. In most rural districts the first secretaries of the district committees were Russians"[2]. In 1972 Chechen and Ingush communists wrote to Moscow about this twice. From 16 to 19 January 1973 several thousand Ingush (participants speak of 15 thousand), joined by Chechens, rallied on the central square of Grozny in front of the building of the region's occupation administration and demanded the return of the Prigorodny district, handed to North Ossetia during the deportation of 1944, or the lifting of the ban on settling there. On the night of 19 January soldiers of the internal troops (predecessors of today's Rosgvardiya) with truncheons and firemen spraying icy water from hoses dispersed those who remained on the square, drove them out of the city and dropped them off in the frost[17]. Then the coloniser went after those who had complained: on 13 March 1973 Moscow adopted a resolution "On Anti-Social Nationalist Manifestations in the City of Grozny", the authors of the letters were expelled from the only permitted party, the organisers of the rally were put on trial[17], and in December KGB chairman Andropov (the KGB being the predecessor of today's FSB) reported on "measures" against "about 400 Ingush"[18]. In those same years the coloniser worked to leave the Chechens and the Ingush without a history, a faith, a language or a livelihood of their own. The USSR rewrote history, imposing its own concept, "the 200th anniversary of the voluntary entry of Chechen-Ingushetia into Russia", and persecuted the Chechen historians who disputed it through decisions of the region's occupation administration[19]. In a quarter of a century the occupier did not allow the highlanders to open a single mosque[20]. The schools to which Chechen and Ingush children returned worked only in Russian from the first grade: the law of the RSFSR of 16 April 1959 declared that "instruction at school is conducted in the pupils' native language" and left the choice of language to parents, but after the return from exile the coloniser opened no schools with Chechen as the language of instruction, so there was nothing to choose from[21]. The factories and oil enterprises of Grozny hired newcomers rather than Chechens: by the end of the 1980s only 16 % of oil-refining workers were Chechens or Ingush, according to official statistics of 1979 up to 28 % of the able-bodied lived off their household plots, and according to the census of 1989 almost a quarter of the people lived outside the republic[2]. The coloniser said aloud what it thought of the people after the dispersal. A. Martazanova, a participant in the events of 1973, recalls: at a meeting of the region's occupation administration on 27 March one of its leaders, Bokov, "said that the Ingush and the Chechens had not yet been rehabilitated, that they had only been pardoned in advance, in the hope of good behaviour", while Rustem Goygov, head of a department in the same administration, who began: "But what about the decisions of the 20th Congress of the CPSU [the congress of 1956 that condemned the deportations of peoples], which…", was not allowed to finish and a month later was removed from his post; the phrase had first been uttered by Solomentsev, head of the government of the RSFSR, who had come to Grozny[17]. Eyewitness Aza Bazorkina recalls that a few days after the dispersal the newspaper Grozny Worker printed, over the signatures of intimidated Ingush, an article "To Serve One's People Honestly", which "says that the Ingush people have not been rehabilitated (as if there had been no 20th Party Congress!) but pardoned"[22]. January 1831 – December 1831 C0045 Abolition of Magdeburg Rights (1831) The abolition of the traditional system of municipal self-government: "The final liquidation of Magdeburg law on the western Ukrainian lands took place in 1786, and in the cities of Central and Left-Bank Ukraine – in 1831 (in Kyiv – 1834)"[23] – the final stage of embedding the cities into the imperial administrative-judicial system, begun as early as the reforms of the 1780s. January 1765 – December 1765 C0031 Abolition of the Cossack Order in Sloboda Ukraine (1765) An imperial reform to liquidate the military-social structure of Sloboda Ukraine: "The conclusions of this investigation, with the participation of a Senate commission, led to the verdict of the Governing Senate on the liquidation of the autonomous order on December 16, 1764, and a series of experimental innovations approved by Catherine II's manifesto of July 28, 1765. On the basis of the Sloboda regiments the Sloboda-Ukrainian Governorate was formed, out of the military forces – 5 hussar regiments of the same names (see Hussars), and the bulk of the Cossack population was transferred to the category of military settlers"[24]. January 1781 – December 1786 C0034 Administrative Dismantling and Enserfment of the Left Bank (1781–1786) The execution of Catherine II's secret instructions for the institutional and cultural assimilation of the land: the liquidation of the regimental order and the introduction of imperial viceroyalties – the Kyiv Viceroyalty was established by the nominal decree to the Senate of September 16, 1781 (PSZRI, coll. 1, vol. XXI, no. 15,228; execution ordered from November)[25][26], "which finally abolished the remnants of the Hetmanate's autonomy and its regimental-sotnia administrative-political and military order"[27]; the secularization of monastery lands in 1786 and the legal binding of peasants by Catherine II's decree of May 3, 1783: "each of the villagers is to remain in the place and station where he is registered by the current last revision"[28]. January 1897 – December 1897 C0067 All-Russian Census and the Erasure of Identity (1897) The empire conducted the general census of 1897, embedded in the doctrine of the "triune Russian people". The linguist Sergei Bulich, in his article for the Brockhaus and Efron Encyclopedic Dictionary, classified Ukrainian speech thus: "the Little Russian dialect of the Russian language"[29]. Historians of the Institute of History of Ukraine of the National Academy of Sciences note: "The census of 1897 recorded not nationality but the respondents' native tongue, and since many Ukrainians named Russian as such, there were in fact more ethnic Ukrainians than indicated in the census"[30]. The census also recorded the reach of the Ukrainian language. According to its consolidated volume, the "Little Russian dialect" - the imperial name for the Ukrainian language - was named as their native tongue by 22,380,551 people out of 125,640,021 counted in the empire, that is 17.8%: the empire's second language by number of speakers after Great Russian (Russian)[31]. Nearly one in four speakers lived outside the nine Ukrainian governorates, and in the Kuban region (now mostly Krasnodar krai of Russia) Ukrainian was the most widespread native language[31]. September 1939 – June 1941 C0081 Annexation and Sovietization of Western Ukraine (1939–1941) The collusion of two totalitarian regimes (the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact), which led to the USSR's invasion of Poland and the seizure of Western Ukraine. To legitimize the occupation, the "People's Assembly of Western Ukraine 1939" was staged, which "on October 27 in Lviv… adopted the Declaration on the reunification of Western Ukraine with the Ukrainian SSR"[32]. Then came the mass deportations: "Between September 1939 and June 1941, up to 1,250,000 people (about 10% of the population) were removed from these lands and Western Belarus… to remote regions of the USSR"[33]. January 1685 – December 1686 C0008 Annexation of the Kyiv Metropolis by the Moscow Patriarchate (1685–1690) The annexation of the independent Ukrainian church through diplomatic pressure and corruption. Patriarch Dositheus of Jerusalem directly accused the Muscovite envoys of simony: "What fault is it to tear away another's eparchy? Is it not a shame before people, is it not a sin before God! You send money and lead people out of their minds, you take charters contrary to the church and to God"[34]. The subordination of the church was justified by geopolitics: "Golitsyn's main project… was the reform of the Ukrainian Orthodox church, or rather – the subordination of the Kyiv metropolitanate to the Moscow patriarch"[9]. January 1837 C1160 Annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's Expedition: 92 Captives, More Than a Thousand Saklias Burned (January 1837) On 23-29 January 1837, the command of the Russian Caucasus Corps sent from the Groznaya fortress into Lesser Chechnya (the lowland-piedmont western part of Chechnya) a detachment under General Feze - 3249 men with 12 guns. Rozen stated the purpose of the campaign in a report to Minister of War Chernyshev of 11 February 1837: "to punish the Chechens of the western part of Chechnya who have evaded obedience"[35]. The expedition journal appended to the report records the week day by day: on the night of 24 January Shalazh-yurt was surrounded - the village was taken "without a shot, laying 14 souls on the spot", 67 inhabitants were led away into captivity, and the village was burned; on 25 January Feze dispatched columns "to discover and destroy the population in the dense forests up both banks of the Shalazha river"; in all, 92 people were taken captive over the campaign, "on the way back more than a thousand saklias were burned along the Martan and Tengin gorges" (saklia - a highlander's house), and the stores of grain and hay were destroyed in the middle of winter[35]. Within the detachment the empire led highlanders against highlanders - 800 horsemen of the Ossetian and Ingush militia (militia - auxiliary units of highlanders in the empire's service): the expedition journal lists in Colonel Shiroky's column "a hundred Cossacks and 800 horsemen of Ossetians and Ingush"[35]. From the aul of Achkhoy, which the troops entered on the fourth day of the annihilation of its neighbors, by the record of the same journal an oath "of submission" and six hostages-amanats were taken (amanat - a person whom the empire took from a community as a guarantee of subordination)[35]. January 1732 – December 1732 C1132 Armed Uprising on the Plain, General Douglas's Expedition, and the Rout of Colonel Koch's Punitive Detachment (1732) In 1732, the lowland part of Chechnya became the center of large-scale armed resistance. The uprising was provoked by the direct discontent of the indigenous population: historian Sh. B. Akhmadov states that those assembled, «openly expressing their discontent with the actions of the tsarist authorities, began to threaten attacks on their fortifications»[36]. Researcher Ya. Z. Akhmadov adds that «in 1732 lowland Chechnya once again turns into the center of a major insurgent movement», and «around 10 thousand highlanders gathered in Chechen-Aul», intending to set out «to destroy the tsarist fortifications»[37]. In response, the occupation apparatus applied military force: the first author indicates that «on July 4, 1732, the tsarist authorities dispatched to Chechnya a military detachment headed by General Douglas, who commanded the troops in the fortress of the Holy Cross»[36], which, according to the cited report, resolved, regarding the insurgents, «without allowing them to multiply, to avert and destroy them by the dispatched detachment»[37]. The punitive action was coordinated with the loyal local elite: Sh. B. Akhmadov notes the participation of Prince Kazbulat, «who led the detachment of tsarist troops headed by Douglas to the village of Chechen-Aul to suppress the highlanders' uprising»[36]. However, the insurgents avoided a direct clash with the empire's main forces: Ya. Z. Akhmadov records that «General Douglas, who had already set out on the campaign, received word that the highlanders had dispersed»[37]. After this, the general sent Colonel Koch's dragoon detachment to punish the inhabitants, which, as stated in the sources, «on July 7 entered the village of Chechen, burned it down completely, and began hastily withdrawing»[36]. The historical episode ended that same year with the complete physical destruction of the punitive forces: Ya. Z. Akhmadov summarizes that during the withdrawal Koch's detachment «was surrounded in dense forests, defeated, and annihilated», and that in the course of the battle «the senior Chechen prince Kazbulat also perished»[37]. January 1918 – March 1918 C0073 Artificial Separatism and the Dismemberment of Territories (January – March 1918) Having been forced to recognize Ukraine's independence under the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, the government of Soviet Russia attempted to retain control over the eastern industrial regions. To this end, a separate separatist entity (the Donetsk–Kryvyi Rih Soviet Republic) was artificially constructed on the territory of the Donbas and the Kryvyi Rih region, with the aim of directly subordinating these lands to the central Russian authorities, bypassing the UNR[38][39]. July 1831 C1153 Assassination of Chechen resistance leader Beibulat Taimiev, prepared by the imperial command (1831) After his escape from surveillance in the fall of 1830, the leader of the Chechen resistance Beibulat Taimiev — bound by his oath to Paskevich, by fractures of both legs, and by illness — took no part in hostilities, but his name alone inspired the insurgents. The historian D. A. Khozhaev wrote: "The tsarist command several times intended to do away with Beibulat, but feared to repress him openly, since this could provoke an undesirable resonance throughout Chechnya. And yet the continued presence of a man like Beibulat in insurgent Chechnya was becoming dangerous for the tsarist command. Preparations began for the murder of Beibulat, which was soon carried out"[14]. On July 14, 1831, not far from the fortification of Tashkichu, Beibulat was killed from ambush by Prince Sali, who was in imperial service. D. A. Khozhaev recorded the official version — the murder was presented as a blood feud — and its exposure: "Prince Sali, who was in tsarist service, was not punished, whereas the other cases of blood vengeance were cruelly prosecuted by the tsarist command. Paskevich wrote of the slain Beibulat that he had been a traitor to the end, and that therefore the killer should not be punished"[14]. September 1837 C1162 Attempted bribery of Shamil with a promise of power over Dagestan to secure his appearance before Nicholas I in Tiflis, and the summoning of the Chechen imam Tashu-Hadji (1837) In September 1837, ahead of Nicholas I's visit to the Caucasus, the empire tried to buy the leader of the highlander resistance: Shamil (Shamil - imam, leader of the resistance of the highlanders of Dagestan and Chechnya to the Russian conquest) was offered "pardon", honors and power in exchange for appearing before the emperor in Tiflis. General Adlerberg conveyed Nicholas I's will to general Rozen in a letter of 10 August 1837: "that Shamil and his chief accomplices Tashav-Hadji, Kibit-Magomet and the Qarakh qadi Abdurrahman be given suggestions to take advantage of His Majesty's arrival in the Caucasus region and to beg the mercy of appearing before the face of the Monarch Himself"[40] - Tashu-Hadji (sheikh, in 1834-1836 the imam of Chechnya, spiritual and military leader of the Chechen resistance) is named first among the "accomplices". General Klugenau obtained a personal meeting with Shamil on 18 September 1837 at a spring near the aul of Karanay; Shamil's chronicler Muhammad Tahir al-Qarakhi recorded the essence of the offer: "Kluki von Klugenau began to speak, asking Shamil to come for a meeting with the Russian Nicholas. He asserted that the emperor would exalt him, Shamil, show him honor, and make him the administrator of the affairs of all Dagestani Muslims. From the emperor, he said, there would be no treachery"[41]. At the same time colonel Pullo demanded of Shamil by letter that he send "to the Groznaya fortress two deputies to be presented to the Sovereign" - and this competing demand, as the imperial historian Yurov admits, "greatly hindered the success" of the recruitment[40]. Shamil refused in a letter to Klugenau of 28 September 1837: "I have resolved not to go to Tiflis even if I am cut to pieces, because I have many times seen treachery from you"[40] - neither he nor Tashu-Hadji appeared before the emperor. August 1991 C0095 Attempted Coup d'État by the GKChP (August 1991) An armed mutiny by the conservative wing of the Soviet leadership, the KGB, and the army aimed at halting the USSR's disintegration and holding the republics by force. The State Committee for the State of Emergency declared: "to introduce a state of emergency in particular localities of the USSR for a term of 6 months from 4 a.m. Moscow time on August 19, 1991… to form the State Committee for the State of Emergency in the USSR"[42]. The putsch's failure opened the way to independence: the Act of Declaration was adopted "proceeding from the mortal danger that had loomed over Ukraine in connection with the coup d'état in the USSR on August 19, 1991"[43]. January 1695 – December 1700 C0010 Azov Campaigns and Fortress Construction (1695–1700) The use of the autonomy as a free resource and labor base for Peter I's ambitions in the south. The population bore extremely heavy logistical obligations: "Provisions for the volunteer troops were supplied by the commoners, who also stocked hay for the winter for the army's artillery." In addition, Moscow established military control by deploying a network of bases near the Zaporizhian Sich: "The Zaporozhians... put forward the demolition of Kamianyi Zaton as a condition for any oath... Mazepa was furious"[44]. January 1913 – December 1914 C0051 Ban on Culture and the Press Before World War I (1913–1914) The Russian Empire continued destroying the indigenous people's culture on the eve of the war: the curator of the Kyiv school district, Derevytsky, in 1913 "issued an instruction in which he declared students' attendance of Ukrainian theatrical performances as inadmissible as spending time in billiard halls or beer houses, and in 1914 categorically forbade all educational institutions of the Kyiv district to mark the 100th jubilee of Taras Shevchenko"[45]; with the outbreak of the war, Nicholas II by a personal decree of 20 July 1914 introduced military censorship with the command's right "to suspend periodical publications"[46] - and that very day the military authorities of the Kyiv military district closed the only Ukrainian daily newspaper, "Rada"[47]. January 1892 – December 1905 C0049 Ban on the Language in Books and Public Speeches (1892–1905) A state campaign to drive the language out of public space and literature: in 1892 the Main Administration for Press Affairs directed the censorship committee to suppress translations into Ukrainian, "reducing the number of such talentless works for purely state purposes"[48]; at the archaeological congress in Kyiv in 1899, scholars from Austrian-ruled Ukraine were forbidden to read papers in Ukrainian - in protest they withdrew from participation[47]; at the unveiling of the Kotliarevsky monument in Poltava on 30-31 August 1903, only guests from Galicia were allowed to speak Ukrainian, while the mayor forbade the locals to do so, citing an order of the ministry of internal affairs[47]. Even children's literature fell under the ban: the 1895 circular prohibited Ukrainian books "for children's reading"[49]. January 1720 – December 1720 C0043 Ban on Ukrainian Book Printing (1720) A campaign to introduce censorship and institutional linguistic assimilation. Peter I's decree of October 5, 1720 banned the printing of books in the indigenous people's language at the key printing houses: "In the Kyiv-Pechersk and Chernihiv printing houses no new books whatsoever are to be printed except previous church editions, and even those old church books are to be corrected before printing for complete conformity with the Great Russian church books, so that there be no discord or distinct dialect in them"[50]. January 1588 – January 1591 C1112 Beginning of the political subjugation of the Nokhchi (1588–1591) The occupation administration of the Tsardom of Muscovy imposed vassalage on the Nokhchi elite under the guise of a military alliance through the procedure of oath-taking (shert). As historian Murat Yasar notes, to the Nokhchi this looked like a military pact: "many local rulers in Muscovy's southern and eastern borderlands, especially in the North Caucasus, regarded the shert more as a military alliance between themselves and one of their potential allies"[51]. The administration, however, unilaterally interpreted this act as unconditional submission: historian Michael Khodarkovsky points out that "in Moscow's eyes the shert now meant an oath of allegiance by the tsar's new and loyal subjects"[52]. Historian Murat Yasar adds that consent was incentivized through bribery: "the signing of the shert went hand in hand with the monetary allowances and gifts that the tsar gave to the local rulers"[51]. To maintain control, the forcible seizure of relatives of Nokhchi leaders was employed: E. N. Kusheva, compiler of a collection of documents, writes that "his nephew Batai was left as a hostage (amanat) in the Terek town"[53]. The subordinated Nokhchi communities were obligated to take part in the military operations of the occupation administration: E. N. Kusheva, compiler of a collection of documents, points to documents "on the possibility of the participation of Murza Shikh... in a campaign of Russian fighting men"[53]. February 2014 – March 2014 C0100 Beginning of the Russo-Ukrainian War: Armed Invasion and Occupation of Crimea (2014) A covert military invasion and the occupation of Crimea, the beginning of Russia's armed aggression against Ukraine: the seizure of administrative buildings by troops without insignia, the installation of a controlled prime minister, and a sham referendum that the UN General Assembly declared void: "the referendum held in the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol on 16 March 2014, having no validity, cannot form the basis for any alteration of the status"[54]. The legal formalization of the seizure was completed in Moscow by the law of March 21, 2014[55]. January 1905 – December 1907 C0068 Black Hundred Terror and Pogroms (1905–1907) The imperial authorities sponsor and cover for radical Russian nationalist organizations for the suppression of the revolution and for terror. The "Union of the Russian People" was "a Black-Hundred organization… The organization received financial support from the state and was patronized by Russian emperor Nicholas II… Mass Jewish pogroms provoked by the 'Union' took place, particularly in Ukraine, in the 'Pale of Settlement'"[24]; of its 400 thousand members, nearly half were in Ukrainian cities[24]. January 1645 – December 1658 C1107 Bribery of Elites, Coercion into Subjecthood, and the Taking of Amanats (1645–1658) The occupation administration of the Tsardom of Muscovy expanded legal control over the societies of the Nokhchi, bribed loyal elites, and coerced the mountain societies into vassalage. The metropole officially rewarded the leaders who served it, granting them privileges and power over dependent people: the register of files of the Ambassadorial Prikaz for 1645 records a petition from the serving Okotsk murza Chepan Kokhostrov to Tsar Mikhail Fedorovich and a report memorandum of the central apparatus «on granting him an increase to his salary and ownership of the uzdens and «people» of his brother, murza Albir Kokhostrov»[53]. In parallel, the administration forced the mountain societies of the Nokhchi (the Shibutians and the Michkizians) into legal subordination. In 1647, under pressure from the Terek voivodes, the Shibutians «placed themselves under your lofty sovereign hand in direct servitude... and swore the shert on the Quran»[53], while the Michkiz people «together with the entire Michkiz land placed themselves in servitude under your lofty sovereign hand... and swore the shert on the Quran»[53]. To guarantee the fulfillment of the imposed obligations, the representatives of the metropole demanded hostages: a dispatch from the Terek voivode Prince Venedikt Andreevich Obolensky and his associates to the Ambassadorial Prikaz of 1647 dryly records the fact of «the giving of an amanat to the Terek town»[53]. The documents record that the metropole instructed the voivodes «to order that amanats be taken from among their kin, men of note... to order that they be kept and given food and drink in the same way as other such amanats»[53], as a result of which the mountaineers «gave a good amanat to the Terek town, Kasa»[53][56]. January 1735 – December 1735 C1133 Bribery of the Nobility and Institutionalization of the Hostage System (1735) In 1735, following the large-scale invasion by the forces of the Crimean Khanate, the diplomatic and administrative apparatus of the Russian Empire used the new balance of power to consolidate its influence among the Nokhchi elites. Historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov states that during this period «the pro-Russian political orientation of the lowland part of Chechnya intensifies»[37]. To bind the local aristocracy, the occupation administration employed institutional bribery: the researcher records that the senior prince Aidemir «was accepted into Russian subjecthood and was assigned a permanent tsarist salary»[37], and, on the whole, «The princes and their uzdens even began to receive monetary allowances from the Russian government»[37]. In parallel, the empire entrenched the system of holding relatives of the nobility: Akhmadov indicates that Prince Aidemir «as a pledge of fidelity to his obligations gave his son Bardykhan as an amanat, while another influential Chechen prince, Alisultan Kazbulatov, gave his brother Bamat as an amanat»[37]. He also adds dry statistical confirmation: «In 1735, two amanats from the Chechen domain were already being held in Kizlyar»[37]. January 1807 – December 1807 C1140 Bulgakov's Punitive Expedition: Devastation of Chechen Villages and Coercion into Allegiance (1807) In February–April 1807, the Russian Empire undertook a punitive expedition deep into Greater Chechnya under the command of General Bulgakov, commander of the Caucasian Line, devastating Nokhchi villages and coercing them into allegiance. Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes of General Bulgakov's troops as having «come with fire and sword to the Chechen land»[14]. The plan of the commander-in-chief in the Caucasus, General Gudovich, was to strike suddenly, before the inhabitants could shelter their families in the mountains: «you would have caught them all by surprise, their cattle and families could not yet have been hidden by them in the mountains, and therefore their punishment and complete success in the matter would have been surer and more convenient»[57]. General Bulgakov, commander of the Caucasian Line, broke through the fortified Khankala Gorge by storm and put villages to the torch; General Ivelich reported that Greater Chechen Ataga had been «consigned to fire», and its inhabitants had submitted, «whose villages were destroyed by fire»[57]. Displeased that instead of a sudden reprisal a bloody war had resulted, General Gudovich, in a directive of March 20, 1807, refused to accept the storming of Khankala «on his own account» and emphasized the punitive, rather than military, character of the assignment: «you were sent not to wage war with the Chechen peoples, but to punish them and bring them into complete submission»[57]. Summing up the expedition, General Bulgakov, commander of the Caucasian Line, reported that by force of arms the Chechens had been «brought to such a state that they will long feel the blow dealt to them, and, of course, will not soon regain strength»[57]. September 1830 – January 1831 C1152 Burning of Lowland Chechnya by Velyaminov's Expedition: Demolition of Villages from the Sunzha to Mairtup, Seizure of Astemir's Family, Collective Penalties Imposed on Chechen Villages, the Cutting Down of Fleeing Inhabitants of Dzulgai-Yurt, and Destruction of Winter Stores (1830-1831) In the fall of 1830, General Velyaminov, who had taken command of the troops operating against Chechnya, began with collective property exactions from the Chechen villages standing on the Terek River near the imperial border. The imperial historian Potto admits: for the driving off by Chechens of ten head of cattle from the stanitsa of Chervlennaya, Velyaminov "immediately ordered that ten head of cattle likewise be taken from the inhabitants of the two villages of Braguny and Novy-Yurt, past which the raiding party had gone, and returned to the Cossacks," and after a herd of horses was driven off in the Nogai steppe, "Braguny again paid with exactly the same number of head"; the owner of Novy-Yurt, Shah-Girei, was summoned to Groznaya and confined in a casemate — a prison cell inside the fortress[58]. On December 18, 1830, a detachment assembled in Groznaya consisting of four infantry regiments — the Moscow, Butyrsky, Tarutino, and Borodino regiments — a composite battalion of the 43rd Jaeger Regiment, five sotnias of line Cossacks, and twenty-two guns, and at night the troops moved on the village of Dzulgai-Yurt, where the Karabulak leader Astemir lived. Potto wrote: the Cossacks, bursting into the village at dawn, rushed to Astemir's house; he himself managed to escape, "but his family — a young son, a daughter, a grandson, and a female cousin — fell into the hands of the Cossacks. Besides them, thirty-nine people were taken prisoner, and about twelve were cut down"[58]. Then the villages of western, Lesser Chechnya were destroyed one after another: Kiter-Yurt "was given over to the flames," Pkhan-Kichu was burned down, at the village of Daut-Martan "the inhabitants managed to flee, but all their property remained the booty of the detachment," Edin-Yurt and Daut-Yurt were burned, "enormous stores of harvested hay" were destroyed, Martan-aul and Dzhargan-Yurt were occupied, the aul of Engeli was exterminated[58]. Between campaigns, the troops cut a clearing through the forest between the village of Aldy and the fortress of Groznaya. In January 1831 the blow was shifted to eastern, Greater Chechnya: Uzeken-Yurt was burned, Besenber with all its hamlets was destroyed. The villages of Avtury, Geldigen, and Mairtup sent their elders with an offer of submission and hostages, but Velyaminov rejected them, demanding the surrender of all Russian captives and deserter soldiers. The condition was a double impossibility, and Potto himself deciphers this: they "could not have had many" captives — captives did not settle in the villages but left through exchange and ransom, which both sides practiced; as for deserters, the Nokhchi did not hand them over — the Chechens, by Potto's admission, "regarded them... as men who had given themselves under the protection of their hearths, and therefore never surrendered them"[58]. Hospitality is a value celebrated in Chechen illi (heroic songs) on a par with courage and fidelity to one's word, and handing over a fugitive meant sending a guest to his death: the historian D. A. Khozhaev wrote of the marching gallows "on which the general [Yermolov] hanged highlanders and fugitive Russian soldiers and Cossacks who were hiding in mountain auls," and recorded that the demand for "the surrender of fugitive Russian soldiers and Cossacks living in the mountain auls" was a constant instrument of the imperial bailiffs (pristavs)[14]. By demanding simultaneously the nonexistent and the inadmissible, Velyaminov engineered a refusal: "this belated and forced submission was not at all part of Velyaminov's designs; he understood the necessity of punishing these auls cruelly, and perhaps that is why he set before them conditions which, in the view of the highlanders, were unthinkable"[58]. Avtury was taken by storm and burned, Geldigen was consigned to the flames with all its stores, and on January 21 Mairtup "with its luxuriant gardens and plantations" was destroyed together with the surrounding auls[58]. Potto sums up the result with an admission: "all of lowland Chechnya, traversed through and through as far as the Kochalykovsky ridge, was given over by Velyaminov to fire and sword"[58]. February 1837 – April 1837 C1161 Coercion of Chechnya into Oaths by Feze's Spring Tour: Amanats from Communities Coerced into the Oath, Destruction of Auls along the Dzhalka, a Livestock Fine (February-April 1837) In February-April 1837, the command of the Russian Caucasus Corps conducted a series of expeditions under General Feze across Chechnya, coercing community after community into an oath to the empire. Rozen stated the sanction in a dispatch to Minister of War Chernyshev: a campaign "beyond the Argun" would be useful "for diminishing the Chechens' trust in the instigators and turning them away from the intention of joining Shamil" (Shamil - imam, leader of the Dagestani and Chechen highlanders' resistance to the Russian conquest)[35]. Rozen's reports to Chernyshev describe the mechanism themselves: after the annihilation of the auls of Akhoy-yurt, Lyumik-yurt, Seid-yurt and Avtur, "the Chechens, gripped by fear from the preceding actions... fell into great despondency" - and the troops took oaths with amanats (amanat - a person whom the empire took from a community as a guarantee of subordination) from Shali on 6 February, Germenchuk on the 8th, Geldigen on the 15th, six auls of the Michik on the 21st, the auls along the Yaman-su and the Aksai on the 25th, and, at the end of March, from the elders of the Goyta forest and the Martan gorge[35]. The summary in the report of 4 March 1837 counts, for eleven February days: "52 souls of inhabitants who did not submit voluntarily were taken captive by our troops... and 52 amanats were taken"[35]. General Feze stated the calculation openly - he acted "with the intention of making use, as far as possible, of the panic fear" (report to Velyaminov of 15 March 1837)[3]. In March the troops passed up the Dzhalka: "the four auls they had abandoned were occupied and annihilated without resistance", and the kutans (winter shelters for livestock) with their grain stores were destroyed[35]. At the end of April a night raid on the Gertli settlement took "18 souls belonging to the families of the brigands" and 465 head of livestock, and "a fine of 132 head of livestock was imposed on the settlement"[35]. The voice of the Nokhchi records the tour as an invasion - the historian D. A. Khozhaev writes: "at the end of February-beginning of March the enemy again invaded Ichkeria. On 1 March, at the village of Aleroy, a battle took place between the detachment of Tashu-Hadji's companion Udi-mullah and the troops of General Fezi" (Tashu-Hadji - sheikh, imam of Chechnya in 1834-1836, spiritual and military leader of the Chechen resistance)[14]. August 1836 C1157 Coercion of Devastated Zandak into Subordination and Tribute by Colonel Pullo (1836) On 23 August 1836, the detachment of Colonel Pullo devastated the aul of Zandak on the Yaman-su river, taking inhabitants captive and driving away livestock (campaign C1156). The village's subordination was engineered by the devastation itself: Pullo calculatedly left some of the houses unburned so that the crushed village would have somewhere to return to beg for "submission". In a report to General Petrov dated 27 August 1836 he admitted: "Being certain that the inhabitants of Zandak, following the common custom of the Chechens, would ask for submission after punishment, and considering such submission useful for the government, I did not order the village burned"[3]. The same report recorded the mechanism of coercion: the devastation of Zandak, which had been considered impregnable, "brought both the inhabitants of the village and all those living in its vicinity into fear and despondency"[3]. Under this fear, as early as 27 August 1836 the elders of the devastated village came to the Groznaya fortress with a forced plea to be accepted into subjecthood; Rozen reported to the Minister of War: "On 27 August the Zandak elders appeared before the commander of the Sunzha Line declaring their submission, which was accepted from them in the established order"[35]. "Submission" was accepted only on the empire's terms: loyalty, a complete break with Tashu-Hadji, the leader of the Chechen resistance, a ban on assemblies, the handover of Russian captives in exchange for the inhabitants of Zandak seized by the troops during the devastation of the village, and payment of tribute at the rate established by the empire for the societies it deemed "submissive". Pullo enumerated: the people of Zandak "pledge for the time to come to remain loyal to us, allowing the inhabitants not the slightest contact with Tashav-Hadji... not to permit rebellious gatherings among themselves, to deliver our captives in exchange for their own taken during the devastation of Zandak, and to pay, on a par with the Aukhovites and other submissive tribes, the established tribute"[3]. Pullo assessed the outcome as the conqueror's gain: "All the above-stated consequences arising from the devastation of the Zandak people have produced important advantages for us"[3]. October 1905 – December 1913 C1175 Collective punishment in the abrek era: fines, quartering of troops and exile for Zelimkhan (1905-1913) In 1905-1913 the Russian Empire dealt reprisals to entire Chechen villages: it fined them, quartered troops at the residents' own expense, exiled relatives and hundreds of families, demolished hamlets. There were two pretexts - the revolution of 1905 and the abrek Zelimkhan. By the beginning of the 20th century forty years had passed since the end of the Caucasus War, but, as historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write, "Chechnya was governed by measures characteristic of a state of martial law", a "military-occupation regime" persisted in the land, and the restrictive measures only grew[2]. Onto this background fell the first Russian revolution of 1905-1907: on 24 October 1905 martial law was imposed across the whole of Chechnya, and from January 1906 field courts-martial went to work[2]. The second pretext was the abrek phenomenon - "abrek" was the empire's word for a highlander declared an outlaw who had gone to the mountains with a weapon. The most famous of them was Zelimkhan from the village of Kharachoy: in 1901, by his own words, he was a family man from a well-off household with a mill and an apiary, but after a quarrel between two families over a betrothal the authorities arrested him together with his old father and relatives; Zelimkhan escaped from the Grozny prison and until his death in 1913 remained the administration's chief enemy in the land[2]. The authorities answered not him but everyone - on top of that there was the weapons ban, which "applied exclusively to the highlanders and the out-of-town settlers and did not extend to the Cossacks"[2]. Against individual villages and entire aul districts, the same historians record, "collective punishments were widely practiced"[2]. Such reprisals were lawless even by the empire's own standards: Article 50 of the Hague Regulations on the Laws and Customs of War on Land - a convention signed and ratified by the Russian Empire - laid down: "No general penalty, pecuniary or otherwise, shall be inflicted upon the population on account of the acts of individuals for which they cannot be regarded as jointly and severally responsible"[59]. And a military directive of late 1907 prescribed, in the event of an uprising, to act by "scattering the bands to the point of total annihilation, and likewise wiping off the face of the earth the villages that sheltered them, bearing in mind that such a method will be not only more effective but also more humane"[2]. The Chechen revolutionary Aslanbek Sheripov summed up the outcome: "The authorities terrorized the peaceful population, and the abreks terrorized these authorities..."[2]. January 1927 – December 1936 C1178 Collectivization of Chechnya (1927-1936) In 1927, after stripping the Chechen people of their weapons (campaign C1177), the USSR began forcibly merging the peasant households of Chechnya into kolkhozes - collective farms controlled by the Russian state ("collectivization"). That same spring the USSR broke off relations with Great Britain and expected war - and its first move was to purge the Chechen "rear": in the summer of 1927 the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB) arrested sixteen religious authorities across Chechnya. Yevdokimov, the OGPU plenipotentiary in the North Caucasus, recorded in a secret report: "The days of military danger of the summer period unusually inspired the Chechen musduh [Muslim clergy] in the sense of bold and open agitation for aid to external forces, for the preparation of an uprising"[60]. Thus the empire ascribed to the Chechens an uprising that did not exist; the real uprisings it provoked itself two years later - with kolkhozes, devastation and the closing of mosques. On 30 January 1930 the supreme organ of the occupation power (the "Politburo of the TsK VKP(b)") adopted a secret resolution "On measures for the liquidation of kulak households in districts of wholesale collectivization"; "kulaks" was what the colonizers called peasants they deemed "well-off". The Politburo resolved to ruin on average three to five percent of peasant households across the USSR and divided their owners into three categories: the first - to concentration camps, up to execution by shooting; the second - to exile in remote places; the third - to resettlement on the worst plots within their own district; across the country it ordered 60 thousand people sent to the camps and 150 thousand expelled from their land, with 6-8 thousand and 20 thousand assigned to the North Caucasus with Dagestan. The Politburo entrusted the reprisal against the first and second categories to the OGPU, and on 2 February 1930 deputy chairman of the OGPU Yagoda signed order No. 44/21 "On measures for the liquidation of the kulaks as a class"[61]. From thousands of Chechen families whom the colonizer deemed well-off it took away voting rights, livestock and land, and expelled the people themselves beyond the borders of their native region. The USSR struck at the religious life of the Chechens as well: it squeezed out the sharia courts - they decided Chechens' cases by Islamic law, - stripped those courts of treasury money and closed mosques. The Nokhchi did not submit and rose in arms three times: in December 1929 Shali, Goity and Benoy revolted, in the spring of 1930 - the mountain okrugs, including Galanchozh, in March 1932 - the Nozhay-Yurt district. All three times the USSR sent troops with artillery and aviation against the insurgents; the toll of the year 1932 alone, from historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov: "the number of killed reached 333, of wounded - 150. The units of the Red Army and the operational groups of the GPU lost in all 27 men killed..."[2]. After the uprising of 1932 the OGPU fabricated the "Chechen nationalist center" - an underground organization that did not exist: thus the empire passed the uprisings off as the fruit of a secret conspiracy[10]. In the case of the "center" the OGPU arrested up to 3 thousand Chechens[2], shot five captured leaders of the uprising and the "members of the center", whom the Chechen historian A. G. Avtorkhanov names one by one; the count of the rank-and-file shot is unknown[10]. Belov, commander of the occupation troops of the North Caucasus Military District (SKVO), wrote in the district command's secret report to the krai committee of the party (the "North Caucasus kraikom VKP(b)") on the results of the military operation of spring 1930: "The causes of the outbreak are... The gravest errors of the old party leadership of the oblast, which pursued a completely incorrect line of wholesale collectivization, without regard for the particularities and the level of development of the national oblast", and further listed: "The administrative imposition of kolkhozes, attempts at collectivization in the mountain districts, the incorrect disenfranchisement of middle peasants, and in a number of cases of poor peasants as well... the attempt at the administrative closing of mosques"[1]. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov named this policy in the title of their chapter: "The collectivization of agriculture. The enserfment of the peasantry by the state"[2]. February 1845 – March 1917 C1173 Colonial oil: the seizure of the Grozny subsoil and the rent of the Cossack host (1845-1917) In 1845-1917 the Russian Empire took Grozny's oil away from the Chechens: it assigned the income from the subsoil to the Cossack host by law and barred the Chechen communities from the industry - neither as owners nor as recipients of rent. On 16 February 1845 paragraph 154 of the "Regulations on the Caucasus Line Host" gave the Cossack host the income from the oil springs near the Groznaya fortress: "as a mark of special favor…the host is granted the income most graciously bestowed upon it from the oil springs near the Groznaya fortress"[16]. The wells from which Chechen owners had once sold oil became a line in the host's budget, and when on 6 October 1893 the first industrial gusher burst from a well of the company of oil industrialist Akhverdov - "in the first two weeks alone it yielded 150 thousand puds of oil"[2] - it turned out that the richest field lay beneath land taken from the Chechen auls. The legal frame was formulated in 1894 by the head of the Terek oblast, General Kakhanov (he headed the oblast from 1889 to 1900[16]), when he refused to extend to the Chechen lands the rules on peasant leasing of the subsoil: "...the state lands populated by the mountain inhabitants were given to them not into ownership by right of property, but only into use..."[2]. Historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova sums up the distribution: "If the total income from the oil industry is taken as 100%, the industrialists received 35%, the treasury 32%, the owners of the land 24% and the middlemen 9%" - the owner of the land was deemed to be the Cossack host, and the Chechen community had no share[16]. Only two villages - Aldy and Novye Aldy - managed to strike deals with the industrialists directly, and these deals show the real price of the subsoil: on 18 April 1915 the assembly of Novye Aldy - a village of 520 households - leased 20 desiatinas to the oil industrialist Stepan Lianozov for 24 years at 5 thousand rubles per desiatina plus 2 kopecks to the community for every pud of oil extracted[16], while the oil industrialist Tapa Chermoyev paid the community 30 thousand rubles up front for the plots near Aldy and by contract guaranteed it a quarter of the income from the extracted oil[16]. To all the other Chechen communities the law left nothing - their share was collected by the Cossack host. January 1658 – January 1660 C1119 Comprehensive Reconnaissance of Territories and an Attempt to Coerce into Subjecthood (1658–1660) The occupation administration of the Tsardom of Muscovy gathered military-strategic and economic intelligence on the mountain societies of the Nokhchi (the Shibutians) and made attempts at their forcible subjugation. In 1658, the central apparatus of the Ambassadorial Prikaz instructed the Terek voivodes to send a mission into the mountains, in order «concerning those little lands... to order that they be examined and truly scouted out — how many of them there are and what kind of people they are... and what fighting capability they have... and what grows in their land, and what craftsmen there are»[53]. The document of the central authority also directly stated «to order that amanats be taken from among their kin, men of note»[53]. To carry out the order, in 1659 the Terek voivodes Melenty Kvashnin and his associates dispatched a military emissary: an extract for the report of the Ambassadorial Prikaz to Tsar Aleksei Mikhailovich of 1660 states that the voivodes «sent a streltsy head into the Shibut land and ordered him to inspect in the Shibut land the Christian faith, and church building, and towns, and places, and to bring them to the faith, and to take an amanat to the Terek»[53]. The emissary carried out the reconnaissance, reporting that «they have no church building, nor to]wns, nor any fighting forces»[53], but he was unable to subjugate the population: «he did not brin[g] the inhabitants of the Shibut land to the faith»[53]. The seizure of new hostages likewise ended without result; the emissary merely stated that the mountaineers «wish [to be] under the lofty sovereign hand, and on the Terek they [have an amanat]»[53]. January 1809 – December 1811 C1141 Consolidation in Chechnya: Bribery of Elders, Economic Control, and Setting Neighbors against One Another (1809-1811) In 1809-1811, the Russian Empire consolidated its power over the lands of the Nokhchi through the bribery of elders, control over the sale of grain and salt, and the setting of neighboring peoples against the Chechens. To incline the Chechens to submission, the commander-in-chief in the Caucasus, General Tormasov, ordered that Chechen elders and clergy be paid «250, and others 150 silver rubles each, as a one-time payment, for which the required sum, 1,400 r. in total»[62]. The empire funneled the sale of grain and salt to the Chechens through controlled barter yards under quarantine, established «for the peaceful Chechens in Naur… for the mountain Chechens in Lashchurin»[62][36]. In a proclamation to the inhabitants of the Chechen land, General Tormasov laid the blame for the devastation of 1807 on the inhabitants themselves — «you yourselves were the cause of the misfortune that befell you the year before last» — and threatened a new invasion, «to bring sword and flame upon the guilty»[62]. January 1736 – December 1740 C1134 Construction of Fortified Stanitsas, Settlement of Cossacks on the Borders, and Holding of Hostages (1736–1740) In the period from 1736 to 1740, the diplomatic and administrative apparatus of the Russian Empire maintained control over the borders of the Nokhchi societies through infrastructure construction and hostage-taking. The established evidence base demonstrates that the metropole began by building new fortifications: historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov records the establishment in 1736 of fortified posts, among them «three new Cossack stanitsas: Borozdinskaya, Kargalinskaya, Dubovskaya»[37]. Historian I. Kh. Tkhamokova emphasizes their engineering-defensive status, recording that each such stanitsa «was, as it were, a small fortress serving for protection against enemy raids»[63]. The construction of infrastructure was followed by the physical settlement of military contingents: the first researcher indicates that garrisons were placed on these frontiers, «and from Kizlyar toward the sea another 430 Cossack families are being settled»[37]. In parallel, the occupation administration continued to physically hold relatives of the local elite seized in previous years: Akhmadov notes, in a list of archival documents, a paper from 1738 identified as «Letter of the Chechen lord A. Bartykhanov to Lieutenant Colonel Bunin about his faithful service to Russia and with a request to release his sister from Kizlyar»[37]. September 1722 – December 1724 C1130 Construction of the Holy Cross Fortress and Forced Resettlement (1722–1724) In 1722–1724, the Russian Empire carried out military-infrastructural colonization and demographic manipulation on the seized frontiers. In the autumn of 1722, construction of a new military base began: historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov states that Peter I «founded the fortress of the Holy Cross on the Sulak»[37]. To ensure forcible control over the territory, the metropole carried out settlement by loyal troops: the researcher indicates that at the fortress «1 thousand families of Cossacks from the Don are being settled»[37]. At the same time, the occupation administration liquidated the former administrative center and forcibly relocated the subordinated Nokhchi societies: the author records that «the Terek town had been razed by 1724, and its entire population, including the Okotskaya sloboda, populated by natives of Chechnya... was transferred to the new fortress»[37]. A controlled buffer zone was taking shape around the new fortification: historian Sh. B. Akhmadov notes that «next to the fortress of the Holy Cross, slobodkas populated by Circassians, Chechens, Ingush, Kabardians, and others very quickly began to appear»[36]. April 2014 – February 2015 C0101 Continuation of the Russo-Ukrainian War: Armed Aggression in the Donbas (2014–2015) The expansion of Russian aggression through the seizure of administrative buildings in eastern Ukraine by armed detachments: "groups of armed men unlawfully carried out a well-organized and coordinated seizure of public buildings and police and security service offices in towns and villages of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions"[64]. The commander of the detachment that crossed the border, I. Girkin ("Strelkov"), later admitted his own role: "It was I, after all, who pulled the trigger of the war. Had our detachment not crossed the border, it would all have ended as in Kharkiv, as in Odesa"[65]. The campaign was accompanied by terror against the local population, the downing of flight MH17, and massive disinformation[66]. In the summer of 2014, the Russian Federation brought in regular troops, which led to the battles near Ilovaisk and Debaltseve. The UN monitoring mission recorded bussed-in crowds from the outset: "people were brought in buses and paid to take part in protests and conduct them according to specific scenarios, including causing violent incidents," while "some protesters allegedly come from the Russian Federation"[67]. January 1835 – August 1836 C1156 Covert reconnaissance of Chechnya by Rosen's topographers and the devastation of Zandak by Pullo's detachment: capture of 31 inhabitants and seizure of livestock (1835-1836) In 1835–1836 the empire combined systematic punitive expeditions in Chechnya with covert reconnaissance of the territory. Corps commander Rosen, in a report to the emperor, admits the practice of clandestine study of unsubdued lands: the undertakings "consisted either in the collection of topographical information... or in covert surveys of the lands of the mountaineers hostile to us"; "in 1836, to survey the direct route leading from Kakheti to Chechnya, a topographer was sent, who, having crossed the snowy ridge, came out onto the Caucasian Line at the fortress of Groznaya, and from there, through Chechnya and the lands of the Kists and the Didoi, returned to Kakheti"; at the same time "I sent from Vladikavkaz Ensign Prince Utsmiev of the Life Guards Grenadier Regiment with a topographer, through Chechnya, to Andia"[35]. Against the movement of Imam Tashu-Hajji, Colonel Pullo, commander of the Sunzha fortified line, conducted constant expeditions; the imperial review of military operations admits: Tashu-Hajji's attempts "were forestalled in good time by the expeditions of the commander of the Sunzha Line, Colonel Pullo, which inflicted total ruin on the inhabitants"[35]. On August 23, 1836, Pullo's detachment, in a covert night march, reached the aul of Zandak on the Yaman-su River, where Tashu-Hajji was staying. Rosen reported to the minister of war: Pullo, "in order to shake the influence of Tashev-Hajji, to quell the unrest among the Chechens, and to instill fear in them, resolved to undertake movements to punish the inhabitants of the village of Zandak"; "the sudden appearance of our troops struck terror into the inhabitants"; the infantry, having driven out the defenders, seized "31 souls of male and female sex as prisoners. In addition, the property of the inhabitants and 384 head of horned cattle fell to our troops as booty"; before the withdrawal, the houses of the murids and of "other principal adherents of Tashev-Hajji" were annihilated[35]. The Chechen writer Abuzar Aydamirov, in his "Chronology of the History of Checheno-Ingushetia," recorded: "Punitive expedition of Colonel Pullo to the auls on the Yaman-Su River. Destruction of the aul of Zandak. Retreat of Pullo's detachment, under the pressure of Tashav-Hajji, to the fortress of Vnezapnaya"[68]. January 1958 – December 1970 C0053 Creation of a Single "Soviet People" (1958–1970) The USSR's official campaign to erase national distinctions: The start was given by the USSR Law "On Strengthening the Connection of School with Life and on the Further Development of the System of Public Education in the USSR" of December 24, 1958: it contained no direct norm on language, leaving the matter to the republics[69]; the republican Law of the Ukrainian SSR of April 17, 1959, by its Article 9, made the choice of the language of instruction a matter for parents[70]. The Third Program of the CPSU, adopted by the 22nd Congress in October 1961, proclaimed "a new stage in the development of national relations in the USSR, characterized by the further drawing together of nations and the achievement of their complete unity" - up to and including "the effacement of national distinctions, especially of language distinctions"[71]. January 1801 – December 1811 C0038 Creation of the Little Russian Governorate-General (1801–1811) Administrative absorption: "the LITTLE RUSSIAN GOVERNORATE-GENERAL – an administrative-territorial and political unit of the Russian Empire, created in 1802 for the incorporation and integration of Left-Bank Ukraine into the Russian Empire"[23]. The outcome is recorded there as well: "During the existence of the governorate-general, the remnants of the Hetmanate's autonomy were finally liquidated"[23]. January 1663 – December 1663 C0023 Creation of the Little Russian Prikaz (1663) Institutional substitution: Ukrainian affairs were handed over to a special agency in Moscow. The Little Russian Prikaz was founded "as one of the departments of the Ambassadorial Prikaz to administer Ukrainian affairs," and through it the tsarist government "exercised control over the political-administrative activity of the hetman's administration and the tsarist voivodes in Ukraine"[23] – the Hetmanate fell under the permanent departmental oversight of the metropole. January 1847 – December 1847 C0060 Crushing of the Cyril and Methodius Society (1847) The secret police's blow against the intellectual elite of the indigenous people: "In March 1847 the society was crushed by the gendarmes. The police managed to identify 12 members of the clandestine organization… The tsarist authorities judged the society's program documents a serious threat to the foundations of autocracy"[27]. The sentences for all the accused were proposed by the chief of gendarmes Orlov in his report to the emperor of May 26, 1847, on which Nicholas I inscribed "Execute"[72]. It was accompanied by trials, exiles, and Shevchenko's dispatch into the army "with the institution over the poet of 'the strictest surveillance with a prohibition on writing and drawing'"[73]. January 1933 – December 1938 C0079 Cultural Terror and the "Executed Renaissance" (1933–1938) The abrupt rollback of the policy of "Ukrainization." The start of the physical extermination and political defamation of the intellectual elite - writers, scholars, film directors, as well as the old national communists (M. Skrypnyk was driven to suicide)[39]. In parallel with the physical terror came the destruction of the Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church, large-scale censorship, the rewriting of history, and the artificial convergence of the Ukrainian language with Russian; works published in the Ukrainian SSR before 1933, in the words of the compiler of the anthology "Executed Renaissance," were "destroyed as a result of Moscow's new course toward the rout and colonial provincialization of Ukraine"[24]. January 1571 – January 1653 C1109 Cyclical Rebuilding and Elimination of Fortifications on the Sunzha River (1571–1653) The Regular Army of the Tsardom of Muscovy carried out the cyclical elimination and renewal of its military presence on the lands of the Nokhchi at the mouth of the Sunzha River.
