The first military base, built in 1567, was soon destroyed: historian E. N. Kusheva notes that "the town of 1567 was demolished around 1571"[56]. Military historian V. A. Potto indicates the reason for the base's elimination: it "was soon destroyed to appease the Turkish sultan"[74]. Later, the military presence on the lands of the Nokhchi was renewed: historian E. N. Kusheva writes that "in 1577-1578... the Russian town was restored on the Terek River at the mouth of the Sunzha"[56]. However, the second military base was also eliminated: historian E. N. Kusheva indicates that this "Russian town was likewise soon destroyed at the demand of the khan"[56]. The subsequent fortification was rebuilt many times: E. N. Kusheva, compiler of a collection of documents, indicates that the military forces of the Tsardom of Muscovy "rebuilt the ostrog in 1590 and 1635"[53], and also notes that in the intervals "the fortress was abandoned for political reasons in 1605"[53]. Another attempt to gain a foothold on the lands of the Nokhchi took place later: E. N. Kusheva, compiler of the collection of documents, records that "in 1651 a Russian ostrog was built anew on the left bank of the Sunzha"[53]. However, it was soon eliminated for good: compiler E. N. Kusheva indicates that "in 1653 the ostrog was burned by Persian troops and was never rebuilt"[53]. January 1828 – November 1829 C1150 Deception and Forcible Detention of Beibulat Taimiev by Paskevich, Splitting Chechnya into Factions, and Coercion into an Oath of Allegiance (1828-1829) After Yermolov's punitive campaign of 1826 and the ebbing of the uprising of 1825-1826, the empire, having failed to subdue Chechnya by force of arms, turned to deception, division, and hostage-taking. The historian D. A. Khozhaev wrote: "Paskevich, trying to lure the principal leader of the Chechen insurgents out of Chechnya, throughout the whole of 1828 offers Beibulat, through intermediaries, a return to 'Russian service.' He is promised the rank of captain, pardon, and honors"[14]. On March 6, 1829, Beibulat Taimiev and 120 elders of Chechnya were forced to accept nominal allegiance in Tarki through the Shamkhal of Tarki. D. A. Khozhaev recorded the motive: the elders "sought to avoid subordination to the tsarist pristavs (superintendents), to avert from Chechnya the threat of constant raids"[14]. Emanuel, commander of the troops on the Caucasus Line, set a condition in his report to Paskevich: "the submission of Bey-Bulat and the other unsubdued Chechens will be recognized as well-intentioned only when they unconditionally take the oath and hand over amanats (hostages)"[75]. In his instruction to Emanuel, Paskevich revealed the calculation of splitting the people: "it is not without use for us to have two factions in Chechnya, which, both remaining submissive to our government, will by internecine discord be restrained from hostile designs against the Russians"[75]. Having summoned Beibulat and the elders of his faction to Tiflis ostensibly for negotiations, Paskevich detained them with the army in the field for the entire Turkish campaign. D. A. Khozhaev wrote: "Realizing that he had been deceived, he tries to return to Chechnya immediately, but he is detained in Tiflis by force"[14]. Paskevich himself acknowledged the scheme in his instruction to Emanuel of August 2, 1829: "I at once resolved to summon to me, under the guise of explanations, their elders and the elder Bey-Bulat known to you, so that, having drawn them away here, I would deprive this tribe of the possibility... of undertaking anything hostile"; "Having kept them in this way for the whole summer, I secured tranquility for the Line on their part"[75]. The same instruction confirmed the regulation on Chechnya: amanats from every elder's district "as a pledge of submission" in the fortress of Groznaya, the son of the Shamkhal as commissar over the Chechens, and travel into imperial territory only with tickets (written passes) from the commissar[75]. The oath was signed by a people that had lived through a wave of arrests, executions, and exiles at the hands of the imperial command. The Chechens wrote to Paskevich in April 1829: they "arrested, took captive, hanged, and exiled to Siberia and other places many of those who, being submissive, served the great Sovereign"[75]. July 1819 – September 1819 C1143 Demonstrative destruction of the aul of Dadi-Yurt and the construction of the Vnezapnaya fortress to force the Nokhchi off the Kumyk plain (1819) After the construction of the Groznaya fortress on the Sunzha in 1818, General Yermolov continued, as historian D. A. Khozhaev writes, to "squeeze unsubdued Chechnya with new fortresses and fortifications," and among these, in 1819, appeared the fortress of Vnezapnaya[14]. Imperial historian Potto names its purpose outright: founded on the eighteenth of July 1819, it "separated the Chechens from the Kumyks" and "blocked [the Chechens'] path to the Dagestanis through the Salatau mountains"[76]. Potto writes that Yermolov "decided to clear the entire Kumyk plain… by making the Chechens leave it for beyond the Kachkalyk mountain ridge," and getting them to take their families away themselves "was possible only by an example of terror"[76]. The Nokhchi aul of Dadi-Yurt was chosen as the demonstrative victim. Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that the aul of 200 households was "one of the richest in Chechnya" and "was famed for its brave and industrious inhabitants and for the beauty and nobility of its girls"[14]. Yermolov ordered Major General Sysoev to surround the aul and, "should they resist, to punish them with arms, giving quarter to no one"[77]. On the fifteenth of September 1819 the aul was surrounded by six Kabardian companies and seven hundred Cossacks, who took it by storming each household under artillery fire[76][14]. Yermolov himself admits the outcome in his "Notes": "all who bore arms were exterminated, and their number could not have been fewer than four hundred men"; of women and children "up to one hundred and forty were taken prisoner… but a far greater number were slaughtered or perished in the houses from the effects of artillery and fire," while the village "consisted of 200 houses" and was "razed to its foundations"[77]. The surviving women and children were led away as prisoners beyond the Terek; historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that during the river crossing 46 captured girls, "unwilling to endure abuse in captivity," perished, "dragging their guards with them into the turbulent river"[14]. After the destruction of the aul, Yermolov finished off the Kachkalyk villages with almost no resistance left; he himself admits: "the example of Dadan-Yurt spread terror everywhere"[77]. February 1919 – December 1919 C1174 Denikin's terror in Chechnya: destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead (1919) In 1919 the Volunteer Army of General Denikin conquered Chechnya with ultimatums, assaults and the burning of villages - the year it left behind ended with 21 destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead. After the fall of the empire (campaign C1189) the peoples of the North Caucasus tried to live in a state of their own: in May 1918 the highland political forces proclaimed the independent Mountain Republic from the Black Sea to the Caspian; its first government was headed by the Chechen Tapa Chermoyev, an oil industrialist (campaign C1173), its parliament by the Ingush Vassan-Girey Dzhabagiev[2]. In February 1919 the Terek oblast was occupied by the Volunteer Army - troops of former imperial officers under the command of Denikin, fighting the Bolsheviks for the return of Russia within its former borders; historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "The main force of the Volunteer Army was made up of Cossacks, and therefore the actions of the Denikinites in the Terek oblast were aimed, first of all, at restoring the privileged position of the Cossacks"[2]. Denikin did not recognize the Mountain Republic: he refused to receive the delegation of its government; General Lyakhov, appointed ruler of the Terek oblast, agreed to regard the republic's parliament as no more than "a consultative organ attached to his person", and as ruler of Chechnya the Volunteer Army appointed General Aliev[2]. At the negotiations with the Mountain government Lyakhov declared: "...There cannot be two masters in one house. Where I pay, I shall be the master. I demand submission to my authority, and whoever does not submit to it, let him blame himself for what will come of it"[2]. The Denikin command recorded of the resistance: "The bitterness of the Chechens and their daring reach the utmost degree"[2]. The year's total was drawn by the Soviet survey of 1920, which historian E. F. Zhupikova cites: "21 destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead Chechens is what the Denikin army left behind it"[78]. January 1614 – December 1616 C1114 Deprivation of the Nokhchi of political agency and the imposition of alien governance (1614–1616) The occupation administration of the metropole liquidated the autonomy of the Nokhchi communities (the Okochans) in the Terek town, establishing alien governance over them and beginning to exploit their resources. Historian E. N. Kusheva states that in 1614 Tsar Mikhail Fedorovich ordered the Kabardian prince Sunchaley Yanglychevich Cherkassky "to be prince over all the Okochans..., to judge them and to have charge of them in military organization and in all matters"[56]. The appointed ruler proceeded to the physical and economic exploitation of the indigenous population. Kusheva points out that he forced those under his rule "to perform all manner of labor for him, to plow the fields and to mow the hay"[56]. Facts of administrative extortion and slave trading are documented: in a petition to Tsar Mikhail Fedorovich, the service Okochans of the Terek town reported that the ruler "having taken from us by force 8 good horses from the herd, sent them off to his kabaks in Kabarda"[79][53], "wrongfully sold four of our Okochan comrades"[79][53] and "took a wife into bondage and sent her off to his kabaks in Kabarda"[79][53]. The document adds that he subjected the Nokhchi to corporal punishment: "he orders us to be thrown into prison and beaten with the knout without thy sovereign knowledge and without guilt"[79][53]. The administration of the metropole itself for years compelled the Nokhchi to serve without pay: a report from the Terek voivode Pyotr Petrovich Golovin to the Astrakhan voivode Ivan Nikitich Odoevsky records that they "serve the sovereign tsar... in all manner of the sovereign's Terek... services... yet for the tenth year have not been granted the sovereign's monetary and grain salary"[79]. The indigenous population was also forced to fight against their own compatriots: E. N. Kusheva, compiler of an academic collection, indicates in the heading of a primary document that there took place "a campaign of the Terek fighting men and the Terek Okochans... against the Endirey ruler Saltan-Magmut and the people of the Okotsk and Michkiz kabaks who had joined him"[53]. In parallel, the metropole imposed tribute on the mountain communities of the Nokhchi: an extract from the book of the Terek town's Prikaz office records that the administration sent men "to the Michkiz lands for the sovereign's yasak"[53]. The compilers of the academic collections dryly state the outcome of the Nokhchi protests: "The petition of the 'Okochans' was not granted"[79]. October 2013 – February 2014 C0099 Derailing the Association with the EU (2013–2014) Economic and political pressure by V. Putin on V. Yanukovych in the autumn of 2013 aimed at derailing the signing of the Association Agreement with the EU. The price was formalized publicly on December 17, 2013: "Ukraine will receive 15 billion dollars from Russia and gas at a reduced price" - the gas price was lowered "to 268.5 dollars per thousand cubic meters" instead of the previous 410, and the money came "from the Russian National Welfare Fund" in exchange for Ukrainian government securities[80]. The refusal to sign the agreement triggered the protests: "between 21 November 2013 and 22 February 2014 large-scale street protests took place, provoked by the decision of then-President Viktor Yanukovych not to sign the association agreement with the European Union," and their suppression ended in shootings - on the Maidan "between January and February 2014 more than 100 people were killed, including by snipers"[64]. January 1718 – December 1718 C0042 Destruction of the Archives of the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra (1718) A covert operation (sabotage) by Muscovite emissaries disguised as monks, aimed at the physical destruction of historical archives. According to testimonies preserved by the Kyiv scholar Lebedyntsev, "the Lavra was set on fire by emissaries from Moscow dressed as monks. The enormous archive and library burned down; the charters and grants… of princes, magnates, and hetmans perished"; historian Hyrych sums up: "The fire destroyed the written memory of the Lavra's independent Ukrainian political and spiritual life"[81]. January 1817 – December 1818 C1021 Destruction of the Nokhchi Villages along the Sunzha and Construction of the Groznaya Fortress in Their Place (1817–1818) Between 1817 and 1818, the Russian Empire forcibly moved the fortified line from the Terek to the Sunzha and secured the seized territory of the Nokhchi communities by building a fortress, accompanying this with the driving off of the population, the taking of hostages, and coercion into submission. Historian D. A. Khozhaev records that the relocation of the line "squeezed unsubdued Chechnya with new fortresses and fortifications," while the fortress of Groznaya was built "on Chechen land," where "eight flourishing Chechen villages… were destroyed, and the population driven off its lands"[14]. Imperial general Yermolov, commander of the Caucasus Corps, testifies in his "Notes" to the deployment of troops ("on May 24 the entire detachment crossed over… moved from the Terek to the Sunzha River"), to the demand that the elders "renew their long-standing oath of submission," and to the taking of amanats (hostages) "from their villages"[77]. Imperial historian Potto confirms the founding of the fortress on June 10, 1818, "with six bastions, which Yermolov named Groznaya"[76]. January 1826 – December 1827 C1149 Destruction of the Refugee Aul of Uzeni-Yurt, Extortion of Hostages from Geldigen, and Capture of Samashki Residents at Harvest (1826-1827) After Yermolov's punitive campaign, which devastated the lowland villages of the Nokhchi in 1826, some inhabitants of the destroyed villages refused to resettle under the conqueror's control and took refuge in the forests. The imperial historian Potto admits: "the inhabitants of some auls destroyed by Yermolov took refuge in the forests and, unwilling to resettle, abandoned even their fields sown with grain"[58]. The village of Uzeni-Yurt on the bank of the Argun became a refuge for these people and a stronghold of the Karabulak leader Astemir, an associate of Beibulat Taimiev in the uprising of 1825. On the night of January 10, 1827, General Laptev, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, covertly led against the village a detachment of 350 line Cossacks with two horse-drawn guns, forcing four hundred Chechens from subordinated communities to take part as well. Potto wrote: they "swam across the Argun and had to take a roundabout route in order to cut off the inhabitants' retreat to the forest"[58]. Warned by a horseman, the inhabitants fled across the Argun. Potto recorded: the Cossacks, overtaking those fleeing, "seized... three women and killed and wounded some fifteen people," after which "the village of Uzeni-Yurt, with all its property and even its livestock, was destroyed to the ground"[58]. That same winter Laptev exacted hostages from the village of Geldigen, rejecting a ransom for a captured young man of Geldigen. Potto wrote: "Laptev rejected all offers and demanded one thing - amanats (hostages)"[58]. In the summer of 1827 his successor, General Engelhardt, set an ambush during the harvest near the aul of Samashki. Potto admits: the inhabitants were freely allowed onto the fields, and then "everything that was in the field turned out to be encircled by a dense Cossack cordon"; the population was released, while the leader Tara-Adzuev and the family of the resistance leader Bakar-Bulatov were taken prisoner, and the grain of the Galgai, who lived by the aul, was "burned... standing in the field"[58]. January 1906 – December 1910 C0050 Destruction of Ukrainian Societies and Segregation (1906–1910) A campaign to suppress the legal civic activity of the indigenous people: in the Poltava and Kharkiv regions the "Prosvita" societies were banned from their very founding, and in 1908–1910, under Stolypin, virtually all "Prosvitas" were closed, except the branches of the Katerynoslav governorate[47]. Justifying the crackdown, Stolypin declared in an address to the Senate that the revival of Ukrainian cultural life was undesirable, for "the three principal branches of Eastern Slavdom, both by origin and by language, cannot but constitute one whole"[47]. Stolypin's circular of 1910 classed Ukrainians among the "aliens" and prescribed "to refuse without fail the registration" of their societies[82]. September 1819 – October 1819 C1144 Devastation of the Kachkalyk villages of the Nokhchi and displacement of their inhabitants beyond the mountains after the Dadi-Yurt terror (1819) After the demonstrative destruction of Dadi-Yurt, General Yermolov moved on to devastate the remaining Nokhchi villages of the Kachkalyk plain and drive their inhabitants off the land. The historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that under Yermolov "cruel punitive raids on peaceful Caucasian auls — with the annihilation of the population, houses, crops, orchards, and forests, the driving off of livestock, and the plundering of property — which disgraced Russian arms, became the rule," and following Dadi-Yurt the Kachkalyk villages of Isti-Su, Noiberdy, Alleroi, and others were "taken by storm and destroyed"[14]. Yermolov himself describes the campaign in his "Notes": on September 30, 1819, he "himself set out with 6 battalions and 16 artillery pieces toward the Kachkalyk villages"; on October 2 he attacked "the village of Goryachevskaya, the strongest of them" (also known as Isti-Su), and a day later devastated Noen-Berdy and Allayar-Aul: "from the first the Chechens were driven out by heavy cannonade, the latter was abandoned by them… Both were utterly devastated"[77]. At the same time, Major General Sysoev invaded Chechen land from Groznaya through Khan-Kale, drawing the forces of the Chechens away from the Kachkalyk plain[77]. The imperial historian Potto confirms: the Apsheron men "went in with bayonets without firing a shot, burst into the aul and committed it to the flames," while Noim-Berdy and Allayar-Aul "were utterly devastated"[76]. One village survived by submitting: Yermolov writes that "the village of Khangeldy begged for mercy… The Aksai owners vouched for its inhabitants, and mercy was granted them"[77], while Potto adds that "the aul of Khosh-Geldy met Yermolov with bread and salt and was spared"[76]. The remaining villages the punitive forces found empty, because the Dadi-Yurt terror had driven the inhabitants off the plain in advance. Yermolov admits that "in none of the villages were there wives and children; the property had likewise been carried away," for "the example of Dadan-Yurt spread terror everywhere"[77]. Potto writes that "the remaining auls were empty - their inhabitants had fled beyond the mountains," and "within a few days the Kumyk plain was completely cleared of the predatory Chechens"[76]. On October 5 the troops returned to Vnezapnaya[77]. January 1826 – May 1826 C1148 Devastation of the Lowland Nokhchi Villages in Yermolov’s Punitive Campaign (1826) In January-May 1826 the Russian Empire conducted a large punitive campaign against the Nokhchi, devastating lowland villages for participation in Beibulat Taimiev’s uprising and forcing the inhabitants into submission. The historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that "in January 1826, having waited for a period inconvenient for the inhabitants of Chechnya, when the frosts made it difficult to shelter families, Yermolov begins a large punitive campaign into Chechnya," occupying the aul of Bolshaya Ataga on January 26 and burning settlements one after another[14]. General Yermolov himself, in a report to Emperor Nicholas I of May 28, 1826, admits the course of the devastation: during the storming of Urus-Martan "the village was burned and its splendid orchards cut down," at Stavna-Kul "16 souls of both sexes were taken prisoner, several people killed," and the village of Shali he "ordered to be exterminated… and its orchards cut down"[83]. The historian D. A. Khozhaev sums up: by May 18, 1826, "flourishing settlements had been destroyed, splendid fruit orchards cut down, fields burned, livestock driven off. People were killed, women and children taken prisoner… People were dying of hunger, cold, and disease"[14]. April 2008 – December 2008 C0098 Diplomatic Attack Against NATO Enlargement (2008) Diplomatic blackmail by V. Putin around the NATO summit in Bucharest aimed at blocking the granting of a Membership Action Plan (MAP) to Ukraine. Two days after the summit, at a meeting with G. Bush in Sochi, the Russian leader denied Ukrainian statehood - Ukraine, in his words, "is not a nation built in a natural manner" but "an artificial country created back in Soviet times"[84] - and directly threatened its rupture: "the country could just split apart," adding that, relying on anti-NATO forces, "Russia would be creating problems there all the time"[84]. At the summit itself, as retold by Kommersant's source, Putin told Bush: "You understand, George, that Ukraine is not even a state!" - in effect threatening "that Russia could begin the severance of Crimea and Eastern Ukraine"[85]. August 1991 C0094 Diplomatic Blackmail (the "Chicken Kiev" Speech, August 1991) The union center's use of international levers to keep Ukraine within the USSR. The culmination was US president Bush's visit to Kyiv, where from the rostrum of the Verkhovna Rada he warned against independence: "Americans will not support those who seek independence in order to replace a far-off tyranny with a local despotism. They will not aid those who promote a suicidal nationalism based upon ethnic hatred"[86]. January 1726 – December 1728 C1131 Economic Discrimination and Reconnaissance of Territories (1726–1728) In the period from 1726 to 1731, the Russian Empire exerted routine administrative and economic pressure on the Nokhchi societies while avoiding large-scale military interventions. The occupation administration imposed harsh taxes on commercial travel by the indigenous population: historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov cites customs documents, stating that in 1726 «from the travel document of the Terek resident, the Okochan Kurman Bogomatov... duties of 24 altyns in money were collected by decree»[37], and also that «a report of February 15, 1726 states that duties were collected from the Terek Okochans Surkai Usmanov...»[37]. The economic strangulation provoked armed resistance: Akhmadov indicates that the highlanders «carried out attacks on the tsarist fortifications, kept the fortress of the Holy Cross «in great oppression»»[37]. In addition, the empire conducted the gathering of military-strategic intelligence: historian Sh. B. Akhmadov notes that in 1728 the officer I. G. Gerber «on the government's assignment... compiled a description of the localities and population... as well as a map of this district»[36]. January 1617 – December 1622 C1115 Economic Exploitation and Creation of Dependency of the Nokhchi (1617–1622) The occupation administration of the Tsardom of Muscovy in the town of Terki used the subordinated Nokhchi (Okochans) to carry out state tasks while artificially keeping them in a state of economic dependency. In their petition to Tsar Mikhail Fedorovich, the Okochan murza Kokhostrov Biytemirov and the serving Okochans of the town of Terki reported constant coercion into military action: «against your sovereign's disobedient ones we fight, we, your sovereign's kholops, not sparing our heads; for you, sovereign, we shed our blood and lay down our heads»[53]. At the same time, the metropole deliberately withheld basic subsistence resources from the Indigenous population for five years. A memorandum from the Ambassadorial Prikaz to the Prikaz of the Kazan Palace records: «the sovereign's grain allowance for the past years — for the 125th, and the 126th, and the 127th, and the 128th, and the 129th year — was not given to them»[53]. The result was the exhaustion of the population: Biytemirov reported that they «have been left without grain, have utterly perished from hunger and every hardship and have fallen, sovereign, into great debt, and we are dying a death of starvation together with our wives and children»[53]. To resolve the crisis, the leader of the Nokhchi set out for Moscow, but perished while returning to the Caucasus. A memorandum from the Ambassadorial Prikaz states that «Kokhostrov-murza together with his man drowned in the Oka River»[53], while representatives of the metropole resolved to confiscate the property of the deceased: «his clothing and all his belongings were taken into our treasury»[53]. The delegate's death was used to further curtail the rights of the Nokhchi. In a petition submitted to Tsar Mikhail Fedorovich, the Okochan murza Chepan Kokhostrov indicated that in the incident «the sovereign's charter of grant was lost together with him»[53], as a result of which the occupation administration artificially lowered the status of his family in order to impose obligations upon it: an official extract of the Ambassadorial Prikaz records that the heirs were «made equal in everything with the Okochans, with the plowing people, and carts and wagons are taken from them», whereas previously from them «no taxes whatsoever had been taken»[53]. September 2004 – December 2004 C0096 Election Interference and Countering the "Orange Revolution" (2004) Direct interference by the Russian Federation in the presidential election of a sovereign state in order to impose a loyal candidate (V. Yanukovych): two weeks before the first round, the head of the Russian state, live on three Ukrainian television channels, campaigned for the incumbent prime minister, declaring that "V. Yanukovych's government achieved more: they managed to fill this growth with good quality"[87]. Chemical poisoning was used against the leader of the democratic forces, V. Yushchenko: the dioxin levels in his blood "were more than 50,000-fold greater than those in the general population"[88]. In response to the protests, Moscow instigated the threat of splitting the country apart - at the Sievierodonetsk congress (28 November 2004) Regions faction leader R. Bohatyriova's words "we will hold a referendum on the creation of a South-Eastern state" were met with applause, while the mayor of Moscow Yu. Luzhkov sat as an honored guest in the presidium[89]. January 1661 – January 1676 C1122 Establishment of Alien Governance and the Mobilization of the Nokhchi for the Crimean Campaigns (1661–1676) The occupation administration of the Tsardom of Muscovy maintained a regime that deprived the subordinated societies of the Nokhchi (the Okochans) of autonomy in the Terek town, prolonging the power over them of a loyal foreign ruler for their subsequent mobilization. In 1661, Tsar Aleksei Mikhailovich issued a charter of grant to the Kabardian prince Kaspulat Mutsalovich Cherkassky, officially prescribing that he «be prince over the Okochans and over the Cherkasses who serve us, the great sovereign, on the Terek, and administer and judge them in military organization and in all our affairs»[53]. Having received control, the appointed ruler became an instrument for implementing imperial objectives: in 1676, the central apparatus of the Ambassadorial Prikaz sent an instruction to Prince Kaspulat Mutsalovich Cherkassky on the need to arrive at the Terek «to administer the oath of allegiance of the population of the North Caucasus to Tsars Ivan and Peter Alekseevich»[79]. In the same period, the subordinated Nokhchi were forcibly thrown into the metropole's military campaigns against the Crimean Khanate. A dispatch from Prince Kaspulat Mutsalovich Cherkassky to the Ambassadorial Prikaz of 1675 states that for the campaign into the Crimean uluses he had at his disposal various fighting men, including «190 Okochan men»[79], and the historian I. Kh. Tkhamokova confirms that in 1675 detachments fought in Crimea that included men «with uzdens, with the newly baptized, and with «Okochans»»[63]. January 1791 – December 1791 C0036 Establishment of the "Pale of Settlement" (1791) The introduction of discriminatory legislation that territorially restricted the rights of the Jewish population: decree No. 17,006 of December 23, 1791 confirmed the ban on Jews enrolling in the merchantry in the internal Russian cities and ports, extending the rights of citizenship and burgher status only to the Ekaterinoslav Viceroyalty and the Tauride region[90]. From the totality of such acts emerged the Pale of Settlement, running predominantly through colonized Ukrainian territories. January 1567 – December 1567 C1105 Establishment of the First Foothold on the Sunzha River (1567) The Regular Army of the Tsardom of Muscovy built the first military base on the lands of the Nokhchi with the support of regular troops. As historian E. N. Kusheva writes, "at the request of Temriuk, conveyed in Moscow in December 1566 by his son Matlov or Mazlov, to build a town 'on the Terek River at the mouth of the Siuiunchi River' 'for protection from his enemies,' in the spring of 1567 voevodas were sent from Moscow for the town-building work — Prince A. S. Babichev and P. Protasyev 'with many men, as well as ordnance, cannons, and arquebuses'"[56]. Historians A. S. Kulikov and V. A. Runov add that the voevodas were sent "with firearms and many men"[91]. Historian E. N. Kusheva states the fact that the base was built on the lands of the Nokhchi: "The Russian town... was built that same year"[56]. January 1741 – December 1748 C1135 Expansion of the Bribery System and Coercion of Highland Societies into Subjecthood (1741–1748) In the 1740s, the diplomatic and administrative apparatus of the Russian Empire scaled up the application of institutional colonial mechanisms to new territories of the Nokhchi. Historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov states that in 1741–1748 there was an «intensification of Russian-Chechen political and trade ties»[37]. The occupation administration expanded the practice of institutional bribery: the researcher records «the granting of Russian salaries to 4 Chechen princes and their uzdens»[37]. This process was accompanied by the legal subordination of new territories through the issuing of ultimatum demands. The author points out that, in response to the highlanders' requests for access to the plain, the empire gave its consent exclusively «on the condition that the highlanders take an oath of Russian allegiance»[37], which led to the formalization of oaths «by new societies of Chechnya, including mountain ones»[37]. Overall, as Akhmadov summarizes, «The process of formalizing relations with Russia at the official level covers the main districts of Chechnya», while, as rigid guarantees of obedience, «amanats (hostages) are handed over as a pledge of fidelity to the oath to the Russian authorities»[37]. September 1818 – December 1818 C1136 Exploitation of the village of Solzha (Sunzhenskaya) as a resource base and its punitive devastation for the armed resistance of the Nokhchi (1818) In 1818, after the fortress of Groznaya had already been built on seized land, the Russian Empire used the nearby village of Solzha (Sunzhenskaya) as a resource base for the garrison, and then devastated it when its inhabitants refused to hand over a fellow villager and took up arms. Historian D. A. Khozhaev records the devastation of Solzha (Sunzhenskaya), as a consequence of which "most of the peaceful surrounding auls fled to the mountains, and the flourishing riverbanks stood deserted for a long time thereafter"[14]. Imperial general Yermolov testifies in his "Notes" that he had previously ordered the troops to spare the village so that the fortress "could obtain from it all the necessary provisions." When soldiers were taking away from a villager an ox "which he called his own," the man shot at a soldier; the inhabitants refused to hand him over, declaring "that they would not give up the man who had shot at the soldier and would defend themselves if the troops came." When the chief of the corps staff "went himself with several companies," he "was met with gunfire." The families and property had been sent away in advance; the defense was held by the men alone. The troops were ordered to cut off the retreat — "to intercept the withdrawal in the forest" — but the defenders had pulled back earlier. Only after this did the troops enter the abandoned village, spending several days carting away from it "grain, forage, and timber fit for construction"[77]. August 1832 – September 1832 C1155 Extermination of 61 settlements of lowland Chechnya and mountainous Ichkeria by Rosen's troops, burning alive of the defenders of Germenchuk, and extortion of hostages from 80 villages (1832) In August 1832, corps commander Rosen led a ten-thousand-strong detachment on a campaign through Chechnya and Ichkeria — the mountainous southeastern part of Chechen land, into which imperial troops had never before penetrated. The historian D. A. Khozhaev wrote: "Rosen's ten-thousand-strong tsarist detachment invaded mountainous Ingushetia and Chechnya, ablaze with the fire of a people's war of liberation. Despite the steadfast resistance of the inhabitants of mountainous Chechnya, who courageously defended every inch of their land, the tsarist troops destroyed several dozen auls and hamlets"[14]. On August 22, after crossing the Argun River, the villages of Belgatoy and Dzhan-yurt were annihilated. On August 23, Germenchuk — the richest village of Chechnya, numbering 600 households — was taken by storm. Rosen reported to Minister of War Chernyshev: "more than 100 bodies were left by them in the village itself," while a group "numbering about 60 men, for the most part people sent by Kazi-Mulla to hearten the inhabitants of Germenchuk," led by Mullah Abdurakhman, "was cut off and surrounded by us in one large house"[35]. The surrounded men refused to surrender and, on the order of General Volkhovsky, were burned alive. The imperial historian Volkonsky, writing from Rosen's dispatches, admits: "Major General Volkhovsky ordered burning firewood and hay to be thrown into the chimneys. This had its effect... but the greater part, together with Mullah Abdurakhman, perished in the flames, continuing to sing verses of the Quran"[92]. For two days "the troops annihilated the houses of the village of Germenchuk"; on August 26, Shali was destroyed "with the exception of 11 households that had paid the fine and the tribute"[92]. Rosen himself acknowledged the pattern of the campaign: the villages, "having been unable to agree among themselves on the release of our prisoners, were punished by the annihilation of their dwellings and plowlands, for which purpose, on the 27th and 28th of this past August, Colonel Shumsky was dispatched... He annihilated Alkhan-yurt, Sala-yurt, Katar-yurt, Lyalsin-yurt, Nazari-yurt, Uzden-yurt, Uruzbey-yurt, and Khyzin-Erzo-yurt"[35]. Further annihilated were Anzeli-yurt and Chingaroy-yurt, the crops and dwellings of Avtury, Said-yurt, the plowlands and houses of Geldigen, Anto-yurt, Askhor-yurt, Taba-yurt, and Kudish-yurt; Mairtup was burned, and in Ichkeria — Shoni, Tsentoroy, Belgatoy, the hamlet of Khamer, Ali-yurt, Bey-Bulat-yurt, Bachin-yurt, Khelboyn-yurt; Benoy was burned[92][35][14]. Rosen summed up the results in his report to Chernyshev of September 27, 1832: "In all, up to the present time, more than 80 Chechen and Ichkerian villages have submitted, a quarter of which had never been in dependence on us; 30 of our prisoners, men and women, have been returned; tribute and fines in money and livestock have been paid... about 5 th. r. s. [five thousand rubles in silver]. 61 unsubmitted villages have been annihilated, many of which, after punishment, declared their submission and fulfilled all demands"[35]. December 1836 C1158 Extermination of the Inhabitants of Kishkeroy-Yurt by Pullo's Detachment: 76 Killed, 40 Captured, Village Burned with Its Stores (December 1836) In late December 1836, Colonel Pullo, in a covert winter raid, exterminated the Chechen village of Kishkeroy-Yurt (Keshkeroy) beyond the Gudermes river. Sanction had been given in advance: on 10 December 1836 Rozen reported to the Minister of War Chernyshev that he "had authorized Col. Pullo to act at once against the unsubmissive Chechen villages"[35]. The pretext for the punishment was declared to be hospitality: the village's inhabitants "had harbored the rebel Tashov-Hadji"[3]. Surrounded at dawn, the village was exterminated together with its people: those fleeing "were caught or exterminated", while "the inhabitants, having barricaded themselves in their houses with their families, were put to the bayonet"[3]; an attempt by Tashu-Hadji to come to the village's relief was repelled by artillery. Rozen himself summed up the outcome: "Upon the occupation of the village of Kishkeroy-Yurt, 76 bodies of the slain were found in it, and 40 souls of both sexes were taken captive; all the property of the inhabitants and the weapons taken from the slain fell to our troops"[3][93]. The village of 63 households, "with a considerable stock of grain and hay," was put to the torch in the middle of winter[3]. Dating: the dispatch is dated in the collection "9 January 1836," but the compilers placed it among documents from late 1836 to early 1837; the raid almost certainly took place on 27-31 December 1836, while the historian Sh. A. Gapurov dates it to December 1835[93]. September 1836 – November 1841 C1159 Failed Attempt at Religious Subjugation of the Highlanders to the Empire through the Hiring of the Preacher Taj ad-Din Mustafin (1836-1841) In 1836, the command of the Russian Caucasus Corps under General Rozen put forward a project to subordinate the entire Sunni clergy of the Caucasus to a "spiritual leader" appointed by the empire: for this role they hired the Kazan efendi (Muslim theologian) Taj ad-Din Mustafin and kept him on the treasury's payroll for about six years. The preacher's task was formulated openly: "to turn the highlanders onto the true path, subordinate them to the Russian government, and destroy or hand over Shamil to us alive" (Shamil - imam, leader of the Dagestani and Chechen highlanders' resistance to the Russian conquest)[4]. In Chechnya, Mustafin was sent to the Groznaya fortress to undermine the spiritual influence of Tashu-Hadji (sheikh, imam of Chechnya in 1834-1836, spiritual and military leader of the Chechen resistance). After a letter from Tashu-Hadji, who under threat of death forbade the preacher to appear on Chechen land, he acted only under military escort and did not show himself in the mountains. The project failed: Golovin, who succeeded Rozen, agreed to release the preacher based on a report by Minister of War Chernyshev of 13 November 1841 - "the teaching of Tajudin Effendi over the course of 6 years did not change the highlanders' attitude toward us in the slightest"[4]. January 1806 – December 1806 C1139 Failed Attempt to Bribe Nokhchi Elders with Economic Promises in Exchange for Allegiance (1806) The Russian Empire, through the commander-in-chief in the Caucasus, General Gudovich, addressed the Nokhchi elders with a proclamation offering economic benefits in exchange for accepting allegiance and ceasing armed resistance: for submission, the elders were promised access to salt, so that they «will be permitted to take from the local salt lakes by tickets, irrevocably, with payment of a very small fixed price», and the right «to drive cattle to this side of the Terek and freely use the vacant pasture lands»[57]. Allegiance was not accepted; by the end of the year the empire moved to preparing an armed invasion, which began in February of the following year. November 1917 – December 1917 C0071 Failure of the Political Seizure of the UNR in Kyiv (November – December 1917) The first attempt by Soviet Russia (the Russian Soviet Republic) to liquidate Ukraine's independence by hijacking power at the All-Ukrainian Congress of Soviets. The Bolshevik government (the Sovnarkom) planned to plant its delegates, artificially create a majority, and legally vote to transfer power to the Soviets under its control. The Ukrainian leadership recognized the threat and mobilized its supporters, leaving the aggressor's delegates in an absolute minority and thwarting the takeover[39][38]. January 1978 – December 1983 C0054 Financial Russification of Schools (1978–1983) The Soviet Union introduced a system of direct material incentives for assimilation: pursuant to the resolution of the USSR Council of Ministers of 13 October 1978 No. 835 "On measures for the further improvement of the study and teaching of the Russian language in the union republics," the Council of Ministers of the Ukrainian SSR, by its resolution of 2 November 1978 No. 518, introduced the study of Russian from the first grades of Ukrainian schools starting with the 1980/81 school year[94]; the all-Union conference "The Russian Language — the Language of Friendship and Cooperation of the Peoples of the USSR" (Tashkent, 22–24 May 1979) spelled out Russification measures down to kindergartens[49]; the resolution of the CPSU Central Committee and the USSR Council of Ministers of 26 May 1983 No. 473 "On additional measures for improving the study of the Russian language in general-education schools and other educational institutions of the union republics" and the resolution of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Ukraine and the Council of Ministers of the Ukrainian SSR of 10 June 1983 raised the salary rates of Russian-language teachers by 15 percent from 1984[49][95]. September 1994 – December 1996 C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Until August 1996 the occupiers bombed the towns and villages of Ichkeria, killed Chechen civilians and held them without charges in filtration camps. In the autumn of 1991, during the collapse of the USSR, Chechens overthrew the Soviet authorities installed in the Chechen-Ingush Republic, elected Dzhokhar Dudayev president and declared the independence of the Chechen Republic. Russia did not recognize it and was preparing a coup[96]. In the autumn of 1994, Russia armed the Provisional Council, a puppet opposition, to overthrow Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria. The Russian army handed the council 10 armored personnel carriers, 40 tanks and 6 combat helicopters with their crews. Officers of the FSK (a predecessor of today's FSB) recruited Russian tank crews for the council (see: "Staging a Coup")[96]. On 1 October the Moscow newspaper Kommersant wrote that the Russian Ministry of Defense "imperturbably rejects all accusations, stating that it has nothing to do with the events taking place in Chechnya"[97]. On 26 November the defenders of Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria, routed the Russian tank crews who were storming the city under the banner of the puppet opposition, and took dozens of Russian servicemen prisoner[96]. On 1 December Russian pilots destroyed all of Ichkeria's aircraft on the airfields[98]. On 9 December Russian President Yeltsin, by Decree No. 2166, ordered the government to use all means of the Russian state, including the army, against the Armed Forces of Ichkeria[99]. The Russian columns moved into Ichkeria a day before the talks that Russia had scheduled for 12 December 1994 (see: "Negotiations as Cover for an Attack")[96]. On the day of the invasion, Yeltsin promised in an address to the citizens of Russia: "I oblige all officials responsible for carrying out the measures to restore constitutional order in the Chechen Republic [this is what Russia called its war against independent Ichkeria] not to use violence against the civilian population and to take it under protection"[96]. Seven days after the address, from 18 December, Russian aircraft bombed the residential districts of Grozny. Deinekin, the commander of the Russian military aviation, said in an interview with the newspaper Moskovsky Komsomolets on 21 March 1995 that the pilots dropped unguided bombs on the city through the clouds when "the ground could not be seen at all"[96]. On 31 December the Russian army stormed Grozny. The defenders of the city routed the occupiers' columns. On 19 January 1995 Russian soldiers captured the ruins of the presidential palace and stormed the remaining districts of the city for another month and a half, until 6 March[96]. The Observer Mission of Russian human rights organizations interviewed 265 refugee families from Grozny. By the mission's estimate, from December 1994 to March 1995 the occupiers killed 25,000-29,000 civilians in the city (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[96]. At the end of March 1995 the Russian army captured Argun, Gudermes and Shali, towns to the east and southeast of Grozny[96]. On 7 April soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) and police officers stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria. On 8 April the occupiers searched the houses. Sadulla Yusupov, an elderly Chechen from Samashki, told Oleg Orlov of the Russian human rights organization Memorial on 13 April: "They were screaming in inhuman voices, swearing, cursing, shouting: 'Come out, you bitches!' and they went up to every house and fired"[100]. The Observer Mission published a list by name of 103 people whom the occupiers killed in the village in two days (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[100]. In June Russian troops captured Vedeno, Shatoy and Nozhai-Yurt, district centers in the mountains in the south (see: "Military Intervention")[96][101]. On 14 June 1995 fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria took about 1,500 hostages in Budyonnovsk, a Russian-controlled town to the northwest of the republic, and demanded an end to the war. Five days later Russia began talks with Ichkeria in Grozny[96]. On 3 July, while the talks were under way, Yeltsin, by Decree No. 663, allowed units of the Russian army "to be stationed on a permanent basis" in the republic[102]. On 30 July the delegations of Russia and Ichkeria signed an agreement on the cessation of hostilities. Russia undertook to withdraw its troops as the army of Ichkeria handed over its weapons[103][104]. Chechen fighters began to hand over weapons, but the Russian units did not leave the republic[96]. On 6 October unknown persons seriously wounded Romanov, the commander of the occupation troops, in Grozny. The next day the leadership of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria called the attempt a provocation aimed at wrecking the peace agreement[105]. On 9 October Yeltsin blamed the attempt on "supporters of [Dzhokhar] Dudayev" (the elected president of the Chechen Republic), and Russia resumed its offensive[96]. From February to May 1996 the Russian army stormed the settlement of Novogroznensky in the east of Ichkeria and the villages of Sernovodsk, Samashki and Bamut in the west (see: "Military Intervention")[96]. In the spring Russian commanders signed "Protocols on Peace and Accord" with villages[96]. A village undertook not to let fighters of the army of Ichkeria in, and Russia promised not to conduct combat operations in it[106]. Contrary to the agreements, Russian pilots bombed villages that had signed the protocols (see: "False Guarantees of Safety")[96]. On 21 April 1996 the Russian military struck a clearing near Gekhi-Chu, a village to the southwest of Grozny, with missiles and killed Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria (see: "Neutralization of the Opposition")[107][96]. On 27 May Chernomyrdin, the chairman of the Russian government, and Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the acting president of Ichkeria, signed a ceasefire agreement in Moscow. On 10 June in Nazran, a town in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, Russia undertook to withdraw its troops from the republic by the end of August 1996[96][108]. On 9 July, six days after Yeltsin won the Russian presidential election, the occupiers launched a new offensive (see: "Sham Ceasefire")[96]. Russian servicemen and police officers took detained Chechens without charges to filtration camps and to pits at military units (see: "Filtration Camp System"). According to a memorandum by Zlydenko, the deputy head of the prison service of the Russian MVD, from 11 December 1994 to 22 July 1995, 1,325 people passed through the camps in Grozny and in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia. The ministry released most of them as innocent and handed one hundred over to investigators (see: "Manufacturing Criminals"). The Russian MVD gave another 141 people to be exchanged for captured Russian servicemen (see: "Hostage-Taking")[96]. In September 1995 the UN Special Rapporteur on torture wrote to the Russian government that many inmates of the camps were systematically beaten to extract a confession of support for Dzhokhar Dudayev (see: "Torture and Abuse")[109]. According to statements by relatives collected by the Chechen society "Victims of War", 1,285 people were listed as missing in June 1996 (see: "Abduction of People")[96]. In January 1998 the UN Working Group on Enforced Disappearances reported that Russia had not established the fate of a single missing person about whom it had been asked[110]. Russian officials and military officers called the authorities of Ichkeria "bandits"[111][112], its army "bandit formations"[96] and "terrorists"[113][114], and Chechen civilians "bandits"[115] and "militants" (see: "Dehumanization")[116]. Generals of the occupation troops passed off the civilians they had killed as fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria (see: "Lies about Its Own Actions")[96]. Russia kept no count of the civilians it killed in Ichkeria[96]. On 3 September 1996 General Lebed, the secretary of the Russian Security Council, named the total number of those who died in the war at a press conference in Moscow: 80,000 people, "give or take 10,000"[117][118]. In its annual report for 1996 the international human rights organization Human Rights Watch estimated the number of civilians killed in Ichkeria since December 1994 at 18,500 to 80,000[119]. In a 1995 resolution the European Parliament condemned Russia's use of the army against Ichkeria[120]. In a 1995 declaration the Parliamentary Assembly of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe called Russia's war in Ichkeria a gross violation of international law[121]. On 25 January 1996 the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions wrote in a report to the UN Commission on Human Rights that the Russian military had killed thousands of citizens of Ichkeria, including when they deliberately and indiscriminately shelled residential districts with heavy weapons and bombed them[122]. Memorial concluded that Russian troops deliberately attacked civilians throughout the war and killed the most of them by bombing and shelling[96]. A Human Rights Watch report of January 1997 says that Russia systematically violated human rights and just as systematically failed to bring the perpetrators to justice[123]. On 12 March 1997 the deputies in Moscow, by Resolution No. 1199-II, declared an amnesty for crimes connected with the war in Ichkeria. Under this amnesty Russian prosecutors closed unfinished cases on the crimes of the occupiers[124][96]. On 29 September 1997 the Directorate of Military Courts of Russia replied to a request from Memorial that over the whole war the courts had convicted 18 Russian soldiers and officers, seven of them for murder (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")[96]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[101]. On 31 August 1996 General Lebed and Aslan Maskhadov, the chief of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, signed the peace agreements in Khasavyurt, a town in Russian-controlled Dagestan. In them Russia acknowledged "the inadmissibility of the use of armed force or the threat of its use in resolving disputed issues". The agreements state that the decision on the independence of Ichkeria was postponed for five years, until 31 December 2001 (see: "Sham Treaties")[125]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic. On 27 January 1997 the citizens of Ichkeria elected the president and parliament of the republic. Aslan Maskhadov became president[96]. Three years after the Khasavyurt agreements Russia attacked Ichkeria for the second time since 1994. On 21 September 1999 Russian pilots began bombing Grozny, and on 29 September the Russian army invaded the republic[96]. August 1914 – March 1917 C1189 First World War in Chechnya: removal of the "unreliable element" into the "Savage Division", extraordinary security and mobilization of strikers (1914-1917) In 1914-1917 the Russian Empire waged the world war both with Chechen hands and at Chechen expense: it carried off to the front, in the "Savage Division", those it considered dangerous, laid the upkeep of the Chechen regiment on the Chechen communities themselves, introduced "extraordinary security" with military courts and censorship in the Terek oblast, and sent striking workers into the army. By 1914 Chechnya had lived for half a century under "Military-Popular Administration" - the colonial regime of the Terek oblast (campaign C1170), without the land taken away for Cossack stanitsas (campaign C1171), and under collective punishments for the abrek phenomenon - the empire's name for a highlander's going into the mountains with a weapon after being declared an outlaw; for a single abrek the empire fined and deported entire villages (campaign C1175). The empire did not extend military conscription to the Chechens: a commission of the Caucasus Military District found it desirable to bring the Muslims of the Caucasus into service "...on the same grounds as the indigenous population of the Empire...", but to exempt the Chechens and the neighboring Kumyks temporarily, since the Chechens were not yet sufficiently "pacified"; the commander of the Caucasus Military District objected: "The exemption of the Chechens from military conscription, even a temporary one... will be as it were a recognition of privileges for the Chechens for their robberies and brigandage, and in the cause of the pacification of the North Caucasus will bring harm rather than benefit"[2]. The decision on the gradual introduction of conscription for the Muslim highlanders the empire took only in 1913, but by the start of the war the administration of the Terek oblast had not even begun to compile the family lists - a kind of household census - and did not dare to declare mobilization: it confined itself to recruiting volunteers[2]. The only mobilization the Russian Empire declared was not for the war but against a strike: in May 1916 it mobilized Grozny workers who held military service deferrals, for taking part in the strike[2]. January 1928 – December 1932 C0077 Forced Collectivization and Dekulakization (1928–1932) An assault on the traditional way of life of the Ukrainian village, which remained the principal bearer of national identity and economic independence. Under the slogans of socialist modernization, Moscow proclaimed the course of "the liquidation of the kulaks as a class": the secret Politburo resolution of January 30, 1930 ordered "to confiscate from the kulaks of these districts the means of production, livestock, farm and residential buildings, processing enterprises, fodder and seed stocks" and to send "60,000 to concentration camps and subject 150,000 kulaks to deportation to remote districts," of which for Ukraine - 15 thousand to concentration camps and 30–35 thousand to deportation[126]. Peasants who put up resistance were dispossessed en masse and deported to Siberia and the North[39]. January 1704 – December 1725 C0017 Forced Labor on Imperial Construction: The Ladoga Canal (1704–1725) The physical and economic exhaustion of the region through the transformation of the Cossack host into unpaid labor for imperial construction projects. The chief of these was the Ladoga Canal: Peter I handed the direction of the works to Münnich, while the digging itself "was carried out chiefly by the hands of Ukrainian Cossacks," and "on the construction works, tens of thousands of people perished from back-breaking labor, hunger and the harsh climate"[23]. In 1721 the acting hetman P. Polubotok "headed a 10,000-strong Cossack corps dispatched by order of Tsar Peter I to the construction of the Ladoga Canal"[127]. For the defiant there were also the Neva construction sites - as hard labor: captured Zaporozhians were "exiled to Sankt-Piterburkh to hard labor forever"[44]. January 1677 – January 1679 C1123 Forcible Mobilization of the Nokhchi for the Russo-Turkish War (1677–1679) The occupation administration of the Tsardom of Muscovy made mass use of the subordinated Nokhchi (the Okochans) as a military resource in conflicts with the Ottoman Empire on distant fronts. In 1678, the Kabardian prince Kaspulat Mutsalovich Cherkassky received a tsarist charter in which the historian I. Kh. Tkhamokova records a reward «for his «many services», for having taken part in the Crimean and Chyhyryn campaigns»[63]. The registers of archival documents for 1678 record a dispatch from the Chuhuiv voivode Ivan Rykhtarov to the Razriad Prikaz «on the march of the regiment of Prince Kaspulat Mutsalovich Cherkassky to Chuhuiv»[79]. The exploitation of military potential continued the following year as well: in 1679, Tsar Fedor Alekseevich issued a decree to the Ambassadorial Prikaz on sending Prince Kaspulat Mutsalovich Cherkassky a charter «on his regiment's performance of guard duty in the vicinity of Chuhuiv and Kharkiv»[79], while a dispatch from Kaspulat Cherkassky himself to the Ambassadorial Prikaz for the same year states «on the arrival of his regiment at Valuyki»[79]. November 1838 – November 1840 C1164 Forcing Chechnya into submission after the fall of Akhulgo and suppression of the general uprising of 1840 (1838-1840) In November 1838 general Golovin, commander of the Separate Caucasus Corps (the head of the imperial troops and administration in the Caucasus), secretly ordered the assassination of Shamil (Shamil - the imam, leader of the resistance of the highlanders of Dagestan and Chechnya to the Russian conquest), and in May 1839 the troops of general Grabbe, commander of the troops of the Caucasus Line (the chain of imperial fortifications on the land of the Nokhchi), invaded Ichkeria (mountainous south-eastern Chechnya). After the rout of Akhulgo (Shamil's mountain residence in Dagestan, August 1839) the empire considered the resistance finished off and pressed Chechnya with winter expeditions - armed marches for money, weapons and people through auls already held since 1836 by the system of amanats, tribute and pristavs (campaign C1163). Muhammad-Tahir al-Qarakhi, Shamil's chronicler, named the reason why the Chechens called for Shamil: "The reason for this was that even before Shamil's coming the Russians had taken from these lower Chechens, as a tax, one ruble (kurush) from every house and one gun from every ten houses"[41]. In February-March 1840 Chechnya rose - the historian D. A. Khozhaev writes: "All of lowland Chechnya was stirring. On the lowland territory of Chechnya occupied by the tsarist colonial troops and subordinated to the Chechen pristav, preparation of an armed uprising began"[14]. The empire answered with punitive marches throughout 1840: the troops of general Galafeyev, who had taken over the left flank of the Caucasus Line, and of general Grabbe burned dozens of auls of Lesser and Greater Chechnya, destroyed crops and stores before winter, and dictated to the insurgents the "Conditions prescribed to submitting highlanders"[3] - hostages, an oath, fines, surrender of weapons. The calculation of the campaign was admitted by general Golovin himself - in a memorandum of 26 April 1841 on the results of the previous year's expedition: "In vain did we expect that after the destruction, in last year's expedition, of the highlanders' food stores, their villages and various property, hunger, cold and extreme poverty would shake the fierce power of the instigator" ("instigator" - the imperial label for Shamil)[4]. The result of the year was summed up by the imperial historian Yurov: "The results of the exhausting expeditions of 1840 on the left flank of the Caucasus line fell far short of the expectations of His Majesty the Emperor and the high command; even more - we did not manage to improve the ominous situation one whit, and our prestige fell in this part of the region"[128]. January 1857 – August 1859 C1168 Forest clearings and famine: Yevdokimov's conquest of Chechnya (1857-1859) In 1857-1859 the empire completed its conquest of Chechnya: forest clearings (prosekas) cut the country into pieces, auls and food stores were burned, exhausted societies were forced into capitulation one after another, and those who surrendered were herded down to the plain under surveillance. The method was formulated by General Yevdokimov himself, who commanded the Chechen Detachment - in a report to Minister of War Sukhozanet of 25 March 1857 he explained the purpose of the clearing: it "took away from the unsubmissive their broad fields, the places of their crops, and, having cut apart, so to speak, the unsubmissive population that nested in forests hitherto inaccessible, put it under the necessity of seeking salvation either by flight into the mountains or by coming out to us onto the glades"[129]. The imperial historian Volkonsky distilled the formula of the period: "wherever our foot steps – impassable forests are cut through, clearings are made... redoubts and fortifications are laid down: nature is overpowered – the Caucasus surrenders"[130]. What subordination would bring, imam Shamil (leader of the resistance of the highlanders of Dagestan and Chechnya to the Russian conquest) told the Chechens at a gathering in Shali in the autumn of 1858 - the speech was written down by his companion and chronicler Hadji-Ali: "they will take away your weapons and will not allow you even to have a knife, All your honored men they will exile to Siberia, and after that you will be like muzhiks"[131]. The condition of the country was conveyed to the imam in a letter by Talkhig Shalinsky, naib of Greater Chechnya: "Chechnya is burning, imam, come put it out"[14]. January 1864 – December 1876 C0063 Formation of the Ideology of Great-Power Chauvinism (1864–1876) Against the backdrop of large-scale territorial conquests, the empire conceptualizes its superiority over the colonized peoples. The ideologue Katkov formulates: "to recognize some element as a distinct nation does not mean granting it freedom, but giving it power, endowing it with binding force. In the recognition of a nation the question of power, of government, of the state is decided"[132] – the recognition of Ukrainians as a nation was ruled out as a question of power. January 1588 – January 1623 C1110 Founding and Fortification of the Terek Town (1588–1623) The occupation administration of the Tsardom of Muscovy established a new military base at the mouth of the Terek River to control the adjacent territories, including the lands of the Nokhchi. Historian E. N. Kusheva writes that the base "was built in 1588–1589... by Mikhailo Burtsev and Kelar Protasyev... the main force of its garrison consisted of streltsy armed with 'fire combat' — pishchal firearms"[56]. The base's infrastructure was systematically expanded: historians A. S. Kulikov and V. A. Runov note that "by the beginning of the 17th century... the Terek fortified town had turned into a rather powerful fortress. Its artillery numbered 40 large guns, and its garrison — more than a thousand streltsy and Cossacks"[91]. To hold its positions, the administration brought in additional military personnel: historian I. Kh. Tkhamokova notes that "in 1589, soon after the town was built, 800 streltsy and Cossacks were to be sent there from Astrakhan, but the Astrakhan voivode sent only 600 men"[63]. A permanent military contingent on state provision was entrenched in this territory: historian I. Kh. Tkhamokova cites a tsar's decree according to which "in 1623, 'upon the petition of the Terek and Greben Cossacks,' a tsar's decree was sent to the Terek ordering the payment of salaries to 30 atamans and 470 rank-and-file Cossacks"[63]. February 2022 – May 2026 C0103 Full-Scale Invasion (from February 24, 2022) On 24 February 2022, the Russian Federation launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine with its regular army from several directions at once - from the north through Belarus towards Kyiv, from the east, and from the south out of Crimea - unleashing the largest war in Europe since the Second World War. The aim of the campaign is the complete destruction of Ukrainian statehood and the erasure of Ukrainian identity. The UN commission recorded the opening this way: "On the same day, Russian troops crossed various border points into Ukraine, including through Belarus, and launched attacks by land, air and sea"[133]. The commission qualifies what it established as follows: the violations "amount to war crimes and include wilful killings, attacks on civilians, unlawful confinement, torture, rape and the forced transfer and deportation of children"[133]. On the character of the strikes the commission writes: they were carried out "with an apparent disregard for civilian harm and suffering"[133]. The OSCE mission puts its finding this way: in the Russian forces' conduct of hostilities there are "clear patterns of IHL violations"; and the mission adds: had they respected "their IHL obligations in terms of distinction, proportionality and precautions in attack," civilian casualties would have been far lower[134]. The campaign is accompanied by the destruction of entire cities (urbicide), ecocide, and a systematic policy of assimilation in the occupied territories[135]. As of May 2026, about 20% of Ukraine's territory remains under occupation[136]. This is the head campaign of the war. Individual sieges, occupation regimes, episodes of mass killing, and cross-cutting policies are carried in campaigns of their own - from the siege of Mariupol and the Bucha massacre to the deportation of children, the filtration system, and the war on the power grid. January 2006 – January 2009 C0097 Gas Wars and Energy Blackmail (2006–2009) The use of the state monopoly Gazprom as a political weapon against Kyiv's independent course. Gas supplies were cut off at the height of winter: "at 10.00am Moscow time on January 1, 2006, Gazprom cut off gas supplies to Ukraine"[137], and three years later "Russian exports to Ukraine were cut off on 1 January. Exports to 16 EU member states and Moldova were drastically reduced on 6 January and cut completely from 7 January"[138]. Supplies ran through opaque intermediaries (RosUkrEnergo), whose use "was long criticized in European government circles and by corporate governance bodies"[138], while RUE's co-owner Dmytro Firtash admitted to the US ambassador that "he needed Mogilevich's approval to get into business in the first place"[139]. January 2020 – February 2022 C0102 Ideological Preparation for the Full-Scale Invasion (2020–2021) A period of intensive ideological conditioning of Russian society and the political elite to justify the complete destruction of Ukrainian statehood. The head of the Russian state published a programmatic article declaring that "Russians and Ukrainians are one people, a single whole," and wrote of the Bolsheviks that "the Bolsheviks' actions in severing from Russia its historical territories are not considered a criminal act"[140]. Deputy Security Council chairman D. Medvedev (Kommersant, 11 October 2021) declared negotiations with Kyiv pointless: "it is pointless for us to deal with vassals. One must do business with the suzerain"[141]. In parallel came the indoctrination of the army and military blackmail through the massing of troops near the borders under the guise of exercises[135]. January 1721 – December 1799 C1108 Imposition of an Image of Backwardness and the “Civilizing” Mission (1721–1800s) In the 18th century, the governmental apparatus of the Russian Empire began employing Enlightenment ideas and the construction of historical myths to ideologically justify the absorption of territories. Historian Michael Khodarkovsky states that by the mid-18th century officials had come to perceive their advance as a mission preordained by destiny to "bring both Christianity and civilization to the ‘wild and uncivilized’ peoples along its borders"[52]. The local population was deliberately assigned an image of backwardness: the researcher points out that in the administration’s documents the Highlanders were described as "inconstant and treacherous," and their actions were explained by references to their "predatory craft, to which they are predisposed by their very nature and upbringing"[142]. In parallel, fictitious grounds for control were being constructed: the author records that in 1748 and the 1770s the Collegium of Foreign Affairs fabricated reports claiming that the Indigenous population of the Caucasus had allegedly professed Christianity in the past, in order to contest the claims of other powers and "legitimize its efforts at their ‘re-Christianization’"[142]. Building on this foundation, in 1784 the imperial governors asserted that, with the dispatch of missionaries, they would be able to spread their influence and shed "the light of divine bliss among all the peoples scattered in the mountains"[142]. January 1890 – December 1900 C0066 Industrial Colonization and Resource Exploitation of the South (1890) At the end of the 19th century, the Russian Empire turns the Ukrainian lands into a raw-materials colony, exploiting the resources of the Donbas and deliberately importing labor: "42 percent of the 425,413 workers counted in the census were born outside Ukraine," and "in 1892, 80 percent of the workforce at the mines and plants of Yuzivka… had arrived from the Moscow region"[143]. April 1986 – December 1986 C0090 Information Blockade Around the Chornobyl Disaster (1986) The ultimate manifestation of the colonial administration's disregard for the lives of the local population. After the explosion at the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant, the union center concealed the scale of the radiation threat: "the concealment of information about the catastrophe from the public was initiated by the country's leadership," and "the maps of radioactive contamination of lands remained classified until 1990"[144]. People were deprived of the right to protection - "the population was not warned of the danger and was given no recommendations," and, "despite the fact that in Kyiv the radiation dose rate increased more than a hundredfold, neither the May Day demonstration nor the Peace Cycling Race was cancelled"[144][145]. June 1919 – March 1921 C0075 Institutional Absorption through a "Military-Political Union" (1919–1921) The final destruction of Ukrainian sovereignty through the imposition of treaties on a so-called military-political union. While formally preserving the status of an independent republic, the leadership of the RSFSR de facto brought the key Ukrainian agencies — military, financial, economic, and transport — under its direct control. On March 18, 1921, Soviet Russia and Soviet Ukraine signed the Treaty of Riga with Poland and divided the Ukrainian lands. Poland, the ally of the Ukrainian People's Republic (UNR) under the Treaty of Warsaw, signed peace with Soviet Ukraine, recognizing it as a state[24][39][38]. January 1830 – December 1830 C1151 Instrumentalization of a Natural Disaster by the Colonizers: Paskevich and Rosen Declare the Earthquake "God's Punishment of the Nokhchi People for Disobedience to the Empire" (1830) At the end of February 1830, the Caucasus was struck by a devastating earthquake that lasted more than a month and caused panic among the mountain peoples. The empire turned the disaster into a weapon of indoctrination and delivered this lie to the people. The historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov wrote: "supporters of the Russian orientation claimed that the earthquake had been caused by the wrath of Allah over the attempt at an armed uprising"[2]. The mechanics of the indoctrination are acknowledged by the colonizers themselves. The imperial historian Volkonsky wrote: "the commander-in-chief accordingly ordered General Rosen 4th to spread entirely opposite rumors among the people, namely, that the earthquake had been sent down by God upon the mountain peoples for their ill-intentioned acts against the Russian government, and hoped by this means to tear his followers away from Kazi-Mulla"[92]. The imperial historian Potto admits that the order was carried out: General Rosen 4th, who commanded the troops on the left flank of the Caucasus Line (the eastern section of the empire's fortified frontier along the Terek and the Sunzha), "resorted to proclamations in which he strove to assure the people that the earthquake had been sent down upon them as punishment for their treason and ill-intentioned acts against the Russian government"[58]. January 1700 – October 1708 C0011 Integration Reforms of Peter I and the Great Northern War (1700–1708) Systematic exploitation of the Hetmanate's potential in a grueling war combined with the simultaneous launch of administrative absorption (the reforms of 1707). The Cossacks dispatched to distant fronts were «wearied, destitute, left horseless, and ruined by year-round military service». Orlyk relayed the starshyna's account of the plans to recut the autonomy: the empire was preparing «to convert the Cossacks into a regular army... to break the military rights and liberties» and «to take the Little Russian towns into its own domain»[44]. January 1817 – December 1828 C0041 Introduction of Military Settlements and Liquidation of the Danubian Sich (1817–1828) A campaign to turn the free population into rightless military settlers. "The trigger was the order abolishing the Buh Cossack Host and turning the Cossacks into military settlers"[32] – the Buh Cossacks' uprising of 1817 was brutally suppressed. There were two acts, on opposite sides of the uprising: the nominal decree of April 17, 1817 transferred the Buh Host's district "into direct military administration" (PSZRI, vol. XXXIV, no. 26,802) - this was the trigger; the decree of October 8, 1817 (no. 27,081), issued after the suppression, formalized the liquidation: "the name of the Buh Cossack Host is abolished"[146]. Later, kish otaman Hladky with part of the Danubian Cossacks "on May 30 (18), 1828 crossed the Kiliya mouth of the Danube, entered the port of Izmail, and joined the Russian army"[147] – this was the end of the last free host: the Danubian Sich "existed from the last quarter of the 18th century until 1828"[147]. January 1687 C0007 Kolomak Articles (1687) Another stage of the assault on autonomy: a treaty with Moscow that eliminated independent diplomacy ("a hetman shall not be elected... nor shall they write anything to anyone on their own behalf"), prohibited declaring one's own subjecthood, and demanded: "to unite the Little Russian people with the Great Russian people by all measures and means... through marriage"[44]. January 1860 – March 1917 C1171 Land plunder: the colonial repartition of land, land hunger and Cossack colonization of the Terek oblast (1860-1917) In 1860-1917 the empire recut the land of Chechnya in favor of the treasury, the Cossack host and loyal notables. The conquest came with a written promise. In January 1859, advancing on Vedeno, the command circulated among the Chechens, in Arabic and Russian, a "Proclamation to the Chechen People": "I declare to you in the name of the Sovereign Emperor, 1) that the Russian government grants you complete freedom to practice forever the faith of your fathers; 2) that you will never be called up as soldiers and will not be turned into Cossacks... 5) that the rights of each of you to the property belonging to you will be inviolable. Your lands, which you own or with which you have been allotted by the Russian authorities, will be confirmed to you by deeds and plans in inalienable possession..."; the document was signed by Baryatinsky, commander-in-chief of the Caucasus Army and viceroy[14]. The land clause of the promise, as historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov render it, ran: "All the lands and forests on the plain where the Chechen people lived before the disturbance of 1839 will be given over to you for eternal use, excepting those occupied by fortifications... but neither Cossack stanitsas nor Chechen auls are to be settled on them"[2]. Historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova writes: "The Chechens treasured and kept this proclamation as the apple of their eye and always appealed to it"[16]. It came out the other way round: historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov draw the balance for lowland and piedmont Chechnya - "100% of the forests (259 thousand desiatinas) and 300 thousand desiatinas out of the 643 thousand desiatinas of the country's agricultural zone were taken away in favor of the treasury, the army and the Cossack host. All this cannot but be considered typical colonial plunder" (a desiatina is a little over a hectare)[2]. The outcome for the people was named from the Duma tribune by deputy Maslov: "You cannot imagine how negligible the landholdings of the Chechens are, especially in the mountains – one tenth, one fifth, a quarter, a third of a desiatina…"[16]. December 1922 – January 1924 C0076 Legal Absorption through the Creation of the USSR (1922–1924) Formal consolidation of the seizure of Ukraine by dragging it into the so-called Union of SSRs. The unification of equal republics with the right of free secession was declared, but in practice the union treaty (December 1922) and the Constitution of the USSR (1924) became instruments of rigid centralization. The Ukrainian SSR was definitively stripped of control over foreign policy, the army, foreign trade, transport, and communications — all these spheres passed to the jurisdiction of union-level people's commissariats in Moscow[39][38]. January 1699 – December 1699 C0026 Liquidation of the Cossacks in Right-Bank Ukraine (1699) The destruction of the Cossack regimental order on the Right Bank by a decision of the Polish Sejm of 1699, on lands that Moscow and Warsaw had divided along the Dnipro by the "Eternal Peace" of 1686.
