Colonel Palii "did not accept the decisions of the general Sejm of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth of 1699 banning the Cossacks on the Right Bank" and "contrary to the terms of the 'Eternal Peace' of 1686 pursued a policy of uniting the Right Bank and the Left Bank"[127]. January 1839 – December 1839 C0059 Liquidation of the Greek Catholic Church (1839) Institutional seizure and spiritual unification: the empire liquidates the independent Uniate church on the Right Bank, transferring the flock and property under the control of the state church. The mechanism is recorded in the fates of monasteries: "in connection with the tsarist regime's liquidation of the Union in this region (1839), the monastery was closed, and its buildings destroyed"[24]; "By the mid-19th century all monasteries of the Basilian order on the territory of the Russian Empire had been liquidated"[148]. November 1764 – December 1764 C0030 Liquidation of the Institution of the Hetmancy and the Second Little Russian Collegium (1764) The final abolition of political autonomy. Catherine II forced hetman Rozumovsky to renounce his office and by the decree of November 10, 1764 established an occupation administration: "we command our Senate, for the proper governance of Little Russia, to establish there a Little Russian Collegium, presided over by our general, Count Rumyantsev"[149]. The program had been set in advance in a secret instruction: "so that they become Russified and cease looking to the forest like wolves"[150]. January 1709 – May 1709 C0014 Liquidation of the Zaporozhian Sich (1709) A military operation of Muscovite troops to completely destroy the Zaporozhian (Chortomlyk) Sich as an autonomous military center in revenge for its support of Charles XII: "Having lost the proxy battle for Zaporizhzhia, Peter decided to follow the path of Baturyn — to destroy the Sich"[9]. Contemporaries recorded the empire's goal directly – Orlyk wrote that Moscow intended "to eradicate the Zaporozhian Host of the Lower Dnipro and to efface its very name forever"[44]. March 1991 C0093 Manipulative Referendum on the Preservation of the USSR (March 1991) Moscow's attempt to legitimize the preservation of a disintegrating empire. The all-Union ballot contained the question: "Do you consider necessary the preservation of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics as a renewed federation of equal sovereign republics in which the rights and freedoms of a person of any nationality will be fully guaranteed"[151]. The Verkhovna Rada of the Ukrainian SSR added its own question – on Ukraine's membership in the Union "on the basis of the Declaration of State Sovereignty of Ukraine"[152], which is what made the outcome ambiguous. The ambiguous wording was approved by the USSR Supreme Soviet in a resolution signed by its chairman Lukyanov[151]. July 1825 C1147 Mass Killing of Elders Summoned to a Demonstrative Execution at Gerzel-Aul (1825) In July 1825, at the height of Beibulat Taimiev’s uprising, the Russian Empire exterminated elders summoned under the pretext of an inquiry. The historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that after the insurgents’ five-day siege of the Gerzel-Aul fortification, "the tsarist generals decided to stage a demonstrative execution to intimidate the highlanders": summoned to the fortification were "318 respected men of the Aksai (Kumyk and Chechen) villages," whom General Lisanevich, "calling out those assembled one by one, threatened in the Kumyk language and subjected to insults"[14]. When General Grekov attempted to "inflict a physical insult" on the Chechen mullah Uchar-Hadji from the village of Mairtup, the latter killed Grekov with a dagger and mortally wounded Lisanevich, after which, "upon Lisanevich’s command ‘Stab them!’, the mass extermination by the soldiers of all the unarmed highlanders present in the fortification began"[14]. The imperial historian Potto confirms that both generals "fell at the hand of a fanatic," after which "the mutiny flared up again with redoubled force"[76]. October 1708 – November 1708 C0012 Mazepa's Defection to Sweden and the Baturyn Massacre (1708) In response to the autonomy's attempt to break vassalage, the regular Muscovite army destroyed the hetman's capital, Baturyn. Peter ordered: "and Baturyn, as a sign to the traitors (since they resisted), burn down entirely as an example to others"[9]. The reprisal was accompanied by terror against the civilian population: "Funck slaughtered more than a thousand people in the small town of Terey (Tereyska sloboda) and burned the town down"[153], and in total "about 15 thousand Ukrainians died in the Baturyn tragedy, including all the women and children"[9]. The massacre ran in parallel with propaganda: "Tsarist letters were circulated among the people claiming that Mazepa had gone over to the Swedes in order to hand Ukraine to Poland, to introduce the Union in Ukraine and eradicate the pious faith; that he was an apostate, a secret Catholic"[154]. April 1783 – December 1783 C0035 Military Annexation of the Crimean Khanate (1783) The seizure of the Crimean Khanate and its forcible incorporation into the Russian Empire: "WE have resolved to take under OUR dominion the Crimean peninsula, the island of Taman, and the entire Kuban side"[155]. With regard to Ukraine, the annexation was secured through the forced mobilization of Cossacks as a military resource, the colonization of the adjacent southern steppes to create a loyal rear, and the erasure of Cossack toponyms: the lands of the destroyed Sich were assigned by Catherine II's manifesto of 3 August 1775 "as convenient to the Novorossiysk Governorate"[156]. For Crimea this meant the liquidation of the state and its ruling dynasty: "in the spring of 1782 Khan Shahin Girey was forced to flee under Russian protection"[157], the manifesto on the taking of Crimea was signed by Catherine II on April 8, 1783 (PSZRI, coll. 1, vol. XXI, no. 15,108)[26], and the khan was exiled to Kaluga; the indigenous population was being squeezed out in waves of emigration - "if before 1787 only 8 thousand had emigrated, by 1792 it was already tens of thousands"[157]. May 1775 – August 1775 C0033 Military Liquidation of the Zaporozhian Sich (1775) The military encirclement and destruction of the Zaporozhian Sich immediately after a joint war. Catherine II's manifesto of 3 August 1775 (PSZRI, coll. 1, vol. XX, no. 14,354) declared: "the Zaporozhian Sich has been utterly destroyed, with the extirpation for the future of the very name of the Zaporozhian Cossacks"[156][158]. The last kish otaman, Kalnyshevsky, "was arrested and sent to the prison of the Solovetsky monastery"[27], where he spent more than 25 years. Hrushevsky describes the mechanics of the treachery: the government "went about the affair slowly, in secret, to catch the Zaporozhians entirely unprepared," and general Tekeli "entered the Zaporozhian lands as a good friend" - then suddenly laid siege to the Sich. The Zaporozhians were even faulted for their own husbandry: they "were establishing their own tillage and thereby severing their dependence on the Russian state"[154]. January 1858 – December 1872 C1022 Muhajirism: the expulsion of Chechens to the Ottoman Empire, the ban on return, and population replacement (1858-1872) In 1858-1872 the empire pushed the Chechens out into the Ottoman Empire and kept the road back closed. Muhajirism comes from the Arabic "muhajir," a migrant who leaves for the sake of faith: that is what those who left were called, and the same name became attached to the whole wave of expulsion. In the summer of 1865 more than 23 thousand people left Chechnya, a fifth of the Chechen people; they left in waves that the imperial chancellery counted as "parties" - there were 28 of them; the operation was led by General Kundukhov, former head of the Chechen okrug, whom the imperial authorities tasked with the expulsion[14][2]. The Chechen expulsion was part of a wider operation: according to official data, in 1858-1865 a total of 493,194 people were expelled from the North Caucasus, of whom 443,082 were members of the Adyghe peoples and Abkhazians[159]. In the west of the Caucasus the instrument was war; in the east - economic strangulation and covert agitation. The goal was formulated in the correspondence of the command of the Caucasus Army on ending the war in the Western Caucasus: "...the question of when the war will end, under the present circumstances, comes down to this – how soon we will manage to send off to Turkey the population hostile to us"[2]. The chief of staff of the Caucasus Corps, Milyutin, admitted the nature of the policy in writing as early as 1857: "our duties to the human race require that we take measures in advance to secure the existence even of the tribes hostile to us, whom we are forcing out of their lands out of state necessity"[16]. A Chechen folk song kept the tally of the culprits: "The Muslim tsar calls us to him, / The Russian tsar begs us to stay! / Without fire or wind Chechnya burst into flame: / The fire was Alkhasov Musa, / The whirlwind's blast was Osmanov Sadulla... / Here it is, the day of the Last Judgement!"[16]. Both are named in the Chechen manner, and both were organizers of the expulsion: Alkhasov Musa is that same General Kundukhov, and Osmanov Sadulla was his assistant, the naib of Lesser Chechnya (a naib is an administrator of a district installed by the authorities). The historian D. A. Khozhayev places the expulsion in the same line as the deportation of 1944: "The genocide against the Chechen people was carried out in the 19th century, during the Caucasus War and after it, during the expulsion to Turkey"[14]. September 1658 – October 1659 C0003 Muscovite–Ukrainian War (1658–1659) Open military aggression by the Tsardom of Muscovy in response to the hetman's attempt to break vassalage. It was accompanied by the fomenting of civil war through sponsorship of the opposition – the revolt of Pushkar and Barabash against Vyhovsky[24] – and by a direct invasion of the Muscovite army, which suffered catastrophic losses at Konotop: "The flower of the Muscovite cavalry, which had made the fortunate campaigns of '54 and '55, perished in a single day"[160]. March 1820 – September 1820 C1145 Night Attack on the Aul of Topli, Burning of Germenchuk, and Coercion of the Nokhchi to Fell Their Own Forests (1820) In the spring of 1820, General Yermolov and Grekov, commander of the left flank, moved troops to cut a road-clearing through the forests of the Nokhchi to the aul of Germenchuk, killing inhabitants and burning auls along the way, while rounding up the neighboring villages to fell this clearing through their own forest. The imperial historian Potto describes how, on the night of March 6, 1820, Grekov’s detachment secretly crossed the Sunzha and suddenly attacked the sleeping aul of Topli: the Grebensky Cossack regiment "burst without resistance into the aul, still sunk in deep sleep," the Cossacks "rushed through the saklias with daggers," and "part of the inhabitants were slaughtered before they could rise from their beds; the others begged for mercy"[76]. Potto then writes that Grekov "gathered the elders of the surrounding villages and ordered them to send workers with axes at once for the felling," and "the smoldering ruins of the village… compelled the Chechens to obey" — the Nokhchi, rounded up under threat of the same reprisal, cut the clearing through their own "dense forest"[76]. Three days later the clearing was ready, and the troops "advanced, burned Germenchug, and drew back to Groznaya," although the aul stood empty and its inhabitants had already left[76]. Yermolov himself, in an instruction to Grekov of March 15, 1820, confirms and sanctions this design of strangulation: "only the squeezing of the Chechens in their essential needs can make plain to them the advantage of submission, and I long ago authorized you to employ every possible means to that end," noting that Grekov had "opened a road even onto the plain"[83]. August 1937 – December 1939 C0080 NKVD National Operations and Institutional Russification (1937–1939) The total purge of ethnic minorities (Poles, Germans, Greeks, Bulgarians) during the Great Terror through targeted national orders of the NKVD. In parallel, in 1938, Moscow officially liquidated every single national district and minority school - by resolutions of the Orgburo of the Central Committee of the VKP(b) of 24 January 1938[161][162] - and by the resolution of the Central Committee of the VKP(b) and the USSR Council of People's Commissars of 13 March 1938 No. 324 made the study of the Russian language compulsory[163]; Kyiv executed the decision by the resolution of the Politburo of the Central Committee of the KP(b)U of 10 April 1938[164], returning to overtly imperial practices of assimilation[165][166]. September 1991 – November 1991 C1183 Non-Recognition and the Attempted Military Invasion: Moscow's Response to the Independence of the Chechen Republic (September-November 1991) After their return from exile the Chechens were ruled for three decades by Russians sent from Moscow; only on 1 July 1989 did an assembly of the region's occupation administration for the first time reject Moscow's candidate and choose a Chechen, Zavgaev, as head of the region[2]. By the autumn of 1991 the USSR was falling apart: the union republics were declaring independence one after another. On 18 August the USSR vice-president Yanaev, together with the heads of the KGB (predecessor of today's FSB), the army and the police, tried to keep the union in Moscow's hands by force: they announced that the nominal head of the USSR, Gorbachev, could not govern "for reasons of health", declared a state of emergency and brought tanks into Moscow, but gave up after three days[42]. Zavgaev, the head of Chechnya installed under the USSR, backed those who wanted to preserve the USSR, and lost: the Chechens came out to non-stop rallies and on 6 September forced his Supreme Soviet to dissolve itself[167]. That same autumn the Chechens elected their own president, Dzhokhar Dudaev, and declared independence from Russia, while the coloniser in the person of the RSFSR went in two months from sending a delegation "to explain the policy" to an attempt to impose a state of emergency on the whole territory of Chechen-Ingushetia with internal troops, but was forced to retreat. On 10 September 1991 the RSFSR president Yeltsin sent to Grozny a delegation headed by state secretary Burbulis and instructed it "to explain the policy of the Russian Federation and of the President of the RSFSR"[168]. On 14 September Khasbulatov, a Chechen from the Moscow leadership, then acting head of parliament, flew to Grozny; on 15 September he personally chaired the last session of the Supreme Soviet of Chechen-Ingushetia, and under pressure from Khasbulatov and from Dzhokhar Dudaev's supporters the deputies dismissed Zavgaev, dissolved themselves and chose from their own ranks a Provisional Supreme Council of 32 members headed by Khusein Akhmadov to hold new elections[169]. Moscow tried to take this council for itself: on 25 September five of its members headed by the council's deputy chairman Chernyi, Khasbulatov's man, came out against Dzhokhar Dudaev's congress; on 26 September Khasbulatov himself threatened by telegram not to recognise the elections, and on 5 October thirteen of the council's thirty-two members, backed by the local KGB, tried to remove Khusein Akhmadov. In response Dzhokhar Dudaev's supporters blocked the central square of Grozny, arrested the republic's procurator and occupied the buildings of the KGB and of the government; Moscow's people in the council, as general Sokolov reported to his command, had no "practical power" left[169][167]. On 6 October the RSFSR vice-president Rutskoi flew to Grozny with the minister of internal affairs and the chairman of the KGB of the RSFSR, but achieved nothing[169], and on 8 October the Moscow leadership, over Khasbulatov's signature, recognised as lawful in Chechnya only the group of procurator Bakhmadov - the man who, according to Sokolov's report, had been "appointed by the Chairman of the Supreme Soviet of the RSFSR Khasbulatov"[167] - and demanded that "the illegal armed formations [this is what the coloniser called the fighters for independence from Russia] surrender their weapons by 24:00 on 10 October 1991"[170]. On 24 October Moscow announced, before any vote had taken place, that the elections set for 27 October "have no legal basis and their results cannot be recognised as lawful"[171]. On 27 October the Chechens elected Dzhokhar Dudaev president, and on 1 November he signed a decree: "to proclaim the state sovereignty of the Chechen Republic from 1 November 1991"[172]. On 2 November Moscow declared the elections "unlawful, and the acts adopted by them not subject to execution"[173]. On 7 November Yeltsin, by decree No. 178, imposed a state of emergency on the whole territory of Chechen-Ingushetia: a curfew, a ban on rallies and strikes, the seizure of weapons, the cancellation of the elections, a Provisional Administration appointed from Moscow, and "the expulsion of violators of public order who are not residents of the given locality... beyond the territory of the Chechen-Ingush Republic at their own expense"[174]. On 8 November the parliament of the Chechen Republic declared the decree unlawful and demanded the withdrawal of the troops within 24 hours[175]. The National Guard of Chechnya and unarmed townspeople blockaded the airlifted internal troops (predecessors of today's Rosgvardiya) at the Khankala airfield near Grozny and in the building of the ministry of internal affairs. The nominal head of the USSR, Gorbachev, refused the RSFSR the use of union troops; on the morning of 10 November the internal troops left Grozny[176], and on 11 November the deputies in Moscow refused to approve Yeltsin's decree, finding it necessary to act "not by applying emergency measures but by political means"[177]. February 1943 – February 1949 C1180 Operation "Chechevitsa": the Total Deportation of the Chechen People and the Special Settlement Regime (1943-1949) On 23 February 1944 the USSR deported the entire Chechen people from their native land to Kazakhstan and Kirghizia (today's Kyrgyzstan). The deportation was total - the numbers show it: the 1939 census counted 387.5 thousand Chechens in Checheno-Ingushetia[1], and by 1 March 1944 the Soviet NKVD (predecessor of today's FSB) reported 387,229 deported Chechens - 478,479 people together with the Ingush[178]. The colonizer named this expulsion Operation "Chechevitsa" ("Lentil"): historian P. M. Polian writes that already in November 1943 Deputy People's Commissar (Minister) of Internal Affairs Chernyshev was discussing with the heads of regional NKVD directorates "questions connected with the planned Operation 'Chechevitsa' - the deportation of some 0.5 million Vainakhs (Chechens and Ingush)"[1]. The supreme organ of the occupation authority (the "Politburo of the TsK VKP(b)") had been discussing the deportation a year before the announced pretext - the accusation that the people had aided the Germans: on 11 February 1943 the talk was already about timing, and Stalin "leaned toward the second proposal" - to deport after the Germans had been driven from the Caucasus[178]. Albogachiev, the former People's Commissar (Minister) of Internal Affairs of the republic, admitted in 1963: "I repeat once more - there were no grounds whatsoever for the deportation of the Chechens and Ingush. This was confirmed by Beria himself during his trial in 1953"[2]. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "All of the above allows us to qualify with confidence the deportation, in this case of the Chechens and Ingush, as the gravest of crimes - genocide"[2]. Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes: "the second attempt to annihilate the Chechens was undertaken in 1944, when the entire people was driven from its native land and deported to Central Asia and Kazakhstan"[14]. On 26 April 1991 the colonizer acknowledged the genocide by its own law - Article 2 of the RSFSR law "On the Rehabilitation of Repressed Peoples" states: "Repressed peoples are recognized to be those peoples... against whom, on grounds of national or other identity, a state-level policy of slander and genocide was carried out, accompanied by their forcible resettlement..."[179]. In 2004 the European Parliament recognized in a resolution: "the deportation of the entire Chechen people to Central Asia on 23 February 1944 on the orders of Stalin constitutes an act of genocide within the meaning of the Fourth Hague Convention of 1907 and the Convention for the Prevention and Repression of the Crime of Genocide adopted by the UN General Assembly on 9 December 1948"[180]. In its resolution of 18 October 2022 the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine condemned "the international crimes committed by the russian federation during the first (1994-1996) and second (1999-2009) wars against the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria, the policy of genocide of the Chechen people, following the criminal actions of the tsarist regime of 1817-1864 and of the soviet authorities of 1944"[181]. October 1659 C0004 Pereiaslav Articles (1659) The imposition of a new enslaving treaty on Yurii Khmelnytsky under the pressure of Muscovite troops. The treaty abolished independence: "the Ukrainian state lost its independence and acquired the status of a political autonomy within the Russian state"[127]. January 1654 C0001 Pereiaslav Council (1654) The oath of Bohdan Khmelnytsky and the starshyna to the tsar. Establishment of control over the Hetmanate through a legal trap: the treaty was asymmetric by design – in response to the demand for a mutual oath, envoy "V. Buturlin, citing the autocratic character of the Russian monarch's power, refused to do so"[127]. The very language of "reunification" is a later imperial overlay: Tsar Aleksei's charter to the Zaporozhian Host (27 March 1654) speaks only of subjects who "have come under our sovereign's high hand"[182]. January 1718 – December 1721 C1128 Plundering Expeditions of Cossacks and Allied Princes (1718–1721) In 1718, the government of the Tsardom of Muscovy organized a large-scale invasion of the lands of the Nokhchi: historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov states that there occurred "a predatory expedition of detachments of Don Cossacks and Kabardian princes allied with Peter I into the ‘Chechen district’ along the Sunzha and the Argun"[37]. As a result of the raid, "800 captives were taken, not counting ‘belongings’"[37]. In 1721, the armed actions continued: the researcher points out that the Astrakhan governor A. P. Volynsky "invited the Don Cossacks and, together with the Terek Cossacks, organized raids to the Agrakhan and Aksai rivers against the Kumyks and Chechens"[37]. January 1631 – December 1640 C1117 Police Registration and Restriction of Settlement (1631–1640) The occupation administration of the Tsardom of Muscovy introduced rigid statistical control and restricted the right of the Nokhchi societies (Okochans, Michkiz, and Shibut) to free movement within the controlled territory. In 1631, Tsar Mikhail Fedorovich issued a decree to the Prikaz of the Kazan Palace on a census of the newcomer population of the town of Terki, directly prohibiting the free residence of unsanctioned migrants. The document prescribed identifying persons «whom it will not be possible to trust», and such people were «to be ordered sent out of the town of Terki, and ordered to go back to wherever each had come from, so that no harm would come to the town from them»[79]. To implement this mechanism, the metropole regularly conducted a total demographic accounting. In the state register of serving people for the region of the Prikaz of the Kazan Palace for 1637, the central authorities recorded in detail the number of inhabitants, including 350 serving «Okotsk people» and 680 newcomer «Okochans, and Tatars, and Michkiz, and Shibut»[53]. In 1640, on the orders of the Terek voivode, the Terek syn boyarsky P. Lukin and the clerk F. Belkov compiled a detailed name-by-name register of the population of the slobodas, rigidly documenting every household of the subordinated Nokhchi (Okochans) to ensure constant surveillance[79][53]. August 1946 – March 1953 C0085 Postwar Ideological Terror ("Zhdanovshchina") (1946–1953) A return to total control over culture after the relative relaxations of the war years: the rout of the Ukrainian creative intelligentsia, accusations of "bourgeois nationalism" (attacks on Rylsky, Yanovsky, the persecution of Sosiura for the poem "Love Ukraine"). In parallel ran a state antisemitic campaign: "On July 18, 1952 the Military Collegium of the USSR Supreme Court passed death sentences on 13 people, including 5 natives of Ukraine… on August 12, 1952 they were all executed"[147], and in January 1953 the "Doctors' Plot" began. January 1800 – December 1864 C1106 Propagandistic Inversion of Roles and Dehumanization (1800–1864) In the 19th century, the occupation administration of the Russian Empire and its propaganda apparatus used inversion of roles and the broadcasting of a logic of superiority to legitimize military aggression. Historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov states that «The anti-colonial and anti-feudal uprisings of the population of Chechnya, referred to in official documents as 'mischief', 'robberies' and 'murders', were perceived by the Russian autocracy as a challenge and an insult... All of this provoked cruel punitive actions incommensurate with the apparent cause»[37]. The practical application of this mechanism is recorded in reports: in 1800, the commander-in-chief of the troops, General B. F. Knorring, justified expeditions against the Indigenous population as protection from their «predatory plunder, villainous brigandage»[37]. In parallel, official historiography constructed an image of backwardness: the researcher points out that pre-revolutionary military science was characterized by an «apologia for the tsarist policy of conquest», under which the defensive struggle of the local population was labeled «the actions of barbarians devoid of 'civilized' notions of independence and freedom»[36]. Literature was used to broadcast chauvinism to the masses. The imperial historian and participant in the events V. A. Potto records that the poet A. S. Pushkin proclaimed in verse: «Submit, Caucasus — Yermolov comes!»[76], while the poet V. A. Zhukovsky glorified the destruction of villages: «Toward the villages — the villages blaze»[74]. Relying on this foundation, General A. P. Yermolov justified repressions on the grounds that «the proconsul of the Caucasus cannot tame the cruelty of the local mores with mercy»[76]. January 1674 C0006 Publication of the "Synopsis" (1674) The creation of the first large-scale ideological justification for the seizure of lands by the Muscovite tsars – the "Synopsis, or a Brief Collection from Various Chroniclers on the Origin of the Slaveno-Rossian People," published by the printing house of the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra in 1674[24]. The author's calculation was political: "to give the Muscovite tsar the motivation to continue the struggle with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth for the liberation from Catholic rule of the remaining part of the 'single Orthodox people'"[183]. January 1617 – December 1618 C1120 Punitive campaign and the devastation of the Nokhchi mountain communities (1617–1618) The occupation administration of the town of Terki undertook an armed invasion of the mountain lands of the Nokhchi. Historian E. N. Kusheva states that the 1618 military campaign of the Terek detachments into the mountains took place «at the request of «the Uvar Nutsal prince and his brother Suleman-murza and the Cherny prince's son Turlov-murza»»[56]. Kusheva adds that «In 1621, the serving Kabardian prince Sunchaley Yanglychevich Cherkassky and his son Prince Sholokh referred in their petitions to their participation in the campaign of the Terek fighting men into the mountains that took place in 1618»[56]. Preparation for the operation included forced mobilization: in a petition to Tsar Mikhail Fedorovich, the Kabardian prince Sholokh reported that «voivode Mikita Dmitreevich Velyaminov sent me... together with my father on your sovereign's service... against your sovereign's disobedient ones, the Michkiz people, against their kabaks»[53]. Having made the crossing «through the mountains and along mountain crevices, through impassable places»[53], the detachments descended upon the settlements. In a similar document, the Kabardian prince Sunchaley Yanglychevich Cherkassky reported that they «burned down and utterly devastated many Shibut, and Kalkan, and Erokhan, and Michkiz kabaks, and took many captives, and killed many other peo[ple]»[53]. Kusheva states that after the detachments «had made war upon «the Shibut, and Kalkan, and Erokhan, and Michkiz kabaks»», the Indigenous population was forced into submission: ««the Shibut, and Kalkan, and Erokhan, and Michkiz people... acknowledged their guilt»»[56], as a result of which the mountaineers «petitioned in submission and gave the shert (oath) and amanats to the town of Terki»[53]. January 1813 – March 1816 C1142 Punitive devastation of the Nokhchi villages along the Sunzha and pitting neighboring peoples against them under Rtishchev (1813-1816) In 1812-1814 Russia was at war with Napoleon and conducted no major campaigns deep into Chechnya. The troops on the Terek were commanded by General Rtishchev, who avoided large campaigns, but raids across the Terek continued under him. Colonel Eristov twice crossed the Terek and devastated Chechen villages; the second time he "exterminated several villages along the Sunzha" and forced the Nokhchi to give up amanats (hostages)[74]. Even the imperial leadership itself condemned these raids. General Rtishchev demanded that the highlanders be won over "not by arms, but by kind treatment"[74], and Emperor Alexander I, upon learning "of yet another raid on peaceful Chechnya by Colonel Eristov," ordered by special rescript "to establish tranquility on the Caucasus Line through friendliness and kind indulgence," that is, he deemed the raid unjustified[14]. The raids did not stop because of this. Beyond the raids, the empire incited neighboring peoples against the Chechens. In 1816 the Nokhchi, led by Beibulat Taimiev, took Major Shvetsov prisoner[14], and in response the commander on the Terek, General Delpozzo, by letter compelled the Kumyk lords of Endirey, Aksai, and Kostek to go to war against the Chechens, demanding that they "put an end to the brigand people"[184]. The Kumyk lords signed "Obligations" in which they undertook to make war on the Chechens, to kill them or hand them over to the Russians, and to let no goods through to them[184]. At the same time Delpozzo did not withdraw his own troops, and in the same report proposed keeping them on the Sunzha "until I exterminate their beastly freedom and independence"[184]. January 1691 – December 1700 C1124 Punitive Raids and the Economic Strangulation of the Nokhchi (1691–1700) At the end of the 17th century, the Tsardom of Muscovy exerted continuous military, diplomatic, and economic pressure on the societies of the Nokhchi. In response to the alliance of the Indigenous population with Russian Old Believer Cossacks, the regular army conducted armed operations: the historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov states that in 1691–1700 «punitive expeditions were carried out in retaliation by the tsarist authorities against the rebel Cossacks and their mountaineer allies»[37] and records «retaliatory punitive raids by tsarist forces»[37]. In parallel, the diplomatic apparatus expanded legal control over the region, formalizing in 1696 «an expression of Russia's protection over the Braguny principality in Chechnya»[37]. Military methods were supplemented by official fiscal pressure: the historian Sh. B. Akhmadov emphasizes that «the Okochans (Akkin Chechens) living in the town of Terki were obligated without exception to pay duties on the various goods and wares they took out for sale to their compatriots in Chechnya and Ingushetia»[36]. The economic strangulation was aggravated by the arbitrariness of the local occupation administration: he adds that «the venality and bribe-taking of the voivodes, who permitted themselves great abuses — all this was a phenomenon far from new»[36]. January 1711 – May 1711 C0027 Pylyp Orlyk's Campaign in Right-Bank Ukraine (1711) A military-diplomatic attempt to restore Ukraine's independence by the forces of the emigration with the support of allies. The campaign failed because of a stab in the back: "the Tatars, disobeying Orlyk, scattered in raiding parties and began taking yasyr captives across Ukrainian villages"[185]. January 1550 – December 1721 C1104 Religious Frontier and the Fabrication of Historical Right (1550–1721) From the mid-16th century until 1721, the diplomatic apparatus of the Tsardom of Muscovy justified military expansion into the North Caucasus with theological rhetoric and invented historical rights. Historian Michael Khodarkovsky states that the government apparatus positioned the tsar as a "universal Christian ruler, who 'upheld the true Christian faith'"[52]. Invasions were motivated by a "divine obligation to rescue Orthodox Christians from infidel captivity"[52]. As a result, as the researcher summarizes, "Moscow's military and political interests could no longer be separated from the ideological and theological rhetoric of expansion"[52], and the North Caucasus "became a religious frontier"[142]. In parallel, fictitious grounds for territorial claims were being constructed: the author records that officials produced false reports for foreign rulers claiming that the indigenous peoples of the Caucasus had allegedly been Muscovite "subjects in the Riazan region since ancient times, and then fled from Riazan and settled in the mountains"[52], which gave the metropole a formal pretext to legalize the absorption of their lands and the construction of its fortifications. January 1769 – December 1786 C0044 Russification of Education and Religion (1769–1786) A systematic campaign of the Russian Empire to root out the indigenous people's language from education and religion: "in 1769 the Holy Synod not only refused permission to print South Russian primers, but ordered the confiscation of those already in people's hands"[48]; by an order of 26 October 1784, the Kyiv metropolitan Samuil Myslavsky directed the rector and prefect of the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy "to take unremitting care of the unfailing and unomitted observance, by teachers and students alike, of the rules of Russian orthography," under the threat of expelling students from the clerical estate[186]; in 1786 the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy was prescribed the empire-wide mode of instruction[49]. January 1877 – December 1878 C0064 Russo-Turkish War and Pan-Slavism (1877–1878) The use of the inhabitants of the Ukrainian governorates in yet another geopolitical war in the Balkans. Imperial expansion was justified by religion and the ideology of Pan-Slavism – Dostoevsky formulated it as a mission: the Slavs "for a long time… will be unable to recognize Russia's selflessness and her great, holy raising, unheard of in the world, of the banner of the greatest idea"[187]. January 1806 – December 1812 C0039 Russo-Turkish War and the Annexation of Bessarabia (1806–1812) The use of Ukrainian resources in yet another geopolitical war of the empire, which ended with the severing of Bessarabia from the Ottoman Empire: "After the incorporation of Bessarabia into Russia on May 16, 1812 (see the Treaty of Bucharest of 1812), Ukrainian Cossacks of the volunteer regiments, of the Ust-Danube Budjak Cossack Host, and of the Danube Cossack Host actively settled the Budjak"[32]. January 1768 – December 1774 C0032 Russo-Turkish War and the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca (1768–1774) The use of Ukrainian resources and Cossack regiments for victory over the Ottomans on the Danube. The diplomatic severing of Crimea from the Ottoman Empire through the recognition of a fictitious "independence": under Article III of the treaty, "All the Tatar peoples: the Crimean, Budjak, Kuban, Yedisan, Jamboyluk, and Yedichkul, without exception, are to be recognized by both empires as free and entirely independent of any outside power"[188] – this "independence" became the prologue to the annexation of the peninsula nine years later. June 1941 – May 1945 C0082 Scorched Earth Tactics and Criminal Mobilization (1941–1945) The Soviet authorities' treatment of Ukraine as a colonial resource during the war. During the 1941 retreat the directive of the USSR Sovnarkom and the Central Committee of 29 June 1941 was in force: "In the forced withdrawal of Red Army units… leave the enemy not a kilogram of grain, not a liter of fuel… All valuable property… that cannot be evacuated must without fail be destroyed"[189]. In 1943–1944, on the liberated territory, the mobilization of the "chornosvytnyky" was carried out: they were "thrown into combat often at once, without undergoing military training… sometimes unarmed, not even changed into military uniform"[190]. January 1793 – December 1795 C0037 Second and Third Partitions of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth (1793–1795) The Russian Empire's collusion with the Hohenzollern and Habsburg monarchies to dismember a neighboring state. Under the second partition, "Russia received the central part of Belarus, the Kyiv, Bratslav, and Podillia voivodeships, and the eastern half of the Volhynian voivodeship – in total 250 thousand km2 and over 3 million inhabitants," and after the third, "the Polish state ceased to exist"[127]. December 1917 – April 1918 C0072 Soviet-Ukrainian War: First Invasion and the Puppet Government (December 1917 - April 1918) In December 1917, Soviet Russia began its first armed invasion of Ukraine, disguising it as an internal war. Defeated in Kyiv, supporters of the Bolsheviks moved to Kharkiv, held an alternative congress there, and created a puppet government - the People's Secretariat: "the first Soviet government of Ukraine," created "as an alternative to the Ukrainian Central Rada and the General Secretariat of the Ukrainian Central Rada"[191]. Thus began the Soviet-Ukrainian War (1917-1921): Soviet Russia passed off the invasion by its own troops as an internal civil war[38][32]. In February 1918, RSFSR troops under the command of Muravyov captured Kyiv and carried out a massacre there; historians call Muravyov "the initiator of mass executions in the city"[191]. The invasion was stopped by the Brest-Litovsk peace treaty (9 February 1918) - the first international act to recognize the Ukrainian People's Republic (UNR) as a subject of international law. At the request of the UNR government, German and Austro-Hungarian troops entered Ukraine, and by the end of April 1918 they had driven the RSFSR troops from all Ukrainian land[32]. After Germany's capitulation in November 1918 these troops left - and Soviet Russia invaded again (campaign C0074). January 1919 – December 1919 C0074 Soviet-Ukrainian War: Second Invasion and Resource Depletion (1919) After Germany's capitulation in World War I, the German and Austro-Hungarian troops that had occupied Ukraine since the spring of 1918 left[32] - and in January 1919 RSFSR troops invaded Ukraine for the second time: the Soviet-Ukrainian War went on[32]. The cover had been prepared in advance: as early as 28 November 1918, the Central Committee of the Bolshevik party (CC RCP(b)) created a "Provisional Workers' and Peasants' Government of Ukraine" in the Russian city of Kursk to provide political cover for the invasion[192]. The goal was the resources of the captured land: the head of the RSFSR government, Lenin, advised Petrograd workers to go to Ukraine for provisions and fuel - "It is foolish to starve and perish in Petrograd when you can win back bread and coal"[193]. The villages answered the grain seizures with uprisings, and the Russian command treated the war against them as frontline work[194]. In the summer of 1919 a second Russian army came to Ukraine - the Armed Forces of South Russia under General Denikin (the "Whites"), who likewise denied Ukrainian statehood[195]. On 30 August 1919 Ukrainian troops took Kyiv, abandoned by the Bolsheviks, but on 31 August the Whites pushed them out - the day went down in history as the "Kyiv Catastrophe"[27]. By the autumn of 1919 the Whites had driven out the RSFSR troops and established their military dictatorship over most of Ukraine[196]. In December 1919 Soviet Russia invaded for the third time (campaign C0104). December 1919 – November 1921 C0104 Soviet-Ukrainian War: Third Invasion and the Final Soviet Occupation (December 1919 - November 1921) In December 1919, having defeated the White army of General Denikin, the troops of Soviet Russia (RSFSR) invaded Ukraine for the third time in two years of the Soviet-Ukrainian War: on 16 December they captured Kyiv - Soviet troops had previously taken it in February 1918 (campaign C0072) and in February 1919 (campaign C0074)[39][197]. The Army of the Ukrainian People's Republic (UNR), no longer able to hold a continuous front, went on a raid behind the lines of the Soviet and White forces - the First Winter Campaign (6 December 1919 - 6 May 1920)[127], while the UNR government concluded an alliance with Poland. In May 1920 Polish troops and the UNR Army liberated Kyiv, but on 12 June Soviet troops captured it again, and by autumn - most of the lands west of the Dnipro[198]. In November 1920 the UNR Army and government were pushed beyond the Zbruch River and retreated to territory under Polish control[199]. The last attempt by Ukrainians to raise an uprising against the Russian invaders was the Second Winter Campaign of the UNR Army: in November 1921 its detachments returned to Ukraine, were encircled, and 359 prisoners were executed near the village of Bazar[196][200]. Thus Soviet Russia, and from 1922 the USSR, entrenched itself on the captured lands of Ukraine until 1991[39][38]. April 1920 – December 1924 C1176 Sovietization of Chechnya: revkoms in place of Soviets, punitive operations and Cheka executions (1920-1924) In 1920-1924 Soviet Russia imposed its control over Chechnya: it installed unelected revolutionary committees (revkoms) in place of elected Soviets, conducted military disarmament operations with the use of aviation, shot people without trial by the hands of the Cheka and took hostages. Seven years earlier Chechnya had gone through the First World War, the two revolutions of 1917 and an attempt to live in a state of its own - the Mountain Republic, proclaimed in May 1918. In 1919 Chechnya was held by the Volunteer Army of General Denikin - troops of former imperial officers who fought the Bolsheviks for the return of Russia within its former borders; its terror left behind 21 destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead (campaign C1174). By the spring of 1920 the Denikinites had rolled back from the North Caucasus, and the emirate of Sheikh Uzun-Haji, which had fought against them, fell apart on its own: the emir died, "The emirate went into the grave with him, without any political consequences for Chechnya and Dagestan"[2]. Power in the land was taken by the Bolsheviks, whom the Chechen villages had until then supported against Denikin. An order of the staff of the North Caucasus Military District prescribed: "The disarmament must begin with lowland Chechnya, so as to secure the Grozny area. The operation must be conducted in real earnest, up to the destruction of the unsubmissive auls"[2]. Commissar of the Caucasus Labor Army Vrachev complained about his own punitive apparatus: the army's special department was carrying out mass shootings of which "... almost nothing is known not only to the Revolutionary Tribunal or the Political Department of the army, but to me or the army commander either"[2]. January 1922 – December 1939 C0052 Stalinist Terror and the End of Ukrainization (1922–1939) The suppression of the national revival in the USSR: the resolution of the Central Committee of the VKP(b) and the Council of People's Commissars of 14 December 1932, signed by Stalin and Molotov, declared that "Ukrainization was carried out mechanically" and ordered "to immediately transfer in the North Caucasus the record-keeping of the soviet and cooperative bodies of the 'Ukrainized' districts, as well as all published newspapers and journals, from the Ukrainian language to Russian"[201]; the annihilation of most Ukrainian writers of the 1920s-1930s went down in history as the "Executed Renaissance"[24]; the resolution of the USSR Council of People's Commissars and the Central Committee of the VKP(b) of 13 March 1938 No. 324 ordered "to introduce the teaching of the Russian language as a subject of study in the schools of the national republics and regions from September 1, 1938"[163]. September 1989 – December 1990 C0091 Stalling Democratic Reforms and Countering the People's Movement (Rukh) (1989–1990) The conservative party apparatus under the leadership of V. Shcherbytsky attempted to contain the growth of the national liberation movement. Because of KGB pressure and the threat of an immediate ban, the founders of the Ukrainian independence movement were initially forced to disguise their goals, naming the organization the "People's Movement of Ukraine for Perestroika": "at first it supported the official course of perestroika, without formally raising the demand of Ukraine's independence," and its program "lacked the demand for a new union treaty and contained a formal provision recognizing the 'guiding role' of the communist party"[191]. Only in 1990, having proclaimed that "what is needed is not perestroika but the complete dismantling of the totalitarian system," did Rukh remove the words "for perestroika" from its name[191]. January 1906 – December 1914 C0069 Stolypin Repressions and Mass Displacement (1906–1914) The suppression of protests and an agrarian reform that economically squeezed Ukrainian peasants off their native lands: "The resettlement movement gained great momentum, and during 1906–12 about 1 million people left Ukraine for Asiatic Russia… The majority of migrants were landless and land-poor peasants (67%)"[24] – nearly a quarter of the resettlers, failing to take root, returned. January 1711 – December 1717 C1127 Strengthening of the Border Line and Reconnaissance of Resources (1711–1717) The metropole temporarily reduced the intensity of direct military strikes, shifting to infrastructural fortification and the study of the region. Historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov states that, owing to the foreign policy situation, "issues related to the mountain peoples ceased to be of primary importance to them"[37]. Nevertheless, the occupation apparatus continued preparations for further expansion. In 1711–1712, the government consolidated the military lines on the border with the lands of the Nokhchi: the researcher points out that "the small Greben Cossack towns along the Terek were consolidated, by order of Tsar Peter I, into 5 stanitsas — from Chervlyonnaya to Kurdyukovskaya"[37]. In parallel, conceptual and economic reconnaissance was under way: in 1714, the tsar’s adviser A. Bekovich-Cherkassky submitted a report in which he considered "drawing the Highlanders over to Russia’s side" to be "in keeping with the vital interests of the Russian state"[37]. In 1717, to inventory the potential of the Nokhchi lands, the government dispatched a specialist: the author records "the survey of mineral springs and other natural riches of the Terek River (including the Bragun warm springs) by Doctor Gottlieb Schober on the assignment of Peter I"[37]. June 1860 – February 1864 C1169 Suppression of the 1860-1861 uprisings, the execution of Baysangur, and the shooting of the zikrists near Shali (1860-1864) For twenty-five years the Chechens and Dagestanis held their own state against the empire - the Imamate created by Imam Shamil: with sharia courts, taxes, an army, and naib governors in the districts. In 1859 the Imamate fell: in April the troops took its capital, Vedeno; in August, near the Dagestani aul of Gunib, Shamil himself surrendered. He was taken to Russia under surveillance: Emperor Alexander II designated Kaluga as his place of residence, where the imam and his family were given a mansion and twenty thousand rubles a year in upkeep - a captivity the sources call "honorable". More than ten years later he was allowed a pilgrimage to Mecca (hajj); in 1871 he died in Medina (the Arabian Peninsula, now Saudi Arabia) and was buried there[41]. After that, Chechnya was held by force. In 1860-1861 uprisings broke out in Ichkeria and the Argun district - they were suppressed by expeditions with the destruction of auls and the eviction of the inhabitants, and those who led them were executed or sent into exile - to the inner provinces of Russia, to Siberia, and to fortresses: Baysangur of Benoy was hanged by sentence of a field court-martial; naib Atabi-Mullah Atayev and Uma Duyev were sent off to different provinces; Sheikh Kunta-Haji - indefinitely, to Ustyuzhna in Novgorod province; his brother - to the Vyborg fortress; rank-and-file followers - to fortress labor with settlement in Siberia. In January 1864, near the village of Shali, troops shot down an unarmed procession of followers of Sheikh Kunta-Haji - a Muslim preacher who taught that God must be remembered aloud, in chorus, with singing and circling in a ring. Such remembrance is called zikr - hence the imperial nickname of his followers, the zikrists. What moved the insurgents was recorded by the imperial side itself: Colonel Belik reported to the head of the Terek oblast in late May 1860 about the Benoy people who had returned to their burnt-out homes - they "earnestly begged permission to settle in their old places, - otherwise they had all sworn to die rather than submit"[2]. The program of the period was set down by the chief of the Main Staff of the Caucasus Army, Kartsov (Kartsev in other sources), in a secret memorandum of 1864: "the only sure means of securing the lasting submission of the Chechens is to organize their mass resettlement, partly to Turkey, partly to the plain, far away from the mountains"[2]. The outcome of the massacre near Shali is summed up by the historian D. A. Khozhayev: "the tsarist authorities provoked the highlanders into an action and staged a slaughter, gunning down with cannon the crowds of murid-zikrists who had advanced on the soldiers' squares with nothing but daggers and empty scabbards"[14] - murids are a sheikh's disciples. May 1953 – December 1954 C0086 Suppression of the GULAG Uprisings (1953–1954) After Stalin's death, the amnesty did not extend to political prisoners, among whom Ukrainians made up an enormous share. This provoked large-scale uprisings within the concentration camp system (Vorkuta, Norilsk, Kengir). In Kengir, the insurgents created a system of self-government, a radio station, and workshops for making weapons, demanding the arrival of a commission of the CPSU Central Committee. During the suppression of the Norilsk uprising, "about 100 people were killed and more than 200 wounded"[202]. In Kengir, the authorities sent in the army: "1,600 soldiers, 3 fire engines, and 5 tanks moved into the zone. It was the only suppression of camp uprisings with tanks in Soviet history"[203]. January 1813 – December 1835 C0058 Suppression of the Haidamak Uprising of Ustym Karmaliuk (until 1835) A years-long punitive campaign of the Russian Empire against the uprising of rightless Ukrainian peasants led by Karmaliuk. He himself "was captured more than once, four times sentenced to Siberian hard labor, from which he escaped, covering thousands of versts on foot," and was "killed by a shot from ambush"[27]. January 1863 – December 1864 C0062 Suppression of the January Uprising (1863–1864) The armed suppression of the liberation uprising on the Right Bank: "The Russian government dealt brutally with the participants of the uprising: hundreds of Poles were executed, thousands exiled to Siberia or given over to the army, and their property confiscated"[127]. That same summer of 1863 came the blow against Ukrainian enlightenment – the Valuev circular suspended the printing of Ukrainian books for the people[204], and the hromadas were driven to self-dissolution[30]. March 1821 – February 1822 C1146 Suppression of the Nokhchi Uprising: Devastation of Villages and Forced Forest Felling by Grekov (1821-1822) In 1821-1822 the Nokhchi rose up against the Russian Empire’s imposition of a fortress line on the Sunzha River and the driving of the plain’s inhabitants into the mountains. The historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that in early 1822 Beibulat Taimiev, with the help of the qadi Abdul-Kadyr of Germenchuk and mullah Mustafa, who had fled the burned Sunzha aul, "attempted to raise a general uprising in Chechnya"[14]. Grekov, commander of the left flank of the Caucasian Line, suppressed this resistance with punitive devastations of villages and the forced cutting of clearings through the forests of the Nokhchi by the hands of the inhabitants themselves. The historian D. A. Khozhaev cites Grekov’s report, in which he himself set out his aim: to drive the Chechens into the forests, where "only snow and cold weather were lacking for the Chechen people to experience all the calamities inevitable in such cases and to feel the necessity of submitting"[14]. The imperial historian Potto confirms the course of the suppression from the conqueror’s side: on March 1, 1821, the troops "surrounded the village of Oisungur… and, as punishment of the inhabitants, who had fled before their arrival, destroyed it completely," felling the forest "in one direction as far as Isti-Su, in the other — as far as the Michik"[76]. In February 1822, when the qadi Abdul-Kadyr met the troops on the Argun with arms in hand, "a cannonball tore off Abdul-Kadyr’s leg… he died on the third day," after which Grekov "burned the villages of Shali and Malye Atagi"[76]. January 1830 – December 1831 C0057 Suppression of the November Uprising (1830–1831) The Russian Empire's regular army suppresses a national liberation uprising: the insurgent detachments in Volhynia, the Zhytomyr region, Podillia, and the Kyiv region "were routed by the tsarist troops in April–May 1831," after which "the tsarist government resorted to brutal repressions against the participants of the uprising"[127]. The era of tightening the screws on the Right Bank begins. January 1829 – December 1829 C0056 Suppression of the Shebelynka Uprising (1829) The forcible suppression of a mass anti-serfdom uprising in Sloboda Ukraine that broke out within the system of military settlements: "The servile condition of the military settlements' inhabitants caused the Buh Cossacks' uprising of 1817, the Chuhuiv uprising of 1819, the Shebelynka uprising of 1829, and others"[32]. The scale is recorded by the EHU: "Up to 3 thousand peasants gathered in Shebelynka," and "on May 30, 1829 a bloody reprisal against the defiant began, during which 109 people died"[192]. January 1708 – December 1708 C1126 Suppression of the Uprising of Murat Kuchukov and Terror against the Indigenous Population (1708) In 1708, the Tsardom of Muscovy employed radical violence to suppress an armed uprising of the Indigenous population. The revolt was caused by the methods previously laid down by the metropole within the campaign C1124: Punitive Raids and Economic Strangulation of the Nokhchi, 1691–1700: systematic abuses by the voevodas and a discriminatory economic policy. Historian Sh. B. Akhmadov states that, because of the duties, "the economic interaction of the Vainakhs with Russia... was practically paralyzed"[36]. In response to the siege of the town of Terki by detachments led by Murat Kuchukov, the government organized large-scale operations: historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov states that "the measures taken by Peter I to combat the Bulavin ‘rebellion’ and other uprisings, including on the Terek against Chechnya, were, in essence, punitive"[37]. The Regular Army carried out sweep operations: he emphasizes that "military detachments were sent to the Terek that physically exterminated any population showing the slightest disobedience"[37]. Military pressure was supplemented by collusion with a third party: the researcher adds that on September 30, 1708, the diplomatic apparatus concluded an agreement with the Kalmyk khan Ayuka that included a clause "on the persecution of Chechens and Nogais"[37]. To neutralize the opposition, the metropole took the leader of the insurgents captive: Akhmadov points out that the tsar "personally decided the fate of the rebel leaders"[37], as a result of which the leader, "taken prisoner while wounded, was hanged"[37]. Total intimidation was ensured through demonstrative terror: the author records that the execution was carried out "by the rib on a hook, in accordance with Peter I’s order to P.M. Apraksin (‘inflict a cruel death penalty’)"[37]. January 1722 – December 1722 C1129 Suppression of the Uprising, Military Intervention, and Forced Formalization of Subjecthood (1722) In 1722, the Russian Empire employed the regular army for the physical suppression of the armed resistance of the Indigenous population. The uprising was caused by the economic policy of the occupation administration: historian Sh. B. Akhmadov states that "the mountain peoples continued to motivate their discontent by the discriminatory measures of the administration of the town of Terki toward trading Highlanders"[36]. As a result of this pressure, "the Chechen and Enderi lords and their subjects refused to swear an oath of submission to the tsarist authorities"[36]. In response, the metropole organized punitive measures: within the framework of Peter I’s Persian campaign, the government dispatched troops to the territories inhabited by Nokhchi communities. Historian Sh. B. Akhmadov records that "on July 23, 1722, a tsarist detachment led by General Veterani... approached the village of Enderi"[36]. Because of the Highlanders’ resistance, a new strike followed: he points out that on August 4, 1722, by decree of Peter I, "a punitive expedition was carried out a second time against the insurgent Chechens and the Enderi people"[36]. Military pressure was accompanied by the total destruction of infrastructure: the researcher states that one of the tsarist detachments "came to Enderi and completely ravaged and burned it, leaving nothing but ashes behind"[36], while in the course of the August raid "3,000 houses were destroyed and the grain in the fields was burned"[37]. The operation was carried out in collusion with a third party: Akhmadov adds that the forces included "an armed detachment of Kalmyks numbering 3,730 men, sent by Ayuka Khan at the tsar’s request"[36]. The radical violence led to the legal subordination of the borderland territories of the Nokhchi: historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov states that after the defeat the local princes swore an oath, "‘including in it, for the first time, their Chechens as well’"[37]. January 1944 – December 1951 C0084 Suppression of UPA Resistance and Operation "Vistula" (1944–1951) A war waged by NKVD/MGB troops against the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) in western Ukraine: chekist-military operations, mass repressive actions, and the forced removal of insurgents' families to Siberia - in 1944–52 "203,662 people were deported from the territory of Western Ukraine to special settlements in remote regions of the USSR"[33]. Its finale was the use of collusion with a third party - Operation "Vistula" (1947), coordinated with the pro-Soviet government of Poland, "the concluding stage of the forced deportation of Ukrainians" "from the ancestral lands of Lemkivshchyna, Nadsiannia, Kholmshchyna, and Pidliashshia," carried out to deprive the UPA of its social base[32]. August 1932 – December 1933 C0078 Terror by Famine: The Holodomor (1932–1933) The use of artificial famine as a weapon of mass destruction for the physical and psychological suppression of national resistance. The launch of a merciless grain-procurement machine, the confiscation of absolutely all food, the introduction of the "blackboard" regime (a total blockade of settlements)[205], and a ban prohibiting peasants from leaving the starving districts: the directive of Stalin and Molotov of January 22, 1933 ordered "not to allow the mass departure of peasants from Ukraine to other regions," declaring the flight of the starving "for bread" a plot "organized by enemies of Soviet power, SRs and agents of Poland"[206]. Physical extermination was accompanied by total psychological terror and show trials[39]. January 1972 – December 1985 C0089 The "General Pogrom" of Human Rights Defenders and Punitive Psychiatry (1972–1985) The apogee of repressions under V. Shcherbytsky. Mass arrests of members of the Ukrainian Helsinki Group and of dissidents: emblematic is the fate of the poet Vasyl Stus, arrested in 1972 "together with other Ukrainian writer-human rights defenders" and a second time in 1980 - for his participation in the Helsinki Group[24]. To neutralize dissenters, punitive psychiatry was applied on a mass scale - declaring healthy people insane in order to isolate them indefinitely and subject them to torture by medication[207]. Many human rights defenders never regained their freedom: Stus "died in the punishment cell of special-regime camp VS-389/36" on the night of September 3–4, 1985[24]. May 1909 – December 1911 C0109 The "Historical Path" (1909–1911) The Kyiv section of the Imperial Russian Military-Historical Society was filling central Kyiv with monuments to "figures of Russian history" and pushed the Shevchenko monument, which the city had already decided to put up, off its allotted site. The queue of eight imperial monuments - from princess Olha to Nestor the chronicler - was submitted in a memorandum of 7 April 1910 by colonel Steletsky, the section's secretary[208]. The "historical path" program grew out of a letter from Zilov, the trustee of the educational district, to governor-general Trepov: Shevchenko should not be placed opposite a "Russian governmental institution," and "it would be necessary to put up a monument to one of the figures of Russian history"[208]. The only monument of the queue actually put up was princess Olha (4 September 1911) - on the site the city had allotted in 1909 for the Shevchenko monument and which the duma gave to the society in 1911, overturning its own decision[208]. January 1911 – December 1911 C0110 The Alexander II Monument in Kyiv (1911) In 1911 the Russian Empire put up in central Kyiv the largest monument to Alexander II in the entire empire. The gratitude on the pedestal was voiced not by Ukraine and not by Kyiv but by the "Southwestern Krai" - the empire's official name for the Ukrainian lands west of the Dnipro[209][210]. The monument was unveiled on 30 August 1911 on Tsarskaya Square; the money was raised by an all-Russian subscription, 200 thousand rubles; the central pedestal bore the coat of arms of the empire, the double-headed eagle, and the inscription "To the Tsar-Liberator, the grateful Southwestern Krai. The year 1911"[211][209]. September 1836 – February 1840 C1163 The amanat-and-tribute system of colonel Pullo in the seized auls of Chechnya (1836-1840) From September 1836 to February 1840 Pullo, commander of the Sunzha Line and then of the left flank of the Caucasus Line (a chain of imperial fortifications on the land of the Nokhchi), built in the auls of Chechnya seized by the empire a system of coercion made of seven interlocking institutions: amanat hostages taken from the most respected families, a tribute of one silver ruble per saklia (house), pristavs - superintendents appointed by the empire, a ban on selling bread to the "nemirnye" (auls that had not submitted to the empire) and on pasturing their cattle on the plain, confiscation of weapons, forced felling of forests and clearings stretching 165 versts, and punishments "according to the degree of guilt" - up to the destruction of the villages themselves. Handing over the command, Pullo summed it up in a memorandum of 1840: "by threatening all the unsubmissive communities with the annihilation of their property, I instilled in them such fear, brought them to such a state, that one after another they began to submit"[3]. The system ended in an uprising. Hadji-Ali, a companion and chronicler of Shamil (Shamil - imam, leader of the resistance of the highlanders of Dagestan and Chechnya to the Russian conquest), recorded: "As the oppressions of general Pullo over the Chechens intensified, so grew the requests of the latter to Shamil to come and free them"[131]. The imperial historian Yurov admitted both the cause and the culprit: "we ourselves assisted Shamil as only his true friends could have done"; "Rumors about the true causes of the uprising of Chechnya reached the attention of the Sovereign Emperor", after which general Grabbe, commander of the troops of the Caucasus Line and Pullo's superior, deemed it necessary "to immediately remove, under a plausible pretext, major-general Pullo from the administration of the left flank"[128]. In February 1840 lowland Chechnya rose and called upon Shamil - the system collapsed together with the career of its builder. December 1917 – January 1918 C0019 The Battle of Kruty and the Killing of Prisoners (January 1918) In late December 1917, as the troops of Bolshevik Russia were advancing on Kyiv, a detachment of yunkers - cadets of the 1st Kyiv Youth Military School named after Bohdan Khmelnytsky (four companies of 150 cadets each, 20 officers, 18 machine guns) - under the command of Sotnyk Averkii Honcharenko took up the defense of Bakhmach station, a railway junction on the border of the UNR and the RSFSR[157]. On January 27, 1918, reinforcements arrived from Kyiv - the first company of the student volunteer battalion under the command of Sotnyk Omelchenko, 115-130 volunteers: students of the Ukrainian National University and Kyiv University and senior-grade pupils of Ukrainian gymnasiums - teenagers, many of them 17 years old[157][212]. The Ukrainian forces took up defense near Kruty station (now the village of Pamiatne in Chernihiv oblast)[157]. On the morning of January 29 a six-thousand-strong detachment of Petrograd and Moscow Red Guards led by Yegorov attacked the positions; the fighting lasted until evening, the defenders repelled several attacks and, on the order of Sotnyk Averkii Honcharenko, withdrew to their echelon - the detachment's train waiting two kilometers away; their losses came to as many as 300 killed, wounded, and captured[157]. A platoon of the student company lost its bearings at dusk and came out at the station already held by the Red Guards; 27 prisoners were shot - among them, according to testimony in the investigation file of commander-in-chief Muravyov, "there were many gymnasium pupils of about 17"; Yegorov, commander of the First Revolutionary Army, authorized the shooting[212]. The teenage cadets managed to delay the offensive: explaining the heavy losses at Kruty and the delay in the advance on Kyiv, Muravyov claimed in his report that the Ukrainian forces had been commanded by "S. Petliura himself" - as the compilers of the collection of the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory note[213]. In February Muravyov's troops approached Kyiv from the Darnytsia side, shelled the city with heavy artillery for five days, and captured it on February 8, 1918[214]. After the UNR concluded the Peace of Brest-Litovsk with the Central Powers, German and Austro-Hungarian troops entered Ukraine, with Ukrainian units in the vanguard; the Bolsheviks abandoned Kyiv, and in early March the Council of People's Ministers returned there, followed a few days later by the Ukrainian Central Rada[215]. On March 19, 1918, by decision of the Ukrainian Central Rada, the bodies of those killed at Kruty were brought to Kyiv and ceremonially buried at the Askold's Grave cemetery[157]. June 1709 – July 1709 C0015 The Battle of Poltava and the Final Defeat of the Hetmanate (1709) The decisive battle of the Great Northern War, in the course of which the military backbone of Ukrainian autonomy was finally eliminated. The defeat of the Swedish-Cossack alliance allowed Moscow to move from suppressing uprisings to the systematic dismantling of the Hetmanate's political agency[44]. January 1888 – December 1888 C0065 The Bohdan Khmelnytsky Monument (1888) In 1888 the Russian Empire put up in central Kyiv a monument to Bohdan Khmelnytsky - a sign of the city's belonging to the empire and of "unity" with Moscow. The pedestal bore programmatic inscriptions: "We will to be under the tsar of the east, the Orthodox one" and "To Bohdan Khmelnytsky – one and indivisible Russia"[216]. The monument was unveiled on 11 July 1888 on Sophia Square; the committee for its construction was headed by Mikhail Yuzefovich - an official of the Kyiv educational district and author of the memorandum that formed the basis of the Ems ukase of 1876[216][217]. January 1722 – December 1724 C0018 The Case of Pavlo Polubotok (1723) Peter I's establishment of the First Little Russian Collegium to seize governance from the hetman's administration: the collegium was created "as the highest appellate instance and the administrative-controlling organ of the Russian state structure in Ukraine"[23]. It was accompanied by the arrest of acting hetman Polubotok and the officers for defending the autonomy: "the officers submitted to Emperor Peter I yet another petition to close the Little Russian Collegium. After this, interrogations of Polubotok began in the Secret Chancellery, and on November 10, 1723 he was arrested and imprisoned in the Peter and Paul Fortress"[127], where the hetman died. The arrest order itself was never published as a separate act - the case was run by the Secret Chancellery; the circumstances were retrospectively set out in Empress Catherine I's manifesto of 8 February 1725: "it was ordered that the General Starshyna - Polubotok, Chernysh and Savych - be in St. Petersburg to answer for it"[218]. January 1853 – December 1856 C0061 The Crimean War and the Suppression of the "Kyiv Cossack Movement" (1853–1856) A grueling geopolitical war of the empire, accompanied by the mass mobilization of the Ukrainian peasantry. Nicholas I's manifesto on the state militia and the decrees on its levy of 29 January 1855 (Nos. 28.991–28.993) gave rise to hopes of freedom - even though the Kyiv governorate was not on the list of governorates called up at all[219]: "the movement for re-Cossackization in March–April engulfed over 500 villages and towns in 8 of the 12 districts of the Kyiv governorate… To suppress the 'Cossack movement' the government threw in regular troops and police"[27]. January 1728 – December 1728 C0028 The Decisive Points (1728) A unilateral imperial act imposed on hetman Danylo Apostol instead of the traditional bilateral treaty. While formally softening the regime of the Little Russian Collegium, the document entrenched harsh imperial restrictions on key points: "Article 19 forbids the hetman relations with other countries"[24], customs revenues went to the tsar's treasury, and personnel appointments were placed under the metropole's control. July 1925 – October 1925 C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) By 1925 Soviet power had stood in Chechnya for its fifth year and remained largely nominal: five years of Sovietization (campaign C1176) - revkoms (revolutionary committees) instead of elected Soviets, arrests of sheikhs, two partial disarmaments - had not given Moscow control over the people, imam Nazhmuddin Gotsinsky, the spiritual head of the armed resistance in Dagestan and Chechnya, was sheltering in the mountains, and the profile of the Mountain district drawn up by the staff of the future operation admitted: "Beyond the Sharo-Argun Soviet power does not exist"[220]. Moscow, meanwhile, was steering a course toward taking power away from the autonomies - historian T. U. Elbuzdukayeva writes: "The unceasing banditry and insurgent movements in the North Caucasus were perceived by the Moscow authorities as a convincing argument in favor of its centralizing efforts, the process of transferring autonomous sovereignty from Caucasian into Moscow hands"[221]. The operation of 1925 became that course in action: the USSR took away the weapons of Chechnya's population with the forces of the army and the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB) - from 25 August the troops passed through 242 settlements, shelled 101 of them with [artillery] guns and machine guns, bombed 16 from aircraft, arrested more than 300 people and shot nearly all of them without trial. Under the guise of maneuvers the troops entered the oblast, surrounded aul after aul, convened the village assembly, presented an ultimatum to surrender weapons according to a ready-made quota, and opened fire on the settlement if it was not met; of the aims Elbuzdukayeva writes: as the centers of the operation the staff had designated in advance the mountain societies "where N. Gotsinsky [the head of the resistance] was presumed to be"[221]. The instruction of 4 August 1925, approved by Uborevich, commander of the North Caucasus Military District (SKVO), prescribed, should the ultimatum not be met, opening artillery fire on the settlement for ten minutes, and allowed repeating it several times[222]. The deception, too, was assigned by document: by an order of 31 July 1925 the staff of the Workers' and Peasants' Red Army (RKKA) approved Uborevich's maneuvers in Chechnya and with the same document assigned the disarmament: "At the same time," the order said, "taking advantage of the concentration of a significant number of troops on the territory of Chechnya (the district of the forthcoming maneuvers), the command of the SKVO, in coordination with the PPOGPU [the plenipotentiary representation of the OGPU] in the North Caucasus, plans to carry out a disarmament and a removal of the bandit element, which by a number of political indications is highly timely"[78]. The sanction was given by Stalin personally: in July 1925 Mikoyan, secretary of the North Caucasus krai committee of the party[223], met him in Sochi and after the conversation telegraphed to Molotov in Moscow: "The political situation in Chechnya has become aggravated. Stalin has given his personal consent to the necessity of the operation"[221]. Many years later Mikoyan summed it up in his memoirs: "This operation fundamentally cleared the air of Chechnya"[224]. January 1876 – December 1887 C0047 The Ems Ukaz and Total Censorship (1876–1887) The complete displacement of the language from the cultural and literary sphere. The Ems ukase prescribed: "Not to permit the import into the empire… of any books whatsoever published abroad in the Little Russian dialect," "To forbid in the empire the printing, in the same dialect, of any original works or translations whatsoever," and "To forbid likewise any stage performances, texts to musical scores, and public readings in the same dialect"[225]. The permitted dictionaries were allowed only "on condition of their being printed in conformity with all-Russian orthography"[49]. Five years later the rules were revised by a Special Conference - it included Solsky, Ostrovsky, the chief procurator of the Synod Pobedonostsev, and Viazemsky, - and the minister of internal affairs Ignatiev reported the result to the emperor on 3 October 1881; assent followed on 8 October[226]. There were no plans to publish the revision, and Ignatiev explained why: "the rules on the use of the Little Russian dialect established in 1876 were not promulgated, and therefore it is not intended to make the projected clarifications known to the general public"[226]. The circular went out to governor-general Drenteln on 16 October stamped "Confidential"[226] - that is, people were judged by rules they were never shown. August 1965 – December 1968 C0088 The First Wave of Repressions Against the "Sixtiers" (1965–1968) The KGB's response to the emergence of a resistance movement among the new Ukrainian intelligentsia. It includes the suppression of the 1965 protests (the public statement by Stus, Dziuba, and Chornovil at the premiere of "Shadows of Forgotten Ancestors") and the pressure on the signatories of the "Letter of 139" in 1968, in which prominent cultural figures spoke out against unlawful political trials[227]. This also includes the crushing of the underground Ukrainian National Front: "in 1967 the UNF was uncovered by the state security organs," and eight of its members received long prison terms[228]. January 1734 – December 1750 C0029 The Governing Council of the Hetman Government and the Lubny Treaty (1734–1750) A long period of direct rule over the Left Bank without the election of a hetman. "The GOVERNANCE OF THE HETMAN'S GOVERNMENT was an organ of power created by the government of Russian empress Anna in 1734 after the death of hetman D. Apostol to govern Left-Bank Ukraine (the Hetmanate) and to prevent new hetman elections"; "in essence its head was the tsar's resident"[127]. At the same time the empire brought Zaporizhzhia back under control: "Anna amnestied the Zaporozhians and allowed them to return to the old Sich grounds (1734) and found the New Sich"[32] – on the eve of war with Turkey the Cossacks were being brought back as a military resource of the crown. July 1937 – December 1940 C1179 The Great Terror in Chechen-Ingushetia (1937-1940) By 1937 Chechnya had been through disarmament (campaign C1177) and the forced merging of peasant households into kolkhozes ("collectivization") with punitive expeditions against insurgent auls (campaign C1178). In 1934 the colonizer merged the oblast with Ingushetia into the united Chechen-Ingush Autonomous Oblast, and in 1936 renamed it the Chechen-Ingush Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic (ChIASSR); today the occupier calls these lands the Chechen Republic and the Republic of Ingushetia within Russia. Through this republic, as through other parts of the USSR, passed the Great Terror: that is what historians call the mass arrests and executions of 1937-1938, for which Moscow assigned each republic and oblast its own number. The repressions began with the resolution of the supreme organ of the occupation power (the "Politburo of the TsK VKP(b)") "On anti-Soviet elements" of 2 July 1937, signed by Stalin[229]. On 11 July 1937 the Politburo, by a separate decision, approved the number of people to be shot in the republic - separately for peasants whom the colonizer deemed "well-off" ("kulaks") and for "criminals"; the historian G. I. Kakagasanov cites it thus: "kulaks - 862 pers., criminals - 555 pers."[229]. On 30 July Yezhov, the People's Commissar (minister) of Internal Affairs of the USSR, issued operational order No. 00447 "On the operation to repress former kulaks, criminals and other anti-Soviet elements"; for the ChIASSR it records: 500 people - to be shot (the order's "first category"), 1,500 - to be confined in camps (the "second category")[230]. Already by mid-August 1937 the arrested were more numerous than recorded in the order, and on 1 March 1938 Moscow assigned the republic a new number - 10,108 people ordered arrested and convicted[231].
