Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write about the days of the deportation of the Chechens: "over the two or three days that the deportation lasted, killing one or two people here and there, the punitive forces destroyed in total no less than a thousand people. And it was announced loudly and distinctly, in Russian: for attempted escape - execution, for failure to obey an order - execution, for expressing protest - execution"[3]. The Chechen historian Dalkhan Khozhaev writes that the threats "were announced in Russian, though many did not understand the language," and the toll of reprisals began within the first hours: "On the Chechen plain hundreds of people (men, women, children and the old) were shot within a few hours"; in the mountains, where people were driven to the roads on foot, "more often than on the plain, they shot down stragglers, the enfeebled, those who misunderstood an order, or simply - 'attempting to escape'"[12]. Historian Z. S. Isakieva writes about the columns from the mountain villages: "Those who could not walk were led out of the column and shot, without even permission to bury them"[2]. T0162.003 Killing of Prisoners and Detainees February 1943 C1180.T0162.003 → C1180 Operation "Chechevitsa": the Total Deportation of the Chechen People and the Special Settlement Regime (1943-1949) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services In April-May 1943 officers of the Soviet NKVD (predecessor of today's FSB), led by Kolesnikov, Deputy People's Commissar (Minister) of Internal Affairs of the republic, in the course of "anti-banditry operations" detained Chechens "suspected of ties with bandits" and shot them "unlawfully, without trial or investigation" - 25 people in two months, "citizens guilty of nothing whatsoever": in the village of Bachi-Yurt, on the orders of cavalry platoon commander Volosov, the convoy shot 17 of 19 detainees, among them a 15-year-old girl; in the village of Belty a convoy headed by Soviet militia section commander Dubasov shot four people "without any pretext whatsoever" and delivered their corpses to the district branch of the NKVD; at the Kuloi hamlet Meishvili, a battalion commander of the NKVD troops (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia), shot the brothers Baisar and Baim Bataev, Dzhamalani Pitalov and Mavla Chebiev[1]. The executioners wrote the shootings off as "attempted escape," and Kolesnikov issued "findings that the use of weapons had been proper"; all this was established by the Chief Military Prosecutor's Office following a letter from the Chechen Dokhtukaev, written from exile - the results were reported in 1957 to Bulganin, head of the government of the USSR, but no one was ever brought to court: the ten-year statute of limitations had expired[1]. T0105 Total Destruction of Infrastructure February 1943 C1180.T0105 → C1180 Operation "Chechevitsa": the Total Deportation of the Chechen People and the Special Settlement Regime (1943-1949) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army During the deportation - Operation "Chechevitsa" - the troops of the Soviet NKVD (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) burned the mountain auls of the Chechens as soon as they had driven the residents under convoy to the trains bound for Kazakhstan and Kirghizia (today's Kyrgyzstan) and had driven off their livestock. The Chechen historian A. G. Avtorkhanov cites the testimony of a Russian student of the Grozny Petroleum Institute who was sent to one of the auls on the day of the deportation: "In the mountain auls this action was carried out differently. All the livestock was evacuated from there, and then the auls were burned, to deprive the 'bandits' of a base for existence. For days on end one could watch auls burning in the mountains"[8]. T0167.001 False Guarantees of Safety February 1943 C1180.T0167.001 → C1180 Operation "Chechevitsa": the Total Deportation of the Chechen People and the Special Settlement Regime (1943-1949) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The USSR lured out by deception the Chechens who were hiding in the mountains from the occupation regime, promising freedom - in the NKVD's (predecessor of today's FSB) papers this was called "legalization." Those who believed the promises were arrested or deported together with their compatriots to Kazakhstan and Kirghizia (today's Kyrgyzstan) in the course of the genocidal Operation "Chechevitsa." The report of Dementiev, head of the Grozny Oblast internal affairs directorate (1956), states: in September-October 1943 alone "30 bands were legalized, comprising 183 men, plus 60 lone bandits"[1]. Historian P. M. Polian writes: the NKVD files "listed 1,300 so-called legalized bandits, that is, men who had come forward, by mutual agreement, with a confession and been released from repression for it. All or nearly all of them were arrested shortly before the deportation or in its course"[1]. In the days of the deportation the troops announced clemency for those who had gone into the mountains - and deported those who came out. A Russian student eyewitness from Grozny, whose testimony was printed in the émigré journal Prometheus in 1949 and is cited by the Chechen historian A. G. Avtorkhanov, writes: "At the same time an amnesty [a promise not to punish] was announced for those who had gone into the mountains, if they came forward voluntarily. Some of them did in fact come forward, but were deported all the same…"[8]. In the summer of 1944 the colonizer repeated the deception: historian P. M. Polian writes that in June "tried and tested" religious authorities, deported in February, were brought from Kazakhstan to Grozny, and they induced hundreds of Chechens in hiding "toward legalization and, hence, deportation"[1]. T0122 Medical and Humanitarian Blockade February 1943 C1180.T0122 → C1180 Operation "Chechevitsa": the Total Deportation of the Chechen People and the Special Settlement Regime (1943-1949) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The colonizer cut the Chechens off from medical care from the first day of the deportation: the Chechen historian Dalkhan Khozhaev writes that the troops, driving people out of their homes, "threw the sick off their hospital beds"[12]. Typhus broke out in the trains - the certificate of the Soviet NKVD (predecessor of today's FSB) of 7 April 1944 on those brought to Kirghizia states: "412 people died and 278 were hospitalized"[13]. With no quarantine and no medicine at the destinations the epidemic spread: by 1 April 1944 about 4,800 people had fallen ill in Kazakhstan, over 2,000 in Kirghizia[3]. The colonizer forbade local residents, on pain of arrest, to help the dying Chechens. The Chechen historian A. G. Avtorkhanov writes: "The local population was categorically forbidden to render help to the dying by giving food, water or medicine. Even a simple display of human sympathy for the perishing women and children was punished with arrests"[8]. T0121 Artificial Famine February 1943 C1180.T0121 → C1180 Operation "Chechevitsa": the Total Deportation of the Chechen People and the Special Settlement Regime (1943-1949) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The USSR, deporting the Chechens and Ingush from their native land, made no provision for food at the places of exile - and from famine and disease in exile almost a third of the deported died within four and a half years. The Special Settlements Department of the Ministry of Internal Affairs tallied the toll for the Kazakh SSR: by 1 July 1949, of the Chechens, Ingush, Balkars and Karachays initially resettled there, 101,036 people had died - 23.3% of those brought in; "the highest mortality was among the deportees from the North Caucasus and the Kalmyks"[1]. The colonizer had taken the people's livestock and food back home: by the resolution of the State Defense Committee of the USSR of 31 January 1944 the people's commissariats (ministries) were obliged "to accept in the North Caucasus from the special settlers livestock and agricultural produce... issuing exchange receipts for what was accepted," while from the confiscated livestock 350 horses "fit for cavalry service" were handed over to the occupier's police cavalry units[10]. Pchelkin, People's Commissar (Minister) of Internal Affairs of the Kirghiz SSR, reported to People's Commissar (Minister) of Internal Affairs of the USSR Beria on 22 April 1944: the food the exiles had brought with them "is running out," "the established ration is critically insufficient," the collective farms are "in no position to help for lack of it, as a result of which in some districts there are instances... of the eating of roots and grasses"[1]. Historian P. M. Polian writes: for lack of food, shelter and fodder the exiles in Kirghizia "had to slaughter up to 90%" of the livestock issued "in compensation for that left behind in their former places of residence," while the funds allocated to them were handed out by local bosses to others - in the Kazalinsk district "one ton of bread was issued to the local party activists," and in the collective farms of the Bazar-Kurgan district "food was issued only to able-bodied special settlers, while those unfit for work were deprived of rations"[1]. In exile the Chechens and Ingush died by the tens of thousands: by the end of 1944 the number of exiles ("special settlers" in the colonizer's terms) had fallen by about 11.5 thousand in Kirghizia and by more than 46 thousand in Kazakhstan[3]. In 1945, among the North Caucasus exiles, 44,652 children died - 2,230 were born; no fewer than 80 thousand people were starving[3]; in the winter of 1948-1949 in the Kazakh SSR (today's Kazakhstan) up to 118 thousand were starving, and 418 people died of hunger[3]. By October 1948 about 146.9 thousand North Caucasus exiles had died in exile; historians put the direct losses of the Chechens and Ingush at 145.7 thousand people, and together with the unborn - at 300 thousand; the people recovered its pre-war numbers only by 1959[3]. T0032 Legal Segregation of the Population February 1943 C1180.T0032 → C1180 Operation "Chechevitsa": the Total Deportation of the Chechen People and the Special Settlement Regime (1943-1949) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The Soviet NKVD (predecessor of today's FSB) obliged the exiled Chechens and Ingush ("special settlers" in the colonizer's terms) over 12 years of age to report monthly to the special commandant's office - the agency's surveillance post at the place of exile; from age 16 the commandant's office opened personal files; the colonizer forbade them to join the Bolshevik party, its youth league (the "Komsomol") and the trade unions, and did not take them into the army[2]. From January 1945 the commandant could, without trial, arrest "offenders" for up to 5 days or fine them up to 100 rubles[3]. By the decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 26 November 1948 the deportation was declared eternal: the Chechens and Ingush were "exiled in perpetuity," with up to 20 years of hard labor for escape and up to 5 years of prison for aiding escapees[3]. T0142 Restriction of Settlement Geography February 1943 C1180.T0142 → C1180 Operation "Chechevitsa": the Total Deportation of the Chechen People and the Special Settlement Regime (1943-1949) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The colonizer locked the exiled Chechens and Ingush into their places of settlement: the commandant's offices forbade absences without their permission, and the mutual surety of the "ten-yard groups" was in force - ten neighboring households answered for one another[3]. People fled anyway: from the spring of 1944 to the end of 1950 - over 20.6 thousand escapes, and the chekists caught nearly all the escapees[3]. In 1948 the colonizer forbade the exiles to live within 100 kilometers of the USSR border and forcibly resettled over 6 thousand people deeper into Kazakhstan[3]. T0030 Administrative-Territorial Division February 1943 C1180.T0030 → C1180 Operation "Chechevitsa": the Total Deportation of the Chechen People and the Special Settlement Regime (1943-1949) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The colonizer abolished the very republic of the Chechens and Ingush and carved up their land among its neighbors: on 7 March 1944 the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR issued the decree "On the Liquidation of the Checheno-Ingush ASSR and the Administrative Organization of Its Territory"[2]: lowland Chechnya went into the newly created Grozny Okrug of Stavropol Krai - a month later the colonizer transformed it into Grozny Oblast[1]; the mountain part was divided between the Georgian SSR (today's Georgia) and the Dagestan ASSR (today's Dagestan within Russia), and the Ingush lands were handed to North Ossetia[3]. The abolition was given legal form by the law of 25 June 1946[2]. T0117.001 Migratory Replacement February 1943 C1180.T0117.001 → C1180 Operation "Chechevitsa": the Total Deportation of the Chechen People and the Special Settlement Regime (1943-1949) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services On 23 February 1944 the colonizer mobilized students and housewives not employed at factories in Grozny and from six in the morning drove them out to the Chechen auls, from which, half an hour after their arrival, the troops took away the arrested Chechens. The Chechen historian A. G. Avtorkhanov cites the testimony of one of the mobilized - a Russian student of the Grozny Petroleum Institute: "Thus we were, according to a carefully worked-out plan, distributed among the auls, 20-30 people per aul"[8]. The student writes about the work they were given in the auls: "The task of the students was to keep the farms in order until the arrival of the settlers from Kursk and Oryol oblasts. We were to gather the livestock, feed it, take in the grain, the implements, and so on"[8]. By mid-May 1944 settlers had arrived in Grozny Oblast numbering 40% of the deported Chechens, including 6,800 families from Stavropol Krai[3]. Into the districts handed to Dagestan the colonizer resettled 65 thousand people from 224 mountain villages of Dagestan[3]. The settlers died too: in the Aukh district in 1944-1947 about 2 thousand - nearly a third - of the resettled Laks, one of the mountain peoples of Dagestan, died of disease[3]. T0045.002 Burning of Books and Archives February 1943 C1180.T0045.002 → C1180 Operation "Chechevitsa": the Total Deportation of the Chechen People and the Special Settlement Regime (1943-1949) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services Having deported the Chechen people in February 1944, the colonizer burned its books and manuscripts. T0043 Erasure and Renaming of Place Names February 1943 C1180.T0043 → C1180 Operation "Chechevitsa": the Total Deportation of the Chechen People and the Special Settlement Regime (1943-1949) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The colonizer erased Chechen and Ingush names from the map. The Chechen lands that had gone to Georgia the colonizer named the Akhalkhevi district[3]. T0164 Pillage February 1943 C1180.T0164 → C1180 Operation "Chechevitsa": the Total Deportation of the Chechen People and the Special Settlement Regime (1943-1949) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army Deporting the Chechen people in February 1944, the colonizer looted its emptied homes. The Chechen historian Dalkhan Khozhaev writes: "In the days of the deportation, parallel to the human stream, columns of military trucks moved toward Grozny in an unbroken flow, loaded with the valuables looted from the emptied homes of the Chechens and Ingush. The items the guards deemed most valuable - carpets, burkas, Caucasian mounted belts, weapons ornamented with gold and silver (daggers, shashkas, flintlock rifles made by Chechen masters of the last century), jewels - were carried in canvas-covered vans"[12]. Drozdov, head of a brigade of the People's Commissariat (Ministry) of State Control of the RSFSR, who inspected the districts handed to Dagestan in August 1944 on the instructions of the government of the RSFSR, reported "unrestrained theft and squandering of the property of the special settlers," begun "soon after the deportation": Yusupov, acting chairman of a district soviet, "fully outfitted himself at the expense of the property of the special settlers" - he was short four hand-operated and four treadle sewing machines, 26 rugs, 30 carpets and 6 bicycles; Khashaev, prosecutor of Dagestan, received a house, an orchard, a vegetable garden and an "ownerless" cow; people's judge Suleimanov formalized his haul with a receipt: "Goods received, money not paid, to which I hereby subscribe"[12]. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov sum up: "Implicated in the unrestrained theft of other people's goods was the entire party-economic and militia top brass of Grozny Oblast, Dagestan, Stavropol, North Ossetia and Georgia"; those caught were dismissed and tried, but "in the end the arrests had to be abandoned, since no one would have been left at liberty to govern"[3]. title: Stalinist Terror and the End of Ukrainization (1922–1939), campaign C0052
content: Stalinist Terror and the End of Ukrainization (1922–1939) The suppression of the national revival in the USSR: the resolution of the Central Committee of the VKP(b) and the Council of People's Commissars of 14 December 1932, signed by Stalin and Molotov, declared that "Ukrainization was carried out mechanically" and ordered "to immediately transfer in the North Caucasus the record-keeping of the soviet and cooperative bodies of the 'Ukrainized' districts, as well as all published newspapers and journals, from the Ukrainian language to Russian"[1]; the annihilation of most Ukrainian writers of the 1920s-1930s went down in history as the "Executed Renaissance"[2]; the resolution of the USSR Council of People's Commissars and the Central Committee of the VKP(b) of 13 March 1938 No. 324 ordered "to introduce the teaching of the Russian language as a subject of study in the schools of the national republics and regions from September 1, 1938"[3]. The official turn was sealed by the resolution of the Central Committee of the VKP(b) and the Council of People's Commissars "On Grain Procurements in Ukraine, the North Caucasus, and the Western Region" of 14 December 1932, signed by Stalin and Molotov: Ukrainization was declared to have been carried out "mechanically," which, in the resolution's own words, "made it easier for bourgeois-nationalist elements, Petliurites and the like to create their legal covers, their counter-revolutionary cells and organizations"[1]. The term "Executed Renaissance" denotes precisely "the repressive policy of communist Moscow aimed at the physical destruction of the Ukrainian intellectual elite of the 1920s–30s (more broadly – of the entire nationally conscious Ukrainian intelligentsia) and the tabooing of its creative achievements"[2]. title: Denikin's terror in Chechnya: destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead (1919), campaign C1174
content: Denikin's terror in Chechnya: destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead (1919) In 1919 the Volunteer Army of General Denikin conquered Chechnya with ultimatums, assaults and the burning of villages - the year it left behind ended with 21 destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead. After the fall of the empire (campaign C1189) the peoples of the North Caucasus tried to live in a state of their own: in May 1918 the highland political forces proclaimed the independent Mountain Republic from the Black Sea to the Caspian; its first government was headed by the Chechen Tapa Chermoyev, an oil industrialist (campaign C1173), its parliament by the Ingush Vassan-Girey Dzhabagiev[1]. In February 1919 the Terek oblast was occupied by the Volunteer Army - troops of former imperial officers under the command of Denikin, fighting the Bolsheviks for the return of Russia within its former borders; historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "The main force of the Volunteer Army was made up of Cossacks, and therefore the actions of the Denikinites in the Terek oblast were aimed, first of all, at restoring the privileged position of the Cossacks"[1]. Denikin did not recognize the Mountain Republic: he refused to receive the delegation of its government; General Lyakhov, appointed ruler of the Terek oblast, agreed to regard the republic's parliament as no more than "a consultative organ attached to his person", and as ruler of Chechnya the Volunteer Army appointed General Aliev[1]. At the negotiations with the Mountain government Lyakhov declared: "...There cannot be two masters in one house. Where I pay, I shall be the master. I demand submission to my authority, and whoever does not submit to it, let him blame himself for what will come of it"[1]. The Denikin command recorded of the resistance: "The bitterness of the Chechens and their daring reach the utmost degree"[1]. The year's total was drawn by the Soviet survey of 1920, which historian E. F. Zhupikova cites: "21 destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead Chechens is what the Denikin army left behind it"[2]. ID: C1174 Start: February 1919 End: December 1919 Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.2 Created: 9 August 2026 Last Modified: 5 September 2026 Discuss on Telegram Actors ID Name Procedures G0014 White Movement (AFSR) 8 Instruments Applied ID Name Procedures S0010 Regular Army 8 Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: T0077 Punitive Expeditions February 1919 C1174.T0077 → C1174 Denikin's terror in Chechnya: destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead (1919) G0014 White Movement (AFSR) S0010 Regular Army At the end of February 1919 four regiments of the Volunteer Army - the division of General Shatilov - attacked the village of Goity with artillery, for its refusal to hand over the Red Army men sheltering there; detachments from the surrounding villages came to its aid, and the Denikinites retreated toward Grozny[1]. On 23 March the army struck from Grozny at Gudermes[1]. From 27 to 30 March battles raged for Alkhan-Yurt: "The shelling of the village was conducted by 24 guns and an armored train that had taken position near the Ermolovskaya stanitsa... the village was captured"; more than 400 of its defenders died[1]. For failure to fulfill the demand to return captured Cossacks the army stormed Tsatsan-Yurt - historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "On 9 April 1919 the White troops attacked and by nightfall captured the village of Tsatsan-Yurt. In the course of the fierce battle more than 500 people died on the Chechen side, including over 400 Tsatsan-Yurt villagers proper"[1]. In October the command threw against Chechnya a force of 15 thousand soldiers and officers taken off the advance on Moscow: "On 5 October stubborn three-day battles began for Chechen-Aul, after which the villages situated near the railway were subjected to a new devastation"[1]. T0105 Total Destruction of Infrastructure February 1919 C1174.T0105 → C1174 Denikin's terror in Chechnya: destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead (1919) G0014 White Movement (AFSR) S0010 Regular Army In its March offensive along the railway the Volunteer Army destroyed villages to the ground: "for several days stubborn battles went on, in the course of which the villages of Berdykel and Ustar-Gordoy ended up completely destroyed, and a number of other villages were captured"[1]. The year's count is kept by the Soviet survey cited by historian E. F. Zhupikova: 21 destroyed auls (27 in another publication of the same source) with 15 thousand dead[2]. The Chechen historian A. G. Avtorkhanov, who wrote of these events in emigration, gives both the motive and a list by name: the highlanders' desire "to arrange their state life at their own discretion" Denikin construed as "national Bolshevism", "hence the policy of burning auls and the extermination of the unsubmissive highlanders", and "to break the resistance of the Chechens and the Ingush, Denikin burned to the ground dozens of the largest centers of Chechnya-Ingushetia - Ekazhevo, Dolakovo, Alkhan-Yurt, Chechen-Aul, Ustar-Gardoy, Gudermes, Gerzel-Aul, Stary-Yurt and others" (Ekazhevo and Dolakovo are Ingush villages)[3]. T0163 Desecration of the Dead February 1919 C1174.T0163 → C1174 Denikin's terror in Chechnya: destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead (1919) G0014 White Movement (AFSR) S0010 Regular Army After capturing Alkhan-Yurt at the end of March 1919 the Volunteer Army for a month did not let the residents bury their dead - historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "As a punishment for the stubborn resistance, the White command for the course of a month did not permit the bodies of the village's fallen defenders to be committed to the earth"[1]. T0022 Terror February 1919 C1174.T0022 → C1174 Denikin's terror in Chechnya: destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead (1919) G0014 White Movement (AFSR) S0010 Regular Army The Volunteer Army answered the uprising in Grozny in December 1919 with mass executions: after the suppression of the rising on the night of 23 December the insurgent leader Gikalo reported: "Right now there are nightmarish reprisals in Grozny: 79 people have been hanged and a mass of people shot"[1]. T0147 Forced Registration of Subjecthood February 1919 C1174.T0147 → C1174 Denikin's terror in Chechnya: destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead (1919) G0014 White Movement (AFSR) S0010 Regular Army On 19 February 1919 General Lyakhov, at a congress of Chechnya's representatives in Aldy, announced the demands of the Volunteer Army, including mobilization: "These demands were put forward in the form of an ultimatum and were not subject to discussion," write historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov, and the congress left the ultimatum without an answer[1]. In April 1919 the command put forward a new ultimatum: "the complete submission of the Chechens to the appointed ruler of Chechnya, the handing over of all Red Army men, Bolsheviks and abreks, as well as of all the valuables carried off into Chechnya by the Red Army... the return of the pilfered materials from the railway and the organization of deliveries of provisions and fodder for the army"; for failure to fulfill a separate demand - to immediately return a group of Cossacks captured in the vicinity of the village - the army took Tsatsan-Yurt by storm[1]. T0156 Forced Surrender of Fugitives and Rebels February 1919 C1174.T0156 → C1174 Denikin's terror in Chechnya: destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead (1919) G0014 White Movement (AFSR) S0010 Regular Army In February 1919 the Volunteer Army demanded, through the Mountain government, the handing over of all Red Army men sheltering in Chechnya: "About 700 people were indeed prepared for handover, but this action met the resolute resistance of the Goity Soviet and the open discontent of the people," write historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov (the Goity Soviet - the soviet of the village of Goity); General Shatilov reported: "...unrest is taking place among the Chechens, as part of them do not want the Bolsheviks handed over"[1]. The demand to hand over "all Red Army men, Bolsheviks and abreks" entered the April ultimatum as well[1]. T0049 Forced Mobilization February 1919 C1174.T0049 → C1174 Denikin's terror in Chechnya: destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead (1919) G0014 White Movement (AFSR) S0010 Regular Army In February 1919 the Volunteer Army announced at the congress in Aldy a mobilization of the highlanders - at the villages' own expense: "the villages were obliged to equip and maintain the mobilized at their own cost"[1]. General Aliev, the appointed ruler of Chechnya, carried out the mobilization: "The 200-300 horsemen assembled in this way (together with Kabardians and Ingush) took part in the suppression of peasant unrest in the Stavropol region"[1]. Historian E. F. Zhupikova conveys the conclusion of the researcher P. Aptekar on the causes of the Chechens' uprising against Denikin: "the forcible mobilizations and requisitions of provisions for Denikin's army"[2]. T0037 Puppet Government February 1919 C1174.T0037 → C1174 Denikin's terror in Chechnya: destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead (1919) G0014 White Movement (AFSR) S0010 Regular Army In 1919 General Denikin refused to recognize the Mountain government and dissolved it[2]; General Lyakhov, appointed ruler of the Terek oblast, agreed to regard the republic's parliament as no more than "a consultative organ attached to his person"[1]. As ruler of Chechnya the Volunteer Army appointed a general from among the Chechens - historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "As Ruler of Chechnya on behalf of the Volunteer Army was appointed a well-known military man - General Eriskhan (Iriskhan) Aliev, a Chechen by origin"[1]. On 29 March 1919 Denikin convened a conference in Grozny - as the same historians write, one "called upon to put an end to the bloodshed and to confirm E. Aliev as ruler of Chechnya" - attended by representatives of 42 villages, mostly supporters of the Atagi Soviet (the Chechen National Council, which sat in Starye Atagi), entrepreneurs and part of the clergy[1]. References Ахмадов Я. З., Хасмагомадов Э. Х. История Чечни в XIX-XX веках. 2005. Жупикова Е. Ф. Повстанческое движение на Северном Кавказе в 1920-1925 годах. 2013. Авторханов А. Г. title: Derailing the Association with the EU (2013–2014), campaign C0099
content: Derailing the Association with the EU (2013–2014) Economic and political pressure by V. Putin on V. Yanukovych in the autumn of 2013 aimed at derailing the signing of the Association Agreement with the EU. The price was formalized publicly on December 17, 2013: "Ukraine will receive 15 billion dollars from Russia and gas at a reduced price" - the gas price was lowered "to 268.5 dollars per thousand cubic meters" instead of the previous 410, and the money came "from the Russian National Welfare Fund" in exchange for Ukrainian government securities[1]. The refusal to sign the agreement triggered the protests: "between 21 November 2013 and 22 February 2014 large-scale street protests took place, provoked by the decision of then-President Viktor Yanukovych not to sign the association agreement with the European Union," and their suppression ended in shootings - on the Maidan "between January and February 2014 more than 100 people were killed, including by snipers"[2]. title: Plundering Expeditions of Cossacks and Allied Princes (1718–1721), campaign C1128
content: Plundering Expeditions of Cossacks and Allied Princes (1718–1721) In 1718, the government of the Tsardom of Muscovy organized a large-scale invasion of the lands of the Nokhchi: historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov states that there occurred "a predatory expedition of detachments of Don Cossacks and Kabardian princes allied with Peter I into the ‘Chechen district’ along the Sunzha and the Argun"[1]. As a result of the raid, "800 captives were taken, not counting ‘belongings’"[1]. In 1721, the armed actions continued: the researcher points out that the Astrakhan governor A. P. Volynsky "invited the Don Cossacks and, together with the Terek Cossacks, organized raids to the Agrakhan and Aksai rivers against the Kumyks and Chechens"[1]. title: Police Registration and Restriction of Settlement (1631–1640), campaign C1117
content: Police Registration and Restriction of Settlement (1631–1640) The occupation administration of the Tsardom of Muscovy introduced rigid statistical control and restricted the right of the Nokhchi societies (Okochans, Michkiz, and Shibut) to free movement within the controlled territory. In 1631, Tsar Mikhail Fedorovich issued a decree to the Prikaz of the Kazan Palace on a census of the newcomer population of the town of Terki, directly prohibiting the free residence of unsanctioned migrants. The document prescribed identifying persons «whom it will not be possible to trust», and such people were «to be ordered sent out of the town of Terki, and ordered to go back to wherever each had come from, so that no harm would come to the town from them»[1]. To implement this mechanism, the metropole regularly conducted a total demographic accounting. In the state register of serving people for the region of the Prikaz of the Kazan Palace for 1637, the central authorities recorded in detail the number of inhabitants, including 350 serving «Okotsk people» and 680 newcomer «Okochans, and Tatars, and Michkiz, and Shibut»[2]. In 1640, on the orders of the Terek voivode, the Terek syn boyarsky P. Lukin and the clerk F. Belkov compiled a detailed name-by-name register of the population of the slobodas, rigidly documenting every household of the subordinated Nokhchi (Okochans) to ensure constant surveillance[1][2]. title: Abolition of the Cossack Order in Sloboda Ukraine (1765), campaign C0031
content: Abolition of the Cossack Order in Sloboda Ukraine (1765) An imperial reform to liquidate the military-social structure of Sloboda Ukraine: "The conclusions of this investigation, with the participation of a Senate commission, led to the verdict of the Governing Senate on the liquidation of the autonomous order on December 16, 1764, and a series of experimental innovations approved by Catherine II's manifesto of July 28, 1765. On the basis of the Sloboda regiments the Sloboda-Ukrainian Governorate was formed, out of the military forces – 5 hussar regiments of the same names (see Hussars), and the bulk of the Cossack population was transferred to the category of military settlers"[1]. title: "Eternal Peace" with Poland (1686), campaign C0009
content: "Eternal Peace" with Poland (1686) The legal legitimation of the partition of territories between the Tsardom of Muscovy and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth behind the Hetmanate's back, definitively turning Ukraine into a rightless object of bargaining. The deal was sealed financially – under the text of the 1686 treaty Moscow undertook "for eternal peace to count out a genuine sum of money, that is, one hundred forty-six thousand Muscovite rubles, and hand it over to the Commonwealth"[1]. "Russian historians usually assess the Eternal Peace as Golitsyn's great diplomatic success, Polish ones – as their major defeat, and contemporary Ukrainian ones – as a national tragedy of Ukraine"[2]. Ukrainian historiography recorded the deal as an ordinary purchase - Hrushevsky: Muscovy "concluded an eternal accord with Poland (paying, in addition, another 146 thousand rubles for Kyiv)"[4]. The treaty also secured an ecclesiastical lever: the Orthodox eparchies in the Commonwealth "according to their spiritual rank and custom, are to receive blessing and ordination from the Metropolitan of Kyiv; and this shall harm none of them in the favor of His Royal Majesty"[5] - while the Kyiv metropolitanate was already subordinated to Moscow. title: Establishment of the "Pale of Settlement" (1791), campaign C0036
content: Establishment of the "Pale of Settlement" (1791) The introduction of discriminatory legislation that territorially restricted the rights of the Jewish population: decree No. 17,006 of December 23, 1791 confirmed the ban on Jews enrolling in the merchantry in the internal Russian cities and ports, extending the rights of citizenship and burgher status only to the Ekaterinoslav Viceroyalty and the Tauride region[1]. From the totality of such acts emerged the Pale of Settlement, running predominantly through colonized Ukrainian territories. title: Founding and Fortification of the Terek Town (1588–1623), campaign C1110
content: Founding and Fortification of the Terek Town (1588–1623) The occupation administration of the Tsardom of Muscovy established a new military base at the mouth of the Terek River to control the adjacent territories, including the lands of the Nokhchi. Historian E. N. Kusheva writes that the base "was built in 1588–1589... by Mikhailo Burtsev and Kelar Protasyev... the main force of its garrison consisted of streltsy armed with 'fire combat' — pishchal firearms"[1]. The base's infrastructure was systematically expanded: historians A. S. Kulikov and V. A. Runov note that "by the beginning of the 17th century... the Terek fortified town had turned into a rather powerful fortress. Its artillery numbered 40 large guns, and its garrison — more than a thousand streltsy and Cossacks"[2]. To hold its positions, the administration brought in additional military personnel: historian I. Kh. Tkhamokova notes that "in 1589, soon after the town was built, 800 streltsy and Cossacks were to be sent there from Astrakhan, but the Astrakhan voivode sent only 600 men"[3]. A permanent military contingent on state provision was entrenched in this territory: historian I. Kh. Tkhamokova cites a tsar's decree according to which "in 1623, 'upon the petition of the Terek and Greben Cossacks,' a tsar's decree was sent to the Terek ordering the payment of salaries to 30 atamans and 470 rank-and-file Cossacks"[3]. title: Comprehensive Reconnaissance of Territories and an Attempt to Coerce into Subjecthood (1658–1660), campaign C1119
content: Comprehensive Reconnaissance of Territories and an Attempt to Coerce into Subjecthood (1658–1660) The occupation administration of the Tsardom of Muscovy gathered military-strategic and economic intelligence on the mountain societies of the Nokhchi (the Shibutians) and made attempts at their forcible subjugation. In 1658, the central apparatus of the Ambassadorial Prikaz instructed the Terek voivodes to send a mission into the mountains, in order «concerning those little lands... to order that they be examined and truly scouted out — how many of them there are and what kind of people they are... and what fighting capability they have... and what grows in their land, and what craftsmen there are»[1]. The document of the central authority also directly stated «to order that amanats be taken from among their kin, men of note»[1]. To carry out the order, in 1659 the Terek voivodes Melenty Kvashnin and his associates dispatched a military emissary: an extract for the report of the Ambassadorial Prikaz to Tsar Aleksei Mikhailovich of 1660 states that the voivodes «sent a streltsy head into the Shibut land and ordered him to inspect in the Shibut land the Christian faith, and church building, and towns, and places, and to bring them to the faith, and to take an amanat to the Terek»[1]. The emissary carried out the reconnaissance, reporting that «they have no church building, nor to]wns, nor any fighting forces»[1], but he was unable to subjugate the population: «he did not brin[g] the inhabitants of the Shibut land to the faith»[1]. The seizure of new hostages likewise ended without result; the emissary merely stated that the mountaineers «wish [to be] under the lofty sovereign hand, and on the Terek they [have an amanat]»[1]. title: Suppression of the Uprising of Murat Kuchukov and Terror against the Indigenous Population (1708), campaign C1126
content: Suppression of the Uprising of Murat Kuchukov and Terror against the Indigenous Population (1708) In 1708, the Tsardom of Muscovy employed radical violence to suppress an armed uprising of the Indigenous population. The revolt was caused by the methods previously laid down by the metropole within the campaign C1124: Punitive Raids and Economic Strangulation of the Nokhchi, 1691–1700: systematic abuses by the voevodas and a discriminatory economic policy. Historian Sh. B. Akhmadov states that, because of the duties, "the economic interaction of the Vainakhs with Russia... was practically paralyzed"[1]. In response to the siege of the town of Terki by detachments led by Murat Kuchukov, the government organized large-scale operations: historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov states that "the measures taken by Peter I to combat the Bulavin ‘rebellion’ and other uprisings, including on the Terek against Chechnya, were, in essence, punitive"[2]. The Regular Army carried out sweep operations: he emphasizes that "military detachments were sent to the Terek that physically exterminated any population showing the slightest disobedience"[2]. Military pressure was supplemented by collusion with a third party: the researcher adds that on September 30, 1708, the diplomatic apparatus concluded an agreement with the Kalmyk khan Ayuka that included a clause "on the persecution of Chechens and Nogais"[2]. To neutralize the opposition, the metropole took the leader of the insurgents captive: Akhmadov points out that the tsar "personally decided the fate of the rebel leaders"[2], as a result of which the leader, "taken prisoner while wounded, was hanged"[2]. Total intimidation was ensured through demonstrative terror: the author records that the execution was carried out "by the rib on a hook, in accordance with Peter I’s order to P.M. Apraksin (‘inflict a cruel death penalty’)"[2]. title: Creation of the Little Russian Governorate-General (1801–1811), campaign C0038
content: Creation of the Little Russian Governorate-General (1801–1811) Administrative absorption: "the LITTLE RUSSIAN GOVERNORATE-GENERAL – an administrative-territorial and political unit of the Russian Empire, created in 1802 for the incorporation and integration of Left-Bank Ukraine into the Russian Empire"[1]. The outcome is recorded there as well: "During the existence of the governorate-general, the remnants of the Hetmanate's autonomy were finally liquidated"[1]. ID: C0038 Start: January 1801 End: December 1811 Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.2 Created: 25 April 2026 Last Modified: 6 August 2026 Discuss on Telegram Actors ID Name Procedures G0009 Russian Empire 2 Instruments Applied ID Name Procedures S0008 Government 2 Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: T0030 Administrative-Territorial Division January 1801 C0038.T0030 → C0038 Creation of the Little Russian Governorate-General (1801–1811) G0009 Russian Empire S0008 Government The erasure of historical borders and the introduction of the imperial vertical: "The governor-general concentrated the entire fullness of administrative power: he was endowed with the right of legislative initiative, determined the degree to which all-Russian laws extended within the governorate-general, and controlled the activity of state institutions, including judicial ones"[1]. T0158 Territorial Marking with Imperial Symbols January 1801 C0038.T0158 → C0038 Creation of the Little Russian Governorate-General (1801–1811) G0009 Russian Empire S0008 Government In 1804-1811 the Russian Empire put up a cast-iron Monument of Glory in the center of Poltava in memory of its victory over the army of Charles XII on 27 June 1709 - with the city's own money and to a design sent from St. Petersburg. By the imperial decree to the Senate of 11 September 1804, "On leaving the villages formerly owned by the city of Poltava under state administration and on releasing the income collected from them to the local Governor-General for the construction in Poltava of a monument in memory of 27 June 1709," the city's revenues were assigned to the monument: "the community of Poltava citizens, through a petition submitted to Governor-General Prince Kurakin, has designated all these revenues for the construction in Poltava of a monument in memory of the day unforgettable for Russia, 27 June 1709, and so we command: the revenues now due for payment, as well as those henceforth collected in favor of this city, shall be released to the local Governor-General until the monument that has been begun is completely finished"[2]. By a second act, the imperial rescript of 9 May 1805 to the Governor-General of Little Russia, "On the construction of a monument in commemoration of the victory won at Poltava by Emperor Peter the Great," the emperor sent a ready-made design and ordered construction to begin: "I forward to you herewith the plans for this monument, drawn up here, charging you... to proceed with its construction on site, except for the bronze ornaments belonging to it, which will be made separately here and delivered to their destination"[2]. That is, Poltava pays, while Petersburg decides what the sign on its land will look like - down to the bronze, which is cast there and shipped ready-made. The monument was founded on 27 June 1804, the cast-iron column was raised in May 1809 under the direction of Moskvin, an engineer of the Luhansk works, and the whole ensemble was opened on 27 June 1811, for the next anniversary of the battle[3][4]. On the medallion of the upper square of the pedestal, inside a serpent ring between two quivers, stood "June the 27th, 1709," and on the opposite side - "Finished in 1809"[3]: the date of someone else's victory was made into the date of the place itself. Both inscriptions, together with the bronze bas-reliefs, disappeared in 1901 - the pre-revolutionary survey records it tersely: "This inscription and the preceding one were destroyed in 1901, and at the same time the bronze bas-reliefs that surrounded them were taken by persons unknown"[3]; they were restored only during the capital repairs of 1953[4]. The monument still stands in Poltava: as of August 2026 it is listed as a monument of national significance under heritage protection number 160010-Н[5], the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance recommended dismantling it in a letter of 29 July 2024[6], but decisions on monuments of national significance are made by the government, and the list of such decisions as of 20 May 2026 does not include the monument[7]. title: Kolomak Articles (1687), campaign C0007
content: Kolomak Articles (1687) Another stage of the assault on autonomy: a treaty with Moscow that eliminated independent diplomacy ("a hetman shall not be elected... nor shall they write anything to anyone on their own behalf"), prohibited declaring one's own subjecthood, and demanded: "to unite the Little Russian people with the Great Russian people by all measures and means... through marriage"[1]. ID: C0007 Start: January 1687 End: January 1687 Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.2 Created: 24 April 2026 Last Modified: 5 September 2026 Discuss on Telegram Actors ID Name Procedures G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy 7 Instruments Applied ID Name Procedures S0009 Diplomacy 6 S0010 Regular Army 1 Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: T0031 Restriction of Sovereignty January 1687 C0007.T0031 → C0007 Kolomak Articles (1687) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0009 Diplomacy The systematic dismantling of the autonomy's democratic institutions. Moscow categorically forbade the Cossacks to elect their leaders independently and to conduct an independent foreign policy: "and without a petition and without a decree of the great sovereigns... a hetman shall not be elected... nor shall they, on their own... write anything to anyone"[1]. The abolition of the historical right to grant asylum: the autonomy was forced to perform the functions of the Muscovite punitive apparatus and to hand over fugitives: "and those fugitives and people of all ranks shall not be received, nor kept among them"[1]. T0041 Implantation of Officials and Military Personnel January 1687 C0007.T0041 → C0007 Kolomak Articles (1687) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0010 Regular Army To ensure constant armed oversight of the autonomy's top leadership and to prevent uprisings, the Tsardom of Muscovy stationed its regular troops directly in the hetman's capital: "with the hetman in Baturyn, for his protection and safety, there shall be a Muscovite streltsy regiment..."[1]. T0010 Denial of a Distinct Identity January 1687 C0007.T0010 → C0007 Kolomak Articles (1687) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0009 Diplomacy The introduction of strict political censorship. Under threat of punishment, the population was forbidden even to say aloud that their lands constituted a separate state entity: "and let no one utter such voices, that the Little Russian land is of the hetman's regiment"[1]. T0117.002 Encouragement of Mixed Marriages January 1687 C0007.T0117.002 → C0007 Kolomak Articles (1687) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0009 Diplomacy The use of demographic engineering to accelerate assimilation. Moscow openly proclaimed a course toward erasing ethnic boundaries by encouraging marriages with Great Russians: "to unite the Little Russian people with the Great Russian people by all measures and means... through matrimony and other conduct..."[1]. T0008 Deprivation of Agency January 1687 C0007.T0008 → C0007 Kolomak Articles (1687) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0009 Diplomacy "In this provision of the articles, the tsarist government's aspiration to turn Ukraine into a region incorporated into the Russian state on ordinary terms was openly declared for the first time"[2]. title: Collective punishment in the abrek era: fines, quartering of troops and exile for Zelimkhan (1905-1913), campaign C1175
content: Collective punishment in the abrek era: fines, quartering of troops and exile for Zelimkhan (1905-1913) In 1905-1913 the Russian Empire dealt reprisals to entire Chechen villages: it fined them, quartered troops at the residents' own expense, exiled relatives and hundreds of families, demolished hamlets. There were two pretexts - the revolution of 1905 and the abrek Zelimkhan. By the beginning of the 20th century forty years had passed since the end of the Caucasus War, but, as historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write, "Chechnya was governed by measures characteristic of a state of martial law", a "military-occupation regime" persisted in the land, and the restrictive measures only grew[1]. Onto this background fell the first Russian revolution of 1905-1907: on 24 October 1905 martial law was imposed across the whole of Chechnya, and from January 1906 field courts-martial went to work[1]. The second pretext was the abrek phenomenon - "abrek" was the empire's word for a highlander declared an outlaw who had gone to the mountains with a weapon. The most famous of them was Zelimkhan from the village of Kharachoy: in 1901, by his own words, he was a family man from a well-off household with a mill and an apiary, but after a quarrel between two families over a betrothal the authorities arrested him together with his old father and relatives; Zelimkhan escaped from the Grozny prison and until his death in 1913 remained the administration's chief enemy in the land[1]. The authorities answered not him but everyone - on top of that there was the weapons ban, which "applied exclusively to the highlanders and the out-of-town settlers and did not extend to the Cossacks"[1]. Against individual villages and entire aul districts, the same historians record, "collective punishments were widely practiced"[1]. Such reprisals were lawless even by the empire's own standards: Article 50 of the Hague Regulations on the Laws and Customs of War on Land - a convention signed and ratified by the Russian Empire - laid down: "No general penalty, pecuniary or otherwise, shall be inflicted upon the population on account of the acts of individuals for which they cannot be regarded as jointly and severally responsible"[2]. And a military directive of late 1907 prescribed, in the event of an uprising, to act by "scattering the bands to the point of total annihilation, and likewise wiping off the face of the earth the villages that sheltered them, bearing in mind that such a method will be not only more effective but also more humane"[1]. The Chechen revolutionary Aslanbek Sheripov summed up the outcome: "The authorities terrorized the peaceful population, and the abreks terrorized these authorities..."[1].
