I say: 'There are no militants here'… Armored personnel carriers... They fire from heavy machine guns. Right in the village. At the house where people live... Either they burn the house down, or the house perishes, anything at all..."[5]. On 7 and 8 April the Russian military killed 103 Chechen civilians in Samashki, whom human rights defenders recorded by name (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[5][1]. On 3 March 1995 the command of the occupation troops demanded that the Chechens in Argun, Gudermes and Shali, towns to the east and southeast of Grozny, persuade the Armed Forces of Ichkeria to leave in order to save people's lives[1][5]. On 23 March the occupiers captured Argun, and on 30-31 March, when the defenders were forced to leave, Gudermes and Shali (see: "Military Intervention")[1]. On 8 April Labunets, the commander of the occupation troops in the south of Ichkeria, threatened in writing to shell Zakan-Yurt, a village to the east of Samashki, with artillery if the Chechens in the village did not hand over their weapons and surrender the fighters of the army of Ichkeria, and on 11 April soldiers of the Russian MVD searched every yard and found no weapons[70][5]. In April 1995 the Chechens in Bachi-Yurt, Koshkeldy and Alleroy, villages in the east of Ichkeria, under threat of bombing bought assault rifles and handed them over to the occupiers, but the Russian military shelled these villages anyway (see: "Total Destruction of Infrastructure")[58][1]. The Internal Troops of the Russian MVD and the Russian police kept Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria where more than 10,000 people and more than 3,000 refugees lived, encircled for more than five months, from 30 September 1995 until the storming in March 1996[69][1]. Artemov, the commander of the occupation troops in the southwest of Ichkeria, threatened the village in writing with artillery and air strikes if the village did not disarm about a hundred fighters of the army of Ichkeria and let Russian vehicles through Sernovodsk[69]. On 11 February 1996 the command of the occupation troops demanded that the Chechens in Novogroznensky, a settlement in the east of Ichkeria, hand over their weapons and expel the defenders, and when the defenders did not leave, the occupiers killed at least 50 Chechen civilians in the settlement by shelling and storming (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[1]. In March 1996 the Russian military demanded that Katyr-Yurt, a village to the southwest of Grozny, hand over assault rifles and ten captured Russian soldiers who were not in the village, and on 28 March a Russian pilot dropped bombs on the village and killed nine people from the Khazhgiriyev family (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[21][1]. In the spring of 1996 the command of the occupation troops and the puppet government in Grozny forced villages to sign a "Protocol on Peace and Accord". Under this document a village undertook to surrender the defenders, hand over weapons and let the Russian military in, and for a single fighter of the army of Ichkeria found in the village the occupiers threatened to shoot Chechens and destroy the village[21]. On 31 March 1996 Russian President Yeltsin, by Decree No. 435, made the signing of such protocols part of his program for Ichkeria[71], and Russian aircraft bombed villages that refused to sign the protocol[1]. On 17 April 1996 the Chechens in Chiri-Yurt, a village to the south of Grozny, released captured Russian servicemen under an ultimatum from General Shamanov, but as the occupiers' vehicles were leaving the village, Russian tank crews with a single shot razed to the ground the house of the family of Abdulla Dakhayev, the representative of the authorities of Ichkeria in Chiri-Yurt[1]. On 19 April the occupiers surrounded Shali, and on 25 April demanded that the town surrender the defenders, hand over weapons and release captured Russian soldiers. On the same day Russian pilots bombed the town (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[72][1]. At the end of April the elders of Komsomolskoye signed a peace agreement with the occupiers, but from 30 April to 1 May Russian pilots bombed the village and wounded four Chechen civilians[73]. On 6 May Russian troops captured Shali without a fight; there turned out to be no defenders or prisoners there[1]. On that day the occupiers surrounded Komsomolskoye and threatened to destroy it if the fighters of the army of Ichkeria did not hand over their weapons by nightfall, but at about three in the afternoon, before the deadline, Russian artillery opened fire and killed several Chechen civilians[21]. On 8 July 1996 Tikhomirov, the commander of the occupation troops, at a press conference in Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny, threatened Ichkeria with retaliatory measures if Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the acting president of Ichkeria, did not return all Russian prisoners on 9 July[74]. From 9 to 15 July Russian troops surrounded and shelled Gekhi, a village to the southwest of Grozny where a unit of the army of Ichkeria was stationed, and Makhkety, a mountain village in the southeast of the republic. In Gekhi the occupiers killed 19 Chechen civilians, in Makhkety 25 (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[38][6][75]. From 10 July the occupation command introduced a curfew in Ichkeria and banned driving into and out of Grozny by car[1][6]. The Russian military destroyed the houses of relatives of the leaders of Ichkeria and the commanders of its army[1][6]. On 15 July 1996 the crews of seven Russian helicopters struck Starye Atagi, a village to the south of Grozny, with missiles and destroyed the house of the mother of Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the acting president of Ichkeria, but the mother and the neighbors survived[6][38]. In the summer of 1996 the Russian military blew up the house of the father of Shamil Basayev, one of the commanders of the army of Ichkeria, in the mountain village of Vedeno[1]. On 19 August 1996 Pulikovsky, the acting commander of the occupation troops, demanded that the army of Ichkeria leave Grozny and gave the citizens of Ichkeria 48 hours to leave the city, where, according to some data, at least 50-70 thousand people remained, and according to others, 300 thousand[1][6][24]. The general threatened after that deadline to strike the city with aircraft, artillery and multiple rocket launchers, which cannot fire with precision, and on the night of 20 August, without waiting for the deadline to expire, the occupiers resumed the shelling and bombing of Grozny[6]. The human rights defenders of Memorial write that the command of the occupation troops made its demands of a whole village and, in case of refusal, threatened reprisals against everyone who lived in it[1]. A Human Rights Watch report of May 1995 says that demands to hand over weapons sometimes serve the Russian military as a pretext for attacking a village or for detaining Chechens[58]. It is unknown how many such crimes the occupation troops committed from December 1994 to August 1996. On 21 August 1996 General Lebed, the secretary of the Russian Security Council, canceled General Pulikovsky's threat to strike Grozny and called it a bad joke to journalists[6][76]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1]. T0023 Filtration Camp System September 1994 C1193.T0023 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0017 Secret Police and Security Services In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers unlawfully detained Chechens and held them without charges in filtration camps and in pits at military units. On 12 December 1994, the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs created filtration camps by directive No. 247. The ministry set them up in prison railcars in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia, in the prisons of Stavropol and Pyatigorsk, cities in the south of Russia, and in the building of a motor depot in Grozny[1][77]. Russian servicemen together with police officers detained Chechens at checkpoints and during "zachistki" ("sweeps", as Russians called house searches and detentions of Chechens). In its detention orders, the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs most often referred to the decree of the president of Russia of 2 November 1993 No. 1815 "On Measures to Prevent Vagrancy and Begging"[78]. The decree concerned vagrants, while most of the detained Chechens had their documents on them[1]. Before sending them to the camps, the occupiers held Chechens for several days in pits and prison vans at checkpoints and at their bases, in places with no official status[1]. There were such pits in the 503rd and 506th regiments of the Russian army near Shali, a town southeast of Grozny[21][1]. From February 1995, the occupiers brought Chechens to Assinovskaya, a stanitsa in the west of Ichkeria, and from there sent them to Mozdok[1]. In the camps, Russian guards beat and tortured detained Chechens during interrogations, including with electric current (see: "Torture and Abuse"). The guards did not treat the wounded[77]. The occupiers did not let detained Chechens tell their relatives where they were. For their families, the people went missing (see: "Abduction of People")[1]. The Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs released most of the detained Chechens from the camps as innocent. From each of them the ministry took a signature saying they had no complaints[1]. According to a certificate by Zlydenko, deputy head of Russia's prison service, from 11 December 1994 to 22 July 1995, 1,325 people passed through the camps in Mozdok and Grozny. The Ministry of Internal Affairs handed a hundred of them over to investigators (see: "Manufacturing Criminals"). The ministry gave another 141 people up for exchange for captured Russian servicemen (see: "Hostage-Taking")[1]. During the storming of Grozny in early January 1995, the Russian troops of General Rokhlin detained men in the bomb shelters near the cannery, where they were hiding from the shelling, and took them to Mozdok[77]. On 3 January, the guards carried more than 60 of them in the back of a single truck and killed at least eight on the way (see: "Killing of Prisoners and Detainees")[1]. On 10 January, the Chechen Umar Kasayev died in the Pyatigorsk prison: the Ministry of Internal Affairs did not give him the medical care he needed[77]. On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria. Officers of the FSK (the predecessor of today's FSB) flew in to the Russian checkpoint near the village with lists of Chechens "subject to filtration"[70][5]. On 8 April, soldiers of the Internal Troops and of police special units from Orenburg and Moscow searched the houses of Samashki. By 10 April, the occupiers had unlawfully detained and taken out of the village more than 200 Chechen men aged 15 to 70, and the escort shot three of them dead on the way (see: "Killing of Prisoners and Detainees")[70][1]. Azman Ansarova from Samashki told the "Memorial" observers that when one of the detained men showed a soldier his passport, "he took the document and tore it to shreds. 'I don't need your documents,' he says. 'You are Chechens — we are going to kill you'… Then they took our sons and drove them away"[5]. The occupiers sent some of the men by helicopter to Mozdok and held others in pits and prison vans near Assinovskaya. On 5 August 1995, Khasan Rasuyev from Samashki told "Memorial" how the guards loaded the detainees into the back of a truck: "And in stacks — into the back. In four layers, I think, one on top of another"[1][5]. Near Assinovskaya, the Russian military released most of the men without certificates of detention, and from Mozdok, by 18 April, the Ministry of Internal Affairs had released 65 Chechens from Samashki as innocent and given 12 up for exchange[1][5]. In April 1995, Russian servicemen took the brother of the Chechen woman Khaza Arsanukayeva from his home in Grozny at night, citing his residence registration in Kalmykia, a Russian-controlled republic by the Caspian Sea. The soldiers beat him at the headquarters of the occupation troops and took him to the filtration camp on the northeastern outskirts of the city, and a week later the guards released him: he could not walk[20]. On 15 March 1996, at the checkpoint near Samashki, the occupiers picked out 91 Chechens from among those leaving the village before the assault and took them to the prisons of Pyatigorsk and Stavropol. Five weeks later, the Ministry of Internal Affairs released them without charges[1]. In March 1996, soldiers of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs detained three Chechens at the checkpoint between Goity and Starye Atagi, villages south of Grozny, and on 7 April Russian servicemen took the Chechen Saidash Shamakhurov from Gikalovo, a village near Grozny. The Russians held all four in Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny, and exchanged them for their own captured soldiers (see: "Hostage-Taking")[28]. In its 1995 comments, the UN Human Rights Committee expressed concern at reports of torture, ill-treatment and arbitrary detention in filtration camps[79]. In early 1997, the human rights defenders of "Memorial" wrote that Russian agencies "are not making substantial efforts to search for Chechens who were detained and went missing"[80]. "Memorial" published the accounts of detainees and lists of Chechens whom the Ministry of Internal Affairs held in the prisons of Pyatigorsk and Stavropol from January to February 1995[77]. On 10 June 1996, in Nazran, a town in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, Russia undertook before Ichkeria to close the filtration camps and the other places where it unlawfully held Chechens[81]. In June, the Ministry of Internal Affairs closed the last camps[1]. Russian courts convicted no one for creating the camps and for the unlawful detentions (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")[1]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1]. T0162.004 Torture and Abuse September 1994 C1193.T0162.004 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0017 Secret Police and Security Services In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers beat and tortured detained Chechens. Russian soldiers together with police officers beat them at checkpoints and during "zachistki" ("sweeps", as Russians called house searches and detentions of Chechens)[5]. The occupiers' escorts beat them in trucks and helicopters. On unloading, the soldiers made them run between two rows of guards, who beat the running men with clubs and rifle butts[1][5]. During interrogations, Russian servicemen and police officers demanded that Chechens admit they had fought, name soldiers of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria and the places where weapons were hidden[1]. In pits, prison vans and tanks, Russian guards held them for several days with their hands tied, blindfolded, without water or food[1][28]. The occupiers released the beaten prisoners without charges or gave them up for exchange for captured Russian servicemen (see: "Hostage-Taking")[1]. Russian servicemen and police officers, from soldiers at checkpoints to military investigators at bases, tortured Chechens from December 1994 to September 1996. On 25 December 1994, near the settlement of Dolinsky northwest of Grozny, Russian soldiers detained and beat Ali Israilov from Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria. The guards of the camp in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia, beat him for three more days and released him. After the beatings, Ali Israilov spent a month and a half in treatment[77]. Until the end of January 1995, the OMON from Ryazan, a Russian police unit, guarded the filtration camp of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs in Mozdok and tortured detained Chechens during interrogations in prison railcars (see: "Filtration Camp System"). The guards whom the Ministry of Internal Affairs sent to replace them on 24-26 January did not torture during interrogations, but beat the prisoners[1]. On 1 January 1995, Russian soldiers detained Zakrail Vairayev near the cannery in Grozny, and the guards in Mozdok and in Pyatigorsk, a city in the south of Russia, beat him so badly that his chest cracked and his tuberculosis flared up. The guards of the Mozdok camp left him, sick, in a prison railcar for eight days and then sent him to a hospital in Nazran, a town in Russian-controlled Ingushetia[77]. From 3 January to 15 February 1995, the guards of the camp near the cannery in Grozny, the escorts and the guards of the prisons in Pyatigorsk and in Stavropol, another city in the south of Russia, beat Magomed Meiriev from Grozny, and in Pyatigorsk they set a dog on him. On 15 February, the occupiers released him in Mozdok with scars from rifle butts and bites[77]. On 23 January 1995, at checkpoint No. 13 between Sernovodsk and the neighboring village of Samashki, officers of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs beat Akhmed Idrisov from Grozny, threatening to kill him, and on 31 January released him as innocent, with broken ribs[77]. In the spring of 1995, the guards of the camp near the cannery in Grozny gave the prisoners urine instead of water[21]. On 25 March 1995, Russian soldiers detained the Chechen Isani Khanoyev in his home in Assinovskaya, a stanitsa in the west of Ichkeria. The guards of the military unit near the stanitsa beat him at night and tortured him with electric current, and on 6 April the Ministry of Internal Affairs released him from Mozdok as innocent[1]. From the end of January 1995, Russian servicemen held detained Chechens in pits and prison vans at military units, where human rights defenders and prosecutors were not allowed. There were such pits in Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny, and near Assinovskaya[1]. On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) stormed Samashki. That day, officers of the Ministry of Internal Affairs detained at a checkpoint Makhmudemin Iziev from Samashki, who was leaving with his family for Sernovodsk, and sent him by helicopter to the field command post of the Russian troops near Assinovskaya[1]. On 8 April, soldiers of the Internal Troops beat Chechen men and teenagers with rifle butts during searches in Samashki, and at the military unit north of the village and near Assinovskaya soldiers set dogs on them[5][70][14]. Near Assinovskaya, the guards held Makhmudemin Iziev for three days without water or food in a prison van at the bottom of a pit. During interrogations, the servicemen beat him in the kidneys and the chest, attached wires to his neck and tortured him with electric current, which left burns[5][1]. On 10 April, the occupiers sent him by helicopter to the filtration camp in Mozdok, and that day six underage Chechens from Samashki were released from there bruised and with bite marks[5][70][14]. Before the visit of representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross on 11-13 April, the camp guards threatened the detained Chechens: "They will leave, and you will stay here"[5]. On 18 April, the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs released Makhmudemin Iziev as innocent. On 20 April, in Sernovodsk, he told the "Memorial" observers about Mozdok: "During interrogations they beat me again and threatened to shoot me. The investigator himself did not beat me; people in masks did the beating when he left the compartment"[1]. In the summer of 1995, the guards near Assinovskaya hung Ramzan Isayev from Alkhan-Yurt, a village southwest of Grozny, by his handcuffs, burned his feet with a torch, squeezed his head with a metal hoop and tortured him with electric current, and then the occupiers gave him up in exchange for a captive from the Russian army[1]. In July 1995, Russian soldiers put Mikael Ivgiev, a journalist of the Chechen magazine "Orga", for two weeks into a tank buried in the ground in Khankala, where the servicemen tortured him with electric current and hung him by his hands tied behind his back; Mikael Ivgiev survived[1]. On 23 December 1995, Russian servicemen detained Ruslan Soslambekov at a checkpoint at the entrance to Grozny and held him for 28 days in a camp of the Ministry of Internal Affairs in garages on the outskirts of the city, where the guards, in front of him, set dogs on prisoners and beat their insides to a pulp, and then released him[20]. In early 1996, the guards of the camp in Grozny hung a Chechen horizontally and beat him, and the doctors of City Hospital No. 9 treated him for broken ribs[28][82]. In February 1996, the occupiers brought for exchange to Shatoy, a district center in the mountains in the south of Ichkeria, a captured Chechen beaten so badly that he was carried out of the armored personnel carrier in people's arms, and the army of Ichkeria gave up Russian soldiers for him[1]. In March 1996, soldiers of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs held three Chechens from the checkpoint between Goity and Starye Atagi, villages south of Grozny, for thirteen days in a railway tank car in Khankala, staged their execution and cut them with a knife, and in April military investigators in Khankala drove needles under the fingernails of Saidash Shamakhurov from the village of Gikalovo. The occupiers gave all four up for exchange (see: "Hostage-Taking")[28]. In May 1995, Sergei Kovalyov, head of the Observer Mission of Russian human rights defenders, wrote that his group had interviewed more than a hundred Chechens, former prisoners of the Russian occupiers. According to him, the occupiers beat and humiliated almost every one of them, and tortured many[83]. In September 1995, the UN Special Rapporteur on torture wrote to the government of Russia that camp guards systematically beat many prisoners to extract confessions of support for Dzhokhar Dudayev[14]. The human rights defenders of "Memorial" write that most of the people who passed through the filtration camps complained of cruel treatment, and that forensic medical examinations confirm their accounts. According to the "Memorial" report, in the pits at military units the occupiers tortured more and more often, and near Assinovskaya also in 1996[1]. In January 1997, the human rights defenders of Human Rights Watch wrote that in 1996 Russian servicemen continued to torture Chechens in Khankala[28]. It is unknown how many such crimes the occupation troops committed from December 1994 to September 1996. The human rights defenders of "Memorial" published the accounts of detained Chechens about beatings and torture in the camps in the winter and spring of 1995[77]. Russian courts convicted not a single occupier for the torture and abuse of Chechens (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")[1]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. Russian servicemen held Chechens at their bases in Grozny and in Khankala at least until the end of September[1]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1]. T0162.003 Killing of Prisoners and Detainees September 1994 C1193.T0162.003 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0010 Regular Army In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers killed detained Chechens without trial. In early 1995, during "zachistki" ("sweeps", as Russians called house searches and detentions of Chechens) in Grozny, Russian servicemen shot peaceful Chechens dead right after detaining them[1]. Russian escorts killed them on the way, in the backs of trucks and in columns on foot[1][5]. At the bases and positions of their units, Russian servicemen beat detained Chechens to death or shot them. The occupiers secretly buried the bodies of the killed near their positions and did not return them to the families (see: "Desecration of the Dead")[1][20][21]. In early January 1995, Russian soldiers detained more than 60 men near the cannery in Grozny. On 3 January, an escort drove them to the filtration camp in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia. When one of the two trucks broke down, the guards laid everyone in the back of the second one, in six layers and more. Those lying in the lower layers suffocated, and the escort shot at those who tried to move[1]. Zakrail Vairayev rode in that truck. On 28 February 1995, in Nazran, a town in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, he told a human rights defender of the American organization Freedom House about the journey. The record of his testimony says: "The vehicle was carrying 63 people. On the way, two suffocated, and six were shot right there, in the vehicle. So the dead rode along with the rest all the way to Mozdok. They beat us the whole way"[77]. Among those shot dead in the back of the truck was Ruslan Kasayev, a young man from Grozny[1]. On 28 January 1995, Russian soldiers led the Khamidov brothers under escort across the grounds of a unit of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) on Mayakovsky Street in Grozny. A neighbor heard one of the brothers shout that they were being led to be shot, and told their father Khusein Khamidov, who from January 1995 had been searching for people missing in Ichkeria and opening mass graves. From the neighbor's words, the father found the grave at the place the Russian military unit had left[1]. On 24 April 1996, in Moscow, Khusein Khamidov told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation: "On 2 April [1995] I dug up a burial of five bodies in the yard of a private house at 16 Mayakovsky Street, and among them were my sons. … Their legs were tied with rope, all their teeth were knocked out, there were marks of severe beatings on their bodies". Of other graves the brothers' father told the tribunal: "On the basis of the exhumations we carried out, I can state that people were shot at the former locations of [Russian] military units. They were taken away in galoshes, in house clothes, with pillowcases pulled over their heads. Many of the exhumed bodies had their hands and feet tied with barbed wire, and there were numerous knife wounds"[21]. On 17 May 1995, the prosecutor of the occupation administration in the Zavodskoy district of Grozny opened a case into the murder of the brothers. Russian military prosecutors received the case and suspended it because they had not found the culprits[1]. In April 1995, Russian servicemen detained three Chechens near the filtration camp on the northeastern outskirts of Grozny; they had come for a released relative. The relative found their bodies in a sewer pipe a kilometer and a half from there: the eyes of the killed had been gouged out and their ears cut off, and each had 15 bullet wounds[20]. On 7-8 April 1995, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs and Russian police officers, during searches in Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, shot detained Chechen men in courtyards, and the Observer Mission of Russian human rights organizations named 27 of them (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[5]. The Russian escort that led detained Chechens from Samashki to a military unit in the hills north of the village shot three of them dead on the way: one of them, wounded, a soldier killed on the order of the escort commander[5][1]. On 9 May 1995, soldiers of the 503rd regiment of the Russian army detained three Chechens from Shali, a town southeast of Grozny, at a checkpoint. After the regiment left on 3 June, relatives found the bodies of two of them secretly buried in a field near Shali, and on 6 June the body of the third at a cemetery; all the bodies bore marks of torture[20][1]. On 23 February 1996, when the Russian 58th Army was advancing on Bamut, a village southwest of Grozny, soldiers of that army put Sharip Batayev, a Chechen from Arshty, a village in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, onto an armored personnel carrier. On 20 March, investigators from Ingushetia found his body in a shallow grave near the position of the reconnaissance troops of the 693rd regiment of the 58th Army: the occupiers had broken his wrists and shot him in the back of the head[1][21]. From 3 to 9 March 1996, Russian troops stormed Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, and soldiers detained a young Chechen woman in the street and took her into a neighboring house, where her body was later found[84][66]. On 20 March, seven Russian servicemen landed from a helicopter at a dairy farm near Nagornoye, a village close to Grozny, lined up the peaceful Chechens who were hiding in a barn and shot the youngest men. Sources differ: Human Rights Watch writes of two brothers killed, while the Chechen Women's Committee named five people shot at the farm and Umar Tuzhuyev, whom the servicemen threw alive out of the helicopter[28][82][21]. On 28 March 1996, the occupiers gave up three Chechens and the bodies of two more detainees in exchange for five of their soldiers, and on one of the bodies Sultan Kacheyev, a commander of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, saw a bayonet wound (see: "Hostage-Taking")[28][82]. On 30 April, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs detained Chechens, residents of the city, at a checkpoint in Grozny and threw them into a pit in Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny. The guards beat two of them to death; the rest were taken out of Khankala on 3 May by the Russian criminal investigation police, and a prosecutor of the puppet government confirmed that both had died of beatings and had had no connection to the army of Ichkeria[1]. On 12 May, Russian troops seized Kharsenoy, a mountain village in the south of Ichkeria, and soldiers shot dead on the road six young Chechens who had left the village, and did not return their bodies to their relatives. In the village, the soldiers shot dead another young Chechen who asked them not to enter the mosque[21]. On 17 August 1996, masked Russian servicemen searched houses near the republican hospital in Grozny. When the occupiers left the block, relatives found in a neighboring yard the bodies of two Chechens, cousins, with their hands tied with wire and marks of torture[34]. On 26 March 1996, the UN Secretary-General transmitted to the UN Commission on Human Rights reports that Russian troops had executed captured Chechen men without trial: peaceful people and soldiers of the army of Ichkeria[68]. The human rights defenders of "Memorial" write that officers of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs and Russian servicemen executed people in Ichkeria without trial. In their conclusion, escorts and guards felt unpunishable in the first hours and days after a detention because the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs counted a detainee's term of custody from the hour he was brought to a filtration camp[1][5]. It is unknown how many detained Chechens the occupiers killed from December 1994 to August 1996. In early 1997, the human rights defenders of "Memorial" wrote of detained and missing Chechens: "Many of them have died, and now it is necessary to find the places of their burial, exhume and identify the bodies"[80]. Russian military prosecutors put Sokolov, the former commander of the 503rd regiment, on trial for the murder of three Chechens from Shali, but a military court returned the case to the prosecutors, and by the spring of 1998 they had not completed it (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")[1]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1]. T0099 Hostage-Taking September 1994 C1193.T0099 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0010 Regular Army In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers took peaceful Chechens hostage and released them in exchange for captured and killed Russian servicemen, weapons or money. Russian servicemen drew up lists of detained Chechens for exchange and put on them people who by their age could not have carried weapons[21]. According to a certificate by the prison service of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs, from 11 December 1994 to 22 July 1995 the ministry handed over 141 prisoners of the filtration camps for exchange for captured Russian servicemen (see: "Filtration Camp System")[1]. Russian police officers and soldiers promised to release a detained Chechen if his relatives brought money, a Russian soldier out of captivity or the body of a dead one[1][21]. The occupiers used the hostages' relatives to find out where the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were holding captured Russians: the relatives searched for captives to rescue their own, while the Russian FSB collected information from them and on 29 July 1995 drew up a certificate on the places where Russian soldiers were being held[1][80]. On 9 January 1995, Russian servicemen detained Shamsu Magomadov in Grozny (see: "Abduction of People"). In the winter of 1995-1996, his sister Madina Magomadova sought her brother's exchange from Colonel Pilyugin of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs. She told "Memorial": "They told me: 'Yes, your brother is alive, we will exchange him — find a soldier [a captured Russian soldier]'. I found a soldier — I went through all those mountains, villages, there is a war on, under fire I searched for a soldier — I found one, brought a photograph. They tell me: 'The soldier is a deserter, he is not subject to exchange…' … 'Go find an officer'. … I found an officer, brought a photograph of the officer... They tell me: sorry, Comrade Magomadova, your brother has been taken away from here, and where he is supposed to be, he has not been brought yet. We cannot find him". The occupiers never released Shamsu Magomadov, and nothing is known of his fate[1]. Russian servicemen and security services put up for exchange the captured relatives and guards of the president of Ichkeria. On 19 February 1995, the occupiers detained in Grozny Makharbi Dudayev, the president's younger brother, and on 6 April the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs put him up for exchange in Malye Atagi, a village south of Grozny, together with 16 prisoners of the filtration camps. The ministry exchanged the prisoners for a captured Russian major and released the president's brother separately[1][34][70]. On the night of 28 May 1996, Russian border guards detained the widow of the president of Ichkeria with her bodyguard at the airport of Nalchik, the capital of Russian-controlled Kabardino-Balkaria, and the Russian FSB released the widow but exchanged the bodyguard for a captured Russian priest[12][85]. Russian soldiers and filtration camp guards demanded ransom for detained Chechens. In late March 1995, the guards of the military unit near Assinovskaya, a stanitsa in the west of Ichkeria, asked detained Chechens who would pay more to get out[1]. In April 1995, the guards of the filtration camp on the northeastern outskirts of Grozny received five million rubles for the release of a detained Chechen[20]. On 15 May 1995, Russian soldiers put a detained Chechen from Shali, a town southeast of Grozny, into a pit at their unit, offered to let him out for money and released him after 18 hours[77]. In December 1995, Russian servicemen detained five elderly Chechens at a checkpoint, and their relatives ransomed them from a filtration camp for ten million rubles[20]. On 17 April 1996, Russian soldiers detained a Chechen woman with her two brothers at the entrance to Grozny and demanded three million rubles for them, and in the evening released all three, and the brother gave them the money[21]. On 18 April, Russian servicemen took six Chechens from their homes in Novye Aldy, a settlement on the southwestern outskirts of Grozny, and their relatives ransomed them from the filtration camp at the city motor depot[21]. The Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs and the command of the occupation troops demanded captured Russian servicemen, their bodies and weapons for detained Chechens. In March 1996, officers of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs demanded that the female relatives of a Chechen, held since January in the filtration camp in Grozny, dig up and bring the bodies of three officers of a Russian police special unit, and in late March, having received the bodies, released him[1]. In March 1996, soldiers of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs detained three Chechens at the checkpoint between Goity and Starye Atagi, villages south of Grozny, and on 28 March the occupiers exchanged them for five Russian soldiers[28]. On 7 April 1996, Russian servicemen took Saidash Shamakhurov from Gikalovo, a village south of Grozny, to Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny, where investigators demanded that he record on tape his request to be exchanged for 15 captured Russian soldiers and 48 construction workers. On 27 April, the occupiers exchanged him for a Russian soldier[28]. In May 1996, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) detained in the center of Grozny 17 to 20 Chechens who were repairing heating pipes and demanded during interrogation that their relatives bring weapons or captured Russian servicemen for them. The next evening the guards let them go[28]. Russian soldiers took hostages during assaults and when encircled. On 7 April 1995, during the storming of Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, the occupiers took four Chechen men hostage, drove them into a pit in a garage and fired at them with assault rifles. One the occupiers killed on the spot, the wounded second one the next day; two survived (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[1]. On 10-12 August 1996, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs, encircled by the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, held about 500 patients, their relatives and medics hostage in City Hospital No. 9 in Grozny. On 12 August, the occupiers left the hospital, taking a hundred hostages as a human shield, and released them near the former driving school where Russian units were stationed, once the defenders had handed over four captured Russian soldiers (see: "Use of People as "Human Shields"")[34][1]. On 11 and 12 August 1996, when the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were liberating Grozny from the occupiers, soldiers of the 101st Brigade of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs took Chechen men from the blocks around the "15th Gorodok", their base on Lenin Street, and held them there as hostages. On 14 October 1996, Magomed Taramov told "Memorial" how on 12 August Russian servicemen took him from his home together with his son Alimkhan: "We are no 'boyeviki' [as Russians called the Armed Forces of Ichkeria], we took no part in the armed actions. They led us out into the street, and there by the wall stood another nine or so people... In all, about twenty-four of us were gathered". For the release of the hostages, the brigade's officers demanded that relatives bring wounded soldiers from the encircled Russian checkpoints and the bodies of the dead, or get the army of Ichkeria to let food through to those posts. Garib Asiyalov, whom the hostages' female relatives called to the talks at the "15th Gorodok", in October told "Memorial" the words of a Russian officer: "…I answer to Kulikov [the head of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs]. We will trade head for head — our wounded or dead one for your living one". According to him, for the wounded and dead soldiers whom the relatives brought by truck, the brigade released 32 hostages[34]. On 16 August, when relatives brought the bodies of eight Russian servicemen to the base, the occupiers released Magomed and Alimkhan Taramov[1]. On 17 August 1996, soldiers of the 101st Brigade searched the blocks near the "15th Gorodok" and took Chechen men from there to the base as hostages. The brigade's officers promised to release them for the bodies of Russian soldiers buried near the bus station and the chemical plant, and on 19 August, when Russian soldiers brought 28 bodies out through the positions of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, they released the hostages. The human rights defenders of "Memorial" published the names of twelve of them[34] and write that at the "15th Gorodok" and in City Hospital No. 9 in Grozny the soldiers of the Internal Troops took hostages on the direct orders of the commanders of their units[1]. In his report of 26 March 1996, the UN Secretary-General cited reports by human rights organizations: Russian troops often detained any Chechen man, whether there was evidence against him or not, in order to exchange him for captured Russian soldiers[68]. The human rights defenders of "Memorial" write that Russian agencies repeatedly used civilian prisoners of the filtration camps as hostages and in most cases offered Ichkeria in exchange Chechens who had not taken part in the fighting. In "Memorial's" conclusion, hostage-taking became a regular practice for the Russian military[1]. Russian prosecutors put none of the occupiers who took hostages in Hospital No. 9 and at the "15th Gorodok" in Grozny on trial (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")[28][1]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. The occupiers shielded themselves with peaceful Chechens from the fire of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria. Russian soldiers led Chechens out of the basements where they were hiding from shelling, took men from their homes and seized doctors and patients in a hospital. The occupiers put them on armored vehicles or placed them in front of themselves so that the soldiers of the army of Ichkeria would not shoot[1][28]. Russian servicemen threatened to burn or shoot the captured Chechens if the defenders fired or did not hand over captives[34]. Russian soldiers released some Chechens from the human shield after a few hours and took others to their bases. There the occupiers put them in pits and beat them (see: "Torture and Abuse")[34]. On 6-8 March 1996, when the army of Ichkeria encircled Russian checkpoint No. 6 in Grozny, an officer of the Russian commandant's office of the city advised the soldiers at the checkpoint over the radio to seize a couple of Chechen families and shield themselves with them. The soldiers at the post did not do so[86][1][87]. From 15 March 1996, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) and the Russian 58th Army stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria (see: "Military Intervention")[1]. On 17 March, Russian soldiers drove Chechens out of the basement of a house on Rabochaya Street, where they were hiding from shelling. A major, the commander of a Russian unit, forced three women and the three Kireyev boys - aged five, eleven and twelve - to climb onto an armored vehicle[1][34]. Leila Gaerbekova, one of the three women on the vehicle, told the human rights defender Andrei Mironov on 4 May 1996: "At gunpoint they put us on a tank [an armored vehicle] on Rabochaya Street. Three children, their mother Koka, me and my sister Anya Gaerbekova. <...> They placed us in front of the tank and said: 'If a single bullet comes from over there, we will burn you'. And there were no bullets from over there, nothing". The soldiers placed almost everyone who had been hiding in the basement in front of the vehicle and led them at gunpoint for about 300 meters, to the canal in the middle of the village. Between 12 and 2 p.m., the major told the Chechens to disperse. Khizir Khachukayev, the commander of the unit of the army of Ichkeria in Samashki, told the human rights defenders of "Memorial" that his soldiers did not fire at the armored vehicles with people on them and were forced to retreat, and put up their main resistance in the center of the village once the occupiers had let the people out of the human shield[1][34]. On 15 March 1996, in Samashki, Russian soldiers led two elderly Chechens, the owner of a house on Vygonnaya Street and his neighbor, out of the house, put them on top of an armored vehicle and drove them around under bullets for six or seven hours. After nine in the evening, the occupiers' commander let both of them go[34]. On 10 August 1996, when the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were liberating Grozny, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs searched City Hospital No. 9 in Grozny. For two days, the occupiers held about 500 patients, their relatives, doctors and nurses hostage (see: "Hostage-Taking"). Movsar Tembulatov, the deputy chief physician, told the human rights defenders of "Memorial" and Human Rights Watch in the hospital on 13 October 1996 how Russian soldiers went down into the basement: "they put me or one of the other doctors in front as some kind of cover, with a submachine gunner behind"[34][1]. On 12 August 1996, soldiers of the army of Ichkeria repelled an attack by Russian troops trying to break through to the occupiers encircled in the hospital. The commander of the Russian servicemen in the hospital agreed to lead his soldiers out in exchange for captives and demanded 100 doctors, nurses, walking patients and their relatives as a human shield for himself. Khadis Malsagov, one of the hostages, told the human rights defenders of "Memorial" on 24 August 1996: "As soon as everyone had moved away from the hospital, they [the Russian soldiers] line the women up and say they will shoot them if the captives are not handed over to them immediately". The soldiers of Khizir Khachukayev handed over all the captives. At the gates of their base, the occupiers released the people from the human shield. When the people were returning to the hospital, Russian troops fired several dozen mortar shells at it, killed the nurse Toita Kutukhanova and wounded two nurses, two doctors and a woman patient (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). On the evening of 12 August and the morning of 13 August, the patients and medics left the hospital for the building of the International Committee of the Red Cross nearby[34][1]. On 12 August 1996, soldiers of the 101st Brigade of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs took men from the blocks of Grozny around the "15th Gorodok", their base on Lenin Street, and shielded themselves with them on the way there (see: "Hostage-Taking")[1]. Two of them, a father and son, the occupiers tied with wire to an armored personnel carrier, drove under fire to Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of the city, and released on 16 August[34]. The 1996 report of "Memorial" says that Russian servicemen and officers of Russian agencies in Ichkeria systematically took hostages and shielded themselves with human shields. According to the report, the occupiers shielded themselves with Chechens during the last six months of the war, from March to August 1996, most often the soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs[34]. The prosecutors of the Russian army did not investigate how Russian troops shielded themselves with Chechens during assaults and held no one accountable for it (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")[28][1]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1]. T0045 Destruction of Historical Memory September 1994 C1193.T0045 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0010 Regular Army In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers destroyed the museums, research institutes and ancient monuments of the Chechens. During the storming of Grozny, Russian artillerymen shelled, and pilots bombed, the center of the city, where the museums and research institutes of Ichkeria stood[1][21]. Russian pilots fired rockets at ancient towers and settlements in the mountains in the south of Ichkeria[21]. The occupiers occupied the ruins of museums and looted what had survived (see: "Theft of Cultural Property")[21]. Russian troops burned almost the entire Central State Archive of the Chechen Republic and the republican libraries in Grozny (see: "Burning of Books and Archives")[1]. Soldiers of the occupation troops destroyed mosques and leveled ancient burial mounds (see: "Destruction of Shrines and Necropolises")[21]. In January 1995, Russian troops destroyed the Chechen National Museum in Grozny. The museum held about 320 thousand exhibits, among them archaeological finds of the ancient and medieval Caucasus, traditional Chechen clothing and old manuscripts[1][21]. The museum's director Isa Adayev told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Prague in May 1996: "From 1 to 4 January 1995, the museum building was shelled quite deliberately from several directions". When the director got to the museum on 7 January, "it was no longer a museum — nothing was left of it — only ruins". On 18 January, Russian special forces seized the ruins[21]. Khotin, deputy director of the museum center of the Russian Ministry of Culture, who inspected the ruins of the museum in late March 1995, told the public tribunal of the Glasnost Foundation in Moscow in February 1996: "The nature of the destruction shows that barrage fire was used there. Next to the museum there is a small park of about 50 fairly old trees. Well, all those trees are cut in half. All of them!"[20]. In early 1995, the occupiers destroyed in Grozny the Research Institute of the Humanities of the Chechen Republic, founded in 1907[1]. In 1995, Russian pilots fired rockets at and bombed Kogo-Maista, an old settlement in the mountains in the south of Ichkeria, far from the fighting. In the strikes, the occupiers destroyed six towers that had stood for thirteen centuries, killed the Chechen boy Deni Murtazov and wounded a woman of his family so badly that she became disabled[21]. The human rights defenders of "Memorial" write that Russian troops destroyed or irreparably damaged in Grozny the university, the pedagogical and petroleum institutes, and the geological museum. In "Memorial's" assessment, Russian troops did not take the rescue of cultural property into account and inflicted irreparable damage on the culture of the Chechen people[1]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1]. T0045.001 Destruction of Shrines and Necropolises September 1994 C1193.T0045.001 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0010 Regular Army In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers destroyed mosques, shelled cemeteries and razed ancient burial mounds south of Grozny to the ground. Russian artillerymen, pilots and helicopter crews shelled mosques in the villages and towns of Ichkeria[20][1]. Approaching a village, the occupiers first of all fired at the top of the mosque, the tallest building, and snipers fired at mosques for no reason[21]. By the estimate of Isa Adayev, director of the National Museum of Ichkeria, by May 1996 Russian troops had destroyed or damaged 70 percent of the republic's mosques[21]. Russian helicopter crews bombed village cemeteries, and snipers fired at them[57][58]. In February-March 1995, a Russian regiment stood for two months and seven days beside three ancient burial mounds, earthen hills over graves, between the villages of Starye Atagi and Chechen-Aul south of Grozny. The Grozny city council had set aside 26 hectares around the mounds for a museum of archaeology, and a fence, signs warning that these were monuments, and building materials had been brought there. Soldiers dug up the middle of the mounds with a special vehicle that accompanies tank regiments, and then razed them to the ground. The occupiers knocked down the fence and the signs with tanks. Soldiers dug trenches between the mounds and used the museum's building materials for dugouts and checkpoints. In May 1996, Isa Adayev told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Prague: "These were deliberate actions. One or two random hits could not have done what was done"[21]. In early February 1995, Russian snipers fired from the hills above Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, at the village cemetery and damaged graves. Because of the shooting, families postponed for a day the funerals of Chechens whom the occupiers had killed with mortar fire on 2 February[57]. In April 1995, Russian helicopter crews bombed Koshkeldy, a village in the east of Ichkeria, and the village cemetery[58]. From 14 to 20 December 1995, artillerymen of the occupation troops shelled the mosque in Gudermes, the second-largest town of Ichkeria, and killed more than 30 townspeople beside it (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[1]. By February 1996, Russian troops had destroyed the mosques and minarets, the towers beside mosques, in Bamut, a village in the west of Ichkeria[20]. From 3 to 9 March 1996, Russian troops stormed Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria. Russian soldiers burned the village mosque together with the bodies of Chechens whom the villagers had brought there for burial (see: "Desecration of the Dead")[88][21]. In May 1996, Sadyt Gisatova, a Chechen woman from Sernovodsk, told the Glasnost tribunal in Prague: "When we came to the mosque to bury the bodies lying there, we saw that the mosque had burned down. All the bodies had burned too. In what countries do they destroy churches and mosques? It is the holy of holies"[21]. By May 1996, the occupation troops, while bombing Grozny, had destroyed the memorial to the victims of the deportation of the Chechens to Central Asia in 1944, and had shot the inscription off the stone. Chechens had built the memorial in 1992 from gravestones that, after the deportation, the colonizers had used to build buildings, roads and pig farms[89][21]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1]. T0045.002 Burning of Books and Archives September 1994 C1193.T0045.002 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0010 Regular Army In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers burned the archives, libraries, books and manuscripts of the Chechens. Russian artillerymen shelled, and pilots bombed, the buildings of the archive, libraries and research institutes in Grozny. The documents, books and manuscripts in these buildings burned[1][21]. Russian commanders, with the help of soldiers, carried ancient books away on trucks toward Mozdok, a town in North Ossetia, and toward Ingushetia, both Russian-controlled (see: "Theft of Cultural Property")[21]. From 31 December 1994, the occupation troops stormed the center of Grozny, where the Central State Archive of the Chechen Republic kept about 656 thousand files on the history of the Chechen and Ingush peoples over more than two centuries. One building of the archive stood on Ordzhonikidze Street, a hundred meters from the palace of the president of Ichkeria[1]. Oleg Orlov, a human rights defender of Memorial, who at the start of the storming was in the basement of the palace together with the group of Sergei Kovalyov, Russia's human rights commissioner, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow in February 1996 that on the night of 4 January 1995 he came out of the basement: "We saw that the whole center of the city was already destroyed, practically all the residential buildings had either burned down or were still burning. … We saw that archive – it had burned down completely"[20]. In February 1995, Yeremchenko, deputy head of the Russian archival agency, came to Grozny and established that in the archive buildings on Ordzhonikidze and Chekhov streets the occupiers had destroyed all the documents together with the backup copies on film. The third building of the archive, on Karagandinskaya Street, survived. It kept about 90 thousand files on the Chechens and Ingush whom the USSR had deported to Kazakhstan in 1944. On 21 September 1995, Yeremchenko, deputy head of the agency, wrote in reply to an inquiry that the occupiers had destroyed 87 percent of the 795 thousand files in all the state archives of the Chechen Republic[1]. In early 1995, Russian troops burned down the entire Chekhov Republican Scientific Library in Grozny with shelling[1]. On 24 April 1996, the ethnographer Yan Chesnov, who studied the Chechens and saw the ruins of the library, told the public tribunal of the Glasnost Foundation in Moscow: "The archive and the republican library have been burned. … The entire book collection has been burned. Books in the Chechen language published in the 1930s in Latin script [in Latin letters], ancient Arabic books. A unique library has perished"[21]. In January 1995, the occupiers destroyed the Chechen National Museum in Grozny with shelling, together with its department of ancient books and manuscripts (see: "Destruction of Historical Memory")[21]. In early 1995, Russian troops destroyed in Grozny the library of the Research Institute of the Humanities of the Chechen Republic. The library kept the works of all the known researchers of the Caucasus, the records of expeditions on the languages of the Chechens and Ingush, and the originals of medieval books and manuscripts[1]. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that in Grozny the scientific and technical library, three university libraries, the libraries of all the research institutes, the republican children's library and the archives of the unions of writers, artists, composers and theater workers burned down. According to Memorial, the occupiers destroyed or irreparably damaged the folklore center with its archive[1]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6].
