of Popular Will September 1994 C1193.T0109 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russia twice held "elections" on the seized land of Ichkeria to pass off the puppet government as chosen by the people[1]. By the autumn of 1995, the Russian army had seized Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria, and the plain in the north of the republic. On 24 October 1995, Russia put Zavgayev at the head of the puppet government in Grozny (see: "Puppet Government")[1]. On 1 November 1995, the puppet parliament, assembled from deputies of the Soviet era, introduced the post of head of the republic. On 5 November, the deputies scheduled the election for this post for 16 December, the day of the elections to the Russian parliament. On 12 May 1996, the puppet deputies scheduled the election of a new parliament for 16 June, the day of the Russian presidential election[1]. From 16 November 1995 until voting day, Russian servicemen at checkpoints let only people registered there into the stanitsa of Assinovskaya and the village of Sernovodsk in the west of Ichkeria, and did not let candidates and campaigners through (see: "Transport Blockade"). From 11 to 20 December, Shkirko, commander of the occupation troops, forbade entry into Grozny without a special pass. The occupiers at checkpoints did not let accredited journalists into the city[1]. On 12 December 1995, the puppet parliament allowed voting at any polling station with any document[1]. The Russian-controlled election commissions of the republic and of Grozny gave numbers of the city's voters that differed twofold: 120 and 250 thousand[1][90]. Both commissions refused to show the voter lists[1]. The staff of the Assistance Group, the mission of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), left Ichkeria for the voting days in December 1995. There were no international observers at the elections. On 9 June 1996, a week before the new elections, the puppet government declared the Assistance Group undesirable (see: "Expulsion of Foreign Missions")[1]. On 6 December 1995, Russian soldiers at checkpoints did not let delegates from the south of Ichkeria into Grozny, and the congress of supporters of Khasbulatov, the former head of the parliament in Moscow, did not take place. On 9 December, Khasbulatov, Zavgayev's main rival, withdrew from the election[1]. From 14 to 17 December 1995, the occupiers held the vote for head of the republic. Russian troops did not control the Shali district southeast of Grozny or the mountain districts in the south, and there was no voting there. Hundreds of thousands of citizens of Ichkeria had fled the war out of the republic and could not vote[1]. On 18 December, the Russian-controlled election commission in Grozny announced that more than 60% of the population had voted and about 90% of them had chosen Zavgayev[1]. On 21 April 1996, Ruslan Akhtakhanov, adviser to Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow about the voting in Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria: "The residents of Samashki said that there had been no elections in their village. <...> a week after the scheduled elections Mr. Zavgayev, sitting in a television studio, thanked the population of the republic that had supported him so vigorously. And he said that the strongest support — 70-80 percent of the population — came from the village of Samashki." According to Ruslan Akhtakhanov, before the elections members of the Russian-controlled village administration went around the village and copied the Chechens' passports and signatures into lists. Ninety-nine percent of those who voted on 17 December, he said, were from these lists[21]. On 14 December 1995, the Russian-controlled administration of Gudermes, the second-largest town of the republic, broadcast by radio that the elections would be held anyway and that no one would shoot at people, while the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated the town from the occupiers that day. On 17 December at nine in the evening, as soon as the polling stations closed, Russian pilots began bombing Gudermes (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[37]. On 10 June 1996, in Nazran, a town in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, the delegations of Russia and Ichkeria recorded in the ceasefire protocol that elections would be held after the withdrawal of Russian troops and the disarmament of the army of Ichkeria[13]. After the signing of the protocol, Lobov, the representative of the president of Russia in Ichkeria, said on Grozny television: "I see no serious reasons for their [the elections'] cancellation or postponement, as the separatists demand" (that is what the Russians called the government and the Armed Forces of Ichkeria)[1]. On 14-16 June, the colonizer held the election of a new parliament of the republic and of the president of Russia, although its army remained in Ichkeria. Irina Dementyeva, correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Izvestia, wrote on 20 June: "As early as the morning of the sixteenth… the head of the republic [Zavgayev] named the percentage of those who had voted — 50. An hour and a half later the chairman of the republican izbirkom [election commission]… told the same journalists: as of 12 noon, 23 percent of the voters had voted". The Russian-controlled election commission in Grozny announced that more than 60% of the voters had voted and that Russian president Yeltsin had received more than half the votes in the Chechen Republic[1]. On 17 and 18 June, the OSCE stated that the elections had not been free and fair and that the decision to hold them had violated the protocols of 10 June on the withdrawal of troops[1][91][92]. On 16 June 1996, Gudermes and the villages of Bachi-Yurt, Alleroy and Tsentoroy in the east of Ichkeria did not vote. The stanitsa of Shelkovskaya in the north of the republic, the town of Shali and the villages of Kurchaloy and Vedeno southeast of Grozny did not vote[6]. After 16 June, officials and public figures of the republic confirmed in writing that there had been no elections in Gudermes, or in 64 villages, stanitsas and settlements of six districts of Ichkeria, including places where, according to official data, Russian troops were stationed. Heads of administrations subordinate to Russia signed some of these papers and certified them with seals bearing the coat of arms of Russia, and one paper was signed by the chairman and secretary of the election commission of the Gudermes district[1]. On 3 July, in the second round of the election, there was no voting in Shali, Novye Atagi, Gekhi and Gekhi-Chu south of Grozny. The election commission closed the polling station in Urus-Martan, a town southwest of Grozny, at four in the afternoon, announcing that 98% of the voters there had already voted. According to the commissions' protocols, in the second round 74% of the voters in the Chechen Republic voted and 73% of them chose Yeltsin, and the Central Election Commission of Russia reported that it had received no information about violations[1]. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that both times the elections were not genuine and the voters could not freely express their will[1]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic. On 27 January 1997, the citizens of Ichkeria elected the president and parliament of the republic. Aslan Maskhadov became president[1]. T0101 Censorship September 1994 C1193.T0101 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0008 Government In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russia decided which journalists could work in Ichkeria, confiscated their footage and persecuted them for reporting on the war. On 1 December 1994, ten days before the open invasion, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, by directive No. 1886-r created the Temporary Information Center[93][1]. On 9 December, by resolution No. 1360, the Russian government instructed the center to issue journalists accreditation, the permit to work in Ichkeria, and to withdraw it immediately for information the center deemed false. The government gave the Russian Interior Ministry (MVD) and the FSK (predecessor of today's FSB) the right to expel from Ichkeria any outsiders they deemed dangerous[33]. On 29 December 1994, the Russian MVD announced that the Temporary Information Center's accreditation gave no right to travel where the Russian Internal Troops (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) were stationed[1]. At the end of January 1995, the Russian government created the Mobile Information Center in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia where the occupiers' headquarters stood. Only this center's accreditation gave journalists the right to be in the "combat zone", and there only under the supervision of servicemen or officials. The occupiers usually counted all of Ichkeria as this zone[1]. The Russian military expelled journalists without accreditation from the republic, and detained journalists with accreditation and confiscated their tapes and equipment, explaining that accreditation from the Ministry of Defense or the MVD was also needed[1]. On 15 December 1994, Soskovets, deputy chairman of the Russian government, announced that the government could strip the NTV television channel of its broadcasting license for its reports on the victims of the war in Ichkeria. After public protest, the government dropped this threat[94]. At the end of May 1995, officers of the Russian FSB arrested NTV journalists near the stanitsa of Assinovskaya in the west of Ichkeria for filming Russian troop positions, although the commander of the Russian division had allowed it. The FSB held the journalists for six hours in a filtration camp and released them (see: "Filtration Camp System")[21]. On 3 June 1995, the Russian military arrested three foreign journalists on the border between Ichkeria and Russian-controlled Dagestan and reprimanded them for not having the proper accreditation. Four days later, on 7 June, the occupiers let the journalists go to Moscow but confiscated their tapes and film[94]. On 25 June 1995, Yelena Masyuk, a journalist of the Russian television channel NTV, recorded an interview with Shamil Basayev, a commander of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, in the Nozhai-Yurt district in the southeast of the republic[94]. In April 1996, the journalist told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow: "To get accreditation to work in Chechnya, you had to get to the military airfield in Mozdok, where the accreditations were issued — but to drive onto the airfield, you already had to have that accreditation." About the road to Shamil Basayev she told the tribunal: "To get to the Chechen village where, by my guess, Basayev was at the time, I had to walk 12 kilometers on foot around the Russian checkpoints"[21]. On 13 July 1995, the Prosecutor General's Office of Russia opened a criminal case against Yelena Masyuk for not telling the investigators where she had taken the interview. At the end of August, the prosecutor's office closed the case without charges and asked the Russian government's press agency to make sure such interviews did not happen again[94]. From 6 to 9 March 1996, while the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were attacking the occupiers in Grozny, Russian officials forbade television crews in the city to film[95]. On 8 August 1996, a Russian soldier at a checkpoint near Grozny told four journalists of foreign media to turn back and threatened to destroy their equipment, and when they turned around, the occupiers fired a grenade launcher at their car and missed. Two hours later, Russian pilots fired on the journalists from helicopters at another entrance to the city but wounded no one[95]. In its report for 1996, the international organization Committee to Protect Journalists wrote that throughout the war Russian troops refused to recognize journalists' accreditation, spoiled their film, destroyed their equipment and fired on their cars from checkpoints and combat helicopters[95]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1]. T0007.002 Occupation as Salvation September 1994 C1193.T0007.002 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0008 Government In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Throughout the war, Moscow declared the invasion and occupation a blessing for the Chechens. On 30 November 1994, Russian president Yeltsin signed secret decree No. 2137 "On Measures to Restore Constitutional Legality and Law and Order on the Territory of the Chechen Republic" (that is what the colonizer called the preparation of the attack on Ichkeria)[1]. On 9 December, by decree No. 2166 the president instructed the Russian government to use all means "to ensure… the rights and freedoms of citizens"[4]. On 27 January 1995, Yeltsin signed decree No. 79 "On Ensuring the Conditions for the Re-creation of Constitutional Organs of Power in the Chechen Republic" (see: "Installation of a New System of Governance")[1][96]. On 12 July 1996, the fourth day of the occupation troops' offensive, the president, by decree No. 1028, named as constitutional organs the government that Moscow had installed in Grozny (see: "Puppet Government")[1][96][42]. On 11 December 1994, the day of the open invasion, Yeltsin addressed the citizens of Russia: "Our goal is to find a political solution to the problems of one of the subjects of the Russian Federation — the Chechen Republic, and to protect its citizens from armed extremism." The president of Russia promised: "I oblige all officials responsible for carrying out the measures to restore constitutional order in the Chechen Republic [that is what Russia called its war against independent Ichkeria] not to use violence against the civilian population and to take it under protection"[1]. A week later, from 18 December, Russian pilots bombed Grozny, and from 19 December until the storming on 31 December they bombed it every day. Human rights defenders of the Russian organization Memorial write: "The bombs and missiles fell mainly on neighborhoods where residential buildings stood and where there were knowingly no military objects" (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[1]. By the estimate of the Observer Mission of Russian human rights organizations, from December 1994 to March 1995 the occupiers killed 25-29 thousand civilian townspeople in Grozny (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[1]. On 11 January 1996, the Russian government replied to the UN Secretary-General's inquiry about human rights in Ichkeria that an extremely complex situation had forced Moscow to use armed force. The reply says that on 29 August 1995 Yeltsin appointed Lobov, secretary of the Russian Security Council, as his representative in Ichkeria to guarantee human rights and prepare free elections (see: "Sham Expression of Popular Will")[68]. On 23 April 1996, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, stated at a meeting of the government commission on settling the war: "The UN Charter also contains the concept of 'peace enforcement', and in this case it can be applied"[1]. Two days later, on 25 April, Russian pilots bombed Shali, a town southeast of Grozny that the occupation troops had surrounded six days earlier (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). The occupiers killed Chechen civilians and, according to the report of the head of the Shali district to the Interfax agency, wounded 29 people[1]. Eleven days later, on 6 May, Russian troops seized Shali without a fight and found no defenders there (see: "Collective Punishment")[1]. On 17 July 1996, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, stated at a meeting of the government commission on settling the war that in six months Russia had liquidated the "anti-constitutional regime" (that is what Russia called the government of Ichkeria) that had threatened its territorial integrity[1]. T0168 Impunity of Perpetrators September 1994 C1193.T0168 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0008 Government In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Throughout the war, Moscow shielded its soldiers, police officers and commanders of the occupation troops from responsibility for crimes against Chechens. In Ichkeria, Shkirko, commander of the Internal Troops of the Russian Interior Ministry (MVD; predecessors of today's Rosgvardia), went by the surname "Shirokov", and Lvov, chief of their staff, by "General Yagodin". Romanov and Labunets, deputy commanders of the occupation troops, were called "Antonov" and "Alekseyev"[1][70]. Military prosecutors closed cases about people whom Russian soldiers had shot dead in cars at checkpoints, citing Articles 23 and 27 of the Russian law on the Internal Troops of the MVD[1]. On 17 December 1994, the Russian military shot up a column of refugees from Grozny near the stanitsa of Nesterovskaya in Russian-controlled Ingushetia. Russian prosecutors suspended the case without finding those responsible[1]. On 3 January 1995, Russian pilots bombed Arshty, a village in Ingushetia inhabited mostly by Chechens (see: "Collective Punishment"), and in a second bombing, on 18 April, killed three women there. Russian prosecutors closed both cases, finding no crime[1]. On 14 January 1995, Lobov, secretary of the Russian Security Council, said that a special commission should establish the truth about the bombings of Grozny. Russia created no such commission[1]. On 24 January 1995, the two sons of Khusein Khamidov disappeared in Grozny. On 2 April, the father dug up a pit in the yard of a house on Mayakovsky Street, where a unit of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD had previously been stationed, and found their bodies (see: "Killing of Prisoners and Detainees"). The prosecutor's office of the puppet government opened a case and gathered evidence. Russian military prosecutors suspended it without finding those responsible[1]. On 24 April 1996, Khusein Khamidov, who had been searching for missing people in Ichkeria since January 1995, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow: "There is not a single case that has been investigated and brought to court… when you hand them documents, hand them a statement about some crime that was committed, they say: 'You tell us who did it, soldiers of the Russian regular army, or of SOBR [the police special forces], or of the MVD'… But who knows who committed the crime — their uniform is one and the same. And on that basis they refuse us"[21]. Russian courts gave Polivtsev, a captain of the 81st regiment of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD, four years for the murder of four Chechens in Grozny on 25 January 1995[1]. On 7-8 April 1995, the Russian Internal Troops stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, and killed 103 Chechen civilians (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians"). On 12 April, a colonel of the Russian MVD at a post near the village introduced himself to human rights defenders as Oblomov, although the surname "Yelansky" was written on the strap of his assault rifle. On 19 April, the Russian prosecutor Dzhapov told Andrei Blinushov, an observer of the Russian human rights organization Memorial, that he did not know how to hold the fighters of the MVD special units to account. The observer wrote in his diary, from the prosecutor's words: "the MVD special units leaving Chechnya destroy all their documentation concerning their actions on the territory of this republic. These units often act in masks, without any insignia on their uniforms, and all the officers use two or three pseudonyms instead of their real surnames"[70]. On 27 April, Ilyushenko, acting prosecutor general of Russia, opened a case on the killings and arson in the village[70]. In mid-May, Russian military investigators questioned some of the victims and witnesses, but did not open the graves and never came to Samashki again. On 14 January 1997, the prosecutors closed the case. On 21 November 1997, Smirnov, deputy chief military prosecutor of Russia, named the reason to Memorial: "the servicemen acted in a state of extreme necessity and necessary defense"[1]. The Russian serviceman Vershinin received three years from a court for shooting dead the boy Zelimkhan Dediyev on 17 April 1995 in the stanitsa of Petropavlovskaya northeast of Grozny[1]. On 14 June 1995, the Prosecutor General's Office of Russia, by directive No. 15-6-95, ordered the prosecutor of the puppet government in Grozny to hand cases of crimes by Russian soldiers over to Russian military prosecutors only if the facts had been established beyond dispute. On 4 July 1996, that government's prosecutor wrote to Skuratov, prosecutor general of Russia, that Russian prosecutors had returned 112 cases to him without investigation, having found no indisputable proof of guilt in them. The letter says that unnamed commanders ordered that investigators not be let into military units and onto checkpoints[1]. The soldiers Korovin, Shulin and Petrov received 14, six and three years for killing two Chechens on the night of 7 July 1995 in the settlement of Rodina near their unit[97][1]. The Russian military did not let into their units the investigators of the puppet prosecutor's office who were investigating the murder of seven Chechens of the Chapanov family in the village of Prigorodnoye near Grozny on 7 July 1995. In January 1996, the puppet prosecutor's office suspended the case[1]. On 17 December 1996, a court gave Permyakov, a fighter of the Russian police special forces, a suspended sentence of a year and a half for the "negligent killing" of Zaurbek Uzuyev, whom he had shot dead at a checkpoint on 8 September 1995 during a rally for the independence of Ichkeria[1]. Military prosecutors suspended the case on the bombing of Roshni-Chu, a village southwest of Grozny, in October 1995[1]. Military prosecutors closed the case on the murder of Sharip Batayev, a Chechen from Arshty, whom scouts of the 693rd regiment of the Russian 58th Army shot dead at the end of February 1996. According to the prosecutors' version, the commander of the scouts was defending himself[1]. In the spring of 1996, Russian prosecutors opened no criminal case on how the occupiers in March had burned Sernovodsk and destroyed Samashki, villages in the west of Ichkeria[21]. On 30 June 1996, the military prosecutor Saprunov wrote to the prosecutor's office of the puppet government that the occupiers had beaten, on the way to Pyatigorsk, a town in southern Russia, half of the 91 Chechens from Samashki whom the Russian military had unlawfully detained on 15 March (see: "Torture and Abuse")[28][82]. In March 1997, Russian prosecutors suspended the case without finding those responsible: those who made the detentions had been "wearing masks on their faces, so their identification is impossible"[1]. On 10 December 1996, Sinitsyn, a prosecutor of the Chief Military Prosecutor's Office of Russia, replied to Memorial's request to investigate how soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD had shielded themselves with civilians in Samashki in March 1996 and with the patients of Grozny City Hospital No. 9 in August 1996 (see: "Use of People as "Human Shields""). Sinitsyn wrote that he had forwarded the human rights defenders' report to the prosecutors of the North Caucasus so that it could be attached to the press reports[28], and on 21 November 1997 Smirnov, deputy chief military prosecutor, replied that in Samashki people had been hiding behind armored vehicles from the shelling[1]. Military prosecutors suspended the cases on the bombings of Katyr-Yurt and Shalazhi, villages southwest of Grozny, in March and April 1996 (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[1]. Shevchenko, prosecutor of the occupation troops, without visiting the scene, stated that the soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD who on 15 July 1996 had shot dead unarmed people in passenger cars on the outskirts of Grozny had used their weapons correctly[38][1]. In mid-July 1996, Russian soldiers held without charges two Chechens from the Vedeno district in the southeast of Ichkeria in an army cell in Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny, and released them at the demand of military prosecutors. The prosecutor's office of the occupation troops recognized only this detention as unlawful, but opened no case, because the culprit, the commandant of Khankala, had died in the fighting in August 1996[1]. On 8 August 1996, the Chief Military Prosecutor's Office of Russia replied to Yuli Rybakov, a deputy of the Russian parliament, that since 11 December 1994 prosecutors had opened 129 cases on crimes by the occupiers against civilians in Ichkeria. Of these, prosecutors had sent 21 cases to the courts, closed 21, left 26 unfinished and suspended 61 - 48 because they had not found those responsible, and 13 because they did not know where the accused were[1]. On 29 September 1997, the Directorate of Military Courts of Russia replied to Memorial's inquiry that over the whole war the courts had convicted 18 soldiers and officers, seven of them for murder[1]. On 26 July 1995, the UN Human Rights Committee expressed regret that no one had been held accountable for the ill-treatment of prisoners and detainees in Ichkeria[79]. The Human Rights Watch report of January 1997 says that Russia systematically violated human rights and just as systematically failed to hold those responsible to account[28]. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that over the whole war Russia held not a single senior commander to account. According to their data, Russian courts convicted no one for the bombings of the villages and towns of Ichkeria, the filtration camps, torture, hostage-taking and human shields[1]. According to Human Rights Watch, at the peace talks in August 1996 the Russian delegation objected to discussing responsibility for crimes[28]. After the peace agreements in Khasavyurt on 31 August 1996 (see: "Sham Treaties")[30], Russia moved the prosecutor's office of the occupation troops to Russian-controlled Dagestan. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that after this the prosecutors almost stopped investigating crimes by Russian servicemen and police officers[1]. On 12 March 1997, deputies in Moscow, by resolution No. 1199-II, declared an amnesty for crimes connected with the war in Ichkeria[29]. Under this amnesty, Russian prosecutors terminated unfinished cases on crimes by the occupiers[1]. T0167.001 False Guarantees of Safety September 1994 C1193.T0167.001 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0008 Government In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers promised the villages of Ichkeria not to touch the Chechens if a village handed over its weapons, sent away the Armed Forces of Ichkeria or let Russian troops in, and then looted, bombed and stormed the villages that had believed them. Russian generals and officers gave their promises to village heads and elders at their posts, by word of mouth or in the form of a written treaty[5]. In mid-January 1995, the elders of Assinovskaya, a stanitsa in the west of Ichkeria, let in Russian troops, who promised through loudspeakers and leaflets not to touch anyone. The occupiers looted houses and abused Chechens, and by 16 February every Chechen family had left the stanitsa (see: "Pillage")[57]. On 21 February 1995, the head of Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, and the elders asked Kosolapov, a general of the occupation forces, at the Russian post near the village what they should do so that there would be no war in the village. The report of the Observer Mission of Russian human rights defenders gives the general's answer: "You have to hand over the heavy weapons, set up a militia team of 40-45 men to guard the village, draw up a protocol of accord with the seals of the imam and the chairman [of the village administration], explain it to the people — that is all that is required of you". On 6-7 March, fighters of the army of Ichkeria from other villages were forced to leave at the demand of the Chechens of Samashki. On 8 March, the head of the village, the imam and five elders signed a treaty with the Russian troops. The village undertook to hand over its heavy weapons and send away the army of Ichkeria, and in exchange the elders asked the Russian troops not to enter Samashki and not to use force against Chechen civilians. General Kosolapov signed the treaty and gave a copy to the head of the village[5]. Eighteen days after the treaty, on 26 March 1995, Russian pilots in six helicopters fired rockets at Samashki and seriously wounded four Chechens. On 28 March, the colonel who commanded the Russian post near the village demanded that small arms be handed over, although the treaty said nothing of this. The head of Samashki collected six assault rifles in the village and handed them to the occupiers. On 6 April, Romanov, deputy commander of the occupation forces, demanded that the village let in the Internal Troops of Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) and hand over 264 assault rifles by seven in the morning of 7 April (see: "Collective Punishment"). The elders replied that there were not that many weapons in the village, and the head of Samashki asked for three days to collect about fifty assault rifles. Romanov refused. On 7 April, the occupiers shelled Samashki with mortars and stormed the village. On 7 and 8 April, the Russian military killed 103 Chechen civilians in the village, whom human rights defenders recorded by name (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[5]. On 11 April, five elders of Samashki handed human rights defenders at the Russian post a written statement: "We believed the MVD of Russia… we forced all the militiamen to leave our village of Samashki. We believed the military that in this case they would not touch the civilian population. And once again a lie. On 7 April the special forces of Russia's MVD began to enter the village"[5][70]. Around 20 April 1995, the elders of Ishkhoy-Yurt, a village in the east of Ichkeria, let in Russian servicemen who promised only to pass through the village[1]. The occupiers fired their assault rifles at the houses and killed a woman who was carrying a child, and the child survived[58]. In the spring of 1996, Russian troops surrounded the villages of Ichkeria and shelled them (see: "Collective Punishment")[21]. Then the occupiers and the puppet government in Grozny signed a "Protocol on Peace and Accord" with the village. The village undertook not to let in fighters of the army of Ichkeria, and in return Russia promised that it would be spared any fighting[11]. On 14 March, Artemov, commander of the occupation forces in the south-west of Ichkeria, gave Russian deputies his word of honor that he would not storm Samashki, because the village was handing over its weapons[21]. On 15 March, the occupiers stormed the village and killed at least 35 Chechen civilians (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[1]. On 31 March 1996, Russian president Yeltsin, by decree No. 435, named "the signing of protocols on peace and accord" one of the main directions of his program for the Chechen Republic[71]. According to the French agency AFP, even before the decree, by 28 March, more than 120 villages of Ichkeria had signed protocols with the occupation forces[98]. On 2 April, Russia and the puppet government signed a "Protocol on Peace and Accord" with Shalazhi, a village south-west of Grozny[1]. On the night of 3 April and on 4 April, Russian pilots bombed the village, destroyed dozens of houses, killed three Chechens and wounded more than three hundred (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[1][21]. By 20 April, according to Zavgaev, head of the puppet government, only 15 villages and towns of Ichkeria had not signed the protocol[1]. On 25 April, Russian pilots bombed Chishki, a village south of Grozny, which had signed a "Protocol on Peace and Accord" shortly before. The pilots killed one Chechen woman and wounded two more Chechens[1]. Human rights defenders of Memorial write: "At times neither a truce, nor the signing of a 'protocol on peace and accord' by a settlement, nor even the occupation of a village or town by the federal [Russian] troops saved it from indiscriminate attacks, air strikes and artillery shelling"[1]. Tim Guldimann, head of the mission of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe in Grozny from January 1996, wrote in 1998 that the commander of the occupation forces and Zavgaev, head of the puppet government, in part forced these protocols upon the villages[11]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1]. T0167.002 Sham Ceasefire September 1994 C1193.T0167.002 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0008 Government In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russia declared ceasefires or signed them with Ichkeria, while the occupation forces went on bombing villages and launched new offensives. Russian president Yeltsin declared an end to hostilities by decree and in televised addresses to the citizens of Russia[1][19]. Russian prime minister Chernomyrdin, commanders of the occupation forces and Russian delegations agreed on ceasefires with representatives of Ichkeria[1]. Russia scheduled ceasefires before Yeltsin's annual address to the Russian parliament on 16 February 1995 and before the Russian presidential election in the summer of 1996[1]. On the night of 10 January 1995, the Russian government declared a 48-hour ceasefire and demanded that the Armed Forces of Ichkeria surrender, and in the daytime the Russian army continued its assault on Grozny[1][21]. On 17 January, Russian prime minister Chernomyrdin agreed with the ministers of Ichkeria on a ceasefire in several stages, and on the night of 19 January Russian pilots dropped concrete-piercing bombs on the presidential palace in Grozny[99][1]. On 13 February, Kulikov, commander of the occupation forces, agreed with Aslan Maskhadov, chief of the Main Staff of the army of Ichkeria, on a "truce" until 19 February, and on 18 February Russian artillerymen shelled the positions of the army of Ichkeria east of Grozny[1]. On 26 April 1995, Russian president Yeltsin signed a decree ending hostilities in Ichkeria from 28 April to 12 May. The decree says: "in the event of armed provocations in the ChR [the Chechen Republic], the actions of the units and formations of the temporary joint forces [Russian troops]… shall be determined in accordance with the situation"[1][100]. General Troshev, who in the spring of 1995 commanded the troops of the Russian defense ministry in Ichkeria, wrote in his memoirs: "We understood that the declaration of the moratorium [the end of hostilities] was of a purely political nature — the country was preparing to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the Great Victory…"[101]. On 9 May, heads of foreign states came to Moscow for the celebration[1]. From 28 April to 12 May 1995, Russian soldiers went on killing Chechen civilians[1]. On 1 May, a Russian sniper killed six-year-old Zulikhan Yunusova in Starye Atagi, a village south of Grozny. Isa Adayev, director of the Chechen National Museum, was at her funeral and in May 1996 told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Prague: "A few days later, at a meeting with the military commandant, it turned out that the soldiers had been drunk and were shooting on a bet: would they hit or not. That is how they killed the girl"[21]. On 10 May, Russian soldiers from the commandant's office of the Staropromyslovsky district of Grozny mortally wounded Sh. Chantiev at the wheel of his car[1]. On 11 May, two days after the celebration in Moscow, Russian pilots bombed Shatoy, a district center in the mountains in the south of Ichkeria[20]. It is unknown how many such crimes the occupation forces committed from 28 April to 12 May 1995. On 12 May, as soon as the decree expired, the Russian army resumed its offensive on the mountain districts of Ichkeria[1]. On 30 July 1995, Russia signed an agreement with Ichkeria on the cessation of hostilities (see: "Sham Treaties"). From 17 August, Russian pilots bombed Roshni-Chu and Tangi-Chu, villages south-west of Grozny, and on 9 October the occupiers launched a new offensive[20][1]. On 31 March 1996, Russian president Yeltsin, by decree No. 435, announced "the cessation, from 24.00 hours on 31 March 1996, of military operations on the territory of the Chechen Republic"[71]. On 1 April, Tikhomirov, commander of the occupation forces, announced that he would continue the war, and on 4 April Russian soldiers stormed Goyskoye, a village south-west of Grozny, and killed 26 Chechens in the fighting[1]. On 27 May, Russian prime minister Chernomyrdin and Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, acting president of Ichkeria, signed a ceasefire agreement in Moscow, and on the evening of 3 June Russian pilots bombed villages of the Nozhay-Yurt and Vedeno districts in the south-east of Ichkeria[13][1][102]. On 10 June in Nazran, Russia undertook to stop the bombing and to remove its checkpoints by 7 July, and on 9 July, six days after Yeltsin's victory in the Russian presidential election, the occupiers launched a new offensive[13][74][1]. On 13 August, Pulikovsky, acting commander of the occupation forces, met Aslan Maskhadov, chief of the Main Staff of the army of Ichkeria, and Ichkeria announced that they had agreed to cease fire from noon on 14 August. On 14 August, Russian pilots bombed Komsomolskoye, a village north-east of Grozny, and killed nine Chechens[97][65]. On 18 August, the command of the occupation forces concluded a ceasefire agreement with the army of Ichkeria, and on the night of 20 August Russian pilots resumed the bombing of Grozny[103][1]. Sergei Kovalyov, head of the Observer Mission of Russian human rights defenders, wrote in the American magazine The New York Review of Books on 11 May 1995 that the ceasefires declared by Russian commanders were disingenuous concessions to domestic and foreign pressures, not the start of a genuine peace process[83]. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that Russia used the "truce" of 1995 to prepare elections and entrench the puppet government, and that Yeltsin's "peace plan" of 1996 remained in force until the election results were tallied in Russia[1]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, Russia signed peace agreements with Ichkeria in Khasavyurt and recognized in them "the inadmissibility of the use of armed force or the threat of its use in resolving disputed questions" (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1]. Three years after the agreements in Khasavyurt, Russia attacked Ichkeria again. On 21 September 1999, Russian pilots began bombing Grozny, and on 29 September the Russian army invaded the republic[1]. T0167.003 Sham Corridor September 1994 C1193.T0167.003 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0010 Regular Army In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers announced "corridors" for Chechens to leave surrounded villages and towns, and then fired on those leaving, detained men at the exit and bombed the villages together with those who had not managed to get out. The "corridors" were announced by the command of the occupation forces when it surrounded a village or town before an assault[1]. Russian commanders passed the conditions for leaving to the head of the village at their checkpoint or announced them through the ITAR-TASS agency, and gave the Chechens from two hours to two days to get out[1][104]. The occupiers began shelling before the appointed time or closed the "corridor" before it ended. Russian generals declared that all Chechen civilians had left, and the troops fired on everyone who remained in the village[1]. On 7 April 1995, a Russian general who refused to give his name gave the Chechens in Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, until four in the afternoon to leave, announcing this at one o'clock, and 15-25 minutes before the deadline the occupiers began shelling the village with mortars. Of the five thousand people in the village, 100-150 managed to get out before the shelling, and even before the appointed hour the Russian military killed two teenagers and mortally wounded a woman who were leaving the village[5]. On 1-2 June 1995, the command of the occupation forces, by agreement with the Assistance Group of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, opened a "corridor" for Chechens to leave the Shatoy district in the mountains in the south of Ichkeria, only in the daytime, from ten in the morning to seven in the evening. Russian tank crews fired on a column of refugees from Borzoy, a village in this district, and pilots bombed it and killed at least four refugees[1]. On 18 December 1995, while Russian troops were shelling Gudermes, the second-largest town of Ichkeria, east of Grozny, the crew of a Russian helicopter fired rockets in an open field at Chechen refugees, mostly women, who were walking from the town along the "humanitarian corridor" eastward to Khasavyurt, a town in Russian-controlled Dagestan. The crew killed the son of one of the refugee women (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[37][21]. On 19 February 1996, on the third day of the assault on the settlement of Novogroznensky in the east of Ichkeria, Kvashnin, commander of the Russian troops in the North Caucasus, declared that all Chechen civilians had left the settlement through two "corridors", and refugees from Novogroznensky denied this. According to the French agency Agence France-Presse, the occupiers killed at least 50 Chechen civilians in the settlement[1]. On 4 March 1996, on the second day of the assault on Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, the occupiers opened a "corridor" and for two hours let vehicles of the International Organization for Migration into the village, and on 5 March they closed the way out. Russian artillerymen and pilots resumed shelling the village, where about 7,000 people remained, and by 9 March, when the occupiers captured Sernovodsk, they had killed at least 45 Chechen civilians there (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[1][66]. On the night of 14 March 1996, the occupiers surrounded Samashki, where about 12,000 people lived. On 14 March, the command of the occupation forces demanded 10 thousand dollars for a "corridor" for the Chechens to leave the village. Chechens from Samashki told human rights defenders of Memorial that the head of the village took this sum to the checkpoint in rubles - 50 million, collected from the villagers (see: "Administrative Corruption and Extortion")[21]. On 15 March at six in the morning, the Russian military at the checkpoint announced to the head of the village that from eight to ten in the morning they would let the Chechens out toward Russian-controlled Ingushetia, and then would begin the assault. Some families went south along another road, but there the occupiers let no one out, and the families returned to the village[1][21]. Zaynap Baysaeva, a Chechen woman from Samashki, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow on 22 April: "Everyone who learned about the corridor — some on a tractor… some in a car, drove up to the checkpoint. But the road was already blocked — the mercenaries [Russian servicemen] were standing there and detaining males from children in the 6th-9th grades to men of 65"[21]. At the checkpoint, Russian soldiers took 91 Chechens off the buses and unlawfully detained them from among those who were leaving through the "corridor". Five weeks later, on 19 April, Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs released them without charges (see: "Filtration Camp System")[28][1]. Sixteen minutes after the end of the "corridor", Russian troops began shelling the village from tanks and howitzers, helicopters and aircraft. About half of the village had not managed to leave (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[1]. On 16 March, Russian soldiers at the checkpoint fired on a column of up to 500 Chechens who were trying to get out of Samashki, and the column returned to the village. On 18 March, several thousand Chechens approached the Russian positions on the southern edge of the village and demanded to be let out. The Russian military allowed women with children to leave and threatened to send the men to a filtration camp, and the women refused to leave without their husbands, fathers, brothers and sons. On the morning of 19 March, the crew of a Russian helicopter fired on the Chechens near the Russian positions, killed one Chechen and wounded six or seven (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians"). Only after this, at noon, did the occupiers open a "corridor", and the Chechens began to leave the encirclement, while a doctor from Samashki took the wounded to the hospital in Achkhoy-Martan, a village in the west of Ichkeria[1]. That day, at another Russian checkpoint, soldiers fired an automatic grenade launcher at women who had been promised a "corridor" to collect their children from the village and return by five in the evening. The occupiers wounded eight to ten women, and the wounded ended up in the hospital in Sleptsovskaya, a stanitsa in Russian-controlled Ingushetia[1][21]. During the assault that began on 15 March, the occupiers killed at least 35 Chechen civilians in Samashki[1]. On 6 May 1996, Russian troops surrounded Komsomolskoye, a village in the Urus-Martan district south-west of Grozny, and demanded that the defenders lay down their arms by nightfall, otherwise shelling would begin at two in the morning. Russian artillerymen opened fire at about three in the afternoon, 11 hours before the deadline, when the Chechens in the village were still preparing to take the children out, and killed Chechen civilians[21]. On 9 July 1996, Russian troops surrounded Gekhi, a village south-west of Grozny, and on 11 July opened a "corridor" only for women, children and the elderly and closed it the same day. The Russian military declared that only men remained in the village, although about 8,000 Chechens had not managed to get out, and from 9 to 12 July the occupiers' artillerymen and pilots killed 19 Chechen civilians in Gekhi[1][6][38]. On 19 August 1996, when the Armed Forces of Ichkeria had surrounded the occupiers in Grozny, Pulikovsky, acting commander of the occupation forces, gave the townspeople 48 hours to leave through the only "corridor", via the suburb of Staraya Sunzha in the east, and threatened to bomb the city afterwards[104]. On the night of 20 August, before the deadline, the occupiers began bombing Grozny and shelling it with artillery, and in the daytime they closed the "corridor"[1][105]. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that no one counted the civilian townspeople whom the occupiers killed in Grozny from 6 to 22 August, and journalists gave the figure of 2,000[1]. On 20 August, the crew of a Russian helicopter near the village of Goyty south of Grozny fired on Chechen refugees from the city who were traveling in buses and cars, and killed ten to twelve people[1]. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that throughout the war the Russian military informed Chechens about the "corridors" poorly or not at all, gave little time to get out before the shelling, and killed Chechen civilians even as they were leaving through the "corridors"[1]. On 21 August 1996, Lebed, secretary of Russia's Security Council, flew to Ichkeria and cancelled the threat to bomb Grozny made by Pulikovsky, acting commander of the occupation forces[6]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1]. T0167.004 Negotiations as Cover for an Attack September 1994 C1193.T0167.004 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0008 Government In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russian president Yeltsin, Russian ministers and generals scheduled negotiations, meetings and peace signings with Ichkeria having already decided to attack, and Russian troops attacked during the negotiations or immediately after them. Russian ministers and commanders of the occupation forces scheduled meetings with Ichkeria in Russian-controlled Ingushetia and North Ossetia. Later the negotiations took place in Grozny through the mediation of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE)[1][106]. Russian delegations demanded that the Armed Forces of Ichkeria hand over their weapons and that the republic recognize itself as part of Russia (see: "Deprivation of Agency")[1]. On 29 November 1994, Russia's Security Council decided to start a war against Ichkeria. In the secret report "Military Aspects of the Operation in Chechnya. Aims, Means and Results", the Russian defense ministry ordered army units and the Internal Troops of Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) to assemble by 6 December, surround Grozny on 7-9 December and capture the city on 10-13 December[1]. On 6 December, two members of the Security Council, Russian defense minister Grachev and Russian interior minister Yerin, met Dzhokhar Dudayev, president of Ichkeria, in the stanitsa of Ordzhonikidzevskaya in Russian-controlled Ingushetia[107][1]. After the meeting, asked by journalists whether there would be a war, Dzhokhar Dudayev replied: "Of course there won't be a war. Why war? For now we have agreed on a peaceful solution…"[108]. Russia scheduled the next negotiations for 12 December in Vladikavkaz, the capital of Russian-controlled North Ossetia, and the day before them the Russian army openly invaded Ichkeria[1]. On the day of the invasion, Russian president Yeltsin said in an address to the citizens of Russia: "Negotiations between representatives of Russia and Chechnya are scheduled for 12 December 1994. We must prevent their disruption"[109]. Human rights defenders of Memorial write about the invasion on the eve of the negotiations: "Actions that were bound to disrupt the negotiations were declared to be aimed at preventing their disruption"[1]. On 12 December, the Russian military detained the delegation of Ichkeria headed by Taymaz Abubakarov, minister of economy and finance, on the border of North Ossetia and Ingushetia in order to let a column of their own troops through into Ichkeria[1][35]. On all three days of the negotiations, 12-14 December, Russian troops advanced on Grozny[110][1], and on the first day the occupiers shelled with artillery and bombed the stanitsa of Assinovskaya in the west of Ichkeria[35]. On 14 December, the delegation of Ichkeria broke off the negotiations over the demand to recognize the republic as part of Russia and left. The delegations never met in Vladikavkaz again[111][1][35]. From December 1994 to April 1996, Russian president Yeltsin and Russian prime minister Chernomyrdin announced negotiations to Ichkeria, and in 1995-1996 Kulikov, Tikhomirov, Kvashnin and Pulikovsky, commanders of the occupation forces, scheduled meetings with the army of Ichkeria, while Russian troops advanced on the days of the meetings. On 27 December 1994, Yeltsin entrusted the negotiations to Yegorov, minister for nationalities, Stepashin, director of the FSK (the predecessor of today's FSB), and Kvashnin, commander of the occupation forces[112]. The next day, FSK director Stepashin told the leaders of Krasnodar krai that what should be discussed was not negotiations but an ultimatum to Ichkeria, and on 31 December the Russian army began storming Grozny[113][1]. On 18 January 1995, Taymaz Abubakarov and Usman Imayev, ministers of Ichkeria, waited in Nazran, a town in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, for two Russian generals whom Chernomyrdin had entrusted with ceasefire negotiations. The generals did not come, and on the night of 19 January Russian pilots dropped concrete-piercing bombs on the presidential palace in Grozny[1]. On 21 February 1995, the Russian military near Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, did not let the delegation of Ichkeria through to a meeting with General Kulikov in Sleptsovskaya, a stanitsa in Russian-controlled Ingushetia. The crews of Russian helicopters fired rockets and machine guns at the road in front of the delegation's cars, and Kulikov refused Ichkeria a meeting[1]. On 22 May 1995, Semyonov, the Russian government's representative in Ichkeria, announced to journalists that negotiations mediated by the OSCE would begin in three days[106], and on 24 May the occupation forces launched an offensive in the mountains in the south of Ichkeria. On 25 May, the delegations of Russia and Ichkeria sat down at the negotiating table in Grozny, and by 12 June the occupiers had captured the mountain district centers of Vedeno, Shatoy and Nozhay-Yurt (see: "Military Intervention")[1]. From 30 September 1995, the Internal Troops of Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Russian police kept Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria on the border with Russian-controlled Ingushetia, encircled (see: "Transport Blockade")[1]. Viktor Kurochkin, a deputy of the Russian parliament, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow in April 1996: "The order to begin large-scale actions of the federal [Russian] troops came in February, precisely when we were agreeing that the checkpoints near Sernovodsk would be removed... But when we arrived to resolve this problem concretely, we were told that an order had come to begin combat operations and to destroy all the bandit formations by 1 April" (this is what Russians called the Armed Forces of Ichkeria)[21]. On the evening of 2 March 1996, the leaders of Sernovodsk agreed on peace for the village with the puppet government in Grozny and with the command of the occupation forces in the south-west of Ichkeria and scheduled the signing for the morning of 3 March. After the agreement, most of the defenders left the village[1]. Sadyt Gisatova, a Chechen woman from Sernovodsk, told the Glasnost tribunal in Prague in May 1996 about the night of 3 March: "That night, for the first time in a long while, my children went to bed undressed. We believed the Russian government and our newly created [puppet government in Grozny] — they promised us peace"[21]. At 5:45 in the morning of 3 March 1996, more than four hours before the signing, the occupiers began storming Sernovodsk in three columns[1]. The defenders of the village killed a Russian colonel in the fighting and captured from him a detailed map of the attack[21]. At 7:30, the defenders repelled the attack. After this, the occupiers shelled the village with artillery, and Russian pilots fired rockets at it from helicopters (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). On 9 March, six days after the start of the assault, Russian troops captured Sernovodsk. From 3 to 9 March, the occupiers killed at least 45 Chechen civilians in the village and wounded 68 (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[1]. On 21 April 1996, while Dzhokhar Dudayev, president of Ichkeria, was talking by satellite telephone with Konstantin Borovoy, a mediator in the peace negotiations between Russia and Ichkeria, the Russian military struck a clearing near the village of Gekhi-Chu south-west of Grozny with missiles and killed him (see: "Neutralization of the Opposition")[12][1]. Two days later, Russian prime minister Chernomyrdin announced that Russia would follow "the tactic of expanding peace combined with tough forceful methods"[1]. On 3 July 1996, in Novye Atagi, a village south of Grozny, the Russian members of the Russia-Ichkeria working group on military questions, headed by General Tikhomirov, declared that they were removing the checkpoints and withdrawing military units from Ichkeria[13]. On 9 July, while Mikhailov, head of the Russian delegation, was assuring Tim Guldimann, head of the OSCE mission in Ichkeria, that Russia wanted to continue the negotiations, Tikhomirov's troops surrounded Gekhi, a village south-west of Grozny, and by 12 July had killed 19 Chechen civilians there (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[1][38]. On 19 July, Kvashnin, commander of the Russian troops in the North Caucasus, announced that he was ready to meet Aslan Maskhadov, chief of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, and to discuss, among other things, "the future of Aslan Maskhadov himself", and the next day the occupiers launched an offensive in the mountains south-west of Shatoy, a district center in the south of Ichkeria (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[114][1]. On 31 July, Ichkeria declined the meeting[115]. From 13 to 17 August 1996, General Pulikovsky, acting commander of the occupation forces, met three times with Aslan Maskhadov, chief of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, at ceasefire negotiations (see: "Sham Ceasefire")[6]. On the evening of 19 August, Pulikovsky gave the people of Grozny 48 hours to leave, and on the night of 20 August, before the deadline, Russian artillerymen and pilots began shelling and bombing the city (see: "Collective Punishment")[104][1]. According to journalists' estimates, from 6 to 22 August the occupiers killed about 2,000 civilian townspeople in Grozny. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that no one kept an exact count[1]. On 1 May 1995, Sergei Kovalyov, a deputy of the Russian parliament, wrote in his testimony to the Helsinki Commission of the US Congress that all attempts to settle the question of Ichkeria's independence by political means, before the war and after it began, were systematically and deliberately torpedoed by the military high command and by others in the government in Moscow[99]. On 22 August 1996, Lebed, secretary of Russia's Security Council, and Aslan Maskhadov, chief of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, agreed on a ceasefire and the withdrawal of Russian troops[1]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1].
