On 21 January 1996, her mother Melkhash Zelimkhanova told human rights defenders of the international organization Human Rights Watch and of "Memorial" there: "When we were in the basement [in Gudermes] it was very cold, and by the time we got here my daughter, Zali, got sick and died a sudden death"[37]. After the capture of Gudermes, Russian servicemen for several days did not let ICRC staff into the city, while the elderly, women and children froze without food or water in the basements of destroyed houses. On 26 December, the ICRC began distributing aid in Gudermes[168]. In December 1995 and January 1996, soldiers at Russian checkpoints hardly ever let through the vehicles of the Belgian section of Médecins Sans Frontières, and the doctors could not get medicines to Gudermes[37]. On the eve of New Year 1996, Russian servicemen and officers of the Ministry of Internal Affairs at the posts around Sernovodsk beat the crews of vehicles that were bringing New Year presents to the children[21]. In 1996, Russian servicemen at the checkpoints checked humanitarian organizations for passes for travel around Ichkeria. Russian agencies issued a pass for two weeks, often a few days before it expired, or did not issue one at all[164]. By 3 January, the occupiers had closed the roads around Grozny and to Gudermes to ICRC vehicles. The commanders of the occupation troops in Grozny and the military leadership in Moscow did not reply until the end of January to the ICRC's requests to name someone to negotiate with[37]. On 5 March 1996, during the assault on Sernovodsk by the Russian units of Artemov, the commander of the occupation troops in the southwest of Ichkeria, the occupiers agreed with the ICRC to cease fire and let its staff through to the wounded and sick, but on 6 March the soldiers at the post did not let the ICRC vehicles through, saying that they had received no orders[21][1]. The Chechens wounded by the occupiers reached doctors only on 9 March, when Russian troops captured Sernovodsk[1], and the ICRC got into the village three weeks after the start of the assault on 3 March[21]. During the assault on Samashki, on 16 March 1996 the occupiers did not let through 17 buses of the International Organization for Migration, which had agreed with the Russian military to evacuate those who remained in the village, and did not let the wounded out through Novy Sharoy, a village to the south, although the Chechens offered 100 million rubles and a car for this[1][21]. On 19 March, when the occupiers opened the way out of Samashki, a doctor of the village hospital took the wounded to the hospital in Achkhoy-Martan, a district center in the west of Ichkeria[1]. In the spring of 1996, Russian troops surrounded the mountain villages of the Vedeno, Shatoy and Nozhay-Yurt districts in the south and southeast of Ichkeria. The soldiers did not let doctors or humanitarian organizations in[1]. On 10 July 1996, Russian troops surrounded Makhkety, a mountain village in the southeast of Ichkeria, and blocked the only road out of it, while soldiers at the Russian checkpoints around Shali, a town southeast of Grozny, did not let vehicles with the wounded through. Seriously wounded Chechens were carried out of Makhkety along mountain paths; four of them died of their wounds in the hospital in Shali[1]. The human rights defenders of Human Rights Watch wrote in their review for 1995 that Russian troops again and again blocked or delayed humanitarian aid to civilians in Ichkeria, especially at the start of the war, and at least once fired on a Médecins Sans Frontières vehicle with a clearly visible emblem of the organization[116]. On 26 March 1996, the UN Secretary-General wrote in a report to the Commission on Human Rights that, according to Human Rights Watch, Russian agencies created bureaucratic obstacles for aid organizations, hindered the distribution of aid and did not allow the sick and wounded to be evacuated from Grozny. Sergei Kovalyov, Russia's human rights commissioner, informed the UN that Russia was obstructing the delivery of humanitarian aid to the war zone, including medicines to save the wounded[68]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1]. T0163 Desecration of the Dead September 1994 C1193.T0163 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0010 Regular Army In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers burned the bodies of the Chechens they had killed, cut off the ears of the dead, secretly buried bodies in unmarked graves and did not give them back to the families. Russian servicemen killed detained Chechens and secretly buried the bodies near their positions, and such graves were often mined[1]. The occupiers did not let relatives onto the grounds of their units, and families found the graves only when the unit had left[1][20]. In captured villages, Russian soldiers threw the bodies of the Chechens they had killed into houses they had set on fire, or doused them with gasoline and set them alight[5][21]. The occupiers cut off the ears of dead Chechens[28][21]. Russian servicemen brought bodies in a "Ural" truck to the Karpinsky cemetery in the west of Grozny from the checkpoints and from the filtration camps to which the occupiers took detained Chechens. Gravediggers laid them in fresh pits, three to five in each[20]. At the start of the war, the Russian army took some of the bodies to Rostov, a city in the south of Russia, to the refrigerator railcars of its 124th medical laboratory, and did not give them back to the families of the dead[169][21]. On 17 December 1994, Russian soldiers in armored personnel carriers shot up a column of cars with refugees from Grozny near the border with Russian-controlled Ingushetia and killed ten people. The occupiers took the bodies away, and the Russian police in Ingushetia found only one of them[1]. On 31 December 1994, the occupiers detained two young Chechens in the basement of a hospital in Grozny, where they were hiding from the shelling. The parents of one of them later collected his body from a morgue in Moscow and buried him at home, while the relatives of the other had still not found him by 2015[170]. From December 1994 to May 1995, the occupiers detained 27 Chechens in Grozny and took them to the filtration camp in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia, and by April 1996 their bodies were brought back from there. Those whom the Russian escort shot or threw out of the vehicles on the way to Mozdok were buried unidentified by villagers, and relatives later found them by descriptions of the bodies and clothes[21]. On 28 January 1995, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) led two brothers, aged 18 and 21, under escort through their unit on Mayakovsky Street in Grozny, shot them and secretly buried them in the yard of a house on the grounds of the unit. On 2 April, when the unit had left, their father Khusein Khamidov found the grave from a neighbor's account, took the bodies out of the ground in the presence of a forensic doctor and buried his sons by his house[1][21][171]. At the end of March 1995, criminal investigators from Moscow began opening the pits with bodies at the cemetery near the cannery in the Zavodskoy district of Grozny. Forensic doctors of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs recorded the cause of death as shooting, death by fire or knife wounds, and some of the bodies had no head[20][21]. On 7 April 1995, the occupation troops stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria. On 7 and 8 April, Russian servicemen went from house to house and killed Chechen civilians (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians"). The 1995 report of the Observer Mission of Russian human rights organizations says: "Numerous accounts by witnesses have been recorded of the deliberate burning by Russian servicemen of the bodies of dead residents." The Mission named 13 people whose bodies the occupiers had burned. On the evening of 7 April, Russian soldiers killed Ali Sugaipov, Emin Nadyrov, Khamzat Kharkharoyev and his son Akhmed, and on the morning of 8 April fellow villagers found their burned bodies in one yard[5]. Russian tank crews wounded 62-year-old Dogu Tsatishayev, and soldiers shot him dead at point-blank range with an automatic rifle in house 93 on Sharipov Street, poured gasoline over the body and set it on fire[5]. On 20 April, Tamara Mutiyeva from Samashki told observers of the Russian human rights organization "Memorial" that Russian servicemen had killed and burned her half-sister. Andrei Blinushov, one of the observers, recorded in his diary: "To this day the sister and mother of the murdered girl are collecting pieces of her bones in the ruins of the house"[70]. On 9 May 1995, soldiers of the 503rd regiment of the Russian army unlawfully detained at a checkpoint Ayub Domayev, Aslambek Suleimanov and Shamkhan Tashukhadzhiyev from Shali, a town southeast of Grozny, and killed all three (see: "Killing of Prisoners and Detainees"). Vladimir Yemelyanenko, a correspondent of the Moscow weekly Moskovskiye Novosti, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow on 21 February 1996 that the military did not let the relatives onto the grounds of the regiment and in answer to their questions "said that no such people had passed through here"[20]. On 3 June, the 503rd regiment left its camp in a field near Shali, and a conscript soldier who had fled the regiment showed the families where the soldiers had buried the three Chechens. Near the camp of the reconnaissance company, at a depth of two meters, the relatives found the bodies of Ayub Domayev and Aslambek Suleimanov. In another place in the field they dug up the car in which the three Chechens had been traveling, crushed by tank tracks. On 6 June, the body of Shamkhan Tashukhadzhiyev was found at the cemetery on the outskirts of Shali[1][20]. In September 1995, Chechen women from Grozny found by the fresh pits at the Karpinsky cemetery five green military shell boxes containing bones and ashes, and handed them over to the OSCE mission. According to the expert examination, one of the boxes contained the remains of people aged 20-23, burned, doused with sulfuric acid and broken into small pieces[20]. In early October 1995, the Czech journalist Petra Procházková filmed at the Orthodox cemetery in Grozny pits with several dozen bodies, to which the occupiers brought new bodies at night in their vehicles, and reported this to the OSCE[21]. At the end of February 1996, Russian servicemen killed the detained Sharip Batayev, a Chechen from Arshty, a village in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, and buried the body at a depth of 20 centimeters on a hillside below the trenches of the reconnaissance troops of the 693rd regiment of the Russian 58th Army. On 20 March, investigators from Ingushetia dug up the body, and on the same day it was buried according to Muslim custom[21]. From 3 to 9 March 1996, Russian troops stormed Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, and burned the mosque there, to which on 4 March villagers had brought the bodies of Chechens killed by the occupiers in order to bury them later[88]. On 11 March, women from Sernovodsk, whom the occupiers had let home for a few hours, found seven burned bodies by the burned-down mosque[21]. During the assault on Sernovodsk, the crews of Russian helicopters wounded an elderly Chechen with rockets at the resort near the village where refugees lived, and the wounded man died on the threshold of his room. The occupiers searched the resort, and after that only burned remains were found where the body had been[21]. On 20 March 1996, Russian soldiers who had landed from a helicopter near a dairy farm by Nagornoye, a village next to Grozny, shot detained unarmed Chechens there: two according to Human Rights Watch, five according to the Chechen women's committee. The killers cut off the ears of the dead and slit their stomachs with a knife[28][21]. On 12 May 1996, Russian troops captured Kharsenoy, a mountain village in the south of Ichkeria, and shot seven young Chechens from the village. Fellow villagers buried one of them, while the bodies of the other six the occupiers never gave back to the relatives[21]. On 15 July 1996, in the northwestern suburb of Grozny, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs from two armored personnel carriers shot unarmed people in passenger cars. The occupiers set fire to the cars with the bodies, and cut off the ears of some of the dead[38][1]. The 1997 report of Human Rights Watch says that from March 1995 to January 1997 the "Victims of War" society headed by Khusein Khamidov helped recover 926 bodies from mass graves in Ichkeria. Forensic doctors in Rostov established the names of 426 of them, and about 80 more mass graves had not been opened by January 1997[28]. In June 1996, the prosecutor's office of the administration installed by Russia in Grozny handed over to Russian prosecutors 342 cases on crimes of the occupiers, among them on cut-off ears and on bodies thrown from helicopters. Russian prosecutors returned more than half of the cases for further investigation, and closed or did not consider the rest (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")[28]. On 3 October 1996, a month after the peace agreements in Khasavyurt, Chernomyrdin, the chairman of the Russian government, and Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the acting president of Ichkeria, signed a statement in Moscow. Under it, Russia undertook to open access to burial sites for examination and excavation at Ichkeria's first request[172]. By mid-October 1996, Russian officials, contrary to the statement, were not letting the "Victims of War" society open the graves: they said they had no bodies, or demanded bribes[28]. In December 1997, several dozen bodies of Chechens, wrapped in blankets, still lay in the refrigerator railcars of the 124th laboratory of the Russian army in Rostov. A delegation of Ichkeria came to Rostov and asked for them back, but the laboratory staff did not return a single body[169]. In 2019, Alexander Cherkasov of "Memorial" reported that several years earlier about a hundred unidentified remains from the time of the war had been taken out of the refrigerators of the 124th laboratory: some were sent to the Chechen Republic, others were buried under numbers in cemeteries in Moscow[173]. In 2014, Russian servicemen found in the Oktyabrsky district of Grozny a mass grave from the first war with the remains of more than 160 people and took them to Rostov for examination. According to the experts, apart from two Russian servicemen, those lying there were most likely civilian men, women and children. On 31 December 2016, the remains of 109 people from this grave were brought from Rostov to Grozny. Relatives identified two of them by genetic profiles and took them, while the other 107 were buried in two temporary mass graves at the cemetery near the village of Pobedinskoye outside Grozny, and the relatives received no lists of the dead[174][175]. T0105 Total Destruction of Infrastructure September 1994 C1193.T0105 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0010 Regular Army In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers destroyed the towns and villages of Ichkeria together with their housing, hospitals and schools[1]. Russian pilots and artillerymen destroyed residential neighborhoods with bombing and shelling (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[1]. In captured villages and towns, Russian soldiers and police officers looted houses (see: "Pillage") and then set them on fire with gasoline, hay or flamethrowers[5][58][21]. After the war of 1994-1996, 60,000 families of Grozny were left without housing[176]. The occupiers destroyed substations, tore down power lines and blew up gas pipelines[20][21]. In December 1994, Russian aviation bombed Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria. On 9 January 1995, Irina from the Third Microdistrict on the outskirts of Grozny told Human Rights Watch in Russian-controlled Ingushetia: "Our region was the first to suffer… either December 17th or 18th, three nine-story apartment buildings of the institute 'Promavtomatika' were bombed out. People all become homeless"[165]. On the night of 20 December, Russian pilots dropped two bombs on a block of one-story houses at the intersection of Moskovskaya Street and Noya Buachidze Street and completely or partially destroyed 18 houses[1]. Russian aviation bombed a substation, and Grozny was left without electricity[20]. On 31 December 1994, the occupiers began the assault on the city. After 20 February 1995, Russian special forces set fire to and blew up houses in Grozny and destroyed pipes and power lines[21]. More than two months after the start of the assault, by 6 March 1995, Russian troops had captured Grozny. On 1 May 1995, the Russian journalist Yevgenia Albats, who had been in the city in January, said at a hearing of a commission of the US Congress: "There is no such city any more. There isn't a single house in Grozny that hasn't been destroyed one way or another by the war"[99]. On 3 February 1995, soldiers of the Russian OMON (police special forces) and of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) searched houses in Petropavlovskaya, a stanitsa northeast of Grozny, and burned 14 houses. In all, the occupiers destroyed 86 houses in the stanitsa[21]. In February 1995, Russian pilots bombed two schools, a sports school, a hospital and a kindergarten in Argun, a town east of Grozny[57]. At the end of March 1995, Russian troops captured Gudermes, the second-largest city of Ichkeria, without a fight, and on 29 and 30 March soldiers burned houses in it with flamethrowers; on Parkhomenko Street two houses were left intact[1][58]. In April 1995, Russian troops shelled for a month Alleroy, a village in the east of Ichkeria with 4,500-5,000 inhabitants. The occupiers completely destroyed a fifth of the houses of Alleroy with rockets[1]. On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs and the OMON stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria. Chechens in Samashki told observers of the Russian human rights organization "Memorial" that the soldiers and OMON men burned houses on 8 April, when they were searching the village. Russian servicemen spent the night in the school on Kooperativnaya Street, and in the morning set it on fire, and the school burned out from the inside[5]. On 10 April, a Chechen woman named Karnukayeva from Rabochaya Street told the Observer Mission of Russian human rights organizations: "The houses are burned. I have nowhere to go now. I am left on the street hungry and cold with 4 children"[5]. Viktor Lozinsky of "Memorial" examined the burned houses of Samashki from 18 April to 1 May 1995. In February 1996, he told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation: "The village was being burned out systematically. The houses were set on fire like this: a window was broken with a rifle butt, and wiping cloth [rags] soaked in some diesel fuel was simply put on the windowsill and set alight"[20]. The Observer Mission published a list drawn up by the administration of Samashki of 198 yards where the occupiers had completely destroyed at least one house, and in 155 of them almost all the houses had burned down[5]. The human rights defenders of "Memorial" write that the Russian military and officers of the Ministry of Internal Affairs burned most of the houses in the village deliberately[1]. From 30 September 1995 to March 1996, Russian Internal Troops and police kept Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, encircled, tore down the power lines near the village and blew up the gas pipeline several times (see: "Transport Blockade")[21]. In December 1995, after the Armed Forces of Ichkeria had liberated Gudermes, Russian troops shelled and bombed the city. According to refugees and journalists' estimates, the occupiers destroyed or damaged about 40 percent of the buildings of Gudermes[37]. From 3 to 9 March 1996, Russian troops stormed Sernovodsk, burned or destroyed 30 percent of the houses of the village, and Russian soldiers set fire to the apartments of refugees on the northern outskirts of the village with hand-held flamethrowers[21]. On 15 March 1996, 11 months after the first assault, Russian troops stormed Samashki again and razed to the ground the House of Culture and the school, which the Chechens had rebuilt. Journalists who came after the assault saw only three surviving houses in the whole village[21]. On 3 and 4 April 1996, Russian pilots bombed Shalazhi, a village in the southwest of Ichkeria, and destroyed dozens of houses, the whole upper part of the village[1][21]. On 6 April 1996, Russian troops captured Zhani-Vedeno, a mountain village of 38 yards in the southeast of Ichkeria, from which the Chechens had fled the shelling, and for a month let no one near it. When the Russian servicemen left, one intact house remained in the village, and in place of most of the houses an observer of "Memorial" found ashes with no traces of shells or bombs[1]. From 9 to 11 July 1996, Russian artillery shelled and aviation bombed Gekhi, a village southwest of Grozny. A correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Izvestia wrote that the occupiers had destroyed more than a third of the village[1][38]. On the night of 11 July, Russian artillerymen shelled Makhkety, a mountain village in the southeast of Ichkeria, with the Grad and Uragan multiple rocket launchers, which cannot fire with precision, and destroyed 150 houses[1][38]. From 6 to 22 August 1996, Russian troops shelled Grozny with heavy artillery and bombed it, and on 21 August Russian pilots dropped incendiary bombs on the blocks of five-story buildings on Saikhanov and Ulyanov Streets, from which the buildings burned out from the inside[1]. The bulletin of the International Committee of the Red Cross of 2 September 1996 says that after the August strikes all 80,000 people in Grozny were left without electricity and medical care: all the hospitals of the city were destroyed or badly damaged[177]. On 26 July 1995, the UN Human Rights Committee, in its comments on Russia, expressed regret that the Russian armed forces had destroyed schools, hospitals and other civilian buildings[79]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1]. T0146 Administrative Corruption and Extortion September 1994 C1193.T0146 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0010 Regular Army In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russian servicemen and police officers extorted money, gold, cars and other valuables from Chechens. At checkpoints, Russian police officers and soldiers took money from drivers for passage and took cars away from Chechens. Such posts stood in Grozny at every stop and on the road from Gudermes to Argun, towns east of Grozny[21]. Russian guards of the filtration camps and of the pits at military units demanded money from detained Chechens for their release (see: "Hostage-Taking")[20][77]. Russian troops surrounded villages and took money from Chechens in exchange for not bombing them and for letting the Chechens leave[21][72]. Russian servicemen demanded weapons that the Chechens did not have and took money instead. Often, a month after the payment, a new Russian unit surrounded the village and demanded money again[21]. On 7-8 April 1995, Russian soldiers who were storming Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, brought the men from Vygonnaya Street out of a basement and demanded gold and money from the women in exchange for not taking the men away. The occupiers took the men, stripped and bound with wire, to the pits near Assinovskaya, a neighboring stanitsa, and to the filtration camp in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia (see: "Filtration Camp System")[70]. In May, the headquarters of the joint grouping of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs in Ichkeria, in a "Memo", prohibited soldiers at the posts from taking belongings and food from Chechens passing through[1]. In the summer of 1995, the puppet government in Grozny began paying compensation from the Russian budget to Chechens whose homes the occupiers had destroyed[176][1]. Officials of the puppet government who distributed the payments usually kept 15 to 50% of each family's money for themselves. By the count of the Chechen journalist Musa Muradov, of the 60 thousand families of Grozny who had lost their housing, no more than one and a half thousand received money[176]. In the autumn of 1995, Russian soldiers at the checkpoints near Achkhoy-Martan and Sernovodsk, villages in the west of Ichkeria, took from everyone who entered or left the village 100,000 rubles (23 dollars) at Achkhoy-Martan and 50,000 rubles at Sernovodsk[68]. Before the assault in March 1996, Chechens in Samashki sold cows to buy weapons, hand them over to the Russian servicemen and save their homes. Zinaida Baisayeva, who lived in the village, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow on 22 April 1996: "Approximately 9-10 times we gave money so that they would not bomb us. But they shelled us anyway every night." On the night of 14 March 1996, the occupiers surrounded Samashki. Russian servicemen told the village head and the elders that they would give a "corridor" so that fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria could leave the village at night, and that they would then check passports and leave. Zainap Baisayeva from this village told the Glasnost tribunal: "For this one-hour corridor they asked, as I was told, 58 million rubles. This money was collected from the residents of the village. My brother gave a million [rubles] — the last he had earned… All the money was handed over to the checkpoint, to whoever was in command there." For a second "corridor", for Chechen civilians to leave the village, the Russian servicemen demanded 10 thousand dollars. Chechens from Samashki told human rights defenders of Memorial that on 14 March the village head took weapons and 50 million rubles (10 thousand dollars) to Russian checkpoint No. 13. On the morning of 15 March, the occupiers gave the Chechens two hours to leave the village (see: "Sham Corridor") and began the assault[21]. In the spring of 1996, the occupiers and the puppet government in Grozny forced villages to sign "Protocols on Peace and Accord" and to surrender weapons (see: "Collective Punishment")[1]. Chechens in Gekhi, a village southwest of Grozny, paid Russian servicemen about a hundred million rubles when signing the "Protocol on Peace and Accord". In Mesker-Yurt, a village southeast of Grozny, the occupiers received a hundred thousand rubles from each house[21]. On 7 April 1996, Russian servicemen ordered Saidash Shamakhurov from Gikalovo, a village south of Grozny, to drive in his own car to Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny. On 27 April, the occupiers exchanged him for a captured Russian soldier (see: "Hostage-Taking"), and three days later returned his car to him, taking 2,000 dollars and one more prisoner for it[28]. In April 1996, the occupiers surrounded Shali, a town southeast of Grozny, and Russian soldiers at the post did not let Chechens out of the town, demanded money from them and fired into the ground in front of them. On 26 April, more than a thousand Chechen women and children left Shali on foot[1][72]. The 1995 report of the observer mission of Russian human rights organizations says that Russian guards extorted money where they held detained Chechens before sending them to filtration camps, because no one controlled these places and they had no official status[77]. Despite the "Memo", Russian servicemen and police officers kept extorting payments at checkpoints until the end of the war in 1996, and Chechens complained about them to human rights defenders[1]. T0020 Staging a Coup September 1994 C1193.T0020 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0017 Secret Police and Security Services In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russian special services and the army gave the puppet opposition money, weapons, instructors, tank crewmen and pilots in order to overthrow Dzhokhar Dudayev, the elected president of the Chechen Republic. In the summer of 1994, Russia's Ministry for Nationalities Affairs and the FSK (a predecessor of today's FSB) helped the puppet opposition recruit armed fighters in Znamenskoye, a village in the northwest of Ichkeria, and in Urus-Martan, a town southwest of Grozny[1]. Russia allocated more than 150 billion rubles to the Provisional Council, the leadership of the puppet opposition, which it had confirmed at a congress on 3 June. In an analytical memorandum, the FSK named the head of the Provisional Council the most suitable candidate for support[1]. On 3 September 1994, the Russian government, in an address to the Chechen people, proposed that Dzhokhar Dudayev resign[1]. On 5 September 1994, the General Staff of the Russian army ordered that 10 armored personnel carriers and 6 combat helicopters with crews be handed over to the Provisional Council[1]. From these helicopters, Russian pilots fired rockets at residential houses in Ichkeria (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). In November, the Russian army handed tanks over to the council[1][178]. In September and October 1994, Russian officers trained more than a hundred fighters of the Provisional Council to drive T-62 tanks and fire army mortars at the "Prudboy" training ground near Volgograd, a city in the south of Russia[179][1]. In October 1994, Savostyanov, the head of the Moscow directorate of the FSK, ordered that Russian soldiers and officers who knew how to maintain armored vehicles and fight in them be found for the Provisional Council. The military counterintelligence of the FSK selected the candidates[180]. From 3 to 9 November, FSK officers travelled around military units near Moscow and signed contracts with tank crewmen[1][180]. In November 1994, Kolesnikov, the Chief of the General Staff of the Russian army, authorized sending the recruits to the Caucasus. Kotenkov, Russia's deputy minister for nationalities affairs, directed the dispatch, and by 16 November the recruits had been brought to Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia near the border of the Chechen Republic[1]. Russia denied that it was sending its servicemen to fight for the Provisional Council (see: "Lies about Its Own Actions"). In the autumn of 1994, FSK officers fought on the side of the puppet opposition[1]. From September 1994 until the assault on Grozny on 26 November, fighters of the Provisional Council and Russian crews attacked Ichkeria. On 2 September, fighters of the council and a column of twelve tanks with Russian crews attacked Grozny. The Armed Forces of Ichkeria stopped them at the settlement of Dolinsky, northwest of Grozny, knocked out a tank and took eight men prisoner, among them, according to initial reports, Russian servicemen[181][135][35][1][46][47]. On 30 September, Russian pilots in four helicopters of the Provisional Council fired rockets at the "Severny" airport in Grozny and destroyed five civilian aircraft and two aircraft of the army of Ichkeria, and fighters of the puppet opposition blocked the entrances to the city[1][2][182]. Dzhokhar Dudayev rejected the Provisional Council's ultimatum to surrender within six hours, and the council's fighters dispersed without attacking Grozny[2][183]. On 15 October, fighters of the Provisional Council stormed Grozny from the south and from the north, and the Armed Forces of Ichkeria repelled the assault. The defenders took several dozen attackers prisoner, among them, according to various reports, 12 to 15 Russian officers[183], and on 16 October the council's fighters retreated to their bases in Znamenskoye and in Gekhi, a village southwest of Grozny[1]. On 17 November 1994, nine days before the assault on Grozny, a group of Russian officers headed by Kolesnikov, the Chief of the General Staff, flew from Moscow to Mozdok[1]. Valery Yakov, special correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Izvestia, wrote about the preparation of the assault in November 1996: "There, in Mozdok, at the 'Arsenal' base, the contract soldiers [recruited Russian servicemen]… trained the Chechen crews [of the Provisional Council]… In all, the contract soldiers received 40 brand-new tanks, 16 of which had 'Russian' crews"[184][180]. On 26 November, fighters of the Provisional Council and Russian tank crewmen under the command of Zhukov, the deputy commander of a Russian army corps from Volgograd, stormed Grozny[1][180]. Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the vice president of the Chechen Republic, wrote in his memoirs that in the morning he saw the start of the assault from the window of his office in the presidential palace: "on the northeastern outskirts of the city, from the direction of Tolstoy-Yurt [a village north of Grozny where the fighters of the Provisional Council were stationed], tank and artillery fire began to thunder"[36]. The tanks reached the center of Grozny, where fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria shot them up with grenade launchers[1]. The defenders routed the attackers and, according to the government of the Chechen Republic, took 68 Russian servicemen prisoner[185]. Among the prisoners were soldiers and officers of the Russian Kantemirovskaya Tank Division from near Moscow[136]. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that without Russia's military help the puppet opposition could not have overthrown Dzhokhar Dudayev[1]. After the defeat of 26 November, the Provisional Council withdrew its fighters to its bases[6][1]. Fifteen days later, on 11 December 1994, the Russian army openly invaded the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria (see: "Military Intervention")[1]. T0123 Deprivation of Drinking Water September 1994 C1193.T0123 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0010 Regular Army In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers left Chechens without drinking water. Russian pilots and artillerymen more than once destroyed substations and the water supply system in Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria, leaving the townspeople without water[20][177]. Russian servicemen fired from armored personnel carriers and helicopters at Chechens who were going for water (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[57][21]. On 31 January 1995, the occupiers shelled Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, from tanks and helicopters, leaving the Chechens in the village without water (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[5]. In February 1995, Russian artillery shelled and aircraft bombed Argun, a town east of Grozny. Chechens in Argun hid in basements and went out for water only between seven and nine in the morning, while the crews of Russian helicopters fired at passers-by in the streets[57]. During the assault on Grozny in February 1995, Russian servicemen in the Katayama settlement within the city limits shot 28-year-old Dzhenchuraeva with the cannon of an armored personnel carrier as she was carrying water. Her brother tried to carry the body home and survived, although the occupiers wounded him in the shoulder. Lipkan Bazaeva, a teacher from Grozny and the wife of the murdered woman's cousin, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Prague in May 1996: "She went for water, believing that a woman would not be killed"[21]. On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) and OMON troops (police special forces) stormed Samashki. On 8 April, Russian soldiers searched houses in the village and set fire to most of them (see: "Total Destruction of Infrastructure"). On the morning of 8 April, Russian servicemen drove Yuzbek Shovkhalov, an elder of Samashki, into the basement of his house on Kooperativnaya Street, and the basement filled with smoke. In April 1995, the elder told the observer mission of Russian human rights organizations how he ran out of there with burns: "I run, thinking, at least there was a flask of water standing there. No, they had carried it out, they're drinking the water. They're all sitting on the other side of the street, sitting, laughing, cracking sunflower seeds"[5][1]. On 10 April, a Chechen woman named Karnukaeva of Rabochaya Street told the mission about soldiers in the neighbors' yard, where she had hidden on 8 April: "They say to the old woman: 'Is this your drinking water?' She says: 'Yes, it's clean water.' 'Go on, you drink it first.' She took a mug, drank some water, then they drank themselves and spilled it, didn't leave a drop. They turned over all those barrels and flasks and poured out the water. In case anything happened, if there was a fire, so that no one could put it out. That's probably what they were thinking"[5]. By 12 April 1995, Russian servicemen had shot through the water barrels in Samashki, and the Chechens in the village had nothing to keep water in[20]. The diary of a Memorial observer records on 14 April that the village was receiving no water, gas or electricity. That day, the command of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs eased entry into Samashki, and Kosov, an adviser to the president of Russian-controlled Ingushetia, organized the delivery of bread and water to the village[70]. In the spring of 1996, a year after Russian troops captured Grozny, there was no water in the city's apartments, and there were two to three liters per person a day. The townspeople walked 5-10 kilometers for water and took it from the dirty Sunzha river, which flows through the city[21]. In August 1996, Russian pilots bombed Grozny, and artillerymen shelled the city (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). A bulletin of the International Committee of the Red Cross of 2 September 1996 says that after these strikes all 80 thousand people in Grozny were left without drinking water, and at the end of August Red Cross engineers reached the city's only working pumping station and began distributing water, three liters per person a day[177]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1]. T0112 Theft of Cultural Property September 1994 C1193.T0112 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0010 Regular Army In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russian servicemen looted museums and the homes of Chechens in Grozny, and specialists of the Russian ministry of culture took the most valuable of the surviving paintings from the ruins to Moscow. From 1 to 4 January 1995, the occupiers shelled the building that housed the Chechen National Museum and the Museum of Fine Arts, and burned both museums almost completely (see: "Destruction of Historical Memory")[1]. Until the spring of 1995, Russian servicemen let none of the Chechens into the ruins of the museums and plundered what had survived. The occupiers took exhibits as trophies, according to rank and position[21]. Russian soldiers loaded exhibits of the National Museum onto armored personnel carriers[21]. Commanders of the occupation troops, with the help of soldiers, took more than one truckload of ancient books from the museum's manuscript department toward Mozdok, a town in North Ossetia, and Ingushetia, both under Russian control[21]. In February 1995, officers of the FSK (a predecessor of today's FSB) packed paintings and other works of art from the ruins into a 20-ton railway container[1]. At the end of March, the Russian ministry for emergency situations brought five specialists from the Russian ministry of culture and Moscow museums to Grozny. The group catalogued the works from the container[20]. Khotin, deputy director of the ministry of culture's museum center and one of the five, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow in February 1996: "We tried to carry out of the ruins everything that could be carried out. At the same time, the state of preservation of the works was practically zero. … We conserved, made presentable and took away about 60 works of fine art"[20]. Isa Adayev, director of the National Museum, told this tribunal in Prague in May 1996: "The art experts who came from Moscow helped to steal things, picking out what they wanted by degree of significance. These experts left behind what they called 'useless junk'"[21]. In 1995, during the capture of Grozny, Russian soldiers twice looted the home library of the Chechen journalist Aslan Dukaev in the city, and his sister saved only a few books[186]. In 1995, after the capture of Grozny, servicemen of unit 3111 of the Dzerzhinsky Division of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) searched the house of a Chechen on the outskirts of the city and took away a collection of ancient manuscripts, books and icons that Mikhail Patalov, a former deputy director of the Grozny Philharmonic, kept there. His complaint passed through eleven levels of the prosecutor's office, the prosecutors opened a case, but it went nowhere[1]. In July 1995, the delegation of Ichkeria at the talks with Russia in Grozny demanded the return of the National Museum's exhibits. The Russian delegation verbally promised to look into it[21]. Seven months later, in February 1996, the removed paintings lay in the storerooms of the Russian ministry of culture awaiting restoration[20]. In July 2002, 43 works from the Grozny Museum of Fine Arts hung in Moscow at an exhibition of the Tretyakov Gallery[187]. T0162.001 Denial of Quarter September 1994 C1193.T0162.001 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0010 Regular Army In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russian leaders and the command of the occupation troops declared that fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria would be shot on the spot and destroyed. The top leaders of Russia declared to journalists in Moscow that the fighters of Ichkeria had to be destroyed[77][132], and the command of the occupation troops declared it in ultimatums and orders to the troops[1]. In February 1995, Kolesnikov, the Chief of the General Staff of Russia, said of the Chechens captured by Russian troops: "Prisoners are treated well, although we don't have to, because by law one could shoot them on the spot as bandits" (this is what Russia called fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria)[77][57]. On 10 January 1996, Russian pilots in helicopters fired missiles at the head of a column of buses that had crossed from Russian-controlled Dagestan into Ichkeria[1]. In the buses were fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria under the command of Salman Raduyev and the hostages they had seized in Kizlyar, a town in Dagestan. Human rights defenders of Memorial write, citing Valery Yakov, a correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Izvestia who spoke with the special forces soldiers: "The special forces landing party set down nearby had orders to destroy the terrorists [this is what the Russians called fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria] who remained alive after the strike"[1]. With the first missiles the pilots destroyed the Russian police car that was escorting the column, and ceased fire. The landing party did not attack the buses. The fighters of the army of Ichkeria with the hostages returned to Dagestan and dug in at Pervomayskoye, a village near the border of Ichkeria[1]. On 15 January 1996, Russian troops under the direction of FSB director Barsukov and Minister of Internal Affairs Kulikov began to storm Pervomayskoye[1]. Human rights defenders of Memorial write: "During the blockade, the attempted assault and the shelling of the village of Pervomayskoye, the main task of the federal side [the Russian troops] was not to free the hostages but to destroy the terrorists. This criminal approach led to the death and wounding of some of the hostages." On 18 January, most of the fighters of the army of Ichkeria broke out of the encirclement and returned to Ichkeria, taking hostages with them. According to a memorandum of the security committee of the Russian parliament, 16 hostages died in Pervomayskoye[1]. On 20 January, Minister of Internal Affairs Kulikov said in an interview with the newspaper Rossiyskiye Vesti that Russian troops had killed 153 fighters of the army of Ichkeria in Pervomayskoye and captured about 40. The occupiers sent all the prisoners to a filtration camp[188]. Russia exchanged the prisoners for the police officers whom Salman Raduyev's fighters had taken with them from Pervomayskoye, and the bodies of the killed fighters for the civilian hostages taken to Ichkeria[1]. On 15 January 1996, the day of the assault on Pervomayskoye, Yeltsin said of Salman Raduyev's fighters: "We still want these terrorists to be punished. And, in general, uprooted from the Chechen land"[132]. On 16 January, Yegorov, head of the Russian president's administration, said that he was "in favor… of all the bandit formations [this is what Russia called the Armed Forces of Ichkeria]… being destroyed"[132]. On 19 August 1996, Pulikovsky, the commander of the occupation troops, demanded that the Armed Forces of Ichkeria leave Grozny, gave Chechen civilians 48 hours to leave the city and announced that he would then strike "at the locations of the militants" with aircraft, artillery and multiple rocket launchers, which cannot fire with precision. On the night of 20 August, without waiting for the deadline to expire, Russian troops again began shelling and bombing Grozny (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[1]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1]. T0021 Neutralization of the Opposition September 1994 C1193.T0021 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0017 Secret Police and Security Services In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russia killed the leaders of Ichkeria, put them on wanted lists and arrested the republic's representatives in Moscow. Russian President Yeltsin, by Decree No. 1226 of 14 June 1994, allowed anyone suspected of ties to criminal groups to be held without charge for up to 30 days[145]. Under this decree, the FSB and the Russian police detained representatives of Ichkeria in Moscow[189][33]. On 1 February 1995, the Prosecutor General's Office of Russia put Dzhokhar Dudayev, the elected president of Ichkeria, on the wanted list in order to arrest and try him (see: "Manufacturing Criminals")[1]. On 17 June 1995, officers of the FSB and the Moscow police arrested Khamad Kurbanov, the representative of the president of Ichkeria in Russia, and two days later Ramzan Muzaev, secretary of the Chechen news agency Chechen-Press[189]. The FSB and police officers held both without charge, released the agency's secretary by 26 July, and the president's representative a month after his arrest[145][190][21]. On 8 October 1995, during the "ceasefire", Russian pilots bombed Roshni-Chu, a village southwest of Grozny, and killed 28 people, among them Magomed Khachuev, head of security of the delegation of Ichkeria at the talks. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that the target of the strike was Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria, who at times lived in the village and was unharmed[1]. On 21 April 1996, Dzhokhar Dudayev, with his wife Alla Dudayeva, his associates and his guards, drove out of Gekhi-Chu, a village southwest of Grozny, to a clearing in the mountains. The president put a satellite phone on the hood of the car and called Konstantin Borovoy, a deputy of the Russian parliament and a mediator in the peace talks. Russian servicemen struck the clearing with missiles[191]. The occupiers killed the president of Ichkeria, Prosecutor General Magomet Zhaniev and Khamad Kurbanov, the republic's former representative in Moscow. Alla Dudayeva was standing twenty meters from the car. In her memoirs, the president's wife wrote: "Suddenly, from the left, came the sharp whistle of an incoming missile. The explosion behind my back and the yellow flame that flared up made me jump down into the ravine... but suddenly the whistle came again"[12]. On 21 and 22 April 1996, Russian troops struck six or seven headquarters of the leadership of Ichkeria in the mountains with missiles and bombs[1]. Alexander Litvinenko, a former FSB officer, wrote in 2002 that the killing of the president had been prepared by an FSB group under the command of Khokholkov, created "to eliminate Dudayev", in Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny. According to him, aircraft of Russian military intelligence guided the missile to a beacon in the president's substituted phone[49]. On 7 May 1996, Russian police officers secretly detained Vagap Tutakov, Ichkeria's representative in Moscow, as he was leaving Kaluga, a city southwest of Moscow[1]. The police officers claimed that they had found weapons in his car[192], and on 8 June they released Ichkeria's representative from custody[1]. On 10 July 1996, Tikhomirov, the commander of the occupation troops, ordered a search for and the detention of Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the acting president of Ichkeria[1][6]. That same day, Russian pilots and artillerymen struck Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev's headquarters in Makhkety, a mountain village in the southeast of Ichkeria[1]. On 15 July, the occupiers captured Makhkety but did not find the acting president there[6]. That day, the crews of seven Russian helicopters destroyed his mother's house in Starye Atagi, a village south of Grozny, with missiles; the mother and the neighbors survived (see: "Collective Punishment")[6][38]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[30]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1]. T0025 Information Isolation September 1994 C1193.T0025 → C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996) G0011 Russian Federation S0010 Regular Army In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers bombed Chechen television, jammed journalists' satellite links and kept them away from the sites of their strikes. Commanders of the occupation forces ordered that journalists not be let into the sites of assaults and bombings. The Russian military and police at checkpoints did not let journalists, including those with accreditation from the Russian government, into the villages and towns that Russian troops were striking (see: "Censorship")[1][21]. Human rights defenders of the American Committee to Protect Journalists write that Russian troops in Ichkeria jammed journalists' satellite transmissions, exposed their film and destroyed their equipment[95]. On 29 November 1994, Russia announced that at 2 p.m. it would cut off all communications with Ichkeria[55]. From 21 to 24 December, Russian pilots struck the television center in Grozny. Deinekin, commander of Russian military aviation, named the aim of these strikes: "to stop the rabid anti-Russian propaganda"[1]. On 3 January 1995, Russian pilots bombed Shali, a town southeast of Grozny. Human rights defenders of Human Rights Watch write that the pilots were apparently trying to hit a radio communication tower, but killed several townspeople at the market and in the hospital (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[57]. On 7 and 8 April, the Internal Troops of Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, and killed 103 Chechen civilians there (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[5]. On 11 April, the occupiers at the post near the village did not let journalists in and admitted them only on 13 April[70][5]. On 8 October, Russian pilots bombed Roshni-Chu, a village southwest of Grozny (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). The occupiers blocked all the roads to the village, and men of the police special forces from the Russian city of Irkutsk at the post did not let journalists in, citing an order[1][193]. From 11 December, before the "elections" of the head of the puppet government on 14-17 December, Russian soldiers at checkpoints did not let journalists without special passes into Grozny (see: "Sham Expression of Popular Will")[1]. From 14 to 20 December, after the Armed Forces of Ichkeria had liberated Gudermes, the second-largest city of the republic, the occupiers shelled and bombed the city, and until 25 December did not let the press in (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[37]. In January 1996, the command of the occupation forces closed Grozny and the east of Ichkeria to the press[37]. From February until the first days of March, the occupiers shelled with artillery the encircled settlement of Novogroznensky in the east of Ichkeria and the villages of Alleroy, Tsentoroy, Bachi-Yurt and Suvorov-Yurt (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). The Russian military did not let journalists in there[1]. From 3 to 9 March, Russian troops shelled Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, with artillery and fired on it from helicopters (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[1]. From 6 to 9 March, while the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were attacking the occupiers in Grozny, Russian officials did not let journalists into the city[95]. On 10 March, the Russian military commandant of Sernovodsk forbade letting journalists, human rights defenders and any foreigners into the village (see: "Expulsion of Foreign Missions")[1]. On 15 March 1996, the Internal Troops of Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Russian 58th Army began the assault on Samashki (see: "Military Intervention")[1]. Sources differ on the number of Chechen civilians the occupiers killed in the village during the assault: 35 according to the villagers' list[1] or about 600 according to a doctor who treated people there (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[6][21]. On 17 and 18 March, the occupiers did not let independent journalists from Moscow through to the village. Maria Eismont, a correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Segodnya, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow on 22 April that on 26 and 27 March the Russian military stopped her on the roads to Samashki, and that she got into the village five days later. In Sernovodsk, Russian soldiers who had taken part in the assault turned the journalists back with the words: "There's no need to go there, there's nothing for you to do there, all the more so since there is nothing at all left to look at." Alexander Trushin, a correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Obshchaya Gazeta, told the Glasnost tribunal on 21 April that in early April the chief of the Russian checkpoint near the village phoned a general and did not let the journalists through: "I asked the captain: 'Did you report why we are going, for what purpose?' He answered: 'Yes, the general knows, and nevertheless the order is not to let you through'"[21]. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that reports of this assault did not reach television and radio[1]. On 21 April 1996, the occupiers killed Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria, during his conversation on a satellite phone with a mediator in the peace talks; according to the version that human rights defenders of Memorial consider likely, the Russian military located the signal of this phone (see: "Neutralization of the Opposition")[191][1]. On 8 August 1996, while the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were liberating Grozny, Russian soldiers did not let four journalists of foreign media into the city through either of its two entrances[95]. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that in the second year of the war Russian troops cut off from the press the areas they deemed undesirable far more tightly and successfully than in the first year[1]. In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[6]. title: Introduction of Military Settlements and Liquidation of the Danubian Sich (1817–1828), campaign C0041
content: Introduction of Military Settlements and Liquidation of the Danubian Sich (1817–1828) A campaign to turn the free population into rightless military settlers. "The trigger was the order abolishing the Buh Cossack Host and turning the Cossacks into military settlers"[1] – the Buh Cossacks' uprising of 1817 was brutally suppressed. There were two acts, on opposite sides of the uprising: the nominal decree of April 17, 1817 transferred the Buh Host's district "into direct military administration" (PSZRI, vol. XXXIV, no. 26,802) - this was the trigger; the decree of October 8, 1817 (no. 27,081), issued after the suppression, formalized the liquidation: "the name of the Buh Cossack Host is abolished"[2]. Later, kish otaman Hladky with part of the Danubian Cossacks "on May 30 (18), 1828 crossed the Kiliya mouth of the Danube, entered the port of Izmail, and joined the Russian army"[3] – this was the end of the last free host: the Danubian Sich "existed from the last quarter of the 18th century until 1828"[3]. title: Cultural Terror and the "Executed Renaissance" (1933–1938), campaign C0079
content: Cultural Terror and the "Executed Renaissance" (1933–1938) The abrupt rollback of the policy of "Ukrainization." The start of the physical extermination and political defamation of the intellectual elite - writers, scholars, film directors, as well as the old national communists (M. Skrypnyk was driven to suicide)[1]. In parallel with the physical terror came the destruction of the Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church, large-scale censorship, the rewriting of history, and the artificial convergence of the Ukrainian language with Russian; works published in the Ukrainian SSR before 1933, in the words of the compiler of the anthology "Executed Renaissance," were "destroyed as a result of Moscow's new course toward the rout and colonial provincialization of Ukraine"[2]. title: The Valuev Circular: Ban on the Language and Schools (1862–1869), campaign C0046
content: The Valuev Circular: Ban on the Language and Schools (1862–1869) A state campaign to destroy the Ukrainian language and culture: in 1862 the authorities closed the Sunday schools that taught in Ukrainian - "for the alleged presence of revolutionary propaganda"[1], the ban on the national press, the official denial of the language's existence – the Valuev circular: "there was not, is not, and cannot be any distinct Little Russian language"[2] – and bonuses to officials "in the ten South-Western governorates for persons of Russian origin, excluding, however, local natives," fixed by the decrees of 1869 and 1886[3]. title: Annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's Expedition: 92 Captives, More Than a Thousand Saklias Burned (January 1837), campaign C1160
content: Annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's Expedition: 92 Captives, More Than a Thousand Saklias Burned (January 1837) On 23-29 January 1837, the command of the Russian Caucasus Corps sent from the Groznaya fortress into Lesser Chechnya (the lowland-piedmont western part of Chechnya) a detachment under General Feze - 3249 men with 12 guns. Rozen stated the purpose of the campaign in a report to Minister of War Chernyshev of 11 February 1837: "to punish the Chechens of the western part of Chechnya who have evaded obedience"[1]. The expedition journal appended to the report records the week day by day: on the night of 24 January Shalazh-yurt was surrounded - the village was taken "without a shot, laying 14 souls on the spot", 67 inhabitants were led away into captivity, and the village was burned; on 25 January Feze dispatched columns "to discover and destroy the population in the dense forests up both banks of the Shalazha river"; in all, 92 people were taken captive over the campaign, "on the way back more than a thousand saklias were burned along the Martan and Tengin gorges" (saklia - a highlander's house), and the stores of grain and hay were destroyed in the middle of winter[1]. Within the detachment the empire led highlanders against highlanders - 800 horsemen of the Ossetian and Ingush militia (militia - auxiliary units of highlanders in the empire's service): the expedition journal lists in Colonel Shiroky's column "a hundred Cossacks and 800 horsemen of Ossetians and Ingush"[1]. From the aul of Achkhoy, which the troops entered on the fourth day of the annihilation of its neighbors, by the record of the same journal an oath "of submission" and six hostages-amanats were taken (amanat - a person whom the empire took from a community as a guarantee of subordination)[1]. Rozen, in a report to Minister of War Chernyshev of 11 February 1837, named the purpose plainly: "to punish the Chechens of the western part of Chechnya who have evaded obedience"[1]. The campaign continued the winter punitive operations after the December extermination of Kishkeroy-Yurt (campaign C1158): within a week, according to the expedition journal appended to the same report, Shalazh-yurt and the dwellings on both banks of the Shalazha were destroyed, more than a thousand saklias (saklia - a highlander's house) were burned, and 92 captives were taken[1]. T0104 Mass Killings of Civilians January 1837 C1160.T0104 → C1160 Annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's Expedition: 92 Captives, More Than a Thousand Saklias Burned (January 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army During the annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's expedition in January 1837, the troops killed inhabitants who offered no armed resistance. The expedition journal, presented by Rozen to Minister of War Chernyshev on 11 February 1837, records: Shalazh-yurt, surrounded on the night of 24 January, was taken "without a shot, laying 14 souls on the spot"[1] - killings in a village that put up no armed fight. On 25 January Feze, according to the same journal, dispatched columns "to discover and destroy the population in the dense forests up both banks of the Shalazha river" - an order for the destruction of the population in so many words[1]. At Urus-Martan, after the inhabitants had fled, the journal records, "23 enemy bodies remained on the spot"[1]. The total number of the killed is not summed up by episode in the journal; some of the fallen fought an armed defense - the technique is recorded on the basis of the killings in a village taken without a shot and of the order to destroy the population. T0099 Hostage-Taking January 1837 C1160.T0099 → C1160 Annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's Expedition: 92 Captives, More Than a Thousand Saklias Burned (January 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army In the course of the annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's expedition in January 1837, the troops took hostages from auls faced with the choice between subjugation and the fate of their neighbors. According to the expedition journal presented by Rozen to Minister of War Chernyshev on 11 February 1837, on 26 January 6 amanats "from the families of the most honored elders" were taken in Achkhoy, and 4 in Phan-kichu (amanat - a person whom the empire took from a community as a guarantee of subjugation; the journal frames the seizure of people with the word "handed over")[1]. Hostages from the most influential families made every community answerable to the empire with the lives of its own people. T0053 Abduction of People January 1837 C1160.T0053 → C1160 Annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's Expedition: 92 Captives, More Than a Thousand Saklias Burned (January 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army During the annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's expedition on 23-29 January 1837, the troops led 92 inhabitants away into captivity. The expedition journal, presented by Rozen to Minister of War Chernyshev on 11 February 1837, counts by episode: at the taking of Shalazh-yurt "67 souls were taken captive", at Urus-Martan "13 souls were captured", at Khankharik-Roshnya and Birzul the detachment "took 12 souls captive"[1]. T0105 Total Destruction of Infrastructure January 1837 C1160.T0105 → C1160 Annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's Expedition: 92 Captives, More Than a Thousand Saklias Burned (January 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army Feze's expedition through Lesser Chechnya on 23-29 January 1837 destroyed housing and livelihood outright. The expedition journal, presented by Rozen to Minister of War Chernyshev on 11 February 1837, records: "Having burned Shalazh-yurt", the troops "destroyed the winter quarters... and the dwellings of the Chechens on both banks of the Shalazha", and "on the way back more than a thousand saklias were burned along the Martan and Tengin gorges" (saklia - a highlander's house)[1]. T0121 Artificial Famine January 1837 C1160.T0121 → C1160 Annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's Expedition: 92 Captives, More Than a Thousand Saklias Burned (January 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army Completing the annihilation of Lesser Chechnya, Feze's troops destroyed the survivors' food as well: on 29 January 1837, according to the expedition journal appended to Rozen's report to Minister of War Chernyshev of 11 February 1837, "by noon the detachment completed the destruction of the dwellings and of the stores of grain and hay along the Martan gorge"[1]. The destruction of food and fodder in the middle of winter left the survivors without means to live through it. T0152 Pitting Neighboring Peoples Against Each Other January 1837 C1160.T0152 → C1160 Annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's Expedition: 92 Captives, More Than a Thousand Saklias Burned (January 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army In Feze's annihilating expedition through Lesser Chechnya in January 1837, the empire led highlanders against highlanders. The expedition journal, presented by Rozen to Minister of War Chernyshev on 11 February 1837, names the composition of Colonel Shiroky's column: "a hundred Cossacks and 800 horsemen of Ossetians and Ingush" (the Ossetian and Ingush militia - auxiliary units of highlanders in the empire's service)[1]. The use of neighboring peoples in a punitive campaign shifted part of the suppression onto the colonized themselves and entrenched enmity between them. T0147 Forced Registration of Subjecthood January 1837 C1160.T0147 → C1160 Annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's Expedition: 92 Captives, More Than a Thousand Saklias Burned (January 1837) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army On 26 January 1837, on the fourth day of the annihilation of Lesser Chechnya by Feze's expedition - two days after the taking of neighboring Shalazh-yurt with 14 killed - the troops, entering the aul of Achkhoy, took from it an oath "of submission" and 6 amanats (amanat - a person whom the empire took from a community as a guarantee of subordination)[1]. The frame is spelled out by the expedition journal itself, presented by Rozen to Minister of War Chernyshev on 11 February 1837: "the troops are proceeding to them not to punish them, but properly to confirm them in submission"[1] - subordination secured under military pressure and framed by the empire as a voluntary act of those who had submitted. References Кавказская археографическая комиссия. Акты собранные Кавказскою археографическою комиссиею. Том VIII (1831-1837). 1881.

title: Mazepa's Defection to Sweden and the Baturyn Massacre (1708), campaign C0012
content: Mazepa's Defection to Sweden and the Baturyn Massacre (1708) In response to the autonomy's attempt to break vassalage, the regular Muscovite army destroyed the hetman's capital, Baturyn. Peter ordered: "and Baturyn, as a sign to the traitors (since they resisted), burn down entirely as an example to others"[1]. The reprisal was accompanied by terror against the civilian population: "Funck slaughtered more than a thousand people in the small town of Terey (Tereyska sloboda) and burned the town down"[2], and in total "about 15 thousand Ukrainians died in the Baturyn tragedy, including all the women and children"[1]. The massacre ran in parallel with propaganda: "Tsarist letters were circulated among the people claiming that Mazepa had gone over to the Swedes in order to hand Ukraine to Poland, to introduce the Union in Ukraine and eradicate the pious faith; that he was an apostate, a secret Catholic"[3]. After a two-hour battle, the remnants of the garrison were slaughtered together with the entire civilian population"[1][4]. The town was looted and burned on Peter's direct order - his letter to Menshikov of 5 November 1708: "and Baturyn, as a mark against the traitors (for they resisted), burn entire, as an example to others"[5]. "In total, about 15 thousand Ukrainians died in the Baturyn tragedy, including all the women and children"[1][4]. T0022 Terror October 1708 C0012.T0022 → C0012 Mazepa's Defection to Sweden and the Baturyn Massacre (1708) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0010 Regular Army The demonstrative destruction of the city as an act of intimidation for the rest of the country. Peter I personally gave the order: "and Baturyn, as a sign to the traitors (since they resisted), burn down entirely as an example to others"[1][4]. Hrushevsky: the Muscovite army, having taken Baturyn "through the treachery of one man," "dealt terribly with the populace: the people were slaughtered, the town razed to the ground, the commanders given over to terrible tortures"[3]. T0045 Destruction of Historical Memory October 1708 C0012.T0045 → C0012 Mazepa's Defection to Sweden and the Baturyn Massacre (1708) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0008 Government A campaign to erase the resistance leader's name (damnatio memoriae): "For two centuries the name and deeds of Mazepa were expunged… His coats of arms were knocked off the churches he had built, his name was painted over in books"[1][4]. title: Construction of Fortified Stanitsas, Settlement of Cossacks on the Borders, and Holding of Hostages (1736–1740), campaign C1134
content: Construction of Fortified Stanitsas, Settlement of Cossacks on the Borders, and Holding of Hostages (1736–1740) In the period from 1736 to 1740, the diplomatic and administrative apparatus of the Russian Empire maintained control over the borders of the Nokhchi societies through infrastructure construction and hostage-taking. The established evidence base demonstrates that the metropole began by building new fortifications: historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov records the establishment in 1736 of fortified posts, among them «three new Cossack stanitsas: Borozdinskaya, Kargalinskaya, Dubovskaya»[1]. Historian I. Kh. Tkhamokova emphasizes their engineering-defensive status, recording that each such stanitsa «was, as it were, a small fortress serving for protection against enemy raids»[2]. The construction of infrastructure was followed by the physical settlement of military contingents: the first researcher indicates that garrisons were placed on these frontiers, «and from Kizlyar toward the sea another 430 Cossack families are being settled»[1]. In parallel, the occupation administration continued to physically hold relatives of the local elite seized in previous years: Akhmadov notes, in a list of archival documents, a paper from 1738 identified as «Letter of the Chechen lord A. Bartykhanov to Lieutenant Colonel Bunin about his faithful service to Russia and with a request to release his sister from Kizlyar»[1]. title: Bribery of the Nobility and Institutionalization of the Hostage System (1735), campaign C1133
content: Bribery of the Nobility and Institutionalization of the Hostage System (1735) In 1735, following the large-scale invasion by the forces of the Crimean Khanate, the diplomatic and administrative apparatus of the Russian Empire used the new balance of power to consolidate its influence among the Nokhchi elites. Historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov states that during this period «the pro-Russian political orientation of the lowland part of Chechnya intensifies»[1]. To bind the local aristocracy, the occupation administration employed institutional bribery: the researcher records that the senior prince Aidemir «was accepted into Russian subjecthood and was assigned a permanent tsarist salary»[1], and, on the whole, «The princes and their uzdens even began to receive monetary allowances from the Russian government»[1]. In parallel, the empire entrenched the system of holding relatives of the nobility: Akhmadov indicates that Prince Aidemir «as a pledge of fidelity to his obligations gave his son Bardykhan as an amanat, while another influential Chechen prince, Alisultan Kazbulatov, gave his brother Bamat as an amanat»[1]. He also adds dry statistical confirmation: «In 1735, two amanats from the Chechen domain were already being held in Kizlyar»[1]. title: The Battle of Poltava and the Final Defeat of the Hetmanate (1709), campaign C0015
content: The Battle of Poltava and the Final Defeat of the Hetmanate (1709) The decisive battle of the Great Northern War, in the course of which the military backbone of Ukrainian autonomy was finally eliminated. The defeat of the Swedish-Cossack alliance allowed Moscow to move from suppressing uprisings to the systematic dismantling of the Hetmanate's political agency[1]. title: Establishment of the First Foothold on the Sunzha River (1567), campaign C1105
content: Establishment of the First Foothold on the Sunzha River (1567) The Regular Army of the Tsardom of Muscovy built the first military base on the lands of the Nokhchi with the support of regular troops. As historian E. N. Kusheva writes, "at the request of Temriuk, conveyed in Moscow in December 1566 by his son Matlov or Mazlov, to build a town 'on the Terek River at the mouth of the Siuiunchi River' 'for protection from his enemies,' in the spring of 1567 voevodas were sent from Moscow for the town-building work — Prince A. S. Babichev and P. Protasyev 'with many men, as well as ordnance, cannons, and arquebuses'"[1]. Historians A. S. Kulikov and V. A. Runov add that the voevodas were sent "with firearms and many men"[2]. Historian E. N. Kusheva states the fact that the base was built on the lands of the Nokhchi: "The Russian town... was built that same year"[1]. title: Creation of the Little Russian Prikaz (1663), campaign C0023
content: Creation of the Little Russian Prikaz (1663) Institutional substitution: Ukrainian affairs were handed over to a special agency in Moscow. The Little Russian Prikaz was founded "as one of the departments of the Ambassadorial Prikaz to administer Ukrainian affairs," and through it the tsarist government "exercised control over the political-administrative activity of the hetman's administration and the tsarist voivodes in Ukraine"[1] – the Hetmanate fell under the permanent departmental oversight of the metropole. title: The Moscow Articles of Ivan Briukhovetsky (1665), campaign C0024
content: The Moscow Articles of Ivan Briukhovetsky (1665) The treaty that became the point of no return in the political, economic, and military absorption of the autonomy: "Under the Moscow Articles, direct control over the military-administrative and financial-economic life of Ukraine (except for the Cossack estate) passed into the hands of the tsarist voivodes"[1]. Garrisons headed by voivodes were introduced into new cities as far as Kodak, taxes went directly to the tsar's treasury, and the Kyiv metropolitanate was to be subordinated to the Moscow patriarch[1]. title: Ideological Preparation for the Full-Scale Invasion (2020–2021), campaign C0102
content: Ideological Preparation for the Full-Scale Invasion (2020–2021) A period of intensive ideological conditioning of Russian society and the political elite to justify the complete destruction of Ukrainian statehood. The head of the Russian state published a programmatic article declaring that "Russians and Ukrainians are one people, a single whole," and wrote of the Bolsheviks that "the Bolsheviks' actions in severing from Russia its historical territories are not considered a criminal act"[1]. Deputy Security Council chairman D. Medvedev (Kommersant, 11 October 2021) declared negotiations with Kyiv pointless: "it is pointless for us to deal with vassals. One must do business with the suzerain"[2]. In parallel came the indoctrination of the army and military blackmail through the massing of troops near the borders under the guise of exercises[3].
