title: Non-Recognition and the Attempted Military Invasion: Moscow's Response to the Independence of the Chechen Republic (September-November 1991), campaign C1183
content: Non-Recognition and the Attempted Military Invasion: Moscow's Response to the Independence of the Chechen Republic (September-November 1991) After their return from exile the Chechens were ruled for three decades by Russians sent from Moscow; only on 1 July 1989 did an assembly of the region's occupation administration for the first time reject Moscow's candidate and choose a Chechen, Zavgaev, as head of the region[1]. By the autumn of 1991 the USSR was falling apart: the union republics were declaring independence one after another. On 18 August the USSR vice-president Yanaev, together with the heads of the KGB (predecessor of today's FSB), the army and the police, tried to keep the union in Moscow's hands by force: they announced that the nominal head of the USSR, Gorbachev, could not govern "for reasons of health", declared a state of emergency and brought tanks into Moscow, but gave up after three days[2]. Zavgaev, the head of Chechnya installed under the USSR, backed those who wanted to preserve the USSR, and lost: the Chechens came out to non-stop rallies and on 6 September forced his Supreme Soviet to dissolve itself[3]. That same autumn the Chechens elected their own president, Dzhokhar Dudaev, and declared independence from Russia, while the coloniser in the person of the RSFSR went in two months from sending a delegation "to explain the policy" to an attempt to impose a state of emergency on the whole territory of Chechen-Ingushetia with internal troops, but was forced to retreat. On 10 September 1991 the RSFSR president Yeltsin sent to Grozny a delegation headed by state secretary Burbulis and instructed it "to explain the policy of the Russian Federation and of the President of the RSFSR"[4]. On 14 September Khasbulatov, a Chechen from the Moscow leadership, then acting head of parliament, flew to Grozny; on 15 September he personally chaired the last session of the Supreme Soviet of Chechen-Ingushetia, and under pressure from Khasbulatov and from Dzhokhar Dudaev's supporters the deputies dismissed Zavgaev, dissolved themselves and chose from their own ranks a Provisional Supreme Council of 32 members headed by Khusein Akhmadov to hold new elections[5]. Moscow tried to take this council for itself: on 25 September five of its members headed by the council's deputy chairman Chernyi, Khasbulatov's man, came out against Dzhokhar Dudaev's congress; on 26 September Khasbulatov himself threatened by telegram not to recognise the elections, and on 5 October thirteen of the council's thirty-two members, backed by the local KGB, tried to remove Khusein Akhmadov. In response Dzhokhar Dudaev's supporters blocked the central square of Grozny, arrested the republic's procurator and occupied the buildings of the KGB and of the government; Moscow's people in the council, as general Sokolov reported to his command, had no "practical power" left[5][3]. On 6 October the RSFSR vice-president Rutskoi flew to Grozny with the minister of internal affairs and the chairman of the KGB of the RSFSR, but achieved nothing[5], and on 8 October the Moscow leadership, over Khasbulatov's signature, recognised as lawful in Chechnya only the group of procurator Bakhmadov - the man who, according to Sokolov's report, had been "appointed by the Chairman of the Supreme Soviet of the RSFSR Khasbulatov"[3] - and demanded that "the illegal armed formations [this is what the coloniser called the fighters for independence from Russia] surrender their weapons by 24:00 on 10 October 1991"[6]. On 24 October Moscow announced, before any vote had taken place, that the elections set for 27 October "have no legal basis and their results cannot be recognised as lawful"[7]. On 27 October the Chechens elected Dzhokhar Dudaev president, and on 1 November he signed a decree: "to proclaim the state sovereignty of the Chechen Republic from 1 November 1991"[8]. On 2 November Moscow declared the elections "unlawful, and the acts adopted by them not subject to execution"[9]. On 7 November Yeltsin, by decree No. 178, imposed a state of emergency on the whole territory of Chechen-Ingushetia: a curfew, a ban on rallies and strikes, the seizure of weapons, the cancellation of the elections, a Provisional Administration appointed from Moscow, and "the expulsion of violators of public order who are not residents of the given locality... beyond the territory of the Chechen-Ingush Republic at their own expense"[10]. On 8 November the parliament of the Chechen Republic declared the decree unlawful and demanded the withdrawal of the troops within 24 hours[11]. The National Guard of Chechnya and unarmed townspeople blockaded the airlifted internal troops (predecessors of today's Rosgvardiya) at the Khankala airfield near Grozny and in the building of the ministry of internal affairs. The nominal head of the USSR, Gorbachev, refused the RSFSR the use of union troops; on the morning of 10 November the internal troops left Grozny[12], and on 11 November the deputies in Moscow refused to approve Yeltsin's decree, finding it necessary to act "not by applying emergency measures but by political means"[13]. ID: C1183 Start: September 1991 End: November 1991 Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.0 Created: 7 September 2026 Last Modified: 7 September 2026 Discuss on Telegram Actors ID Name Procedures G0011 Russian Federation 3 Instruments Applied ID Name Procedures S0008 Government 2 S0010 Regular Army 1 Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: T0031 Restriction of Sovereignty September 1991 C1183.T0031 → C1183 Non-Recognition and the Attempted Military Invasion: Moscow's Response to the Independence of the Chechen Republic (September-November 1991) G0011 Russian Federation S0008 Government On 10 September 1991 the RSFSR president Yeltsin sent to Chechen-Ingushetia a delegation headed by state secretary Burbulis and instructed it "to explain the policy of the Russian Federation and of the President of the RSFSR at the present stage"[4]; the delegation came back with nothing[3]. On 8 October the Moscow leadership, over Khasbulatov's signature, resolved "until the election of a new composition of the Supreme Soviet of the Chechen-Ingush Republic, to regard the Provisional Supreme Council of the Republic as the only lawful body of state power on the territory of the Chechen-Ingush Republic" and ordered "the illegal armed formations [this is what the coloniser called the fighters for independence from Russia] to surrender their weapons to the bodies of internal affairs by 24:00 on 10 October 1991"[6]. The Chechens did not surrender their weapons: on 9 October the leadership of the National Congress of the Chechen People replied that the resolution had been adopted "with the sole aim of preserving colonial domination over the Chechen people, over the peoples of the Caucasus and their natural riches", announced the mobilisation of men from 15 to 55 and put the National Guard on combat alert[14]. On 10 October Moscow instructed vice-president Rutskoi and the RSFSR government "to ensure the necessary conditions for the restoration of legality and law and order in the Chechen-Ingush Republic"[15]. On 15 October the chairman of the KGB of the RSFSR (predecessor of today's FSB) Ivanenko suspended the work of the KGB of Chechen-Ingushetia "until 27 October 1991" and by his own order appointed an acting chairman for it[3]. On 19 October Yeltsin addressed the leadership of the congress with an ultimatum: "I demand from the leaders of the Executive Committee of the National Congress of the Chechen People and the groupings supporting them the cessation of unlawful actions and unconditional submission to the law… all measures provided for by the laws of the RSFSR will be taken"[16]. On 24 October Moscow resolved that the elections set for 27 October "have no legal basis and their results cannot be recognised as lawful", and entrusted the preparation of different elections to the Provisional Supreme Council and to the RSFSR deputies from the republic[7]. The Chechens voted anyway: on 27 October, according to the electoral commission of the Chechen Republic, 72 % of voters turned out, and 90.1 % voted for Dzhokhar Dudaev[3]. On 1 November Dzhokhar Dudaev signed a decree: "Guided by the Declaration on the state sovereignty of the republic and by the will of the citizens of the Chechen Republic expressed in direct and universal elections, to proclaim the state sovereignty of the Chechen Republic from 1 November 1991"[8]. On 2 November Moscow answered with a resolution: "To recognise the elections to the supreme body of state power (the Supreme Soviet) and of the President of the republic held in the Chechen-Ingush Republic on 27 October 1991 as unlawful, and the acts adopted by them as not subject to execution"[9]. On 7 November Yeltsin, in decree No. 178, named as the reason for the state of emergency an aggravation "caused by the unlawful actions of the executive committee of the National Congress of the Chechen People and its leaders, who seek, by organising mass disorders, with the use of violence, to remove the lawfully acting state bodies from power", and in point 6 banned any elections: "elections of bodies of state power and of local self-government shall not be held during the whole period of the state of emergency"[10]. None of these bans worked: the elections took place, the president and the parliament of Chechnya were at work, and on 11 November the deputies in Moscow refused to approve the decree itself[13]. T0037 Puppet Government September 1991 C1183.T0037 → C1183 Non-Recognition and the Attempted Military Invasion: Moscow's Response to the Independence of the Chechen Republic (September-November 1991) G0011 Russian Federation S0008 Government On 15 September 1991 the deputies of the Supreme Soviet of Chechen-Ingushetia, at their last session, chaired in person by Khasbulatov, a Chechen from the Moscow leadership, then acting head of parliament, dissolved themselves and chose from their own ranks a Provisional Supreme Council of 32 members headed by Khusein Akhmadov to hold new elections[5]. Filatov, in 1991 secretary of the parliament's leadership in Moscow, recalled: "with the energetic participation of Khasbulatov the Supreme Soviet of the republic was dispersed — what remained was the so-called Small Council, some artificial formation that was to work until new elections were held"[17]. Khusein Akhmadov took the side of Dzhokhar Dudaev's congress and on 4 October signed a resolution on the KGB (predecessor of today's FSB): "to terminate the activity of the KGB of the ChIR [Chechen-Ingush Republic] and of all its structures on the territory of the Chechen Republic"[18]. Then Moscow began to build its own power out of this council. On 25 September five of its members headed by the council's deputy chairman Chernyi, Khasbulatov's man, came out against Dzhokhar Dudaev's congress; on 26 September Khasbulatov himself threatened by telegram not to recognise the elections; on 5 October thirteen of the council's thirty-two members, backed by the local KGB, tried to remove Khusein Akhmadov[5]. On 8 October the Moscow leadership, over Khasbulatov's signature, having heard vice-president Rutskoi back from Grozny, declared lawful in the republic only the council "under the chairmanship of comrade B. D. Bakhmadov" - a procurator whom they themselves had installed - and instructed it "to take all necessary measures to stabilise the situation"[6]. General Sokolov, head of the occupation army's training centre in Grozny, reported to his command: "the chairman V. D. Bakhmadov was appointed by the Chairman of the Supreme Soviet of the RSFSR R. I. Khasbulatov", and the council itself "has no practical power"[3]. On 9 October the leadership of the National Congress of the Chechen People, Dzhokhar Dudaev's congress, called Bakhmadov's council "unlawful, puppet" and demanded that it "dissociate itself from the attempt to resurrect" the Supreme Soviet "dissolved by the people"[14]. After the elections of 27 October Bakhmadov's council addressed the residents of the republic: the elections "are unconstitutional and have no lawful force, not a single decree of the so-called president D. Dudaev, not a single resolution of the parliament of the so-called Chechen Republic has legal force or is subject to execution"[19]. On 7 November the RSFSR president Yeltsin, by decree No. 178, resolved: "To introduce... on the territory of the Chechen-Ingush Republic, as a special form of administration, a Provisional Administration of the Chechen-Ingush Republic"; as its head he appointed his own representative in the republic, Arsanov, as deputy the republic's minister of internal affairs Ibragimov, and instructed them "to form the Provisional Administration of the Chechen-Ingush Republic within 3 days"[10]. On 8 November the parliament of the Chechen Republic, chaired by Khusein Akhmadov, replied: "The leadership of Russia, following the lead of the overthrown totalitarian forces and proceeding from imperial interests, has introduced it [the state of emergency] on the territory of a republic whose sovereignty was proclaimed as far back as November 1990" - and declared the decree "unlawful and having no legal force"[11]. Neither Bakhmadov's council nor Arsanov's Provisional Administration ever got to work in Chechnya: on 11 November the deputies in Moscow refused to approve Yeltsin's decree[13]. T0019 Military Intervention September 1991 C1183.T0019 → C1183 Non-Recognition and the Attempted Military Invasion: Moscow's Response to the Independence of the Chechen Republic (September-November 1991) G0011 Russian Federation S0010 Regular Army On 7 November 1991 the RSFSR president Yeltsin signed decree No. 178, point 1: "To introduce, from 05:00 on 9 November 1991 until 05:00 on 9 December 1991, a state of emergency on the whole territory of the Chechen-Ingush Republic". By the same decree he imposed a curfew, banned rallies and strikes, ordered "the temporary seizure of firearms and cold weapons from citizens, enterprises and organisations", searches of vehicles and dwellings, and "the expulsion of violators of public order who are not residents of the given locality to their place of permanent residence or beyond the territory of the Chechen-Ingush Republic at their own expense", and instructed the minister of internal affairs and the chairman of the KGB (predecessor of today's FSB) of the RSFSR to submit "proposals on bringing in additional forces"[10]. On 8 November the parliament of the Chechen Republic, chaired by Khusein Akhmadov, demanded that Yeltsin "within 24 hours withdraw all armed formations from the territory of the sovereign Chechen Republic" and resolved "to inform the parliaments and peoples of the world of the armed interference of the leadership of Russia in the internal affairs of the sovereign Chechen Republic"[11]. The journalist Tsyganok, in the article "Ten Days That Cancelled the Peace", quotes the summary of the RSFSR ministry of internal affairs for the morning of 10 November: "To ensure the regime of the state of emergency, units of the MVD [ministry of internal affairs] of the RSFSR with a total strength of about 1.2 thousand men have been sent to the North Caucasus region"[12]. According to the chronicle of events, on 8-9 November "two military transport aircraft with special-forces detachments on board, but without weapons, landed at the Khankala military airfield near Grozny… the airfield is blockaded by Dzh. Dudaev's guardsmen, leaving the aircraft is impossible, so on the morning of 9 November the aircraft fly away"[3]. The National Guard of Chechnya and unarmed townspeople surrounded the building of the ministry of internal affairs in Grozny; on 9 November the first deputy minister of internal affairs of the RSFSR Komissarov reported to Moscow: "We are blockaded in the building of the MVD [ministry of internal affairs] of the ChIR [Chechen-Ingush Republic]. We are surrounded by a crowd of about 4,000 people, fuel tankers are standing opposite"[12]. On 9 November the Moscow leadership recorded that "the heads of the executive bodies (Barannikov [minister of internal affairs of the USSR], Bakatin [chairman of the KGB of the USSR], Komissarov [first deputy minister of internal affairs of the RSFSR]) in a difficult critical situation failed to carry out their direct official duties"[20]. The nominal head of the USSR, Gorbachev, refused the RSFSR the use of union troops, and on 10 November at 10:45 the internal troops (predecessors of today's Rosgvardiya) began their withdrawal from Grozny[12]. On 11 November the deputies in Moscow resolved "to recognise the approval of the Decree as impossible", established "a special regime of entry into and exit from the Chechen-Ingush Republic, excluding the import and export of weapons" and ordered "a parliamentary and an internal (through the MVD of the RSFSR and the KGB of the RSFSR) investigation to establish the persons responsible for taking insufficiently prepared political and military-technical decisions on the introduction of the state of emergency"[13]. title: The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925), campaign C1177
content: The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) By 1925 Soviet power had stood in Chechnya for its fifth year and remained largely nominal: five years of Sovietization (campaign C1176) - revkoms (revolutionary committees) instead of elected Soviets, arrests of sheikhs, two partial disarmaments - had not given Moscow control over the people, imam Nazhmuddin Gotsinsky, the spiritual head of the armed resistance in Dagestan and Chechnya, was sheltering in the mountains, and the profile of the Mountain district drawn up by the staff of the future operation admitted: "Beyond the Sharo-Argun Soviet power does not exist"[1]. Moscow, meanwhile, was steering a course toward taking power away from the autonomies - historian T. U. Elbuzdukayeva writes: "The unceasing banditry and insurgent movements in the North Caucasus were perceived by the Moscow authorities as a convincing argument in favor of its centralizing efforts, the process of transferring autonomous sovereignty from Caucasian into Moscow hands"[2]. The operation of 1925 became that course in action: the USSR took away the weapons of Chechnya's population with the forces of the army and the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB) - from 25 August the troops passed through 242 settlements, shelled 101 of them with [artillery] guns and machine guns, bombed 16 from aircraft, arrested more than 300 people and shot nearly all of them without trial. Under the guise of maneuvers the troops entered the oblast, surrounded aul after aul, convened the village assembly, presented an ultimatum to surrender weapons according to a ready-made quota, and opened fire on the settlement if it was not met; of the aims Elbuzdukayeva writes: as the centers of the operation the staff had designated in advance the mountain societies "where N. Gotsinsky [the head of the resistance] was presumed to be"[2]. The instruction of 4 August 1925, approved by Uborevich, commander of the North Caucasus Military District (SKVO), prescribed, should the ultimatum not be met, opening artillery fire on the settlement for ten minutes, and allowed repeating it several times[3]. The deception, too, was assigned by document: by an order of 31 July 1925 the staff of the Workers' and Peasants' Red Army (RKKA) approved Uborevich's maneuvers in Chechnya and with the same document assigned the disarmament: "At the same time," the order said, "taking advantage of the concentration of a significant number of troops on the territory of Chechnya (the district of the forthcoming maneuvers), the command of the SKVO, in coordination with the PPOGPU [the plenipotentiary representation of the OGPU] in the North Caucasus, plans to carry out a disarmament and a removal of the bandit element, which by a number of political indications is highly timely"[4]. The sanction was given by Stalin personally: in July 1925 Mikoyan, secretary of the North Caucasus krai committee of the party[5], met him in Sochi and after the conversation telegraphed to Molotov in Moscow: "The political situation in Chechnya has become aggravated. Stalin has given his personal consent to the necessity of the operation"[2]. Many years later Mikoyan summed it up in his memoirs: "This operation fundamentally cleared the air of Chechnya"[6]. ID: C1177 Start: July 1925 End: October 1925 Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.1 Created: 13 August 2026 Last Modified: 5 September 2026 Discuss on Telegram Actors ID Name Procedures G0010 USSR 14 Instruments Applied ID Name Procedures S0010 Regular Army 9 S0017 Secret Police and Security Services 5 Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: T0006 Dehumanization July 1925 C1177.T0006 → C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army On 31 July 1925 the Revolutionary Military Council of the USSR explained the operation being prepared by the properties of an entire people - the order says: "The Chechen oblast is a hotbed of criminal banditry spreading to the districts neighboring Chechnya... In their mass the Chechens are inclined to banditry as the main source of easy gain, which is furthered by the presence of a large quantity of weapons. Mountain Chechnya is a refuge for the most hardened enemies of Soviet power"[2]. The label from the order passed into the operation's working nomenclature: the instruction of 4 August 1925, approved by Uborevich, commander of the North Caucasus Military District, Volodin, member of the district's Revolutionary Military Council, and Yevdokimov, plenipotentiary representative of the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB) for the krai, puts people in one row with rifles and "removes" them with a single verb - point 8 of the instruction reads: "If the conditions of the surrender of weapons are fulfilled, no house-to-house search is conducted, and only the bandit and vicious element is removed"[3]. Thus criminality was declared a property of the people, and its men - an "element" subject to removal. T0001 Imposition of a Backwardness Narrative July 1925 C1177.T0001 → C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army On 31 July 1925 the Revolutionary Military Council of the USSR, in the order justifying the operation to disarm Chechnya, declared the Chechens incapable of proper farming: "The rich lands granted to the Chechens on the plain after the revolution are not used by them in full; they run their agriculture in backward forms, are not industrious"[2]. The accusation stands in a military order as one of the grounds for sending in troops: the lands were "granted" to the people by the authorities themselves, their way of farming was declared backward by the same authorities, and the conclusion drawn from this assessment was a military operation. Historian T. U. Elbuzdukayeva, who publishes the order, also cites its continuation: "political indications" had ripened - the population's weariness of war and the demand to fight "banditry"[2] - that is, even by the document's own logic the war was to be waged not on economic backwardness, yet it is backwardness that is set down as a justification. T0007 Imposition of Its Own Picture of Reality July 1925 C1177.T0007 → C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The documents of its staff described a military operation with artillery shelling as the bringing of peace: the "Main Tasks of the Special Operational Groups of the OGPU in the Operation in the Chechen Autonomous Oblast", approved by Yevdokimov, plenipotentiary representative of the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB) for the krai, Uborevich, commander of the North Caucasus Military District, and Volodin, member of the district's Revolutionary Military Council, open with the words that the mass operation "in its final result must bring general pacification to Chechnya and create the appropriate conditions for the peaceful Soviet-economic construction of the oblast"[3]. The same frame was prescribed to be spoken aloud in every aul: under the disarmament instruction of 4 August 1925 the representatives of the authorities, having entered a village surrounded by troops, announced to the assembly the purpose of their coming - "the removal of weapons with a view to the Chechen authorities securing a normal working life for the toiling population", and the artillery shelling was given a name within this frame: "warning fire as a measure of influence"[3]. The organizer of the operation, Mikoyan, secretary of the North Caucasus krai committee of the party, brought this picture to its final formula in his memoirs: "It was a brilliant operation without any bloodshed"[6] - in the same chapter he himself describes the Chechen old men taken hostage by the Chekists and the shelling of a Chechen village by the troops of the USSR. T0019 Military Intervention July 1925 C1177.T0019 → C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army On 25 August 1925 the USSR sent troops into the Chechen Autonomous Oblast to take away the weapons of its inhabitants; the operation was conducted by the army and the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB) under the overall command of Uborevich, commander of the North Caucasus Military District, and Yevdokimov, plenipotentiary representative of the OGPU for the krai[2]. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write of the forces gathered against the Chechen villages: "In all, about seven thousand Red Army men with 240 machine guns and 24 [artillery] guns were brought in to take part in it. In addition, two aviation detachments and an armored train were at the disposal of the operation's commander. Tactically the troops, as well as the operational groups of the GPU, were divided into seven groupings"[7]. Historian T. U. Elbuzdukayeva gives, from the military documents, a different count: 6183 Red Army men with 137 heavy and 102 light machine guns, 14 mountain and 10 light [artillery] guns, and beyond that 341 OGPU officers assembled from across the whole North Caucasus[2]. Mikoyan, secretary of the North Caucasus krai committee of the party and one of the operation's organizers, recalled that "It was agreed to send two divisions into Chechnya 'for exercises'. The exercises were to include contact with the population, amateur performance evenings, concerts, closeness with the local youth, which was to strengthen still further the trust in Soviet power"[6]; the same legend was scattered from the air - the account of a surviving companion of imam Nazhmuddin Gotsinsky, printed in 1936 in the Warsaw journal Severny Kavkaz, says: "To calm the population, proclamations were scattered from aeroplanes, in which it was written that ordinary maneuvers were taking place and the inhabitants were asked not to worry and to stay in their homes"[8]. The head of Chechnya itself - Eldarkhanov, chairman of the Chechen TsIK (the highest organ of power of the autonomous oblast) - was not informed of the preparations: "The center and the organs of the OGPU did not consider it necessary to inform even the chairman of the Chechen TsIK, T. Eldarkhanov, of the action being prepared. The concentration of troops in Grozny was explained by forthcoming maneuvers"[2]. At the same time the disarmament instruction of 4 August 1925 wrote the Chechen TsIK into every step of the execution: its representatives enter the surrounded aul together with the command and convene the assembly, sit on the weapons-reception commissions, are obliged to provide profiles of the districts, and after "all the enumerated measures of influence" receive the authority to dissolve village executive committees and install revkoms[3]. Even before the troops went in, the OGPU had described every village: historian E. F. Zhupikova relates - "The organs of the OGPU gathered information about the most influential mullahs and sheikhs, about the honored elders, about the guides without whom it was impossible to penetrate into the mountains"[9]; for every settlement a questionnaire was drawn up with the number of inhabitants and households, the composition of the population by taips (clans) and the quantity of weapons planned for removal[3]. T0155 Forced Disarmament July 1925 C1177.T0155 → C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army Over the three weeks of the operation, from 25 August to 12 September 1925, the troops of the USSR took from the inhabitants of Chechnya 25299 rifles, 4319 revolvers and pistols, a machine gun and about 80 thousand cartridges[7]; the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB) reported to Stalin in rounded numbers: "In Chechnya during the operation 24000 rifles, 4000 revolvers, about 70000 cartridges, 2 machine guns were removed"[10], while Mikoyan, secretary of the North Caucasus krai committee of the party and one of the operation's organizers, counted in his memoirs "more than 30 thousand rifles, more than 10 machine guns"[6]. By the assessment of historian E. F. Zhupikova, what was removed amounted to "approximately 75% of what the population had before the start of the operation and approximately half of the weapons removed in all the highland oblasts"[9]. Under the disarmament instruction of 4 August 1925 the inhabitants were announced "the exact figure of the firearms and ammunition subject to removal", taken from the OGPU questionnaires, and given no more than two hours to surrender them[3]; Mikoyan describes the same quota with the words "they would present each village with the demand to surrender all weapons in the quantity known from agent intelligence"[6]. The taking of weapons began even before the troops went in, with the inhabitants divided up by lists: from those entered in the lists of the "vicious element" and their relatives "the local revkoms took the weapons away, while registering those of the remaining inhabitants"[9]. The inhabitants themselves asked to give up their weapons without shelling: in early September 1925 the delegates of the Goity society Eski Karlagov, Khatu Dobriyev and Dzhabi Otgayev appealed to the district's Revolutionary Military Council with a request: "Now, at the disarmament, which we consider right, we ask that this be taken into account and petition that an exception be made by allowing the voluntary surrender of weapons without the taking of repressive measures"; the answer came by telegram, "most urgent", over the signatures of Uborevich, commander of the North Caucasus Military District, Volodin, member of the district's Revolutionary Military Council, and Yevdokimov, plenipotentiary representative of the OGPU for the krai: "The Red Army knows well the revolutionary services of the village of Goity. The surrender of weapons must be carried out voluntarily on 9 September with delivery of the weapons to Grozny. The weapons necessary for self-defense will be left to the aul of Goity"[1]. T0165 Indiscriminate Attacks July 1925 C1177.T0165 → C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army The targets of the artillery and aviation were often not military objectives but inhabited settlements as such: the instruction of 4 August 1925, approved by Uborevich, commander of the North Caucasus Military District, Volodin, member of the district's Revolutionary Military Council, and Yevdokimov, plenipotentiary representative of the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB) for the krai, prescribed - "If the population of the aul does not fulfil the demand to surrender weapons in the established time in full, or fulfils it partially, the detachment command, by way of threat, opens artillery fire (or, in the absence of artillery, machine-gun fire) for 10 minutes with high bursts and half-strikes", and added: "depending on the situation the warning fire, as a measure of influence, may be opened several times as well"[3]; the document names no military objective and no target inside the village at all. Of the 242 disarmed settlements 101 came under rifle, machine-gun and artillery fire, 16 under strikes from the air[7]; by the count of historian E. F. Zhupikova, "104 one-pud bombs [about 1.7 tonnes] were dropped on the 16 auls where the leaders of the insurgents were hiding"[9]. A one-pud aerial bomb is about 16 kilograms, the weight of a round of a modern 120 mm mortar; on average six to seven such bombs fell per aul. The aviation was directed by Petrozhitsky, chief of the district's air force, and historian T. U. Elbuzdukayeva lists the targets by name: "In the course of the operation the aircraft of the 3rd, and from 6 September also of the 5th aviation detachments delivered air strikes on the auls of Zumsoy, Dai, Tagir Khoy, Akki Bougi, Oshni, Khimoy, Nizheloy, Ragekhoy, Urus-Martan and Nozhay-Yurt"[2]. What the "warning fire" looked like in a single aul can be seen from the dispatch on Achkhoy-Martan of 25 August 1925: "15 shrapnel rounds were fired at the aul, first four with a high burst, then to strike. After two Chechen women had been wounded, the inhabitants began to hand over their weapons"[11]. Historian A. Yu. Lashkov writes of the strike on the aul of Dai: "Initially, because of heavy fog, the neighboring settlement of Chubakhkimeroy was mistakenly subjected to the air strike"[12]. T0077 Punitive Expeditions July 1925 C1177.T0077 → C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army Through the resisting villages the troops moved in raids with house-to-house searches and arrests. The instruction on mass searches, issued for the operation by the staff of the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB), ordered houses to be cordoned off and everyone found in them to be detained and searched, and speaks of arrests in points 7 and 8: "All who counteract in one measure or another the successful conduct of the mass operation are brought to account and arrested", "Malicious concealers of weapons are arrested"; of what was taken during a search the same document says: "During searches and arrests only all correspondence is taken, including correspondence in the Arabic language, as well as all weapons found during the search"[3]. The information department of the OGPU, in its "Survey of the Political Condition of the USSR for September 1925" stamped "Top Secret", summed up the operation with the words "On our side losses are 20 men"[10], and reported nothing about the killed and wounded in the shelled and bombed auls. The count of losses for the operation as a whole is given by historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov from a journal publication of 1995: six killed civilians, 30 wounded, a further 12 killed assigned to the "bandits", with the troops' own losses at five killed and nine wounded[7]. T0105 Total Destruction of Infrastructure July 1925 C1177.T0105 → C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army Disarming Chechnya, the troops of the USSR destroyed the villages that had not met the ultimatum, up to complete demolition: the aul of Khakmedy - more than 300 households - was destroyed entirely, in the aul of Dai 20 houses were destroyed, Urus-Martan stood for three days under artillery fire and air strikes. A surviving companion of imam Nazhmuddin Gotsinsky - the spiritual head of the resistance in Dagestan and Chechnya, whom the troops pursued into the mountains - related in 1936 in the Warsaw journal Severny Kavkaz: "Then the fire was transferred to the nearest auls, of which the aul of Khakmedy (more than 300 households) was completely destroyed"[8]. The aul of Dai, the center of resistance of the fifth combat sector, historian A. Yu. Lashkov describes from the documents of the military archive: "From the shelling and bombings the aul of Dai suffered substantially: 20 houses turned out destroyed, there were a small number of human casualties"[12]. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "...the aul of Urus-Martan was subjected to artillery shelling and air strikes for three days, the aul of Dai was bombed three times, for two days artillery shelled the auls of the Zumsoy society"[7]. T0159 Collective Punishment July 1925 C1177.T0159 → C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army Even before the operation the village assemblies together with the revkoms (unelected committees installed in place of elected Soviets - campaign C1176) drew up lists of the "vicious element" - inhabitants noted in robberies; historian E. F. Zhupikova writes: "They and their relatives bore material responsibility for all cases of theft on the territory of Chechnya"[9] - the relatives paid for others' thefts by the fact of kinship and an entry in the list. One could leave the list only by an oath with an obligation to inform: "If the 'vicious element' took an oath that for a year he would not rob and would inform on thieves, he was struck from the list"[9]. When the troops reached the mountains, the destroyed was counted by the same category: as the result of the bombing of 16 auls "119 houses of the 'vicious element' were blown up"[9]; historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov confirm the number - "119 houses were blown up"[7]: a house was blown up because its owner was entered in the list. T0099 Hostage-Taking July 1925 C1177.T0099 → C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services To get at imam Nazhmuddin Gotsinsky, who was sheltering in the mountains of Chechnya, the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB) took old men from the villages and held them hostage under the threat of destroying the villages with artillery. Mikoyan, secretary of the North Caucasus krai committee of the party and one of the operation's organizers, described it himself: "to catch him, the Chekists invited to their quarters old men from the villages where he might be hiding and, declaring them hostages, warned them that if they did not say where Gotsinsky was, they would destroy the villages with artillery, and would arrest them and put them on trial. For a whole day they tried to persuade the old men, but all was without result. Then an aeroplane was sent to that district. They were terribly afraid of the aeroplane. Only after several shells had been fired at the village so that, without destruction of the houses, the inhabitants should feel its power, did the old men say in which gorge Gotsinsky was hiding"[6]. The word "hostages" is also in the documents of the operation itself: on 4 September 1925 Mironov, head of the Chechen oblast department of the OGPU, reported: "I report: the population is giving up Nazhmudin. I am now conducting negotiations with the representatives. The matter is being conducted through the hostages I have released... Let aeroplanes appear at 15 hours, but not strike. For effect let some 6-7 of them come"[1]. For the Sharoy district the count of hostages is known from the documents of the military archive: historian A. Yu. Lashkov writes that "the command of the military grouping demanded of the population of the Sharoy district the surrender of the well-known bandit Gotsinsky. In doing so, 40 men from among the honored elders were taken hostage. However, the demand to surrender Gotsinsky was not satisfied within the appointed time, and therefore the troops resorted to intensified repressions. In two days 22 puds of bombs [about 360 kilograms - like 22 rounds of a modern 120 mm mortar] were dropped on the district"[12]. The surviving companion of Gotsinsky names a different number and adds what is not in the Soviet papers: from the destroyed aul of Khakmedy "105 hostages were taken", and the hostages were threatened with shooting - his account says: "the Bolsheviks wrote of the shooting of the hostages in the event of resistance in their proclamations"[8]. The word "hostages" is not in the disarmament instruction of 4 August 1925, approved by the operation's commanders, - it allows only arrests of "influential persons of the aul" as an extreme measure: the hostage-taking was done over and above what was written, and its traces remained in the dispatches of the executors and the memoirs of an organizer. T0156 Forced Surrender of Fugitives and Rebels July 1925 C1177.T0156 → C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0010 Regular Army On 8 September 1925 Soviet aviation dropped eight one-pud bombs - 16 kilograms each, like a round of a modern 120 mm mortar - on Nozhay-Yurt, to force the village to hand over Gibertiev, the former head of the district militia[13]. Urus-Martan was coerced in the same way: historian A. Yu. Lashkov writes that after artillery fire and bomb strikes "the leadership of Urus-Martan yielded and handed over the bandits on 9 September"[12]. Of the representatives of the local authorities the instruction on mass searches, issued for the operation by the staff of the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB), says: they are brought into the removal as those "obliged to point out the dwellings of persons subject to removal, as well as those persons (relatives and others) with whom the person subject to removal may be hiding"[3] - the community itself was made the executor of the removal. The price of this demand is named by historian E. F. Zhupikova: "By force of the highland custom of hospitality, the population of Chechnya, even if it was hostile to the leaders of the insurgents and the chiefs of the bandits, could not hand them over to the authorities. Breaking the custom would have disgraced the highlander for many generations and would have threatened his clan with blood vengeance from the man he had handed over"[9]. T0021 Neutralization of the Opposition July 1925 C1177.T0021 → C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services In the two months of the operation of 1925 the USSR arrested and shot the leaders of the resistance of Chechnya and Dagestan. Imam Nazhmuddin Gotsinsky, the spiritual head of the resistance in Dagestan and Chechnya, was arrested by the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB) on 5 September 1925. His hiding place was given up by the old men held hostage in the Sharoy district under the threat of the shelling of their villages. On the same day Uborevich, commander of the North Caucasus Military District, Yevdokimov, plenipotentiary representative of the OGPU for the krai, and Volodin, member of the district's Revolutionary Military Council, reported to Moscow: "The operation in the Sharoy district has ended successfully. After 5 days of repressions and agent work, today at 14 hours a report was received through the aircraft that Gotsinsky has been taken"[12]; he was arrested by an operational group of the GPU under the command of M. Ushaev[7]. Historian T. U. Elbuzdukayeva writes: "N. Gotsinsky was urgently taken to Rostov-on-Don, where on 15 October 1925 he was sentenced to be shot"[2]. Arrests are provided for by the disarmament instruction of 4 August 1925 as well - it allows "the conduct of arrests of influential persons of the aul, reactionarily disposed", with the proviso to resort to this measure "as an extreme one, with the observance of maximum tact"[3]. Under shelling even the innocent surrendered: historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that in Urus-Martan, "after the artillery and aviation shelling of the settlement, the sheikhs Solsa-Haji Yandarov and Bilu-Haji Gaytayev surrendered to the authorities - soon, incidentally, released owing to their complete innocence"[7]. T0160 Sham Trials July 1925 C1177.T0160 → C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The instruction on mass searches, issued for the operation by the staff of the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB), establishes that until the end of the investigation the arrested are concentrated at the staffs of the OGPU district groups, and of what follows point 19 says: "The procedure for conducting the investigation and the further routing of the arrested is provided for in the regulations on the troikas for the extrajudicial examination of cases"[3]. The "Main Tasks of the Special Operational Groups of the OGPU", approved by Yevdokimov, plenipotentiary representative of the OGPU for the krai, Uborevich, commander of the North Caucasus Military District, and Volodin, member of the district's Revolutionary Military Council, include the same procedure directly in the list of tasks: "The removal of the counter-revolutionary, bandit and other criminal anti-Soviet element... the registration of the same, the conduct of the investigation and the extrajudicial examination of their cases and their transportation to the place of destination"[3]. Through this procedure passed 183 of the more than three hundred arrested in the course of the operation - the investigation of their cases ended in extrajudicial shooting[7]. The OGPU had received the right of extrajudicial reprisal a year earlier - by a secret resolution of the Presidium of the TsIK of 9 May 1924 (campaign C1176); the operation's instruction applied it to the arrested. T0162.003 Killing of Prisoners and Detainees July 1925 C1177.T0162.003 → C1177 The disarmament of Chechnya: a military operation with artillery shelling and bombing of auls (1925) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The USSR shot nearly all those arrested in the course of the operation of 1925 - people already in the hands of the troops and the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB). Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "The total number of arrested exceeded 300. Of the total number of arrested, 105 were shot on the spot; against 183 an investigation was opened, which also ended in extrajudicial shooting; 21 were exiled"[7]. Even the OGPU's own count found few "active" ones among them: the survey submitted to Stalin names 50 "active bandits and prominent counter-revolutionary figures", while "In all, 400 bandits and elements abetting them have been arrested"[10] - those shot were mostly not leaders but rank-and-file detainees whose guilt was established by no court. So was killed the operation's chief prisoner as well: imam Nazhmuddin Gotsinsky - the spiritual head of the resistance in Dagestan and Chechnya, detained on 5 September 1925 and sentenced in Rostov-on-Don - was shot, in the words of a highlander emigre writing in the Paris journal Prométhée in 1930, "Il fut fusillé sans jugement dans les souterrains du Guépéou de Rostov" - without trial, in the cellars of the GPU in Rostov[14]. title: Devastation of the Lowland Nokhchi Villages in Yermolov’s Punitive Campaign (1826), campaign C1148
content: Devastation of the Lowland Nokhchi Villages in Yermolov’s Punitive Campaign (1826) In January-May 1826 the Russian Empire conducted a large punitive campaign against the Nokhchi, devastating lowland villages for participation in Beibulat Taimiev’s uprising and forcing the inhabitants into submission. The historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that "in January 1826, having waited for a period inconvenient for the inhabitants of Chechnya, when the frosts made it difficult to shelter families, Yermolov begins a large punitive campaign into Chechnya," occupying the aul of Bolshaya Ataga on January 26 and burning settlements one after another[1]. General Yermolov himself, in a report to Emperor Nicholas I of May 28, 1826, admits the course of the devastation: during the storming of Urus-Martan "the village was burned and its splendid orchards cut down," at Stavna-Kul "16 souls of both sexes were taken prisoner, several people killed," and the village of Shali he "ordered to be exterminated… and its orchards cut down"[2]. The historian D. A. Khozhaev sums up: by May 18, 1826, "flourishing settlements had been destroyed, splendid fruit orchards cut down, fields burned, livestock driven off. People were killed, women and children taken prisoner… People were dying of hunger, cold, and disease"[1]. ID: C1148 Start: January 1826 End: May 1826 Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.1 Created: 27 June 2026 Last Modified: 5 September 2026 Discuss on Telegram Actors ID Name Procedures G0009 Russian Empire 7 Instruments Applied ID Name Procedures S0010 Regular Army 7 Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: T0077 Punitive Expeditions January 1826 C1148.T0077 → C1148 Devastation of the Lowland Nokhchi Villages in Yermolov’s Punitive Campaign (1826) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The Russian Empire sent troops to ravage the lowland villages of the Nokhchi, choosing the moment most vulnerable for the inhabitants to strike. Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that «in January 1826, having waited for a period inconvenient for the inhabitants of Chechnya, when the frosts made it difficult to shelter families, Yermolov launches a large punitive campaign into Chechnya», occupying the aul of Bolshaya Ataga on January 26[1]. General Yermolov himself, in a report to Emperor Nicholas I dated May 28, 1826, reported that the troops were methodically cutting roads and occupying villages: on April 12 «the village of Kurchali was occupied without a shot», on the 16th «the troops moved to the village of Gekhi», and on the 24th he «moved to the village of Malaya Roshni, which was found empty»[2]. T0105 Total Destruction of Infrastructure January 1826 C1148.T0105 → C1148 Devastation of the Lowland Nokhchi Villages in Yermolov’s Punitive Campaign (1826) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that after February 17, 1826, Yermolov's troops «ravaged and destroyed the auls of Lesser Chechnya - Urus-Martan, Roshni, Gekhi, Belakai, Daut-Martan, and Shelchikhi», and by the end of the campaign «flourishing villages had been destroyed»[1]. General Yermolov himself, in a report to Emperor Nicholas I dated May 28, 1826, confirmed: during the storming of Urus-Martan «the village was burned», Bolshaya Roshni was «put to the torch», and the village of Shali, whose inhabitants «give an amanat, asked for time, and deceived», he «ordered to be destroyed»[2]. The imperial historian Volkonsky specifies that Shali stood empty by the time the troops arrived: Yermolov «did not find a single inhabitant there: all had scattered through the forests», after which he «burned their dwellings»[3]. T0140 Destruction of the Natural Landscape January 1826 C1148.T0140 → C1148 Devastation of the Lowland Nokhchi Villages in Yermolov’s Punitive Campaign (1826) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that by May 18, 1826, the Nokhchi's «splendid fruit orchards had been cut down, fields burned»[1]. General Yermolov himself, in a report to Emperor Nicholas I dated May 28, 1826, admitted that at Urus-Martan «its splendid orchards were cut down», and for the village of Shali he gave the order «to cut down the orchards»[2]. T0164 Pillage January 1826 C1148.T0164 → C1148 Devastation of the Lowland Nokhchi Villages in Yermolov’s Punitive Campaign (1826) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The Russian Empire drove off livestock and plundered the ravaged villages of the Nokhchi. Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that by May 18, 1826, «livestock had been driven off», and after the troops returned, Yermolov «sent a detachment of 500 Cossacks against Daut-Martan», and «the village was ravaged and plundered»[1]. T0053 Abduction of People January 1826 C1148.T0053 → C1148 Devastation of the Lowland Nokhchi Villages in Yermolov’s Punitive Campaign (1826) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that by May 18, 1826, «women and children had been taken captive» from the Nokhchi[1]. General Yermolov himself, in a report to Emperor Nicholas I dated May 28, 1826, specified the number: in the surprise attack on the village of Stavna-kul on May 2, «16 souls of both sexes were taken captive», and in the attack on Malaya Ataga on May 16 he «captured 15 souls of both sexes»[2]. The imperial historian Volkonsky confirms the seizure at Stavnokol: the sudden movement «brought us sixteen captives»[3]. T0121 Artificial Famine January 1826 C1148.T0121 → C1148 Devastation of the Lowland Nokhchi Villages in Yermolov’s Punitive Campaign (1826) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The Russian Empire condemned the Nokhchi inhabitants to famine by ravaging their villages, crops, and stores. Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that after Yermolov's campaign, deprived of shelter and food, «people were dying of hunger, cold, and disease»[1]. T0152 Pitting Neighboring Peoples Against Each Other January 1826 C1148.T0152 → C1148 Devastation of the Lowland Nokhchi Villages in Yermolov’s Punitive Campaign (1826) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The Russian Empire set a neighboring people against the Nokhchi in order to weaken their resistance. Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that Yermolov, «attempting to provoke a clash between the Chechens and the Ingush… forcibly conscripted the Ingush into a militia and sent them together with tsarist detachments against Chechen auls», although the Ingush «refused to go against their kin… deserting from the militia»[1]. References Хожаев Д. А. Чеченцы в Русско-Кавказской войне. 1998. Кавказская археографическая комиссия. Акты собранные Кавказскою археографическою комиссиею. Том VI, часть вторая (1816-1827). 1875. Волконский Н. А. Война на Восточном Кавказе с 1824 по 1834 г. в связи с мюридизмом. 1886.

title: "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917), campaign C1170
content: "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) In 1858-1917 conquered Chechnya lived under a regime the empire itself named "military-popular administration": administrative power over the people lay in the hands of officers of the active army. The system was named by Baryatinsky, viceroy in the Caucasus - historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "A. I. Baryatinsky called the system of governing the highlanders that he was creating 'military-popular' and considered it temporary", and add what the name contained: "Contemporaries, without embarrassment, called this system of administration 'military'"[1]. The system was defined by a later viceroy, Vorontsov-Dashkov: it was "based on the concentration of administrative power in the hands of individual officers, under the supreme direction of the commander-in-chief of the Caucasus Army, and on allowing the population to manage its internal affairs according to its own adats" (adats - the customary law of the highlanders)[2]. The imperial general Chernyavsky explained why the regime was needed: "for these savage peoples such privileges are still premature... What is needed here is a power that commands, bridles and governs"[2]. Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes of the order thus imposed: "In the restless Terek oblast a 'military-popular' regime was established, which was in essence a state-of-emergency regime"; the outcome of the war he states separately: "A colonial 'military-popular' regime was established in the land"[3]. ID: C1170 Start: April 1858 End: March 1917 Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.3 Created: 3 August 2026 Last Modified: 18 September 2026 Discuss on Telegram Actors ID Name Procedures G0009 Russian Empire 13 Instruments Applied ID Name Procedures S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations 11 S0010 Regular Army 2 Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: T0036 Installation of a New System of Governance April 1858 C1170.T0036 → C1170 "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations On 1 April 1858 the "Regulation on the Administration of the Caucasus Army" created a special section for the mountain peoples at the Main Staff - historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova calls this "the first legislative confirmation of the system of 'military-popular administration' that had in fact taken shape as the land was being conquered"[2]. In 1859, "in connection with the reform of the local administration and the entry into force of the Regulation on the Main Directorate of the Viceroy of the Caucasus", State Control was "deprived of the ability to monitor the activities of the local authorities": within the viceroy's Main Directorate a special control department was set up, answerable not to the central agency but to the head of the Main Directorate himself[2]. On 16 January 1860 Emperor Alexander II approved the regulation by which the Left Wing of the Caucasus Line (the chain of imperial fortifications on Nokhchi land) was renamed the Terek oblast[2]. On 24 May 1860 Baryatinsky, viceroy in the Caucasus, ordered the creation at the Main Staff of the Caucasus Army of a "Chancellery for the Administration of the Caucasus Highlanders" - later it was called the "Caucasus Mountain Administration", then the "Caucasus Military-Popular Administration"[2]. On 25 December 1860 the "provisional staffing tables of the military-popular administration of the Terek oblast" were approved: the oblast was divided into six okrugs (districts) - Kabardian, Vladikavkaz, Chechen, Kumyk, Ichkerian and Argun[2]. T0151 Imposition of Alien Governance April 1858 C1170.T0151 → C1170 "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "in 1867 Major General Prince Tumanov was appointed head of the Middle military otdel, while of the eight heads of the mountain okrugs six were colonels and two were majors"[1]. The head of the Terek oblast united civil, military and Cossack authority in one pair of hands and, in the words of the same historians, could against the highlanders "at his own will use... arms and raise against them the troops and Cossacks subordinate to him, hand highlanders over to a military court and administratively expel 'undesirable elements' from the oblast"[1]. From September 1866 the viceroy received the right to replace highlanders in the posts of pristavs (superintendents appointed by the empire) with incomer officers - historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova records the result: for a long time highlanders could rise no higher in the administrative system of the Terek oblast than the office of village elder[2]. The elders themselves were hand-picked by the authorities and sworn to "unquestioning execution... of all instructions and demands of the administration"; the population was left no choice - "The local authorities did not consider it possible to grant even the right to elect aul elders, since they 'found no sufficient guarantees that this would not entail serious inconveniences in the matter of governing the highlanders'"[2]. The court system was crowned by the same officers: in 1862 an oblast Main People's Court was created, all of whose members were appointed by the head of the oblast, and in 1870 - okrug "Mountain verbal courts" chaired by officers of the administration; historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov conclude: "Thus the court system created for the highlanders of the Terek oblast was not merely not removed from the control of the military authorities but, on the contrary, directly subordinated to them"[1]. The 1895 regulation on village communities handed the right of assembly to a limited number of "elected representatives", and the okrug head could strip an "elected representative" of his office and dissolve the entire village assembly[1]. T0030 Administrative-Territorial Division April 1858 C1170.T0030 → C1170 "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations The oblast was recut in 1862, 1869, 1888 and 1899[2]. From 1 May 1888 the Vedeno and Argun okrugs were merged into the Grozny okrug - under the formula quoted by historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova, "to shield the Cossacks from the 'corrupting' influence of the highlanders"[2]. The Chechen villages on the right bank of the Terek, which were slated for transfer to the Kizlyar and Pyatigorsk otdels (Cossack divisions), were set apart as a special uchastok (sub-district) and temporarily left under the head of the Grozny okrug; the mountain okrugs were divided into uchastoks, while the Cossack otdels were divided by the pattern of manning military units, into sotnias (Cossack hundreds) and regiments[2]. From 1 January 1899 the oblast was recut once more: four otdels - Pyatigorsk, Mozdok, Kizlyar, Sunzha - and four okrugs: Vladikavkaz, Khasav-Yurt, Nalchik, Grozny[2]. T0043 Erasure and Renaming of Place Names April 1858 C1170.T0043 → C1170 "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations The Groznaya fortress, founded by General Yermolov on the Sunzha on 10 June 1818[4], became the town of Grozny in 1870[1]. On 21 March 1888, by decree of Emperor Alexander III, the names of peoples were erased from the names of the okrugs of the Terek oblast: the Chechen okrug was renamed the Grozny okrug, the Ingush - the Nazran, the Kabardian - the Nalchik, the Kumyk - the Khasav-Yurt, the Military-Ossetian - the Vladikavkaz[2]. Okrugs named after the peoples living in them received the names of imperial fortresses and slobodas - the map of governance ceased to call the peoples by name. T0032 Legal Segregation of the Population April 1858 C1170.T0032 → C1170 "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations From 1882 "especially important" cases in which the accused were highlanders were transferred to the field court-martial; in 1893, with the emperor's permission, a significant share of highlanders' criminal cases was withdrawn from the general civil courts - into whose jurisdiction these cases passed, the source does not specify[2]. Punishment could also be imposed without any court: the head of the oblast jailed highlanders for up to one month at his personal discretion, and imposed penalties on aul communities for harbouring[2]; on 19 November 1893 the rules of administrative deportation to Eastern Siberia on accusation or suspicion of stealing horses and livestock were extended to the Terek oblast[2], and according to historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov the decision on administrative exile for a term of up to five years was taken by the commander of the Caucasus Army, and the place of exile was Chechen Island in the Caspian[1]. The 1894 "Temporary Regulation on Measures to Restrain the Native Population of the Terek Oblast from 'Predation'" - its draft was submitted for approval by the head of the Terek oblast, general Kakhanov - according to historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova, wrote the collective liability of the village community for committed crimes into law[2]; historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov record the mechanics: mountain villages paid for stolen livestock "if the tracks of the stolen livestock turned out to be lost near the given village", while "the possibility that the thieves might not be highlanders at all was completely ignored"[1]. Indigenous inhabitants were barred from holding the posts of pristav and okrug head and from serving as justices of the peace[2]; the 1888 regulation on the administration of the Terek and Kuban oblasts established, in the words of historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova, "a narrowly caste-based military-Cossack administration, without the participation not only of representatives of the mountain peoples but of the non-Cossack element as well... the highlanders were placed outside the operation of the general laws"[2]. In the 1890s the administration, by a separate order, forbade Cossacks to keep kunachestvo with highlanders (kunachestvo - sworn brotherhood, an institution of friendship between households)[2]. Service was segregated too: the "political unreliability" of the Caucasus Muslims led the authorities to give up forming line units from them, and from 1886, by order of the Minister of War, recruits from the Terek oblast were assigned only to troops stationed in the Caucasus[2]. Zemstvos were never introduced in the oblast at all; the proposal on zemstvo institutions in the Terek oblast, submitted to the State Duma in 1914, was not adopted before the revolution[2]. T0035 Forced Passportization April 1858 C1170.T0035 → C1170 "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations The 1894 "Regulation on Residence Permits" enshrined estate inequality: nobles, officials and merchants received passport books of unlimited duration, while highlanders ascribed to village communities received five-year books or short-term passports and bilets (written passes) for absence[2]. Historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova states the regime's effect from the oblast's records: "Terek highlanders, should they appear beyond the Kuban or in other parts of the Russian Empire without passports, were considered vagrants and malefactors and were punished as such"; she also writes: "The passport system served the administration of the Terek oblast as a favourite means of constraining even persons well known to it"[2]. Inside the oblast a regime of absences operated: leave of up to a month was granted by the village elder, for a longer term - by the okrug head; unauthorized absence was punished by fine, arrest or public works, and a highlander could not move from one community to another without the consent of two village communities - the one he was leaving and the one he was joining[1]. T0142 Restriction of Settlement Geography April 1858 C1170.T0142 → C1170 "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations As early as 1880, by decree of the viceroy, all highlanders were expelled from the Shatoy sloboda - "owing to the decrease of Russians in the sloboda" - with a ban on settling there henceforth[2]. On 14 May 1893 the eviction of highlanders from the towns and slobodas of the oblast began; the bans were lifted piecemeal over decades: for Grozny - on 18 March 1901, for the Vozdvizhenskaya sloboda - on 27 February 1906, for Vedeno and Shatoy - only on 10 May 1916[2]. The head of the oblast justified the repeal not by the rights of the evicted - he petitioned for the repeal of the law of 14 May 1893 as one "serving as a brake on the Russification of the tribes"[2]. By order of 26 August 1898 the head of the garrison of the Shatoy fortification banned entry into the fortification without a bilet - the population of three uchastoks was left without access to the post and telegraph office, the savings bank and the pharmacy[2]. T0155 Forced Disarmament April 1858 C1170.T0155 → C1170 "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations On 17 August 1884 the "Binding Decree on the Sale, Storage and Carrying of Combat Firearms in the Caucasus Krai" was approved: combat rifles - only under police permits, and the sale and purchase of army-pattern weapons were banned[2]. On 1 July 1899 the decree was tightened: previous permits were annulled, annual renewal was required, and weapons without a permit were confiscated and sold for the benefit of the treasury[2]. In 1892, by order of the head of the Terek oblast, all weapons with which highlanders appeared in Russian settlements were confiscated, including weapons brought for sale; from 1893 the authorities were allowed to search homes for weapons[2]. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov record the contrast: highlander militiamen in imperial service carried weapons at all times, "unlike ordinary highlanders, who could not appear armed outside their villages"[1]. T0056 Taxation April 1858 C1170.T0056 → C1170 "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations Historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova writes: from the 1860s the administrative apparatus in Chechnya and Ingushetia "was maintained chiefly on funds collected from the people"[2]. The empire did not trust the highlanders with military service - and taxed them in money instead: by the laws of 2 and 9 June 1887 a monetary levy in place of military service was introduced for the Muslims of the Terek oblast, its size "did not exceed 22 kopecks per 'dym'"[2] ("dym" - a separate household, homestead)[2]; historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov confirm: "in 1887 the Russian government introduced a special monetary levy for them"[1]. From then on the levies only grew: "From 1887 to 1905 the sum of taxes rose from 228.1 to 678.8 thousand rubles, that is, it nearly tripled over these years", while the podymnaya tax - the tax on each household - "in the Terek oblast reached in the 1890s up to 70 kopecks per desiatina, while at that time in the interior provinces of the country it was no more than 17 kopecks, or four times less"[2]. On top of the levy, village communities bore obligations in kind: maintaining the elder and the village board, the roads, ditches and watch posts[1]. T0146 Administrative Corruption and Extortion April 1858 C1170.T0146 → C1170 "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: fine moneys were spent on maintaining exiles and secret agents, and at times covered officials' embezzlement - in 1893 the head of the Nadterechny uchastok, lieutenant Tomashevsky, embezzled over 300 rubles collected from Chechen villages[1]. The nature of the power was admitted from within by colonel Belik, appointed in 1860 the first head of the Chechen okrug; he later wrote: in Chechnya "there reigns for the most part not law but arbitrary rule, often founded on the dishonesty of the chief, and thereby we only sow in the people distrust of ourselves, even hatred"[1]. T0158 Territorial Marking with Imperial Symbols April 1858 C1170.T0158 → C1170 "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations On 15 March 1873 the coat of arms of the Terek oblast was approved: "In a black shield, a silver wavy bend to the right. An Imperial standard on a golden staff. The shield is crowned with the ancient Tsar's Crown and surrounded by golden oak leaves joined by the Alexander ribbon"[2]. Historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova reads the meaning of the sign thus: the silver bend is the Terek, which had long been a border, and now "both its banks were united by the Imperial standard, and the Terek became fully Russian - such is the basic meaning of this coat of arms"[2]. The draft coat of arms of the city of Grozny was made by B. V. Köhne, an official of the Heraldry Office: on an azure shield a silver mountain between two golden sea lilies, and in the dexter canton - the arms of the Terek oblast[2], so that the city's emblem carried the imperial symbol of the oblast. The land was marked with the figure of the conqueror as well. The first monument to Yermolov in Grozny was "the carefully preserved dugout in which he lived during the founding of the Groznaya fortress"[2], and later a bronze bust of the general was set up by the dugout. What this sign meant, Ibragimova puts thus: the bust recalled the most tragic years of the conquest of the Caucasus and was a symbol of the dramatic fate of the mountain peoples, and the monument to the general who "with barbaric cruelty exterminated whole peoples in the name of the conquest of the Caucasus" became for Chechens "a kind of 'eyesore'"[2]. The sign outlived the empire: under Soviet rule the monument "was blown up by night with enviable regularity and just as regularly restored by night"[2]. T0022 Terror April 1858 C1170.T0022 → C1170 "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army At the start of the twentieth century the Terek authorities began to bring in military detachments and Cossack units for mass searches of highland auls - formally to confiscate weapons and to "detain fugitives"[1]. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write what this turned into: sweeping searches of mountain villages "were as a rule accompanied by looting and other unlawful acts by soldiers and Cossacks, which was encouraged in every way by the Terek authorities, who constantly sought a pretext for applying harsher measures against the highlanders"[1]. How literally this encouragement worked is visible in November 1902: during a search staged by Cossacks at the bazaar of the village of Shaami-Yurt mass disturbances broke out, the ataman of the Samashkinskaya stanitsa, Gridnev, forbade his men to use firearms, and the clash ended without bloodshed - after which the head of the Terek oblast removed Gridnev from his post and expressed displeasure to the Cossacks who had taken part in the disturbances for their "passivity"[1]. The sanction came from the very top: when the head of the Terek oblast reported that the clashes between Chechens and Cossacks were bringing material damage and human casualties and that these groups of the population should be kept apart, Nicholas II replied that "it is precisely this neighbourhood that keeps up in the Cossacks their old ancestral daring, and therefore there is no need whatever to take measures to soften the situation"[4]. Bloodshed in Chechen villages was for the authorities not an incidental cost but the working condition of the land. T0164 Pillage April 1858 C1170.T0164 → C1170 "Military-Popular Administration": the Colonial Regime of the Terek Oblast (1858-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The military teams and Cossack units brought in at the beginning of the 20th century for sweeping searches of the mountain auls robbed the residents with the authorities' encouragement: historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that the searches "were as a rule accompanied by robberies and other unlawful actions of soldiers and Cossacks, which was encouraged in every way by the Terek command"[1]. References Ахмадов Я. З., Хасмагомадов Э. Х. История Чечни в XIX-XX веках. 2005. Ибрагимова З. Х. Царское прошлое чеченцев. Власть и общество. 2009. Хожаев Д. А. Чеченцы в Русско-Кавказской войне. 1998. Ибрагимова З. Х. Мир чеченцев. XIX век. 2007.

title: Suppression of the Shebelynka Uprising (1829), campaign C0056
content: Suppression of the Shebelynka Uprising (1829) The forcible suppression of a mass anti-serfdom uprising in Sloboda Ukraine that broke out within the system of military settlements: "The servile condition of the military settlements' inhabitants caused the Buh Cossacks' uprising of 1817, the Chuhuiv uprising of 1819, the Shebelynka uprising of 1829, and others"[1]. The scale is recorded by the EHU: "Up to 3 thousand peasants gathered in Shebelynka," and "on May 30, 1829 a bloody reprisal against the defiant began, during which 109 people died"[2]. ID: C0056 Start: January 1829 End: December 1829 Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.2 Created: 25 April 2026 Last Modified: 1 August 2026 Discuss on Telegram Actors ID Name Procedures G0009 Russian Empire 1 Instruments Applied ID Name Procedures S0010 Regular Army 1 Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: T0077 Punitive Expeditions January 1829 C0056.T0077 → C0056 Suppression of the Shebelynka Uprising (1829) G0009 Russian Empire S0010 Regular Army The use of the regular army to suppress the peasants' anti-serfdom uprising in Sloboda Ukraine (the Shebelynka uprising of 1829) – one in a series of revolts caused by the "servile condition" of the military settlements' inhabitants[1]. References Інститут історії України НАН України. Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 1. 2003. – редкол.: Смолій В. А. (голова) та ін. Інститут історії України НАН України.
