title: Stolypin Repressions and Mass Displacement (1906–1914), campaign C0069
content: Stolypin Repressions and Mass Displacement (1906–1914) The suppression of protests and an agrarian reform that economically squeezed Ukrainian peasants off their native lands: "The resettlement movement gained great momentum, and during 1906–12 about 1 million people left Ukraine for Asiatic Russia… The majority of migrants were landless and land-poor peasants (67%)"[1] – nearly a quarter of the resettlers, failing to take root, returned. ID: C0069 Start: January 1906 End: December 1914 Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.1 Created: 25 April 2026 Last Modified: 31 July 2026 Discuss on Telegram Actors ID Name Procedures G0009 Russian Empire 2 Instruments Applied ID Name Procedures S0008 Government 1 S0017 Secret Police and Security Services 1 Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: T0141 Creation of Economic Hopelessness January 1906 C0069.T0141 → C0069 Stolypin Repressions and Mass Displacement (1906–1914) G0009 Russian Empire S0008 Government The economic squeezing of peasants onto the imperial frontier under the guise of free choice: "during 1906–12 about 1 million people left Ukraine for Asiatic Russia. The largest number of resettlers came from Left-Bank Ukraine, whose peasantry suffered from land scarcity"[1]; land and credit were unobtainable at home, while "Low land prices beyond the Urals and encouraging government credits… attracted the poor peasantry and prompted it to migrate"[1] – state coercion was disguised as voluntary resettlement. T0128 Liquidation of National Civic Organizations January 1906 C0069.T0128 → C0069 Stolypin Repressions and Mass Displacement (1906–1914) G0009 Russian Empire S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The forcible suppression of protests and repressive measures against national self-organization of the same period: Stolypin's "instruction to the governors… demanding a halt to the registration of 'alien,' including Ukrainian, national cultural-educational societies"[1]. title: Punitive Raids and the Economic Strangulation of the Nokhchi (1691–1700), campaign C1124
content: Punitive Raids and the Economic Strangulation of the Nokhchi (1691–1700) At the end of the 17th century, the Tsardom of Muscovy exerted continuous military, diplomatic, and economic pressure on the societies of the Nokhchi. In response to the alliance of the Indigenous population with Russian Old Believer Cossacks, the regular army conducted armed operations: the historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov states that in 1691–1700 «punitive expeditions were carried out in retaliation by the tsarist authorities against the rebel Cossacks and their mountaineer allies»[1] and records «retaliatory punitive raids by tsarist forces»[1]. In parallel, the diplomatic apparatus expanded legal control over the region, formalizing in 1696 «an expression of Russia's protection over the Braguny principality in Chechnya»[1]. Military methods were supplemented by official fiscal pressure: the historian Sh. B. Akhmadov emphasizes that «the Okochans (Akkin Chechens) living in the town of Terki were obligated without exception to pay duties on the various goods and wares they took out for sale to their compatriots in Chechnya and Ingushetia»[2]. The economic strangulation was aggravated by the arbitrariness of the local occupation administration: he adds that «the venality and bribe-taking of the voivodes, who permitted themselves great abuses — all this was a phenomenon far from new»[2]. title: Truce of Vilna (1656), campaign C0002
content: Truce of Vilna (1656) Separate peace negotiations between Moscow and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth on ending the war and dividing spheres of influence, held in complete isolation from the Ukrainian side: "The plenipotentiary representatives of the Ukrainian Cossack state, headed by R. Haponenko, were not admitted to the negotiating table"[1]. The hetman asked that the Cossack envoys be given mandates as full participants of the congress - "but the tsar's government once again let this request pass unheeded," and the delegates "sat idle beside the commissioners, not admitted to the official sessions"[2]. The negotiations were held at Niemieza near Vilna from August 1656; the armistice was signed on October 24[1]. title: Truce of Andrusovo (1667), campaign C0005
content: Truce of Andrusovo (1667) An agreement on the partition of the Hetmanate along the Dnipro between the Tsardom of Muscovy and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth without Ukrainian participation: "The Russian state received significant territorial acquisitions… However, Right-Bank Ukraine, Polotsk, Vitebsk, and other Belarusian cities with Russian garrisons remained with the Commonwealth"[1]. The legal entrenchment of Ukraine's split and the transformation of Zaporizhzhia into a buffer zone: "under the treaty of 1667 it was under the joint rule of Moscow and Warsaw"[2]. Hrushevsky records the reaction to the partition: "there was great resentment against the Muscovite government for agreeing to cede Right-Bank Ukraine to Poland in the armistice of 1667: it divided Ukraine with Poland and did not keep what it had promised when taking Ukraine under the tsar's hand"[3]. ID: C0005 Start: January 1667 End: January 1667 Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.4 Created: 24 April 2026 Last Modified: 5 September 2026 Discuss on Telegram Actors ID Name Procedures G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy 4 Instruments Applied ID Name Procedures S0009 Diplomacy 2 S0008 Government 2 Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: T0039 Collusion with a Third Party Behind the People's Back January 1667 C0005.T0039 → C0005 Truce of Andrusovo (1667) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0009 Diplomacy The official partition of Ukrainian lands between two neighboring states. The treaty was signed exclusively by representatives of Moscow and Warsaw: "Concluded on January 30 (February 9) in the village of Andrusovo, near Smolensk, for 13.5 years. The Russian delegation was headed by okolnichy A. L. Ordin-Nashchokin, the Polish one by commissioner Yu. Hlebowicz"[1]. The opinion of the autonomy itself was completely ignored: "The interests of the hetmans and of Ukraine were, of course, not taken into account"[4]. A separate knot of the collusion was Kyiv: article 7 of the Andrusovo treaty (30 January 1667) stipulated that "the very city of Kyiv… is to be handed over and vacated… that is, within two years, counting from the present treaty… in the coming year 1669, on the 15th day of April"[5]; "Muscovy then did not give it back"[3] - and in 1686 it legalized what it had withheld, "paying for Kyiv once more" (see the "Eternal Peace" campaign). The "territory for money" scheme was laid down in the same document: article 34 records Tsar Aleksei's consent to grant "a worthy treasury for the satisfaction of the szlachta exiles… from the part of Ukraine ceded to His Tsarist Majesty's side"[5] - with the sum deferred to future embassies. T0008 Deprivation of Agency January 1667 C0005.T0008 → C0005 Truce of Andrusovo (1667) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0009 Diplomacy In the legal partition of Ukrainian lands, the opinion of the people themselves or of their leaders was demonstratively ignored. The Hetmanate was treated exclusively as an object: "The interests of the hetmans and of Ukraine were, of course, not taken into account"[4]. T0030 Administrative-Territorial Division January 1667 C0005.T0030 → C0005 Truce of Andrusovo (1667) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0008 Government The legal codification of the territory's division. Moscow deliberately fragmented a once unified country, turning such important regions as Zaporizhzhia into rightless buffer zones under joint administration: "...Zaporizhzhia (which under the treaty of 1667 was under the joint rule of Moscow and Warsaw)"[2]. T0056 Taxation January 1667 C0005.T0056 → C0005 Truce of Andrusovo (1667) G0008 Tsardom of Muscovy S0008 Government Having gained political power over the Left Bank, Moscow immediately attempted to seize the right to collect taxes in order to extract resources directly: "the attempts of Russian voivodes... to introduce their own taxation system in Ukraine led only to revolts (for example... the attempted census of 1666...)"[2]. title: Forcible Mobilization of the Nokhchi for the Russo-Turkish War (1677–1679), campaign C1123
content: Forcible Mobilization of the Nokhchi for the Russo-Turkish War (1677–1679) The occupation administration of the Tsardom of Muscovy made mass use of the subordinated Nokhchi (the Okochans) as a military resource in conflicts with the Ottoman Empire on distant fronts. In 1678, the Kabardian prince Kaspulat Mutsalovich Cherkassky received a tsarist charter in which the historian I. Kh. Tkhamokova records a reward «for his «many services», for having taken part in the Crimean and Chyhyryn campaigns»[1]. The registers of archival documents for 1678 record a dispatch from the Chuhuiv voivode Ivan Rykhtarov to the Razriad Prikaz «on the march of the regiment of Prince Kaspulat Mutsalovich Cherkassky to Chuhuiv»[2]. The exploitation of military potential continued the following year as well: in 1679, Tsar Fedor Alekseevich issued a decree to the Ambassadorial Prikaz on sending Prince Kaspulat Mutsalovich Cherkassky a charter «on his regiment's performance of guard duty in the vicinity of Chuhuiv and Kharkiv»[2], while a dispatch from Kaspulat Cherkassky himself to the Ambassadorial Prikaz for the same year states «on the arrival of his regiment at Valuyki»[2]. title: Military Liquidation of the Zaporozhian Sich (1775), campaign C0033
content: Military Liquidation of the Zaporozhian Sich (1775) The military encirclement and destruction of the Zaporozhian Sich immediately after a joint war. Catherine II's manifesto of 3 August 1775 (PSZRI, coll. 1, vol. XX, no. 14,354) declared: "the Zaporozhian Sich has been utterly destroyed, with the extirpation for the future of the very name of the Zaporozhian Cossacks"[1][2]. The last kish otaman, Kalnyshevsky, "was arrested and sent to the prison of the Solovetsky monastery"[3], where he spent more than 25 years. Hrushevsky describes the mechanics of the treachery: the government "went about the affair slowly, in secret, to catch the Zaporozhians entirely unprepared," and general Tekeli "entered the Zaporozhian lands as a good friend" - then suddenly laid siege to the Sich. The Zaporozhians were even faulted for their own husbandry: they "were establishing their own tillage and thereby severing their dependence on the Russian state"[4]. The manifesto records the operation matter-of-factly: "On June 4, Our Lieutenant-General Tekeli, with the troops entrusted to him by us, occupied the Zaporozhian Sich"[1]. Hrushevsky: "The Sich was destroyed, and on 3 August a tsarist decree announced its abolition, 'with the annihilation of the very name of the Zaporozhian Cossacks'"[4]. title: Economic Exploitation and Creation of Dependency of the Nokhchi (1617–1622), campaign C1115
content: Economic Exploitation and Creation of Dependency of the Nokhchi (1617–1622) The occupation administration of the Tsardom of Muscovy in the town of Terki used the subordinated Nokhchi (Okochans) to carry out state tasks while artificially keeping them in a state of economic dependency. In their petition to Tsar Mikhail Fedorovich, the Okochan murza Kokhostrov Biytemirov and the serving Okochans of the town of Terki reported constant coercion into military action: «against your sovereign's disobedient ones we fight, we, your sovereign's kholops, not sparing our heads; for you, sovereign, we shed our blood and lay down our heads»[1]. At the same time, the metropole deliberately withheld basic subsistence resources from the Indigenous population for five years. A memorandum from the Ambassadorial Prikaz to the Prikaz of the Kazan Palace records: «the sovereign's grain allowance for the past years — for the 125th, and the 126th, and the 127th, and the 128th, and the 129th year — was not given to them»[1]. The result was the exhaustion of the population: Biytemirov reported that they «have been left without grain, have utterly perished from hunger and every hardship and have fallen, sovereign, into great debt, and we are dying a death of starvation together with our wives and children»[1]. To resolve the crisis, the leader of the Nokhchi set out for Moscow, but perished while returning to the Caucasus. A memorandum from the Ambassadorial Prikaz states that «Kokhostrov-murza together with his man drowned in the Oka River»[1], while representatives of the metropole resolved to confiscate the property of the deceased: «his clothing and all his belongings were taken into our treasury»[1]. The delegate's death was used to further curtail the rights of the Nokhchi. In a petition submitted to Tsar Mikhail Fedorovich, the Okochan murza Chepan Kokhostrov indicated that in the incident «the sovereign's charter of grant was lost together with him»[1], as a result of which the occupation administration artificially lowered the status of his family in order to impose obligations upon it: an official extract of the Ambassadorial Prikaz records that the heirs were «made equal in everything with the Okochans, with the plowing people, and carts and wagons are taken from them», whereas previously from them «no taxes whatsoever had been taken»[1]. title: Beginning of the political subjugation of the Nokhchi (1588–1591), campaign C1112
content: Beginning of the political subjugation of the Nokhchi (1588–1591) The occupation administration of the Tsardom of Muscovy imposed vassalage on the Nokhchi elite under the guise of a military alliance through the procedure of oath-taking (shert). As historian Murat Yasar notes, to the Nokhchi this looked like a military pact: "many local rulers in Muscovy's southern and eastern borderlands, especially in the North Caucasus, regarded the shert more as a military alliance between themselves and one of their potential allies"[1]. The administration, however, unilaterally interpreted this act as unconditional submission: historian Michael Khodarkovsky points out that "in Moscow's eyes the shert now meant an oath of allegiance by the tsar's new and loyal subjects"[2]. Historian Murat Yasar adds that consent was incentivized through bribery: "the signing of the shert went hand in hand with the monetary allowances and gifts that the tsar gave to the local rulers"[1]. To maintain control, the forcible seizure of relatives of Nokhchi leaders was employed: E. N. Kusheva, compiler of a collection of documents, writes that "his nephew Batai was left as a hostage (amanat) in the Terek town"[3]. The subordinated Nokhchi communities were obligated to take part in the military operations of the occupation administration: E. N. Kusheva, compiler of a collection of documents, points to documents "on the possibility of the participation of Murza Shikh... in a campaign of Russian fighting men"[3]. title: Administrative Dismantling and Enserfment of the Left Bank (1781–1786), campaign C0034
content: Administrative Dismantling and Enserfment of the Left Bank (1781–1786) The execution of Catherine II's secret instructions for the institutional and cultural assimilation of the land: the liquidation of the regimental order and the introduction of imperial viceroyalties – the Kyiv Viceroyalty was established by the nominal decree to the Senate of September 16, 1781 (PSZRI, coll. 1, vol. XXI, no. 15,228; execution ordered from November)[1][2], "which finally abolished the remnants of the Hetmanate's autonomy and its regimental-sotnia administrative-political and military order"[3]; the secularization of monastery lands in 1786 and the legal binding of peasants by Catherine II's decree of May 3, 1783: "each of the villagers is to remain in the place and station where he is registered by the current last revision"[4]. title: Suppression of the November Uprising (1830–1831), campaign C0057
content: Suppression of the November Uprising (1830–1831) The Russian Empire's regular army suppresses a national liberation uprising: the insurgent detachments in Volhynia, the Zhytomyr region, Podillia, and the Kyiv region "were routed by the tsarist troops in April–May 1831," after which "the tsarist government resorted to brutal repressions against the participants of the uprising"[1]. The era of tightening the screws on the Right Bank begins. title: Land plunder: the colonial repartition of land, land hunger and Cossack colonization of the Terek oblast (1860-1917), campaign C1171
content: Land plunder: the colonial repartition of land, land hunger and Cossack colonization of the Terek oblast (1860-1917) In 1860-1917 the empire recut the land of Chechnya in favor of the treasury, the Cossack host and loyal notables. The conquest came with a written promise. In January 1859, advancing on Vedeno, the command circulated among the Chechens, in Arabic and Russian, a "Proclamation to the Chechen People": "I declare to you in the name of the Sovereign Emperor, 1) that the Russian government grants you complete freedom to practice forever the faith of your fathers; 2) that you will never be called up as soldiers and will not be turned into Cossacks... 5) that the rights of each of you to the property belonging to you will be inviolable. Your lands, which you own or with which you have been allotted by the Russian authorities, will be confirmed to you by deeds and plans in inalienable possession..."; the document was signed by Baryatinsky, commander-in-chief of the Caucasus Army and viceroy[1]. The land clause of the promise, as historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov render it, ran: "All the lands and forests on the plain where the Chechen people lived before the disturbance of 1839 will be given over to you for eternal use, excepting those occupied by fortifications... but neither Cossack stanitsas nor Chechen auls are to be settled on them"[2]. Historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova writes: "The Chechens treasured and kept this proclamation as the apple of their eye and always appealed to it"[3]. It came out the other way round: historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov draw the balance for lowland and piedmont Chechnya - "100% of the forests (259 thousand desiatinas) and 300 thousand desiatinas out of the 643 thousand desiatinas of the country's agricultural zone were taken away in favor of the treasury, the army and the Cossack host. All this cannot but be considered typical colonial plunder" (a desiatina is a little over a hectare)[2]. The outcome for the people was named from the Duma tribune by deputy Maslov: "You cannot imagine how negligible the landholdings of the Chechens are, especially in the mountains – one tenth, one fifth, a quarter, a third of a desiatina…"[3]. ID: C1171 Start: January 1860 End: March 1917 Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.2 Created: 4 August 2026 Last Modified: 18 September 2026 Discuss on Telegram Actors ID Name Procedures G0009 Russian Empire 7 Instruments Applied ID Name Procedures S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations 7 Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: T0052 Expropriation of Resources January 1860 C1171.T0052 → C1171 Land plunder: the colonial repartition of land, land hunger and Cossack colonization of the Terek oblast (1860-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations According to the summary by historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov, of the 643 thousand desiatinas (a desiatina is a little over a hectare) of lowland and piedmont Chechnya, Chechen villages were left 347 thousand, Cossack stanitsas were handed 222 thousand - a third, officers as private owners got 28 thousand, fortifications 17 thousand, and the treasury about 30 thousand desiatinas of "reserve" land[2]. The same partition was described by the office itself: the Terek land-survey administration, counting only the lowland part of Greater and Lesser Chechnya (a narrower scope than the lowland and piedmont Chechnya of the historians' summary), summed up: "The entire lowland part of Greater and Lesser Chechnya, with the adjoining Lesser-Chechen forest, comprises an area of 271086 desiatinas. Of it, at various times, 650 desiatinas went to 6 Cossack stanitsas, 1560 desiatinas of forest to the Terek Cossack Host, 8645 desiatinas were granted into private ownership for the services of individual persons, 8266 desiatinas were given to towns and settlements, 234970 desiatinas were allotted to 43 Chechen auls, and 16965 desiatinas were held by the forestry department. Thus, there is no free land left…"[3]. The forests were confiscated wholesale: "in Chechnya and Ingushetia tsarism appropriated forests with a total area of 225.5 thousand desiatinas (they became 'state' forests) and handed another 33.5 thousand desiatinas along the Sunzha and its tributaries to the Cossack host. The forests were placed under armed guard, and the unfortunate peasants caught felling wood were pursued with heavy penalties"[2]. From the mountain auls, according to historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova, "50989 desiatinas of pasture were confiscated to the treasury", and the same pastures were then handed back to the communities "on terms of quitrent use"[3]. What people had cleared with their own hands was taken too: in 1874 in the Vedeno okrug the owners of 250 desiatinas of plots cleared from under forest were told to swear on the Quran that the clearing had been done with the permission of the communities - "in the whole okrug only Sh. Dolatmurzayev, a resident of the village of Belgatoy, was able to swear... all the other plots, whose owners to their honor did not risk giving a false oath, were declared communal"[2]; after the uprising of 1877 the residents of Dyshni-Vedeno had 74 certificates for cleared plots taken away "as punishment, for support of the insurgents"[3]. In 1888 the Chechen communities petitioned the emperor: building materials and firewood they were "forced to buy from private owners or from the treasury, whereas formerly they had used them free of charge"[3]. In 1891 the Vladikavkaz Railway Company received a concession for a branch line from Beslan station through Grozny to Petrovsk[4]. On 15 June 1891 Alexander III, by a personal decree to the Minister of Ways of Communication, ordered the expropriation of land for the route: "Having authorized the construction of the Petrovsk railway, in place of its previously indicated direction from Vladikavkaz to Petrovsk, along the direction from Beslan station... to Petrovsk, we command: 1) that the proper arrangements be made for the expropriation... of the lands necessary for this purpose"[5]. The trackbed, the station and the entire railway infrastructure landed on lands that by then were registered to the Terek Cossack Host and the Groznenskaya stanitsa - the very lowland land that had been taken from Chechen auls and handed to the host: historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that "the railway trackbed (and, accordingly, the station and all the railway facilities) passed over lands belonging to the Terek Cossack Host", and "the Grozny city railway station was built on the land of the Groznenskaya stanitsa"[2]. The bargaining over the price went on between the railway, the town and the Cossacks: the town authorities demanded "60 rubles for every square sazhen of town land expropriated for the construction of the station, the locomotive depot with workshops, the goods station and the access tracks", while the Cossacks of the Groznenskaya stanitsa offered the builders their plot free of charge - counting on oil-refining and other enterprises rising around the station[2]. The money for the expropriation went to the holders of what had been seized; the Chechen communities had no part in that settlement. T0117.001 Migratory Replacement January 1860 C1171.T0117.001 → C1171 Land plunder: the colonial repartition of land, land hunger and Cossack colonization of the Terek oblast (1860-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations The Kakhanovskaya stanitsa "was founded in 1860 on the site of the village of Umakhan-Yurt in the bend of the lower Sunzha" and found itself almost encircled by 14 Chechen villages, which took in the evicted people of Umakhan-Yurt[3]. Six stanitsas of the Kizlyar otdel "were situated on the lands of the expelled Chechen population", and the Baryatinskaya stanitsa, planted right up against the large village of Stary Yurt, took away part of the Stary Yurt residents' lands[3]. In all, on the Sunzha Line, by the count of historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova, "the highlanders lost 262946 desiatinas of lowland land"[3]. T0032 Legal Segregation of the Population January 1860 C1171.T0032 → C1171 Land plunder: the colonial repartition of land, land hunger and Cossack colonization of the Terek oblast (1860-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations The allotment norm was written out by estate and origin: "Cossacks are allotted 30 desiatinas (a desiatina is a little over a hectare) per soul, while natives get no more than 2-5 desiatinas"[3]; the gap was also entrenched by the general rules of allotment: by the count of the newspaper Kazachy Vestnik for 1884, on which historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova relies, Russian residents of the Caucasus krai received "24–30 desiatinas of land allotment per soul, whereas natives got 12–18 desiatinas per dym, which on average numbered 5 men" (a dym is a hearth, a household)[3]. In 1886 in the Grozny okrug "an average Chechen family with many children... had 11 desiatinas of land, while the average Cossack family owned more than 92 desiatinas"[2]. By Order No. 418 of the viceroy of 1863, "the right to buy land plots from the local population was received by Russian officers and officials of the oblast administration"[3] - an ordinary Chechen could not be a buyer of that same category of land; the rules of 1 March 1902 instituted the buying-up of privately owned lands "for the needs of the Caucasus Cossack hosts, at the expense of their capital funds"[3]. T0141 Creation of Economic Hopelessness January 1860 C1171.T0141 → C1171 Land plunder: the colonial repartition of land, land hunger and Cossack colonization of the Terek oblast (1860-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov give a summary based on the materials of the Caucasus Military District (RGVIA, f. 1300, op. 7, d. 3) and the work of A. I. Khasbulatov: "According to the data of 1877, in Mountain Chechnya, including Ichkeria, with a population of almost 100 thousand people, there was on average 0.3 desiatinas (a desiatina is a little over a hectare) of arable land per capita... such fantastic landlessness as in Mountain Chechnya was known to no other region of the Russian Empire"[2]. In 1901 on the Chechen plain "a family (usually quite numerous) had from 7 to 14 desiatinas"[3]. The count by family budget was kept by the oblast statistics service itself: "A Cossack family had a gross income of 918 rubles from its land allotment... and was left with a surplus of 140 rubles. The richest Chechen family on the plain, according to the Terek Oblast Statistical Committee (1903), received an income of 262 rubles from its land allotment while spending 414 rubles on its upkeep; the deficit came to 152 rubles"[3]. T0038 Economic Control January 1860 C1171.T0038 → C1171 Land plunder: the colonial repartition of land, land hunger and Cossack colonization of the Terek oblast (1860-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations In 1895 the Cossacks leased out 420 thousand desiatinas (a desiatina is a little over a hectare) of "yurt" (stanitsa allotment) lands, the official rent for which came to over 140 thousand rubles a year; on top of that, "reserve" lands went out on lease - up to 65 thousand desiatinas annually[2]. By 1913 the stanitsas were leasing out 424 thousand desiatinas of host lands and collecting 806.5 thousand rubles in rent, and the main tenants were Chechens - up to 77 percent of peasant households[2]. Leasing became so widespread that the administration of the Terek oblast grew alarmed: historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that the authorities "seriously feared that, by renting the same plots for many years, the highlanders might in the end lay claim to them", and, besides, sought to attach to the oblast as many "out-of-town" peasants as possible, "and therefore at the end of the 19th century an ordinance came out forbidding Cossacks to lease their land directly to the highlanders"[2]. The use of land taken from the Chechens was made conditional on the authorities' permission, and that permission was revoked as soon as use threatened to turn into right. T0146 Administrative Corruption and Extortion January 1860 C1171.T0146 → C1171 Land plunder: the colonial repartition of land, land hunger and Cossack colonization of the Terek oblast (1860-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations The ban on leasing land directly to the highlanders, introduced at the end of the 19th century, produced middlemen: "The result of this decision was the appearance of a large number of intermediaries through whom the land still reached the highlanders, but at a higher price"[2]. Who profited from it is named by historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova: "Speculative leasing became widespread; it was practiced by officials of the government and administration and by officers, who rented large areas at 10-15 kopecks per desiatina and sublet them to the highland population at a price several times the original"[3]. The difference in price was pocketed by officials and officers of the very administration that had taken the land away. T0015 Bribery of Elites January 1860 C1171.T0015 → C1171 Land plunder: the colonial repartition of land, land hunger and Cossack colonization of the Terek oblast (1860-1917) G0009 Russian Empire S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations By the viceroy's authorization of 6 April 1867, writes historian Z. Kh. Ibragimova, "8674 desiatinas were given out into private ownership, for services, to influential local people of Chechnya" (a desiatina is a little over a hectare); 57 Chechens received it, and Ibragimova names the viceroy in the Caucasus, Baryatinsky, as the initiator of the handouts[3]; the largest allotments went to the Chechen ruling families - the Taymazovs (6550 desiatinas), the Bekovich-Cherkasskys (over 6350), the Turlovs, the Eldarovs; land was also handed out to Russian officers - "Colonel Ippolitov received more than 1 thousand desiatinas of land in the Argun okrug"[2]. The hierarchy of the handouts followed estate lines: to the largest highland owners - "from 1 to 5 thousand desiatinas, depending 'on the degree of significance and the services rendered by each to the government'", to persons of the second category (the highland notability, the first being Russian nobles) - up to 1 thousand[3]. Land also paid the lower administration: "village elders received five shares each of arable and hay lands"[2], aul secretaries - up to 75 desiatinas[6]. References Хожаев Д. А. title: Black Hundred Terror and Pogroms (1905–1907), campaign C0068
content: Black Hundred Terror and Pogroms (1905–1907) The imperial authorities sponsor and cover for radical Russian nationalist organizations for the suppression of the revolution and for terror. The "Union of the Russian People" was "a Black-Hundred organization… The organization received financial support from the state and was patronized by Russian emperor Nicholas II… Mass Jewish pogroms provoked by the 'Union' took place, particularly in Ukraine, in the 'Pale of Settlement'"[1]; of its 400 thousand members, nearly half were in Ukrainian cities[1]. In Odesa, "Low-ranking policemen and soldiers failed to interfere with the pogromists and in many instances participated in the looting and killing"[3], and the commander of the district's troops told policemen: "all of us sympathize in our souls with the pogrom"[3]. T0022 Terror January 1905 C0068.T0022 → C0068 Black Hundred Terror and Pogroms (1905–1907) G0009 Russian Empire S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The intimidation of the population and suppression of the liberation movement by radical monarchist organizations whose program rested on the principles of "the unity and indivisibility of the Russian Empire, the preservation of autocracy… great-power chauvinism, antisemitism, militant Orthodoxy"[1]. The outcome was "the mass Jewish pogroms provoked by the 'Union,' particularly in Ukraine, in the 'Pale of Settlement'"[1]. References Інститут історії України НАН України. title: Sovietization of Chechnya: revkoms in place of Soviets, punitive operations and Cheka executions (1920-1924), campaign C1176
content: Sovietization of Chechnya: revkoms in place of Soviets, punitive operations and Cheka executions (1920-1924) In 1920-1924 Soviet Russia imposed its control over Chechnya: it installed unelected revolutionary committees (revkoms) in place of elected Soviets, conducted military disarmament operations with the use of aviation, shot people without trial by the hands of the Cheka and took hostages. Seven years earlier Chechnya had gone through the First World War, the two revolutions of 1917 and an attempt to live in a state of its own - the Mountain Republic, proclaimed in May 1918. In 1919 Chechnya was held by the Volunteer Army of General Denikin - troops of former imperial officers who fought the Bolsheviks for the return of Russia within its former borders; its terror left behind 21 destroyed auls and 15 thousand dead (campaign C1174). By the spring of 1920 the Denikinites had rolled back from the North Caucasus, and the emirate of Sheikh Uzun-Haji, which had fought against them, fell apart on its own: the emir died, "The emirate went into the grave with him, without any political consequences for Chechnya and Dagestan"[1]. Power in the land was taken by the Bolsheviks, whom the Chechen villages had until then supported against Denikin. An order of the staff of the North Caucasus Military District prescribed: "The disarmament must begin with lowland Chechnya, so as to secure the Grozny area. The operation must be conducted in real earnest, up to the destruction of the unsubmissive auls"[1]. Commissar of the Caucasus Labor Army Vrachev complained about his own punitive apparatus: the army's special department was carrying out mass shootings of which "... almost nothing is known not only to the Revolutionary Tribunal or the Political Department of the army, but to me or the army commander either"[1]. ID: C1176 Start: April 1920 End: December 1924 Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.3 Created: 8 August 2026 Last Modified: 5 September 2026 Discuss on Telegram Actors ID Name Procedures G0013 Soviet Russia (RSFSR) 7 G0010 USSR 1 Instruments Applied ID Name Procedures S0017 Secret Police and Security Services 4 S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations 2 S0010 Regular Army 2 Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: T0036 Installation of a New System of Governance April 1920 C1176.T0036 → C1176 Sovietization of Chechnya: revkoms in place of Soviets, punitive operations and Cheka executions (1920-1924) G0013 Soviet Russia (RSFSR) S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations Soviet Russia placed an unelected extraordinary body over Chechnya: on 3 April 1920 a congress in Grozny "proclaimed the transfer of all power to the Chechen Revolutionary Committee of five members"[1]. When at the elections to the Soviets in July 1920 "the overwhelming majority of seats in the Soviets went to... representatives of the so-called 'kulak-mullah and nationalist elements'", the elected Soviets were dissolved - historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov record: "within a short span the peasant Soviets were dissolved twice (in August 1921 and in July 1922) and the power of the revkom was restored again"[1]. In the autumn of 1920 "the Aldy congress was dispersed, and several Grozny party workers... arrested" on the orders of Ordzhonikidze, head of the Caucasus Bureau of the Communist Party's Central Committee[1]. The Mountain ASSR, which had given legal form to the highlanders' autonomy, "did not last long and in 1924, having fulfilled its tasks as conceived by the party leadership, ceased to exist"[1]. T0155 Forced Disarmament April 1920 C1176.T0155 → C1176 Sovietization of Chechnya: revkoms in place of Soviets, punitive operations and Cheka executions (1920-1924) G0013 Soviet Russia (RSFSR) S0010 Regular Army Soviet Russia disarmed Chechen villages by military operations through all five years of the campaign. Historian E. F. Zhupikova writes: the Caucasus Labor Army "conducted" disarmament operations "...in 1920; in March-August 1921 the Chechen auls of Gordali, Tsentoroy, Belgatoy, Dargo, Benoy, Vedeno, Groznensky and Shali, which had taken part in the mutiny of N. Gotsinsky, were disarmed"[2]. In May 1922 the troops sent into Chechnya were headed by Gikalo - secretary of the Mountain oblast committee (obkom) of the party[3], who in the war with Denikin had commanded insurgent detachments in the mountains of Chechnya[2]: "The villages of Makhkety, Goity and Katyr-Yurt were subjected to disarmament, with combat aviation used against the latter. Besides the seizure of a significant quantity of weapons, up to 30 'bandits' were captured and shot, and their property was confiscated by the authorities"[1]. The year 1924 "ended in the Chechen Autonomous Oblast with a large military operation to seize weapons, in the course of which almost 3 thousand rifles and about 400 revolvers and pistols were collected"[1]. T0022 Terror April 1920 C1176.T0022 → C1176 Sovietization of Chechnya: revkoms in place of Soviets, punitive operations and Cheka executions (1920-1924) G0013 Soviet Russia (RSFSR) S0017 Secret Police and Security Services Soviet Russia carried out executions for show: "During the Chechen congress in Grozny, by verdict of the local Cheka, 7 Chechens were demonstratively shot. The execution made such '...a devastating impression on the masses of Chechens who had not yet had time to disperse after the congress' that the command of the Caucasus Labor Army demanded that henceforth death sentences on Chechens be carried out as far away from Chechnya as possible"[1]. T0021 Neutralization of the Opposition April 1920 C1176.T0021 → C1176 Sovietization of Chechnya: revkoms in place of Soviets, punitive operations and Cheka executions (1920-1924) G0013 Soviet Russia (RSFSR) S0017 Secret Police and Security Services Over Sheikh Ali Mitaev, a member of the Chechen revkom, the GPU set "thorough surveillance", and in the spring of 1924 it "took the decision 'on the removal' of A. Mitaev from Chechnya. The official agreements with him were treacherously broken; he was suddenly arrested, taken to Rostov-on-Don and, after a brief investigation, shot"[1]; historian E. F. Zhupikova dates the arrest to 19 April 1924 and cites the GPU's formula of accusation - "for his connection with counter-revolutionary organizations"[2]. The historians call the character of the reprisal and its perpetrators by their proper names: "The murder of A. Mitaev by the Chekists," write Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov[1]. T0099 Hostage-Taking April 1920 C1176.T0099 → C1176 Sovietization of Chechnya: revkoms in place of Soviets, punitive operations and Cheka executions (1920-1924) G0013 Soviet Russia (RSFSR) S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations In 1923-1924 the Chechen revkom made hostage-taking an official practice of the fight against "banditry": "Measures were taken to register all criminals present in Chechnya, and the practice was introduced of taking hostages from among the close relatives of bandits in hiding"[1]. T0164 Pillage April 1920 C1176.T0164 → C1176 Sovietization of Chechnya: revkoms in place of Soviets, punitive operations and Cheka executions (1920-1924) G0013 Soviet Russia (RSFSR) S0010 Regular Army In 1920 the Red Army looted the Chechen villages where it was stationed: the units quartered in Chechnya, historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write, "received almost no property or food allowance", which pushed them into "self-supply" - "...the Red Army not only ran riot, but took away grain, cattle and so forth, terrorizing the population with senseless killings"[1]. In the summer of 1920, in Tsentoroy, the Chechens routed a unit of the Caucasus Labor Army "engaged in outright plunder"[1]. The property of the killed was taken too: during the disarmament of May 1922 "up to 30 'bandits' were captured and shot, and their property was confiscated by the authorities"[1]. T0160 Sham Trials April 1920 C1176.T0160 → C1176 Sovietization of Chechnya: revkoms in place of Soviets, punitive operations and Cheka executions (1920-1924) G0010 USSR S0017 Secret Police and Security Services On 9 May 1924 the Soviet Union, by a secret resolution of the Presidium of the Central Executive Committee (TsIK), gave the OGPU "the right of extrajudicial reprisal against bandits and their accomplices, namely: expulsion from the given locality, confinement in a concentration camp for a term of up to 3 years, and the application of the supreme measure of punishment - shooting", and prescribed that the republics declare localities "unfavorable in respect of banditry", where the GPU organs "are entitled to decide at their own discretion any case of banditry"[4]. The Chechen authorities already in that same May telegraphed the center: "Sanction the creation of a tribunal or a political troika"[5]. The troikas that went to work, "composed of an official of the procuracy, the GPU and the first party leader, — as a rule, passed sentences in absentia — on the basis of the submitted documents, often without even questioning the accused. Of any participation of a defense in the proceedings there could be no talk"[1]. T0162.003 Killing of Prisoners and Detainees April 1920 C1176.T0162.003 → C1176 Sovietization of Chechnya: revkoms in place of Soviets, punitive operations and Cheka executions (1920-1924) G0013 Soviet Russia (RSFSR) S0017 Secret Police and Security Services The special department of the Caucasus Labor Army carried out mass shootings uncontrolled even by its own command: army commissar Vrachev complained that of them "...almost nothing is known not only to the Revolutionary Tribunal or the Political Department of the army, but to me or the army commander either"[1]. During the disarmament of May 1922 people were first captured and then shot: "up to 30 'bandits' were captured and shot, and their property was confiscated by the authorities"[1]. References Ахмадов Я. З., Хасмагомадов Э. Х. История Чечни в XIX-XX веках. 2005. Жупикова Е. Ф. Повстанческое движение на Северном Кавказе в 1920-1925 годах. 2013. title: Destruction of Ukrainian Societies and Segregation (1906–1910), campaign C0050
content: Destruction of Ukrainian Societies and Segregation (1906–1910) A campaign to suppress the legal civic activity of the indigenous people: in the Poltava and Kharkiv regions the "Prosvita" societies were banned from their very founding, and in 1908–1910, under Stolypin, virtually all "Prosvitas" were closed, except the branches of the Katerynoslav governorate[1]. Justifying the crackdown, Stolypin declared in an address to the Senate that the revival of Ukrainian cultural life was undesirable, for "the three principal branches of Eastern Slavdom, both by origin and by language, cannot but constitute one whole"[1]. Stolypin's circular of 1910 classed Ukrainians among the "aliens" and prescribed "to refuse without fail the registration" of their societies[2]. The crackdown received its doctrinal grounding: Stolypin declared in an address to the Senate that the revival of Ukrainian cultural life was undesirable, for "the three principal branches of Eastern Slavdom, both by origin and by language, cannot but constitute one whole"[1].Stolypin's circular to the governors (20 January 1910) — a complete ban on self-organization: "when considering petitions for the registration of any alien societies whatsoever… one must… refuse without fail the registration of their charters"[2]. T0032 Legal Segregation of the Population January 1906 C0050.T0032 → C0050 Destruction of Ukrainian Societies and Segregation (1906–1910) G0009 Russian Empire S0008 Government The official classing of the indigenous population as aliens: Stolypin prescribed to the governors to refuse the registration of "any alien societies whatsoever, including Ukrainian and Jewish ones, regardless of the aims they pursue"[2]. References Шевельов Ю. В. Українська мова в першій половині двадцятого століття (1900-1941). Стан і статус. 1987. Столыпин П. А. Столыпинский циркуляр. 1910. – циркуляр министра внутренних дел П. А. title: "Only Pardoned": Alien Rule and the Suppression of Chechen and Ingush National Life (1965-1989), campaign C1182
content: "Only Pardoned": Alien Rule and the Suppression of Chechen and Ingush National Life (1965-1989) In 1965-1989 the Chechens and the Ingush, whom the coloniser had merged into a single region (the Chechen-Ingush ASSR), were ruled by Russian officials sent from Moscow. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "in the early 1970s, of the 60 ministries and agencies of the Council of Ministers of the ChIASSR only 17 were headed by Chechens or Ingush. In most rural districts the first secretaries of the district committees were Russians"[1]. In 1972 Chechen and Ingush communists wrote to Moscow about this twice. From 16 to 19 January 1973 several thousand Ingush (participants speak of 15 thousand), joined by Chechens, rallied on the central square of Grozny in front of the building of the region's occupation administration and demanded the return of the Prigorodny district, handed to North Ossetia during the deportation of 1944, or the lifting of the ban on settling there. On the night of 19 January soldiers of the internal troops (predecessors of today's Rosgvardiya) with truncheons and firemen spraying icy water from hoses dispersed those who remained on the square, drove them out of the city and dropped them off in the frost[2]. Then the coloniser went after those who had complained: on 13 March 1973 Moscow adopted a resolution "On Anti-Social Nationalist Manifestations in the City of Grozny", the authors of the letters were expelled from the only permitted party, the organisers of the rally were put on trial[2], and in December KGB chairman Andropov (the KGB being the predecessor of today's FSB) reported on "measures" against "about 400 Ingush"[3]. In those same years the coloniser worked to leave the Chechens and the Ingush without a history, a faith, a language or a livelihood of their own. The USSR rewrote history, imposing its own concept, "the 200th anniversary of the voluntary entry of Chechen-Ingushetia into Russia", and persecuted the Chechen historians who disputed it through decisions of the region's occupation administration[4]. In a quarter of a century the occupier did not allow the highlanders to open a single mosque[5]. The schools to which Chechen and Ingush children returned worked only in Russian from the first grade: the law of the RSFSR of 16 April 1959 declared that "instruction at school is conducted in the pupils' native language" and left the choice of language to parents, but after the return from exile the coloniser opened no schools with Chechen as the language of instruction, so there was nothing to choose from[6]. The factories and oil enterprises of Grozny hired newcomers rather than Chechens: by the end of the 1980s only 16 % of oil-refining workers were Chechens or Ingush, according to official statistics of 1979 up to 28 % of the able-bodied lived off their household plots, and according to the census of 1989 almost a quarter of the people lived outside the republic[1]. The coloniser said aloud what it thought of the people after the dispersal. A. Martazanova, a participant in the events of 1973, recalls: at a meeting of the region's occupation administration on 27 March one of its leaders, Bokov, "said that the Ingush and the Chechens had not yet been rehabilitated, that they had only been pardoned in advance, in the hope of good behaviour", while Rustem Goygov, head of a department in the same administration, who began: "But what about the decisions of the 20th Congress of the CPSU [the congress of 1956 that condemned the deportations of peoples], which…", was not allowed to finish and a month later was removed from his post; the phrase had first been uttered by Solomentsev, head of the government of the RSFSR, who had come to Grozny[2]. Eyewitness Aza Bazorkina recalls that a few days after the dispersal the newspaper Grozny Worker printed, over the signatures of intimidated Ingush, an article "To Serve One's People Honestly", which "says that the Ingush people have not been rehabilitated (as if there had been no 20th Party Congress!) but pardoned"[7]. ID: C1182 Start: January 1965 End: July 1989 Contributors: decolonial.ist project Version: 1.0 Created: 6 September 2026 Last Modified: 6 September 2026 Discuss on Telegram Actors ID Name Procedures G0010 USSR 8 Instruments Applied ID Name Procedures S0008 Government 6 S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations 2 Procedures Carried Out Text search (name, technique or description): Filter by peoples: Date range (by start): — Sort by date: T0151 Imposition of Alien Governance January 1965 C1182.T0151 → C1182 "Only Pardoned": Alien Rule and the Suppression of Chechen and Ingush National Life (1965-1989) G0010 USSR S0008 Government After the return of the Chechens and the Ingush from exile the USSR did not let the indigenous inhabitants hold key leading posts in government and industry, reserving them for Russian settlers. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "The leading posts (first secretary of the obkom of the CPSU [head of the region's occupation administration], minister of the MVD, republican prosecutor, head of the KGB [predecessor of today's FSB], minister of finance, secretary of the Grozny gorkom of the CPSU [head of the city] and chairman of the Grozny gorispolkom [head of the city administration], head of Grozneft, military commissar of the republic and some others) are reserved for Russian officials"; for the Chechens and the Ingush, 70 % of the population, "roughly 30% of posts were reserved"[1]. According to the letter of 26 communists of 1972, which the historians quote, "in the early 1970s, of the 60 ministries and agencies of the Council of Ministers of the ChIASSR [the Chechen-Ingush republic] only 17 were headed by Chechens or Ingush. In most rural districts the first secretaries of the raikoms [heads of districts] were Russians"[1]. The historians write: "That is precisely why the CC of the CPSU [the central authority in Moscow] keeps sending new first secretaries of the obkom [heads of the region] to Chechen-Ingushetia" - in 1966-1989 these were Apryatkin, Vlasov and Foteev, sent in from other regions[1]. When the Ingush at the rally of January 1973 demanded that locals be appointed to leading posts, Bokov, a leader in the region's occupation administration, replied at a meeting of party functionaries on 21 January: "In their speeches they went so far as to say that a measure should be carried out here to take account of leading cadres from among the Chechens and the Ingush, that is, to carry out indigenisation"[2]. Historian A. B. Kuznetsova writes, citing the witness B. Kh. Toriev: "Chechens and Ingush were subjected to harsh discrimination in admission to the CPSU - they were admitted only from among the workers, so that those who held engineering positions were forced to go and work at a factory as labourers in order to be able to join the party"[8]. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that only by the mid-1980s did Chechens and Ingush head 155 of the 194 village soviets and 11 of the 19 city and district soviets, while "the most significant posts at the middle and republican level, as well as the leadership of Grozny and of the regional committee of the CPSU, remained with the Russian nomenklatura"[1]. The historians write that on 1 July 1989 the region's occupation administration at its meeting "for the first time in the entire history of the Chechen-Ingush party organisation rejected the candidate proposed by the CC of the CPSU (N. I. Semenov) and elected Doku Zavgaev first secretary"[1]. T0021 Neutralization of the Opposition January 1965 C1182.T0021 → C1182 "Only Pardoned": Alien Rule and the Suppression of Chechen and Ingush National Life (1965-1989) G0010 USSR S0008 Government In 1972-1981 the Chechens and the Ingush twice wrote to Moscow about discrimination and protested on the square; each time the coloniser expelled from the only permitted party and put on trial the protesters, not the region's occupation leadership. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that in March 1972 26 Chechen and Ingush communists "wrote a collective letter addressed to the CC of the CPSU [the central authority in Moscow], in which they directly accused the party leadership of Chechen-Ingushetia not only of chauvinism but also of corruption. The result of the appeal, however, was not what the authors of the collective letter had counted on: it was not the leaders of the republic who were punished, but they themselves"; S. Bokaev, S. Pliev, N. Umarkhadzhaev, B. Kostoev and B. Lyanov were expelled from the party[1]. On 16 January 1973 the Ingush gathered on the central square of Grozny, in front of the building of the region's occupation administration, and Chechens joined them; rally participant Salman Mamatiev recalls: "on the second day there were almost as many Chechens on the square as Ingush"[2]. Eyewitness Aza Bazorkina recalls: "From a makeshift rostrum on Lenin Square, on 16, 17 and 18 January, day and night, the grievance of dispossessed, deceived people pours out", and on the night of 19 January the militia and the internal troops (predecessors of today's Rosgvardiya) cleared the square: "The doubting young people, who did not want to disperse without reliable information, were beaten with rubber truncheons and doused with icy water from fire hoses, herded into buses, driven out of the city and let out there, soaking wet, into a twenty-degree frost in an open field"[7]. On 13 March 1973 Moscow adopted a resolution "On Anti-Social Nationalist Manifestations in the City of Grozny"; on 27 March the region's occupation administration resolved to accept it "for unswerving guidance and execution" and recorded: "For nationalist actions and active participation in anti-social manifestations the following have been expelled from the party: Pliev S. Kh., Gazdiev A. M., as well as Kushtov A. S. - physician at city hospital No. 2, Abadiev B. - director of the puppet theatre, Uzhakhova - teacher at boarding school No. 15, Egiev - former chairman of the construction committee of SMU-7 [trade-union committee of a construction directorate], Daurbekov - former head of department at the Nazran district newspaper"[2]. Historian A. B. Kuznetsova gives the tally: "23 people were expelled from the CPSU, 18 from the VLKSM [the Komsomol, the youth organisation of Soviet power], 9 people were removed from leading positions and 14 people were prosecuted"[8]. On 27 December 1973 KGB chairman Andropov (the KGB being the predecessor of today's FSB) reported to Moscow: "After the well-known events that took place in the city of Grozny in January 1973, in which about 400 Ingush from the Prigorodny district of the North Ossetian ASSR took an active part, as a result of measures taken by the state security organs new attempts to carry out socially dangerous acts, especially in February 1973 on the anniversary of the eviction of the Ingush and also on the eve of the holidays of 1 and 9 May, were prevented"[3]. In June 1981 23 communists wrote to Brezhnev about the corruption of Vlasov, head of the region's occupation administration; historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "The CC of the CPSU this time too backed the republican leadership, accusing the authors of the letter of nationalism (although among its signatories were people of various nationalities, including Russians and Ukrainians). Two people were expelled from the party"[1]. T0004 Rewriting of History January 1965 C1182.T0004 → C1182 "Only Pardoned": Alien Rule and the Suppression of Chechen and Ingush National Life (1965-1989) G0010 USSR S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations From 1973 the coloniser justified the deportation and did not let the Chechens speak of it or of the military seizure of the region, and from 1979 it imposed a "concept" of "the 200th anniversary of the voluntary entry of Chechen-Ingushetia into Russia" and persecuted the historians who disputed it. At a meeting of the region's occupation administration on 27 March 1973 one of its leaders, Bokov, justified the eviction of 1944: "All this, in our view, forced the government to take this extreme measure in order to put an end to the anti-Soviet actions of the political bandit groups [the authorities' name for armed opponents], which found shelter among a significant part of the Chechen-Ingush population", and the minutes of the same meeting named the bearers of "nationalist" ideas one by one: "the writer Khalid Oshaev, expelled from the party, the former deputy director of a plant Kostoev B., the university lecturer and candidate of sciences Vagapov Ya."[2]. Historian A. B. Kuznetsova writes that at the discussion of the two-volume "Essays on the History of the Chechen-Ingush ASSR" in 1973 the speakers criticised the "belittling" of the role of the Russian people and the works of the historian V. I. Filkin, "while not a word was said at the discussion about the deportation"[8]. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that the region's occupation administration launched a persecution of the Chechen intelligentsia "under the guise of a discussion around the 'concept' of the 200th anniversary of the voluntary entry of Chechen-Ingushetia into Russia", whose author was considered to be the archaeologist Vinogradov, and he "relied even on the authority of the CC of the CPSU [the central authority in Moscow]"[1]. In February 1979 L. I. Lavrov, a historian of the Academy of Sciences, wrote on instructions from his superiors a review of the "Justification Memorandum" for the jubilee: the oaths of the 18th century "did not lead to the actual entry of the region into the Russian Empire, since even after the oaths no officials of the tsarist administration appeared there", and "the planned celebration of the jubilee, in the light of the above, appears historically unjustified"; historian V. P. Krikunov, who published the memorandum in 1990, writes: "The first copy of the memorandum got lost and, when the question of whether or not to celebrate the 200th 'jubilee' was being decided, was not taken into account (or rather, it was taken into account, and that, evidently, is why it got lost)"[9]. Historian Viktor Shnirelman writes: "In those years Vinogradov became the chief adviser of the obkom of the CPSU [the region's occupation administration] on ideology and social sciences, which in effect made him the first censor of scholarly and publishing activity in the republic"; "Such Chechen and Ingush historians as M. N. Muzaev, A. Z. Vatsuev, Ya. Z. Akhmadov, Kh. Akiev, Ya. S. Vagapov, Kh. S. Akhmadov and others were subjected to persecution"; the 1977 book by the linguist Kyuri Chokaev, "The Language and History of the Vainakhs", "was declared in the obkom… a model of 'rabid nationalism', and the entire print run was destroyed on the spot"[10]. Historians D. B. Abdurakhmanov and Ya. Z. Akhmadov also write that for disagreeing with the "concept" "there were officially pilloried [publicly disgraced] … the Chechen-Ingush State University lecturer F. P. Bokov, professors N. P. Gritsenko and V. P. Krikunov"[4]. Shnirelman writes that Vlasov, head of the region's occupation administration, reproduced the concept "in his speech at the III plenum of the Chechen-Ingush obkom of the CPSU on 14 July 1979" and "gave instructions to propagate it widely in the local media", and in 1982 the jubilee of the "voluntary entry" was combined with the 60th anniversary of the republic: "On this occasion the republic was awarded the Order of the Red Banner of Labour; its leaders received awards too. In particular, Vlasov was presented with the Order of Lenin"[10]. On 29 June 1984 the region's occupation administration recorded in its minutes on the work of the Institute of History, Sociology and Philology: "Vagapov Ya. S., Akhmadov Ya. Z., Vatsuev A. Z. permit themselves politically harmful judgements, dispute the scholarly validity of the concept of the voluntary entry of the Chechens and the Ingush into Russia"[4]. Historians D. B. Abdurakhmanov and Ya. Z. Akhmadov write that only in 1990 did "the same organ of the CPSU revoke its decision concerning the institute and its staff as mistaken"[4]. T0100 Seizure of Religious Institutions January 1965 C1182.T0100 → C1182 "Only Pardoned": Alien Rule and the Suppression of Chechen and Ingush National Life (1965-1989) G0010 USSR S0008 Government After the return of the Chechens from exile the coloniser did not allow a single mosque to be opened and, through its officials, decided who could pray and where. Muzarov, an official supervising religion, wrote in a report of 25 August 1983: "In Chechen-Ingushetia in the pre-October period [before 1917] Muslim ideology reigned supreme. There were 2,675 mosques, 60 thousand murids [members of religious brotherhoods], 38 sheikhs [religious mentors, heads of brotherhoods], 2,850 mullahs [Islamic clergymen] and 140 religious schools. After the restoration of the republic's autonomy in 1957 it so happened that on the territory of the Chechen-Ingush ASSR there was not a single mosque"[5]. The mosques did not vanish by themselves. Most of them the coloniser had closed before the war: historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that religious schools "after the closure of most mosques… moved into the homes of mullahs and Islamic scholars"[1]. Historian Dalkhan Khozhaev writes that during the exile "medieval crypts and pre-revolutionary mosques, tombs and shrines… were blown up"[7]; historians Akhmadov and Khasmagomadov add that in Grozny "the city mosque was destroyed"[1]. The surviving buildings the coloniser took over as clubs and warehouses. On 21 January 1967 277 believers of the Nazran district submitted an application to open a mosque in the village of Barsuki; Asaulka, an official supervising religion, reported to Moscow that the district administration, by its decision of 10 June 1967, had refused "to consider the application on the grounds that, as established by an inspection, 'many signatures under the application were made not by the persons indicated in the application but forged, and the surnames of some persons are fictitious'"[11]. On 11 November 1969 the government of the region, subordinate to Moscow, in a resolution "On Measures to Strengthen Control over Observance of the Legislation on Religious Cults", recorded that in the districts "ministers of the cult in a number of cases arbitrarily engage in building and opening prayer houses, hold collective rites in public places, organise pilgrimages of believers to so-called 'holy places'", while "effective measures aimed at the gradual cessation of their activity are not being taken"[12]. On 18 May 1977 Bobov, an official supervising religion, reported to Kerimov, the head of that government: "in the republic there are no Muslim religious associations or ministers of the cult registered with the authorities, while at the same time, contrary to the law, 263 Muslim religious societies and groups operate unofficially"[13]. On 19 August 1980 Bobov reported to Moscow: in the republic "there are 62 buildings of former mosques… 17 used as clubs and schools, 25 as storage premises, 8 as factory workshops, post offices, shops, 2 handed over to the use of believers"[14]. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that the region's occupation authorities "directly forbade the opening of mosques in Chechen and Ingush villages, and did not allow the numerous murid [religious] communities to perform religious rites openly either"[1]. T0116.004 Ban on the Indigenous People's Religious Practice January 1965 C1182.T0116.004 → C1182 "Only Pardoned": Alien Rule and the Suppression of Chechen and Ingush National Life (1965-1989) G0010 USSR S0008 Government In 1958-1989 the coloniser declared Chechen shrines closed, put people on trial for printing the Quran and kept believers on file. On 10 December 1958 the Moscow agency supervising religion sent its officials in the regions a circular headed thus: "On Measures to Stop Pilgrimage to So-Called 'Holy Places'"; its task: "to achieve the cessation of pilgrimage and the closure of so-called 'holy places'"[15]. In Chechnya this circular fell upon the grave of the mother of Sheikh Kunta-Haji, founder of the largest Chechen brotherhood. The same agency's report for 1973 says: the grave "was declared 'closed' by the local authorities about fourteen years ago. However, from 1961 the religious activists began restoring it without permission… In 1970-1971 this so-called 'holy place'… was visited by over 10 thousand people… On the way the pilgrims, often with the participation of adolescents, perform the collective religious rite of 'zikr' [a joint prayer with circular movement and chanting]"[16]. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "The performance of the 'loud' zikr [prayer aloud] of the Qadiri tariqa [brotherhood] (the order of Kunta-Haji) was suppressed with particular severity"[1]. On 29 June 1979 the Oktyabrsky district court of Grozny tried Alaudin Bogatyrev, Salaudin Dubaev and Anatoly Yushkin; the verdict states that Bogatyrev "with the aim of engaging in a prohibited trade… was engaged in the production by printing methods, on a significant scale, of literature of religious content in the Arabic language": from 1971 to 1978 they had clandestinely printed 2,500 copies of the Quran, 600 copies of parts of it and 500 Arabic textbooks, and the court ruled "to subject" Bogatyrev "to 6 years of deprivation of liberty with confiscation of property, to be served in a strict-regime corrective labour colony", and Dubaev and Yushkin to four years each[17]. On 5 April 1983 Moscow adopted a resolution "On Measures for the Ideological Isolation of the Reactionary Part of the Muslim Clergy"; Muzarov, the official supervising religion in the region, reported on 25 August 1983: "59 murid [religious] groups and societies have organisationally ceased their activity and the activity of more than 100 ministers of the cult [mullahs] has been neutralised… Work was carried out to put all extremist elements and fanatics on file, a map of murid [religious] organisations was drawn up"; "The number of murids [members of brotherhoods] has fallen - from 20 thousand to 9 thousand"[5]. The Chechens did not submit: on 5 May 1989 the agency supervising religion counted 311 brotherhood groups in the republic, "uniting about 8,300 people", of which "the 'Kunta-Haji' brotherhood - 183 groups"[18]. T0117.001 Migratory Replacement January 1965 C1182.T0117.001 → C1182 "Only Pardoned": Alien Rule and the Suppression of Chechen and Ingush National Life (1965-1989) G0010 USSR S0008 Government In 1965-1989 the coloniser brought workers from Russia to the factories of Grozny and gave them housing, while pushing the Chechens out of the republic to seek work and permanent residence in other regions. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "in the 30 years since the return of the Chechens and the Ingush to their Homeland, only 16% of the workers of the oil-refining and petrochemical enterprises of Chechen-Ingushetia were Chechens or Ingush", in the radio-engineering industry 14 %, in instrument-making 6 %, while the missing workers and engineers "were brought in from Russian regions by way of organised recruitment. Moreover, some specialists received the keys to their flats right at the railway station"[1]. The historians write: "Every year more than 100 thousand people, organised in construction brigades, left Chechen-Ingushetia for construction work"[1]; historians D. B. Abdurakhmanov and Ya. Z. Akhmadov write that a family of five or six, on a state-farm worker's wage of 60-80 roubles, was left with "either 'shabashka' - hard 14-16-hour labour on construction sites in rural districts of the country, or departure for permanent residence in Kalmykia, the Rostov, Astrakhan and Volgograd regions to work on livestock farms"[4]. From the second half of the 1980s the region's occupation administration, under agreements with the Kalinin, Novgorod and Omsk regions, sent villagers to settle in the Non-Black-Earth zone[1]. The census of 1989 counted 956,879 Chechens in the USSR, of whom 734,501 lived in Chechen-Ingushetia: almost every fourth lived outside the republic[19]; the historians write: "the main cause of migration was unemployment"[1]. T0032 Legal Segregation of the Population January 1965 C1182.T0032 → C1182 "Only Pardoned": Alien Rule and the Suppression of Chechen and Ingush National Life (1965-1989) G0010 USSR S0012 Occupation and Controlled Administrations In 1965-1989 the coloniser, by law and by administrative decisions, kept the Chechens out of the cities and factories of their own republic. The coloniser had restricted the residence registration of Chechens in Grozny as early as 1958; historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "these restrictions in fact ceased to operate only in the 1980s"[1]. Historian A. B. Kuznetsova writes that in the early 1970s "the leadership of the ChIASSR [the Chechen-Ingush republic] (in agreement with the union centre [Moscow]) declared that the labour resources of the republic (read: the unemployed) had to be used locally"[8]. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "Already in 1979 up to 28% of all able-bodied inhabitants of the Chechen-Ingush ASSR, according to official statistics, derived their main income from work on their personal household plots, that is, were in fact unemployed. Ten years later the level of hidden unemployment, by some estimates, had risen to 40%"[1]. T0114.003 Conversion of Schools to the Metropole's Language January 1965 C1182.T0114.003 → C1182 "Only Pardoned": Alien Rule and the Suppression of Chechen and Ingush National Life (1965-1989) G0010 USSR S0008 Government After the return of the Chechens from exile the coloniser switched all the schools of the republic to Russian from the first grade, reduced the Chechen language to a few lessons a week and in the schools of Grozny did not teach it at all. The law of the RSFSR of 16 April 1959 declared that "instruction at school is conducted in the pupils' native language" and left the choice of language to parents, but after the return from exile the coloniser opened no schools with Chechen as the language of instruction, so there was nothing to choose from[6]. Sociolinguist Musa Ovkhadov writes: "After the restoration of the autonomy of Chechen-Ingushetia Russian became the language of instruction in the schools of the republic from grade 1"; "In the schools of the capital of the republic, the city of Grozny, until the end of the 1980s the Chechen language was not taught (in 1989 121 thousand Chechens lived in Grozny out of its population of 400 thousand)"[20]. Educationalist Isita Muskhanova writes: "teaching in all the schools of Chechen-Ingushetia was conducted in Russian from the first to the last year of study, while the study of the native language and native literature was allotted only a few hours a week"; the republican newspapers of the first half of the 1960s wrote that to return to the national school "would mean taking a step backwards"[21]. Philologist Zulay Khamidova, who spent nine years fighting for Chechen lessons in city schools, recalls: "In kindergartens the language of upbringing was Russian, and if a child knew only the native language, he was punished and required to speak only Russian"; after her efforts the Chechen and Ingush languages were introduced in city schools "as a subject, 1 hour a week, whereas 5 hours a week were allotted to Russian"[22]. By Musa Ovkhadov's count, the entire school course of Chechen language and literature from grade 1 to grade 10 in the 1970s-1980s amounted to 1,497 hours, on average 3.5 hours a week[20]. The result is visible in the official statistics of the USSR: in the Chechen and Ingush languages 154 books and pamphlets were published in 1940, 49 in 1970, 37 in 1980 and 39 in 1985[20]; the republic's television in the 1980s broadcast in Chechen for 20-25 minutes a day[23]. The Chechens did not give up their language: according to the census of 1989, 938,765 of the 956,879 Chechens named Chechen as their native language[8]. References Ахмадов Я. З., Хасмагомадов Э. Х. title: Destruction of the Refugee Aul of Uzeni-Yurt, Extortion of Hostages from Geldigen, and Capture of Samashki Residents at Harvest (1826-1827), campaign C1149
content: Destruction of the Refugee Aul of Uzeni-Yurt, Extortion of Hostages from Geldigen, and Capture of Samashki Residents at Harvest (1826-1827) After Yermolov's punitive campaign, which devastated the lowland villages of the Nokhchi in 1826, some inhabitants of the destroyed villages refused to resettle under the conqueror's control and took refuge in the forests. The imperial historian Potto admits: "the inhabitants of some auls destroyed by Yermolov took refuge in the forests and, unwilling to resettle, abandoned even their fields sown with grain"[1]. The village of Uzeni-Yurt on the bank of the Argun became a refuge for these people and a stronghold of the Karabulak leader Astemir, an associate of Beibulat Taimiev in the uprising of 1825. On the night of January 10, 1827, General Laptev, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, covertly led against the village a detachment of 350 line Cossacks with two horse-drawn guns, forcing four hundred Chechens from subordinated communities to take part as well. Potto wrote: they "swam across the Argun and had to take a roundabout route in order to cut off the inhabitants' retreat to the forest"[1]. Warned by a horseman, the inhabitants fled across the Argun. Potto recorded: the Cossacks, overtaking those fleeing, "seized... three women and killed and wounded some fifteen people," after which "the village of Uzeni-Yurt, with all its property and even its livestock, was destroyed to the ground"[1]. That same winter Laptev exacted hostages from the village of Geldigen, rejecting a ransom for a captured young man of Geldigen. Potto wrote: "Laptev rejected all offers and demanded one thing - amanats (hostages)"[1]. In the summer of 1827 his successor, General Engelhardt, set an ambush during the harvest near the aul of Samashki. Potto admits: the inhabitants were freely allowed onto the fields, and then "everything that was in the field turned out to be encircled by a dense Cossack cordon"; the population was released, while the leader Tara-Adzuev and the family of the resistance leader Bakar-Bulatov were taken prisoner, and the grain of the Galgai, who lived by the aul, was "burned... standing in the field"[1].
